stem: A 32-year-old G2P1 woman attends a Calvary Mater Newcastle maternal medicine clinic at 8 weeks gestation. Past history: unprovoked pulmonary embolism 3 years ago, treated with warfarin for 6 months. Subsequent thrombophilia screen normal. No further VTE events. She has been on apixaban 5 mg BD since the PE for indefinite extended prophylaxis after a recurrence-risk consultation. She has a body mass index of 31, is currently a non-smoker, and her previous pregnancy 5 years ago (before the PE) was uncomplicated. She has no liver disease, normal renal function, no other comorbidity. Her booking bloods are normal.

data_table.Examination: Unremarkable. No calf swelling, no other signs of VTE.
data_table.Investigations: Hb 122, platelets 240, INR 1.0 (off warfarin), Cr 68, LFT normal. Thrombophilia screen historically normal.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate anticoagulation strategy throughout this pregnancy, satisfying ALL constraints: efficacy for VTE prevention given prior idiopathic PE, fetal safety, postpartum continuation feasibility, and Australian PBS access?

options.text: Continue apixaban 5 mg BD throughout pregnancy and breastfeeding; restart warfarin at 6 weeks postpartum
Switch to therapeutic enoxaparin 1 mg/kg BD throughout pregnancy, continue at least 6 weeks postpartum, switch back to apixaban after delivery if breastfeeding ceased
Switch to warfarin throughout pregnancy with INR target 2.5-3.5; pause warfarin at 36 weeks for elective delivery and bridge with enoxaparin
Stop apixaban now without replacement; restart at 6 weeks postpartum since recurrence risk is acceptable in pregnancy
Aspirin 150 mg daily as VTE prophylaxis throughout pregnancy

subtopic_detail: VTE prophylaxis strategy in pregnancy with prior idiopathic PE on DOAC

stem:
A 36-year-old G3P2 woman at 32 weeks gestation is admitted to John Hunter Hospital maternal medicine ward with 6 weeks of progressive arthralgia (small joints of hands, both wrists, both knees, symmetrical), facial rash worse with sun exposure, and 2 days of pleuritic chest pain with mild pericardial friction rub on auscultation. She has been on a single antihypertensive agent for gestational hypertension since 22 weeks gestation, and the medication was titrated to current dose 4 weeks before symptom onset.

She has no past history of autoimmune disease, no family history. Today: BP 138/86 on current treatment, HR 92, T 37.4, mild butterfly rash sparing nasolabial folds, MCP and PIP joint tenderness without effusion. Investigations: ANA 1:640 homogeneous, anti-histone antibody strongly positive, anti-dsDNA negative, ENA negative, complement (C3, C4) normal, ESR 78, CRP 32, urine no proteinuria.

data_table.Examination: Butterfly malar rash sparing nasolabial folds, MCP+PIP joint tenderness symmetric without effusion, soft pericardial friction rub.
data_table.Investigations: ANA 1:640 homogeneous, ANTI-HISTONE strongly positive, anti-dsDNA NEGATIVE, ENA negative, complement C3 C4 normal, ESR 78, CRP 32, urinalysis no proteinuria/casts.

lead_in: Which class of antihypertensive most plausibly explains this drug-induced syndrome, given the antibody pattern?

options.text: Calcium-channel blocker (nifedipine)
Methyldopa (centrally-acting alpha-2 agonist used in pregnancy)
Beta-blocker (labetalol)
Diuretic (hydrochlorothiazide)
ACE inhibitor (ramipril)

subtopic_detail: Drug-induced lupus erythematosus from methyldopa in pregnancy

stem:
A 33-year-old woman is day 5 postpartum after a spontaneous vaginal birth at 39 weeks, complicated by gestational hypertension treated antenatally with labetalol. She is exclusively breastfeeding her well term infant. She represents to her GP with persistent BP readings of 152/98 to 158/102 on three separate occasions. She has a documented angioedema reaction to enalapril 4 years ago. She has stage 3a chronic kidney disease (eGFR 48) from reflux nephropathy diagnosed in childhood, well controlled gout for which she takes allopurinol, and she has asthma requiring a salbutamol inhaler twice weekly with one ICU admission 3 years ago for a severe exacerbation.

Her current labetalol 200 mg orally bd is not controlling her BP and she reports worsening fatigue and bronchospasm with exertion that she attributes to labetalol.

data_table.Examination: BP 156/100, HR 78, no oedema, chest clear, no headache, no visual disturbance, no epigastric pain, no hyperreflexia.
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 130 micromol/L (baseline 115), eGFR 48, urine ACR 8 mg/mmol, FBC normal, LFTs normal, urate 0.42 mmol/L, urine protein:creatinine ratio 25 mg/mmol.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate antihypertensive substitution?

options.text: Nifedipine modified-release 30 mg orally once daily
Hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg orally once daily
Perindopril 4 mg orally once daily
Atenolol 50 mg orally once daily
Methyldopa 250 mg orally tds

subtopic_detail: Antihypertensive choice with stacked breastfeeding, CKD, asthma, ACEi-allergy, gout constraints

stem: A 28-year-old woman, G2P0 with one previous first-trimester miscarriage, presents to the Early Pregnancy Assessment Service at the Royal Hospital for Women in Sydney with 4 days of right iliac fossa pain and minimal PV spotting. LMP was 7 weeks and 2 days ago. She is haemodynamically stable, has no shoulder tip pain, and her abdomen is soft with right iliac fossa tenderness only. She has completed her family and would prefer non-surgical management if appropriate.

data_table.Examination: BP 116/72, HR 84, abdomen soft, RIF tender, no peritonism, cervix closed on speculum, minimal old blood in vault.
data_table.Investigations: Beta-hCG 4800 IU/L (rose from 2900 IU/L over 48 hours), FBC Hb 128 g/L, LFTs normal, creatinine 62 micromol/L, blood group A positive. Transvaginal ultrasound: empty uterus, right adnexal mass 28 mm with surrounding free fluid in pouch of Douglas measuring 12 mL, no fetal pole within the adnexal mass.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate management decision based on Australian criteria?

options.text: Laparoscopic salpingectomy after consent
Single-dose methotrexate 50 mg per square metre IM
Expectant management with serial beta-hCG every 48 hours
Laparoscopic salpingotomy with tube preservation
Repeat ultrasound in 7 days

subtopic_detail: Methotrexate threshold criteria for ectopic pregnancy management

stem:
A 31-year-old woman is referred to a maternal medicine clinic at the Calvary Mater Newcastle at 16 weeks gestation with a known diagnosis of Sjogren syndrome made 4 years ago. She is asymptomatic, on hydroxychloroquine 200 mg daily, and has had no thrombotic events. Autoantibody profile from her rheumatologist 6 months ago: ANA 1:1280 speckled, anti-Ro (SSA) strongly positive at 240 U/mL, anti-La (SSB) positive at 90 U/mL, anti-dsDNA negative, anticardiolipin negative, lupus anticoagulant negative, anti-Smith negative, anti-RNP negative.

Her previous pregnancy 3 years ago ended in elective termination at 9 weeks. She has no children. She is on no other medications and has no thyroid disease.

data_table.Examination: No active synovitis, no rash, mild dry eyes only.
data_table.Investigations: ANA 1:1280 speckled, anti-Ro (SSA) 240 U/mL strongly positive, anti-La (SSB) 90 U/mL positive, dsDNA neg, anticardiolipin neg, LA neg. TFT normal.

lead_in: Based on the antibody pattern, which is the single most important antenatal surveillance step beyond standard screening?

options.text: Serial uterine artery Doppler at 20 and 24 weeks for placental insufficiency risk
Weekly fetal echocardiography focused on PR interval from 16 to 26 weeks
Monthly maternal serum complement (C3 / C4) levels for lupus flare detection
Maternal aspirin 150 mg from 12 weeks for preeclampsia prevention
Serial fetal MRI from 20 weeks for neural-tube and brain anomalies

subtopic_detail: Anti-Ro associated congenital heart block surveillance

stem: A 28-year-old G2P1 woman is admitted to John Hunter Hospital at 29+5 weeks gestation in established preterm labour. Birth is anticipated within 6 hours. She has received the first dose of betamethasone 11.4 mg IM 30 minutes ago. The obstetric registrar is preparing to commence an infusion of a magnesium-based agent whose primary intended fetal effect is described as: 'a calcium-channel modulator that stabilises immature cerebral microvasculature, attenuates glutamate-driven excitotoxicity at NMDA receptors, and reduces free-radical-mediated white matter injury in the periventricular region.' Maternal observations are normal, no preeclampsia features, no contraindications to magnesium therapy.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7, HR 88, BP 118/72, RR 18, SpO2 99% room air. Patellar reflexes 2+.
data_table.Examination: Cervix 4 cm dilated, 80% effaced, cephalic, station -1; CTG reactive.
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC normal. Mg baseline 0.85 mmol/L. Patellar reflexes preserved.

lead_in: Based purely on the mechanism described, which is the single most likely clinical indication?

options.text: Eclampsia seizure prophylaxis in severe preeclampsia at term
Tocolysis to delay preterm birth by 48 hours for steroid effect
Fetal neuroprotection from cerebral palsy in anticipated preterm birth under 30 weeks gestation
Maternal treatment of supraventricular tachycardia in pregnancy
Maternal treatment of acute severe asthma with bronchodilator effect

subtopic_detail: Magnesium sulfate fetal neuroprotection mechanism vs other indications

stem:
A 32-year-old G2P2 woman is reviewed in Calvary Mater Newcastle maternity ward day 4 post elective lower-segment caesarean section for breech at term. She has a temperature of 38.6 degrees Celsius, mild lower abdominal tenderness, no offensive lochia, and breastfeeding well. Pre-operative antibiotic prophylaxis was cefazolin. Wound site is dry without erythema. There is no calf swelling and no respiratory symptoms.

Urinalysis is negative. Foley catheter was removed day 2. Her temperature has now been over 38 degrees for 12 hours despite paracetamol. Blood pressure 118/76, heart rate 96 sinus, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 98 percent.

data_table.Examination: Mild lower abdominal tenderness without peritonism; uterus appropriate involution, lochia rubra without offensive odour; wound clean; calves soft, no swelling; chest clear.
data_table.Investigations: FBC: WCC 14.2 x10^9/L; CRP 88 mg/L. UEC normal. Urinalysis negative. Blood cultures sent. Pelvic USS pending.

lead_in: Based on the timing relative to delivery and the constellation of negative findings, which is the single most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Wound infection at the caesarean operative site with cellulitis
Endometritis from ascending genital tract organisms after caesarean
Mastitis from ongoing breastfeeding with milk stasis
Deep vein thrombosis from postpartum hypercoagulable state
Urinary tract infection following recent indwelling catheter use

subtopic_detail: Puerperal fever timing-based differential
Diabetes preconception counselling
stem: You are the obstetrics registrar reviewing a 28-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes on a basal-bolus insulin regimen. She is planning her first pregnancy in the next 6 months. Her last HbA1c is 8.4 percent. She has background diabetic retinopathy and microalbuminuria. She is on perindopril 5 mg daily and atorvastatin 20 mg nocte. Her partner is well.

data_table.Examination: Well; BMI 26; no peripheral oedema; fundoscopy background retinopathy
data_table.Investigations: HbA1c 8.4%, eGFR 84, urine ACR 5.2, TSH 1.4, fT4 normal, beta-hCG negative
data_table.Medications: Insulin glargine 24 units nocte; insulin aspart 6 to 10 units with meals; perindopril 5 mg daily; atorvastatin 20 mg nocte

lead_in: What is the most important preconception management package?

options.text: Cease perindopril and atorvastatin before conception; commence folic acid 5 mg daily; target HbA1c below 6.5 percent if achievable safely
Continue current medications; commence folic acid 500 micrograms daily; advise conception once HbA1c is 7 percent
Continue perindopril and atorvastatin until conception; commence folic acid 500 micrograms daily; target HbA1c below 8 percent
Switch insulin to oral metformin and gliclazide before pregnancy; commence folic acid 5 mg daily; target HbA1c below 7 percent
Defer pregnancy planning until microalbuminuria resolves; continue all current medications and review HbA1c quarterly only

subtopic_detail: Acute fatty liver of pregnancy recognition
stem: You are the obstetric registrar called to ED to review a 32-year-old G2P1 at 36+4 weeks with 5 days of nausea, vomiting, malaise and now confusion. Her partner reports she is sleepy and not making sense. She has had no antenatal complications. She has no headache, no visual disturbance, no abdominal pain. Her BP is 132/82, urine dipstick shows trace protein only. Her bloods are striking.

data_table.Examination: Jaundiced sclerae, mild RUQ tenderness, no peripheral oedema, fetal heart 146 with variable decelerations on CTG
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 2.4, ammonia 96, ALT 380, AST 420, ALP 280, bilirubin 78, INR 2.4, fibrinogen 1.4, platelets 168, Cr 124 (baseline 64), urate 0.46, lactate 4.6, urine dipstick protein trace; haptoglobin normal; LDH 480

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Administer betamethasone 11.4 mg IM and observe for 24 hours for spontaneous improvement; defer delivery for steroid effect
Correct hypoglycaemia and coagulopathy; arrange immediate delivery typically by caesarean; transfer to a centre with HDU and adult ICU
Administer magnesium sulfate 4 g IV bolus and arrange induction of labour with vaginal delivery aim within 24 to 48 hours
Administer N-acetylcysteine 150 mg/kg IV loading dose; observe for 48 hours and consider delivery if liver function does not improve
Arrange urgent liver biopsy to differentiate AFLP from HELLP syndrome before deciding on delivery timing and mode

subtopic_detail: Ovarian torsion - imaging and management
stem: You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 24-year-old woman in ED with 6 hours of sudden severe right iliac fossa pain, nausea and one vomit. Her LMP was 14 days ago and beta-hCG is negative. She is not on contraception and has no STI risk. Her transvaginal ultrasound shows a 6 cm right ovarian dermoid cyst, an enlarged oedematous right ovary, and absent venous Doppler flow on the right with maintained arterial flow.

data_table.Examination: Tender right iliac fossa with guarding; cervix closed; no PV bleeding; no cervical excitation
data_table.Investigations: Beta-hCG negative; WCC 12.4; CRP 22; transvaginal US right ovary 6 cm dermoid, enlarged ovary, absent venous Doppler flow, arterial flow preserved; left ovary normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Conservative management with IV opiate analgesia; arrange outpatient gynaecology follow-up to monitor cyst progression by ultrasound
MRI pelvis to confirm diagnosis and degree of vascular compromise before booking elective laparoscopy within 24 to 48 hours
Urgent laparoscopy with detorsion and ovarian conservation; cystectomy of the dermoid cyst at the same procedure if feasible
Urgent laparotomy with right salpingo-oophorectomy due to ovarian non-viability and the presence of a complex cystic mass
Diagnostic laparoscopy first; if torsion is confirmed convert to laparotomy and proceed with right oophorectomy and biopsy

subtopic_detail: Emergency contraception choice and timing
stem: You are the GP registrar reviewing a 22-year-old woman who attends today for emergency contraception. She had unprotected vaginal intercourse 96 hours ago. Her LMP was 14 days ago in a regular 28-day cycle. She is on no regular medications, has BMI 32 and is not breastfeeding. She has no contraindications to copper IUD. She is keen on the most effective option available.

data_table.Examination: Well; no abdominal tenderness; cervix appears normal on speculum exam
data_table.Investigations: Beta-hCG negative today; STI screen pending

lead_in: Which is the most effective emergency contraceptive option for this patient?

options.text: Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg oral once now and advise abstinence or barrier method until next menstrual period commences
Levonorgestrel 3 mg oral once now (double dose for BMI above 26) plus combined oral contraceptive quick start tomorrow
Ulipristal acetate 30 mg oral once now and advise no progestogen-containing contraception starts for 5 days afterwards
Insertion of a copper intrauterine device within 24 to 48 hours by trained inserter; also screen and treat for chlamydia presumptively
Misoprostol 800 micrograms vaginally once now and arrange beta-hCG quantitative testing in 14 days for confirmation of contraception

subtopic_detail: Refractory atonic PPH after first-line uterotonics
stem:
You are the obstetrics registrar called to the birthing suite for a 32-year-old G3P3 at 5 minutes post normal vaginal delivery of a 4200 g infant after a prolonged second stage. She has had a brisk PV bleed of approximately 1200 mL. The uterus is boggy and not contracting despite fundal massage. She has received oxytocin 10 IU IM with delivery of placenta.

The placenta appears complete. Her BP is 92/56 and HR 122. The team has called for help, set up large-bore IV access, and the massive transfusion protocol has been activated.

data_table.Examination: Uterus boggy at umbilicus; ongoing PV blood loss; no cervical or vaginal laceration on inspection; placenta examined and complete
data_table.Investigations: Hb 88 (was 124 antenatal), platelets 184, fibrinogen 2.4, INR 1.1; group and hold sent; massive transfusion protocol activated; blood gas pH 7.32 lactate 2.4
data_table.Medications: Oxytocin 10 IU IM with delivery; no current antihypertensive history; no contraindication to ergometrine

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next pharmacological step?

options.text: Carboprost 250 micrograms intramyometrial; repeat every 15 minutes to a maximum of 8 doses; avoid in asthma or pulmonary hypertension
Calcium gluconate 10% 10 mL IV over 10 minutes; defer further uterotonics until ionised calcium is rechecked at 30 minutes
Misoprostol 800 micrograms rectal; observe over 30 minutes for response; avoid further uterotonic during this interval
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV over 10 minutes alone and observe for 30 minutes before further uterotonics; recheck fibrinogen at 60 minutes
Ergometrine 250 micrograms IM and start oxytocin infusion 40 IU in 1 L crystalloid over 4 hours; reassess at 5 minutes for tone

subtopic_detail: Request for antenatal treatment of streptococcal colonisation
stem: A 29-year-old woman in her first pregnancy telephones about her routine swab result. She has no symptoms, no allergies and wants the organism dealt with before the birth.

data_table.Swab: Vagino-rectal swab at 36 weeks grew group B streptococcus
data_table.Urine: Midstream urine culture at 28 weeks showed no growth

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice?

options.text: A course now will not clear it; intravenous cover is given in labour
A course of oral amoxicillin now will clear it well before the birth
Vaginal chlorhexidine washes in the last month will remove the organism
Her partner needs treating as well so that she is not colonised again
Repeat the swab weekly and treat orally if it is still growing later

subtopic_detail: Bishop score and induction method choice
stem: You are the obstetric registrar planning induction of labour for a 34-year-old G3P2 woman at 41 weeks and 3 days. The pregnancy has been uncomplicated and she has had two previous normal vaginal deliveries. CTG today is reassuring and ultrasound estimated fetal weight is 3650 g. She has had no previous caesarean. On vaginal examination, the cervix is 1 cm dilated, 1 cm long, firm, mid position, and the head is at station -2.

data_table.Examination: Bishop score 4 (dilatation 1, length 1, consistency 0, position 1, station 1); intact membranes; head free
data_table.Investigations: CTG normal; AFI 8 cm; EFW 3650 g

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence intravenous oxytocin 2 milliunits/min and titrate every 30 minutes to contractions; artificial rupture of membranes at 4 cm
Perform amniotomy and commence walking; reassess contraction pattern after 4 hours and add oxytocin if not in labour
Arrange membrane sweep weekly and continue expectant management until 42 weeks before considering further intervention
Proceed directly to elective caesarean section under spinal anaesthesia; book theatre within the next 4 hours
Cervical ripening with vaginal prostaglandin or balloon catheter; reassess Bishop score in 6 to 12 hours before progressing

subtopic_detail: PPROM at 32 weeks management bundle
stem: You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 29-year-old G1P0 woman at 32+1 weeks gestation who has presented with a gush of clear fluid 2 hours ago and ongoing damp pad. She has no contractions and no bleeding. The fetal movements are normal. The pregnancy has been uncomplicated. Speculum examination confirms pooling of fluid in the vagina and a closed cervix.

data_table.Examination: Speculum: pooling of clear amniotic fluid, no bleeding, closed cervix; abdomen soft, no contractions
data_table.Investigations: CTG reassuring; FBC normal; CRP 4; group B Strep swab taken; ultrasound: AFI 6 cm, fetal weight 1850 g

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate management bundle?

options.text: Admit; corticosteroids and oral erythromycin 250 mg 6-hourly for 10 days; expectant management to 34 weeks if stable
Discharge home with twice-weekly outpatient review and instructions to return if temperature 38 or above; expectant care
Immediate caesarean section after a single corticosteroid dose; transfer to a tertiary neonatal centre for late preterm delivery
Augment with intravenous oxytocin; aim for vaginal birth within 24 hours; corticosteroids only if cervix is unfavourable
Empirical intravenous ampicillin and gentamicin for chorioamnionitis; defer corticosteroids until temperature trend established

subtopic_detail: Severe pre-eclampsia magnesium loading and target
stem: You are the obstetric registrar in birth suite reviewing a 28-year-old G2P1 woman at 34 weeks with new severe-range hypertension and frontal headache that has not responded to paracetamol. Her booking BP was 110/68. She has 3+ proteinuria on dipstick. She is otherwise well and the CTG is reassuring. She has no asthma. The blood tests have just returned.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 168/112 repeated, HR 92, RR 18, SpO2 99% RA, T 36.8
data_table.Examination: Brisk reflexes; no clonus; mild facial oedema; abdomen soft; fundal height 33 cm
data_table.Investigations: Plt 124, ALT 84, urate 0.42, Cr 76, LDH 320, PCR 380 mg/mmol; urgent labetalol bolus given
data_table.Medications: Pregnancy multivitamin; nifedipine PR 20 mg given 20 minutes ago

lead_in: Which magnesium regimen and seizure-prevention rationale is most appropriate?

options.text: Magnesium sulfate 1 g IV bolus over 5 minutes then 0.5 g/hour infusion; recheck reflexes and respiratory rate at 4 hours
Magnesium sulfate 4 g IV over 20 minutes then 1 g/hour infusion for 24 hours; monitor reflexes and respiratory rate hourly
Phenytoin 15 mg/kg IV loading dose over 30 minutes; commence maintenance phenytoin 100 mg every 8 hours for 7 days
Diazepam 10 mg IV bolus and commence midazolam 5 mg/hour infusion; reassess BP control after sedation
Reserve magnesium for after a first seizure; commence intravenous hydralazine and aim for BP below 140/90 in the next hour

subtopic_detail: Refractory PPH escalation pathway
stem: You are the obstetric registrar called urgently to a birth suite. A 33-year-old G3P3 woman delivered a 4200 g infant 25 minutes ago after a prolonged second stage with vacuum extraction. Estimated blood loss is now 1500 mL and ongoing. She received 10 IU IM oxytocin at delivery and 40 IU oxytocin infusion plus 250 mcg ergometrine IM 10 minutes ago. The uterus is still atonic. There are no obvious tears. She has no pre-existing hypertension and no asthma.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 92/58, HR 124, RR 22, SpO2 98% on 4 L/min, T 36.4
data_table.Examination: Uterus boggy, fundus at umbilicus; placenta delivered intact; vagina and perineum inspected, no major tear
data_table.Investigations: Hb 78, plt 156, fibrinogen 2.0, INR 1.2, blood group and screen, two large bore IV lines in situ
data_table.Medications: Oxytocin 40 IU infusion at 250 mL/h; ergometrine 250 mcg IM given 10 min ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next pharmacological and procedural step?

options.text: Repeat ergometrine 250 mcg intramuscular; continue oxytocin infusion and reassess uterine tone in 15 minutes
Take to theatre for laparotomy and B-Lynch suture; defer further pharmacological uterotonics pending operative intervention
Carboprost 250 mcg intramuscular and intrauterine balloon tamponade; continue oxytocin infusion and activate massive transfusion protocol
Tranexamic acid 4 g intravenous bolus; reassess uterine tone and bleeding in 30 minutes before further escalation
Manual uterine compression and bimanual massage only; cease pharmacological therapy and observe for spontaneous tone return

subtopic_detail: VBAC contraindication recognition
stem: You are the obstetric registrar in antenatal clinic reviewing a 30-year-old G3P2 woman at 36 weeks who wants to plan a trial of labour after caesarean. Her first caesarean at 38 weeks was for failure to progress, with a classical incision used because of marked adhesions. Her second was an elective lower-segment caesarean. The current pregnancy is uncomplicated and the baby is cephalic with estimated weight 3300 g. The placenta is anterior and fundal. She is keen to avoid another caesarean.

data_table.Examination: Uterus appropriate for dates; cephalic presentation; fetal heart rate 142 bpm; pelvis adequate clinically
data_table.Investigations: Ultrasound: anterior fundal placenta, no praevia, cervix 30 mm long, EFW 3300 g

lead_in: What is the most appropriate counselling and plan?

options.text: Plan vaginal birth after caesarean with continuous CTG; epidural analgesia available; oxytocin augmentation as required
Plan vaginal birth after caesarean with mechanical cervical ripening; avoid prostaglandins; reassess if spontaneous labour delays
Plan vaginal birth after caesarean only if she goes into spontaneous labour at term; elective caesarean if she has not laboured by 41 weeks
Counsel that classical caesarean precludes trial of labour; plan elective repeat caesarean at 36 to 37 weeks
Refer for external cephalic version at 37 weeks if breech; otherwise allow spontaneous labour with intrapartum review

subtopic_detail: Placenta praevia with antepartum haemorrhage
stem: You are the obstetric registrar called to ED to review a 31-year-old G2P1 woman at 33 weeks gestation with painless bright red vaginal bleeding starting 1 hour ago. The 20-week scan reported anterior low-lying placenta and a follow-up scan at 32 weeks confirmed complete placenta praevia. She estimates 250 mL of blood loss and is now pad changing every 20 minutes. The fetus is moving normally. She has no contractions and no abdominal pain.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft, non-tender; uterus not contracting; vagina with ongoing fresh bleeding; speculum not performed yet; no vaginal examination done
data_table.Investigations: Hb 102, plt 168, group and screen on the way; CTG shows reassuring fetal heart rate 140 bpm with normal variability

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Vaginal examination to assess cervical dilatation; commence intravenous oxytocin to expedite delivery vaginally
Discharge home after observation if bleeding settles within 2 hours; outpatient ultrasound follow-up in 1 week
Administer external cephalic version to facilitate vaginal birth; corticosteroids and observe for delivery within 24 hours
Activate massive transfusion and proceed to immediate caesarean section under general anaesthesia regardless of fetal status
Admit; large bore IV access, fluid resuscitation, group and crossmatch 2 units; corticosteroids and anti-D if Rh negative

subtopic_detail: Primary postpartum haemorrhage initial management
stem: You are the obstetric registrar in the birth suite called urgently to a multiparous woman who delivered a 4200 g baby vaginally 15 minutes ago after a 3-hour labour. The placenta has been delivered and appears complete. She is now bleeding heavily with an estimated 900 mL blood loss collected in the drape. Her uterus feels poorly contracted on abdominal palpation. Her bladder is empty. There are no obvious lacerations on initial visual inspection of the perineum.

data_table.Examination: Uterus boggy and palpable at umbilicus; perineum intact on initial inspection; placenta delivered appears complete; bladder empty
data_table.Investigations: Group and screen on file; Hb on admission 118; FBC and coags pending; IV cannulae x2 in situ
data_table.Medications: IV oxytocin 5 units active management given at delivery

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate next step?

options.text: Transfer to theatre for examination under anaesthesia and manual exploration of the uterine cavity without further uterotonics
Insert a Bakri intrauterine balloon as the first uterotonic step without prior medical therapy attempts
Commence bimanual uterine massage and give IV oxytocin 10 units bolus then 40 units in 1 L saline infusion over 4 hours
Administer intramuscular ergometrine 250 micrograms first-line before any further oxytocin or uterine massage
Administer intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g over 10 minutes and observe for response before any uterotonic escalation

subtopic_detail: Lactational mastitis management
stem: You are the GP reviewing a 32-year-old primiparous breastfeeding woman 3 weeks postpartum. She presents with a 36-hour history of right breast pain, redness in the upper outer quadrant, fever and rigors. She is otherwise well. She is continuing to breastfeed but the affected breast is exquisitely tender during feeds and she is considering stopping breastfeeding on that side. Ultrasound is not immediately available in your clinic. There is no skin necrosis or lymphangitic spread above the breast.

data_table.Examination: Right upper outer quadrant: erythema 8 by 6 cm, warm, indurated, no fluctuance; nipple intact, no cracking; no axillary lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Clinical diagnosis; FBC and CRP pending; breast milk not cultured

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Cease breastfeeding from both breasts; bind the breasts and prescribe bromocriptine to suppress lactation
Encourage continued breastfeeding plus oral di(cloxacillin) 500 mg every 6 hours for 5 days; review at 48 hours
Refer urgently for needle aspiration of the inflamed area without antibiotic therapy pending culture results
Prescribe oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 160/800 mg twice daily for community MRSA cover empirically
Trial 48 hours of warm compresses and ibuprofen alone without antibiotics; reassess only if symptoms worsen

subtopic_detail: Anti-D prophylaxis post sensitising event
stem: You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 28-year-old G2P1 RhD-negative woman at 32 weeks gestation who presents 6 hours after a moderate motor vehicle accident with seatbelt restraint. She has mild lower abdominal tenderness but no per vaginal bleeding. The CTG is reassuring and ultrasound shows no retroplacental haematoma. Her booking blood group is O Rhesus negative with no antibodies on routine screening at 28 weeks (after standard antenatal anti-D). The fetus is known to be RhD positive on cell-free DNA testing.

data_table.Examination: Soft uterus with mild tenderness; no per vaginal bleeding; CTG reassuring; abdomen non-peritonitic
data_table.Investigations: Group O Rh negative; antibodies negative on 28-week screen; Kleihauer test result 3.5 mL fetal blood; ultrasound: no retroplacental haematoma, EFW 1900 g
data_table.Medications: Routine antenatal anti-D given at 28 weeks (625 IU)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Give an additional 625 IU intramuscular anti-D within 72 hours and assume the routine 28-week dose covers any further sensitising event during this admission
Calculate additional anti-D dose based on Kleihauer (125 IU per 1 mL fetal red cells) and administer within 72 hours; recheck Kleihauer in 48 hours
Withhold further anti-D because routine 28-week dose has been given and the Kleihauer simply reflects normal background fetal cell transfer
Give 1500 IU intramuscular anti-D once as a fixed dose without Kleihauer-based calculation and arrange routine follow up only
Defer anti-D pending repeat antibody screen at 36 weeks; administer only if anti-D antibodies are detected at that time

subtopic_detail: Umbilical cord prolapse emergency
stem: You are the obstetric registrar in the birth suite called urgently to a multiparous woman at 38 weeks who has just had spontaneous rupture of membranes during artificial rupture for slow progress. She is 4 cm dilated. The midwife reports feeling a pulsating loop of cord at the introitus. The CTG shows a sustained fetal bradycardia of 80 bpm. The woman is not contracting at this moment. The on-call anaesthetist and theatre team have been called. The operating theatre is 5 minutes away.

data_table.Examination: Pulsating cord palpable at the introitus; cervix 4 cm dilated; head at -2 station; CTG bradycardia 80 bpm sustained
data_table.Investigations: Bedside clinical assessment; no time for further imaging

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Wait for the cervix to reach full dilatation then perform instrumental vaginal delivery once the head is engaged at the spines
Replace the cord above the presenting part through the cervix; complete labour vaginally if bradycardia resolves within 5 minutes
Augment labour with oxytocin to expedite vaginal delivery while monitoring the fetal heart with continuous CTG and frequent review
Manually elevate the presenting part with a vaginal hand; position knee-chest or left lateral; activate category 1 caesarean
Administer terbutaline 250 micrograms subcutaneously and reassess fetal heart rate in 10 minutes before deciding on delivery mode

subtopic_detail: Endometrial hyperplasia on tamoxifen
stem: You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 58-year-old postmenopausal woman taking tamoxifen 20 mg daily for 4 years following ER-positive breast cancer. She presents with 3 weeks of intermittent painless vaginal spotting. She has no other medications, no obesity (BMI 24), no family history of Lynch syndrome, and no diabetes. Pelvic ultrasound shows an endometrial thickness of 10 mm with heterogeneous appearance. Pipelle biopsy demonstrates atypical endometrial hyperplasia (endometrial intraepithelial neoplasia).

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft; bimanual: anteverted uterus, non-tender, no adnexal mass; speculum: small amount of fresh blood at cervix
data_table.Investigations: TVUS endometrium 10 mm heterogeneous; Pipelle: atypical hyperplasia (EIN); FBC, UEC, LFT unremarkable; CA-125 22
data_table.Medications: Tamoxifen 20 mg daily; calcium and vitamin D

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Insert a levonorgestrel intrauterine system and repeat endometrial sampling at 6 months as first-line conservative therapy
Refer to gynaecological oncology for total hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy after multidisciplinary discussion
Switch tamoxifen to letrozole and repeat endometrial biopsy in 3 months without surgical intervention
Provide oral medroxyprogesterone 20 mg daily for 3 months and reassess endometrial thickness on ultrasound
Repeat the Pipelle biopsy in 3 months to confirm persistence before any surgical referral or specialist consultation

subtopic_detail: Pre-eclampsia with severe features
stem: You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 26-year-old primiparous woman at 34 weeks. She presents with frontal headache, epigastric pain and visual disturbance. Her booking BP was 110/70. Her booking renal function and uric acid were normal. Today she is hyperreflexic with brisk reflexes and 3+ clonus. Antenatal aspirin 100 mg nocte was started at 14 weeks for prior unexplained pregnancy loss. CTG is reassuring. She has not yet had antenatal corticosteroids.

data_table.Examination: Hyperreflexic with 3+ clonus; mild facial oedema; epigastric tenderness; CTG reassuring
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 92, ALT 168, creatinine 96, uric acid 0.42, urine PCR 320 mg/mmol; lactate normal; coags normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management plan?

options.text: Commence oral labetalol 200 mg three times daily and arrange induction of labour within 24 hours regardless of cervical favourability
Administer betamethasone 11.4 mg IM only; defer antihypertensive and magnesium until corticosteroid course is complete in 24 hours
Discharge with home BP monitoring and increased aspirin to 150 mg daily; daily community midwife review for fetal movements only
Proceed directly to category 1 caesarean section without antihypertensive or magnesium prophylaxis to avoid maternal seizure risk
Administer IV labetalol or hydralazine to lower BP, IV magnesium sulfate 4 g load then infusion, and betamethasone for fetal lung maturation; plan delivery

subtopic_detail: Endometriosis-associated chronic pelvic pain
stem: You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 32-year-old woman with 4 years of cyclical dysmenorrhoea, deep dyspareunia, and dyschezia worsening over the past 6 months. She has tried ibuprofen 400 mg as needed and a combined oral contraceptive in standard 21/7 regimen with partial benefit. She does not desire pregnancy in the next 2 years and contraception is acceptable. Transvaginal ultrasound shows a 3 cm left ovarian endometrioma. Examination demonstrates uterosacral nodularity. She has had no surgery.

data_table.Examination: Tender posterior fornix; palpable uterosacral nodules; bimanual: fixed retroverted uterus; left adnexal fullness
data_table.Investigations: TVUS: 3 cm left ovarian endometrioma, kissing ovaries; CA-125 68; pregnancy test negative
data_table.Medications: Combined oral contraceptive 30 mcg ethinyl estradiol/levonorgestrel cyclic; ibuprofen PRN

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Switch to continuous combined oral contraceptive (no pill-free interval) plus regular paracetamol and reassess pain at 3 months
Refer immediately for laparoscopic excision of endometriosis and cystectomy of the left ovarian endometrioma without further medical trial
Commence GnRH analogue (goserelin 3.6 mg monthly) plus tibolone add-back therapy for 6 months as first-line escalation
Recommend acupuncture and pelvic floor physiotherapy alone for 6 months without changing hormonal therapy
Stop the combined oral contraceptive and commence the levonorgestrel intrauterine system as monotherapy for endometriosis symptoms

subtopic_detail: Recurrent miscarriage workup
stem: You are the GP referring a 34-year-old woman who has had 3 consecutive first-trimester miscarriages, the most recent 8 weeks ago. She has no living children. Her menstrual cycle is regular. Her BMI is 23. She does not smoke. She and her partner are not consanguineous. There is no family history of thrombosis. She is preparing to conceive again and asks what investigations are warranted before the next attempt. She is currently on no medications and her TFTs done last year were normal.

data_table.Examination: Unremarkable; no thyroid mass; no signs of androgen excess
data_table.Investigations: Previous miscarriages at 8, 10 and 9 weeks; no products sent for cytogenetics; baseline TFT normal a year ago
data_table.Medications: Pregnancy multivitamin and folate 500 mcg daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate workup?

options.text: Antiphospholipid antibodies, parental karyotype, thyroid function tests, and pelvic ultrasound for uterine anomalies
Inherited thrombophilia screen (factor V Leiden, prothrombin G20210A, protein C and S, antithrombin) as the first-line workup
Endometrial biopsy for chronic endometritis and uterine natural killer cell quantification as the primary investigation workup
Routine hysteroscopy and pelvic MRI for all couples after a second miscarriage without prior ultrasound or biochemical assessment
Sperm DNA fragmentation testing and male hormone profile as the first-line investigation in unexplained recurrent miscarriage

subtopic_detail: First trimester aneuploidy screening interpretation
stem: You are the GP shared-care obstetric registrar reviewing a 32-year-old primigravida at 12+3 weeks gestation. She has had her first trimester combined screen at her chosen radiology clinic and brings the report. The fetus has appropriate crown-rump length for dates. She has no chronic medical conditions, no family history of chromosomal abnormality and is in a low-risk demographic for aneuploidy. She is keen to know what monitoring she requires for the remainder of pregnancy.

data_table.Examination: Fundus not yet palpable abdominally; no clinical concerns
data_table.Investigations: Nuchal translucency 1.6 mm, PAPP-A 1.0 MoM, free beta-hCG 1.1 MoM; calculated risk trisomy 21 1 in 8500, trisomy 18 1 in 25000
data_table.Medications: Pregnancy multivitamin with folate 500 micrograms and iodine

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her antenatal care?

options.text: Order non-invasive prenatal testing (cell-free DNA) because the combined screen alone is insufficient to exclude common trisomies in a low-risk woman
Refer for diagnostic amniocentesis at 16 weeks gestation to provide karyotype confirmation despite the reassuring screening risk estimate
Continue routine antenatal care and arrange the second trimester morphology ultrasound between 18 and 22 weeks gestation as scheduled
Arrange a fetal detailed cardiac scan at 14 weeks gestation regardless of normal nuchal translucency to screen for congenital cardiac anomalies
Repeat the nuchal translucency scan at 13+6 weeks gestation to confirm the initial measurement before continuing routine antenatal care

subtopic_detail: Combined hormonal contraception eligibility with migraine
stem: You are the GP reviewing a 22-year-old nulligravid woman who requests the combined oral contraceptive pill for cycle regulation and contraception. She reports migraine headaches approximately once a month with no visual or sensory aura, lasting under a day and managed with paracetamol. She does not smoke, has BMI 24, BP 118/72, and no personal or family history of venous thromboembolism, stroke, ischaemic heart disease or breast cancer. She has read online that all migraine sufferers must avoid the pill and would like clarification.

data_table.Examination: Unremarkable; no focal neurology; no breast lumps; thyroid normal
data_table.Investigations: Cervical screening up to date; STI screen negative; not pregnant
data_table.Medications: Paracetamol PRN for migraine; nil regular

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refuse combined hormonal contraception and prescribe progestogen-only options because any migraine history places her in WHO category 4 absolute contraindication
Recommend depot medroxyprogesterone acetate intramuscular injection every 12 weeks as the only safe option for any woman with a migraine history
Insert a copper intrauterine device today as the only reliable contraception that avoids any hormonal influence on migraine frequency or stroke risk
Decline to prescribe combined contraception and recommend barrier methods alone with neurology referral before any hormonal contraceptive can be considered
Prescribe the combined oral contraceptive pill and counsel her to stop immediately and seek review if she develops any new aura, focal neurology or worsening headache

subtopic_detail: Heavy menstrual bleeding first-line treatment
stem: You are the GP reviewing a 38-year-old para 2 woman whose menstrual bleeding has been heavy for the past 18 months, soaking through a super pad every two hours on her three heaviest days and passing thumb-sized clots. She has regular 28-day cycles, no intermenstrual bleeding and no post-coital bleeding. She has completed her family and her cervical screening is current. Pelvic ultrasound shows a normal uterus with a thin regular endometrium and normal ovaries.

data_table.Examination: No conjunctival pallor; abdomen soft and non-tender; bimanual unremarkable; cervix healthy
data_table.Investigations: Hb 105 g/L, MCV 78, ferritin 8 microg/L, TSH 1.8; pelvic ultrasound normal; cervical screening current

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line management?

options.text: Prescribe tranexamic acid 1 g three times daily during menses only with oral iron and review the response to monotherapy in three months
Insert a levonorgestrel intrauterine system today and commence oral iron replacement with three-month review of bleeding and ferritin response
Refer for endometrial ablation as first-line definitive management given completed family and a uterus with no submucosal pathology on imaging
Arrange outpatient hysteroscopy with endometrial biopsy as the next step before any medical or device-based therapy can be safely commenced
Prescribe combined oral contraceptive pill for cycle and bleeding control with iron replacement and review at three months for symptom response

subtopic_detail: Secondary postpartum haemorrhage workup
stem: You are the GP reviewing a 30-year-old para 1 woman 14 days after an uncomplicated spontaneous vaginal birth at term. Over the past 24 hours her vaginal loss has changed from light brown to fresh red, soaking through two regular pads per hour. She passed a 50 cent piece sized clot this morning. She has mild lower abdominal cramping but no fever, no foul-smelling discharge and no urinary or bowel symptoms. She has been breastfeeding exclusively and feels otherwise well.

data_table.Examination: Uterus palpable two finger-breadths above the symphysis pubis, mildly tender; speculum shows fresh blood from os, no foreign body; no perineal trauma
data_table.Investigations: Hb 102 g/L (booking 124), white cell count 9.5, CRP 12; urine pregnancy test positive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Request urgent magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis with gadolinium contrast to characterise the uterine cavity and adjacent soft tissue anatomy
Refer for outpatient hysteroscopy in three weeks to directly visualise the cavity and obtain endometrial biopsy under direct vision
Send high vaginal and endocervical swabs alone and treat empirically for endometritis without imaging before culture results return next week
Arrange same-day transvaginal pelvic ultrasound to assess the endometrial cavity and exclude retained products of conception causing the secondary bleed
Reassure that this is the normal pattern of late lochia rubra and review in seven days only if the bleeding has not settled or fever develops

subtopic_detail: HELLP syndrome diagnosis and delivery planning
stem: You are the obstetric registrar called to see a 34-year-old G2P1 at 33+2 weeks who presents with 12 hours of epigastric pain radiating to the back, nausea and three episodes of vomiting. Booking blood pressure was 110/65 and previous antenatal visits have all been unremarkable. Fetal movements are normal. On arrival to the assessment unit her blood pressure has climbed and she now reports a frontal headache. Bloods drawn in triage are returning while you assess her.

data_table.Examination: Epigastric tenderness; brisk reflexes with no clonus; CTG reassuring at 33+2; fundus appropriate for dates
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 78, Hb 110, AST 220, ALT 195, LDH 800, haptoglobin under 0.1, urine protein:creatinine 60 mg/mmol, creatinine 80

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management plan?

options.text: Commence magnesium sulfate seizure prophylaxis, give betamethasone, control blood pressure with IV labetalol and plan delivery within 48 hours after corticosteroid course
Admit for serial bloods, intravenous fluids, oral nifedipine and conservative observation until 37 weeks gestation to maximise fetal benefit from intrauterine growth
Refer urgently to general surgery for upper abdominal imaging and laparoscopic cholecystectomy on the assumption of biliary colic causing the presentation
Arrange urgent plasma exchange and high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone targeting thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura before any consideration of delivery decision
Admit overnight for telemetry monitoring, antiemetics and analgesia, and review the haematology and biochemistry trend on rounds the following morning before escalation

subtopic_detail: Recurrent pregnancy loss investigation pathway
stem: You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 33-year-old woman in clinic referred for three consecutive first-trimester pregnancy losses at 8, 10 and 9 weeks gestation over the past two years. Her cycles are regular every 28 days. She and her partner are not consanguineous and there is no family history of recurrent miscarriage. She has no symptoms suggestive of thyroid disease, polycystic ovary syndrome or autoimmune disease. She is otherwise well, takes no regular medication and has BMI 24. She and her partner wish to plan a fourth pregnancy.

data_table.Examination: Unremarkable; thyroid normal; no hirsutism or acanthosis nigricans; bimanual unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: TSH 1.6, prolactin within reference range, HbA1c 5.2 percent; previous pregnancy ultrasounds showed fetal pole with no heartbeat at second-trimester gestation; no products sent for histopathology in prior losses

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial workup?

options.text: Empirically commence low-dose aspirin and low molecular weight heparin from positive pregnancy test in the next conception without any further investigation now
Send only a serum endometrial natural killer cell panel and refer for empirical intravenous immunoglobulin treatment in the first trimester of the next pregnancy
Test antiphospholipid antibodies, parental karyotype, three-dimensional pelvic ultrasound for uterine anomaly and thyroid function before the next conception is attempted
Arrange hysterosalpingogram alone as the sole next investigation and defer all blood tests until imaging has excluded a structural cavity abnormality on radiology
Reassure her that three losses still falls within the population background rate and decline any investigation until she has had a fourth consecutive first-trimester loss

subtopic_detail: Preterm labour tocolysis and neuroprotection
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar at a regional hospital reviewing a 28-year-old G2P1 at 31+4 weeks gestation who presents with two hours of regular painful contractions every five minutes. Speculum confirms a closed cervix on visualisation but transvaginal ultrasound measures cervical length of 18 mm with funnelling. Membranes appear intact, there is no per vaginal bleeding and there are no signs of chorioamnionitis.

CTG is reassuring at 31+4 with normal baseline and reactivity. The nearest tertiary neonatal centre with level 3 NICU is 90 minutes away by road.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft between contractions; fundus 32 cm; cephalic presentation; cervix closed on speculum, cervical length 18 mm with funnel on TVUS
data_table.Investigations: FBC and CRP normal; high vaginal swab and GBS sent; urinalysis negative; CTG reassuring

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management plan?

options.text: Give betamethasone and arrange immediate caesarean section locally to deliver the infant before progressive cervical change leads to imminent vaginal birth in the unit
Commence indometacin tocolysis and admit locally for steroids and bedrest with no plan for transfer or for fetal neuroprotection beyond the steroid course
Allow labour to progress without tocolysis, give betamethasone alone and prepare for vaginal birth locally with neonatal resuscitation team attending the delivery
Start oral nifedipine and admit overnight for observation, deferring corticosteroids and magnesium sulfate until the labour pattern is confirmed in 12 hours
Commence nifedipine tocolysis, give betamethasone, administer magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection and transfer to the tertiary neonatal centre in utero

subtopic_detail: NCSP intermediate-risk pathway with HPV other oncogenic and LSIL
stem: A 32-year-old G2P2 woman presents to your GP clinic for routine cervical screening test. She has had two prior negative CSTs (5 years and 10 years ago), normal Pap smears before that, no abnormal bleeding, regular menses, and is in a monogamous relationship with her husband. She has no past history of CIN or sexually transmitted infections. She is current with vaccinations including HPV.

data_table.Examination: Cervical examination normal at speculum, smooth, no friability
data_table.Investigations: Cervical screening result: HPV-positive (non-16/18 oncogenic types - 'other oncogenic HPV'); reflex liquid-based cytology: low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (LSIL); no high-grade cellular changes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Routine recall for repeat cervical screening test in 5 years given negative prior screening pattern
Repeat cervical screening test in 6 months as accelerated surveillance without colposcopy referral now
Repeat cervical screening test in 12 months to assess for human papillomavirus persistence or progression
Refer for immediate colposcopy for cervical biopsy and assessment without further interval surveillance
Refer for LLETZ procedure as definitive cervical treatment without preceding colposcopic assessment now

subtopic_detail: ADIPS 75g OGTT diagnostic thresholds and pathway
stem: A 32-year-old G2P1 woman at 26 weeks gestation undergoes her routine 75g oral glucose tolerance test in your antenatal clinic. She has BMI 27 at booking, previous baby weighed 4250 g at 39 weeks with no documented gestational diabetes diagnosis at that pregnancy. There is no family history of type 2 diabetes. She is asymptomatic.

data_table.Examination: Fundal height 26 cm; fetal heart present, normal CTG; weight gain 9 kg this pregnancy
data_table.Investigations: 75g OGTT - fasting plasma glucose 5.2 mmol/L; 1-hour 9.8 mmol/L; 2-hour 8.7 mmol/L; HbA1c at booking 5.4 percent; urinalysis no glucosuria, no proteinuria; routine bloods unremarkable

lead_in: What is the appropriate interpretation and next step?

options.text: Normal OGTT results - reassure the patient and continue routine antenatal care without specific intervention
Diagnose impaired fasting glucose and recommend dietary advice and exercise alone without further monitoring
Diagnose pre-existing type 2 diabetes - immediate metformin and endocrinology referral with twice-weekly bloods
Diagnose gestational diabetes, refer to diabetes-in-pregnancy clinic and commence dietary review with self-monitoring
Diagnose hyperglycaemia and recommend repeat OGTT at 32 weeks gestation without lifestyle intervention

subtopic_detail: Severe HG admission with Wernicke prevention
stem: A 28-year-old G1P0 woman at 9 weeks gestation presents to your ED with 5 days of unrelenting vomiting (10-15 times daily), 5 kg weight loss from booking weight 8 weeks ago, inability to keep down fluids, and feeling weak. She has tried oral pyridoxine and ondansetron wafers at home without benefit. She has no abdominal pain, no fever, and her pregnancy was confirmed by transvaginal ultrasound at 7 weeks showing intrauterine viable pregnancy.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.6, BP 92/56, HR 118, postural drop 25 mmHg, weight loss 5 kg
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes, tachycardic, no abdominal tenderness, no organomegaly
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis 3+ ketones; Na 128, K 3.1, urea 8.4, creatinine 92; bicarbonate 18; TSH 0.2 (mildly suppressed), free T4 22 (mildly raised); LFTs ALT 78 ALP 110; FBC normal; pelvic ultrasound viable IUP single fetus

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Admit, commence intravenous saline at 4 mL/kg/hour with oral pyridoxine and metoclopramide and discharge once tolerating sips of fluid
Admit, give intravenous Hartmann's with potassium replacement, intravenous thiamine 100 mg, and intravenous ondansetron 8 mg three times daily
Outpatient management with subcutaneous ondansetron home injection device and weekly urea, electrolytes and creatinine blood tests
Refer urgently to endocrinology for the thyroid abnormalities before initiating any antiemetic or fluid management decisions now
Commence oral metformin and reassure that hyperemesis gravidarum typically resolves by 12 weeks gestation without admission

subtopic_detail: Uterotonic escalation when ergometrine contraindicated
stem: A 32-year-old G3P2 woman delivers a healthy 4150 g male infant by uncomplicated vaginal birth with active third-stage management. Twenty minutes after delivery you are called to a brisk vaginal bleed estimated at 1200 mL over 20 minutes. The uterus is poorly contracted and boggy. The placenta was delivered intact and complete. There is no obvious tear. She has chronic hypertension on labetalol and her booking BP was 158/95.

data_table.Examination: Boggy fundus above umbilicus, atonic on bimanual compression; no trauma identified at speculum exam; bladder empty after catheter
data_table.Investigations: Estimated blood loss 1200 mL and continuing; Hb on booking 110; clotting screen sent; cross-match in progress
data_table.Medications: Labetalol; recent received oxytocin 10 IU IM as part of active third stage

lead_in: After bimanual uterine compression and IV access, what is the most appropriate next pharmacological step?

options.text: Administer ergometrine 250 micrograms intramuscularly as the first-line second uterotonic in primary PPH
Administer misoprostol 800 micrograms per rectum as the first-line additional uterotonic in primary PPH
Administer intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g as the immediate first-line agent before any further uterotonic
Administer intravenous carboprost 250 micrograms in haemodynamically unstable PPH as the first-line agent
Administer intravenous oxytocin 5 IU bolus then 40 IU in 500 mL Hartmann's infusion as the immediate next uterotonic

subtopic_detail: Rotterdam criteria diagnosis and initial management
stem: A 23-year-old woman presents to your GP clinic with 18 months of irregular cycles (every 35-65 days), acne, and increasing facial hair. She has gained 8 kg in 12 months and her BMI is 29. She is sexually active using condoms. Periods are heavy when they occur. She is not seeking conception now but wants to know her options for the future.

data_table.Examination: Hirsutism Ferriman-Gallwey score 12; moderate acne; acanthosis nigricans on neck and axillae; no thyromegaly; no virilisation
data_table.Investigations: LH 12 IU/L, FSH 6 IU/L, total testosterone 2.4 nmol/L (high-normal), SHBG 28 nmol/L (low), prolactin normal, TSH normal, free androgen index elevated, DHEAS normal, 17-OH progesterone normal; fasting glucose 5.8 mmol/L, HbA1c 5.6 percent, lipids normal; pelvic ultrasound: ovarian volume right 12 mL, left 13 mL, multiple peripheral follicles bilaterally

lead_in: Based on the Rotterdam criteria, what is the most appropriate diagnosis and initial management?

options.text: Diagnose secondary hypogonadism and refer to endocrinology for specialist input before any pharmacological intervention
Diagnose congenital adrenal hyperplasia and refer for an ACTH stimulation test before initiating any pharmacological treatment
Diagnose insulin resistance as a standalone diagnosis and commence empirical metformin 500 mg twice daily without further workup
Diagnose hypothalamic anovulation and recommend weight gain to restore the hypothalamic axis function
Diagnose PCOS by Rotterdam criteria, address lifestyle, and consider the combined oral contraceptive pill for cycle control

subtopic_detail: Timing of prophylaxis during cervical ripening in a colonised woman
stem: You admit a 31-year-old woman at 41 weeks for induction of labour for prolonged pregnancy. A cervical ripening balloon has just been placed and she is comfortable.

data_table.Swab: Vagino-rectal swab at 36 weeks grew group B streptococcus
data_table.Findings: No contractions, membranes intact, temperature 36.6 degC

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan for her intravenous antibiotic?

options.text: Start it when contractions establish or the membranes rupture
Start it now, at the time the ripening balloon has been inserted
Start it when the balloon comes out, whatever the cervix is doing
Start it only if she develops a fever at some point during labour
Start it in the second stage, once she has begun pushing the baby out

subtopic_detail: Imaging pathway for suspected PE in pregnancy
stem: A 32-year-old G2P1 woman at 24 weeks gestation presents to your ED with sudden onset right-sided pleuritic chest pain and mild breathlessness for 2 hours. She has no calf swelling. There is no haemoptysis. She has no prior VTE history and no family history. Her body mass index is 24. There is no recent travel or surgery.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8, BP 120/76, HR 105, RR 22, SpO2 96 percent RA, PEFR normal
data_table.Examination: Mild tachycardia; chest clear to auscultation; no calf swelling; normal heart sounds; gravid abdomen consistent with dates; fetal heart present 145 bpm
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus tachycardia, no S1Q3T3; CXR clear bilateral lung fields; FBC normal; arterial blood gas pH 7.43, PaO2 88, PaCO2 36; d-dimer raised at 1200 ng/mL (typical for pregnancy); troponin negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next imaging investigation?

options.text: Bilateral compression ultrasound of lower limb veins, and if negative proceed to ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) scan
Computed tomography pulmonary angiogram (CTPA) as first-line investigation given specificity in pregnancy
Magnetic resonance pulmonary angiogram (MRPA) as the first-line investigation to avoid radiation exposure
Bilateral compression ultrasound of lower limb veins as the sole investigation regardless of pulmonary symptoms
D-dimer testing alone, with anticoagulation commenced based on the result without further imaging in pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Pharmacotherapy choice for hyperemesis gravidarum in early pregnancy
stem: You are the antenatal day-unit registrar reviewing a 28-year-old primigravida at 9 weeks gestation with persistent vomiting unable to tolerate oral fluids for 36 hours. She has lost 4 kg from booking weight. She has not tried any antiemetic so far. There is no history of liver disease and no abdominal pain. She has been managing on diet modification and ginger which are now ineffective.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 108, BP 102/68 lying, postural drop 18 mmHg, T 36.8
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes, no abdominal tenderness, uterus non-palpable
data_table.Investigations: Urine ketones 4 plus, urine specific gravity 1.030, sodium 134, potassium 3.1, urea 7.4, creatinine 82, ALT 38, TSH 0.6
data_table.Medications: Nil regular; folate 5 mg daily and pregnancy multivitamin

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next pharmacological step?

options.text: Metoclopramide 10 mg IV three times daily without oral antiemetic until tolerating diet again
Pyridoxine 25 mg three times daily and doxylamine 12.5 mg up to four times daily with IV fluids
Methylprednisolone 16 mg three times daily orally as the appropriate step in refractory presentation
Ondansetron 4 mg IV every 8 hours as the preferred initial antiemetic given the severity of symptoms
Prochlorperazine 12.5 mg IM as a single dose then plan oral antiemetic on discharge from the unit

subtopic_detail: GBS intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis with severe penicillin allergy
stem: You are the obstetric registrar admitting a 31-year-old G2P1 woman at 39 weeks gestation in early labour with intact membranes. Her routine vaginal-rectal swab at 36 weeks grew group B streptococcus. She reports a documented episode of laryngeal oedema and hypotension when given amoxicillin in childhood. Sensitivities on the swab show clindamycin resistance but vancomycin susceptibility.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal T 36.8, HR 84, BP 118/72; fetal heart rate baseline 138 with normal variability
data_table.Examination: Cervix 4 cm dilated, head at -1 station, intact membranes
data_table.Investigations: GBS positive 36 weeks (clindamycin resistant, vancomycin susceptible); FBC normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate intrapartum antibiotic regimen?

options.text: IV vancomycin 20 mg/kg every 8 hours starting now and until delivery as appropriate IAP
Oral azithromycin 500 mg twice daily as the practical option while awaiting IV access placement
IM benzathine penicillin 2.4 million units as a single dose to cover the expected duration of labour
IV clindamycin 900 mg every 8 hours starting now as the recommended next-line beta-lactam alternative
IV cefazolin 2 g every 8 hours starting now noting the absence of severe penicillin allergy features

subtopic_detail: Initial management plan for PPROM at 33 weeks without infection
stem: You are the obstetric registrar admitting a 29-year-old G2P1 at 33+0 weeks gestation with a clear gush of fluid 6 hours ago and ongoing leakage confirmed by sterile speculum pooling. She is afebrile and not contracting. Cardiotocography shows a reassuring trace. She has no history of penicillin allergy and the GBS swab from 28 weeks was negative.

data_table.Examination: Sterile speculum: pooling, fern positive; closed cervix; uterus non-tender
data_table.Investigations: FBC normal, CRP 6, MSU clear, ultrasound presenting cephalic, EFW 2050 g, AFI 4 cm

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management plan?

options.text: Admit and plan immediate induction of labour given prolonged rupture risk and a viable fetal weight estimate
Admit and start broad-spectrum amoxicillin clavulanate antibiotic prophylaxis with corticosteroids for fetal lung maturation
Admit, start IV erythromycin 250 mg every 6 hours, give betamethasone 11.4 mg IM, and plan expectant management until 34 weeks if stable
Admit and commence magnesium sulfate neuroprotection without antibiotic prophylaxis or corticosteroid administration
Discharge home with twice weekly review and oral erythromycin if asymptomatic given the reassuring cardiotocograph today

subtopic_detail: Management of oncogenic HPV not 16/18 with reflex LBC LSIL on routine cervical screen
stem: You are the GP registrar reviewing a 39-year-old woman with a routine cervical screening test today. She has no symptoms, no postcoital bleeding, and her last screen 5 years ago was negative. She is well, has two children, and has had a Mirena for the last 2 years for menorrhagia.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft, vagina healthy, cervix appears normal at speculum
data_table.Investigations: Today: oncogenic HPV detected (not 16 or 18). Reflex liquid-based cytology: low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion. No prior abnormal screening.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Repeat the cervical screening test in 5 years given the long interval and her absence of any symptoms
Repeat cervical screening test in 12 months as per the AU National Cervical Screening Program protocol
Refer to colposcopy within 8 weeks for evaluation of low-grade cytology in an HPV-positive woman over 30
Arrange large loop excision of the transformation zone for both diagnostic and therapeutic purposes
Repeat the cervical screening test in 6 months because she has a long-acting intrauterine device in place

subtopic_detail: Timing and counselling for Mirena insertion for heavy menstrual bleeding
stem: You are the GP registrar seeing a 41-year-old woman with 6 months of heavy menstrual bleeding flooding through tampons every hour for two days per cycle. She has no postcoital or intermenstrual bleeding. Pelvic ultrasound is unremarkable with a 6 mm endometrial thickness on day 5 and no fibroids. Her ferritin is 8 micrograms/L and she has commenced oral iron. She is in a stable relationship and does not desire further pregnancy and has chosen the Mirena.

data_table.Examination: BMI 26; mobile, anteverted uterus; no adnexal masses
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 96, ferritin 8; pelvic ultrasound day 5 endometrium 6 mm, no fibroids; cervical screening up to date
data_table.Medications: Ferrous sulfate 325 mg daily started today

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan for Mirena insertion?

options.text: Insert only after 6 weeks of oral iron therapy to allow haemoglobin to fully recover before any procedure
Insert after a 3 month trial of tranexamic acid alone given that hormonal devices are second-line for menorrhagia in AU practice
Insert at any time in her cycle today if pregnancy can be confidently excluded and start contraceptive cover immediately
Insert after endometrial biopsy because all women over 40 with heavy menstrual bleeding require histological sampling first
Insert only during days 1 to 7 of menses because this is the only time pregnancy can be excluded reliably

subtopic_detail: Counselling for trial of labour after one prior lower segment caesarean section
stem: You are the obstetric registrar counselling a 31-year-old G2P1 at 38 weeks gestation about mode of delivery. Her previous birth was an emergency lower segment caesarean section 2 years ago for category 1 fetal compromise after 6 hours of labour at 6 cm cervical dilation. The current pregnancy is uncomplicated, the fetus is cephalic, and her booking BMI is 27. She would like an evidence-based discussion of trial of labour after caesarean compared with elective repeat caesarean.

data_table.Examination: Symphysiofundal height 38 cm, cephalic presentation, head 4/5 palpable, cervix posterior, closed, 2 cm long
data_table.Investigations: Ultrasound at 36 weeks: EFW 3300 g, posterior placenta clear of internal os, normal liquor

lead_in: Which statement is the most accurate counselling point to share?

options.text: Induction of labour with prostaglandin E2 gel is the recommended approach to maximise VBAC success rates
The probability of successful vaginal birth in a planned trial of labour is approximately 70 to 75 percent in this clinical setting in AU
Continuous electronic fetal monitoring is not required during a planned trial of labour after one prior caesarean
The absolute risk of uterine rupture during a planned trial of labour after one caesarean is approximately 5 percent in AU practice
Maternal mortality is significantly higher with planned trial of labour after caesarean than with elective repeat caesarean

subtopic_detail: Next pharmacological step in refractory primary postpartum haemorrhage
stem: You are the obstetric registrar at a delivery suite resuscitation 25 minutes after vaginal birth complicated by ongoing brisk uterine bleeding. The third stage was actively managed with IM oxytocin. Despite 40 international units of oxytocin in 1 litre of crystalloid, two doses of ergometrine 250 micrograms IM, bimanual compression, and bladder catheterisation the uterus remains poorly contracted with continued vaginal blood loss. Cumulative measured loss is 1800 mL. She has no history of hypertension and her booking BP was 110/70.

data_table.Examination: Uterus boggy, soft, palpable above umbilicus despite bimanual compression; placenta delivered complete; no obvious laceration on exam
data_table.Investigations: Fibrinogen 1.4 g/L, platelets 110, INR 1.4; bedside Hb 78
data_table.Medications: Oxytocin 40 units in 1 L crystalloid infusing; ergometrine 500 micrograms IM total; tranexamic acid 1 g IV given at 10 minutes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next pharmacological action while transfusion is activated?

options.text: Administer further ergometrine 500 micrograms intramuscular now as the appropriate next uterotonic step
Administer recombinant activated factor VII 90 micrograms/kg now as the next pharmacological step in refractory haemorrhage
Administer a second dose of intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g now and repeat the dose at 30 minutes if needed
Administer misoprostol 800 micrograms rectally now as the immediate next prostaglandin uterotonic step
Administer carboprost 250 micrograms by intramuscular injection now and repeat every 15 minutes up to 8 doses if bleeding continues

subtopic_detail: Timing of delivery for stable gestational hypertension at term
stem: You are the obstetric registrar in antenatal clinic reviewing a 33-year-old G2P1 at 37+5 weeks gestation with three consecutive office BP readings of 150/96 measured 4 hours apart over the last week. She is asymptomatic with no visual symptoms, headache, or epigastric pain. The fetus is growing normally and CTG today is reassuring. Her booking BP was 110/68 and she has no prior hypertension.

data_table.Vital signs: BP today 152/98 right arm, 150/96 left arm; HR 84; afebrile
data_table.Examination: No epigastric tenderness; reflexes 2 plus; no clonus; fundus 38 cm
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, LFTs, urate normal; urine protein/creatinine ratio 18 (under 30 mg/mmol); CTG reassuring

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue expectant management to 40 weeks and start labetalol 200 mg twice daily while monitoring blood pressure trends weekly
Admit for inpatient observation for 48 hours and reassess for proteinuria evolution before any decision on delivery
Plan elective caesarean section now because of the established maternal hypertension in the third trimester
Discharge home with twice weekly clinic review and home BP diary aiming for spontaneous labour at 41 weeks
Plan induction of labour today or tomorrow given gestational hypertension confirmed at term gestation in AU practice

subtopic_detail: Antenatal surveillance schedule for uncomplicated MCDA twins
stem: You are the obstetric registrar counselling a 30-year-old G1P0 at 12 weeks gestation about her newly identified monochorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy after a dating scan showed a single placenta with a T-sign. Both fetuses are growing concordantly with normal nuchal translucency. She wants to understand the surveillance plan for the remainder of pregnancy.

data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender uterus 14 cm
data_table.Investigations: Dating scan 12 weeks: MCDA twins, both with normal anatomy at this gestation, T-sign confirmed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate surveillance schedule?

options.text: Four weekly ultrasound from 20 weeks for growth assessment with delivery planned at 38 weeks if uncomplicated
Weekly ultrasound from 24 weeks with growth surveillance and middle cerebral artery Doppler for twin anaemia syndrome
Eight weekly ultrasound through pregnancy with elective caesarean at 39 weeks regardless of fetal growth pattern
Fortnightly ultrasound from 16 weeks for fetal growth, liquor volume, and umbilical artery Doppler assessment until delivery
Monthly CTG from 28 weeks without routine ultrasound after the 20 week morphology scan if all is well

subtopic_detail: Discrimination of acute fatty liver of pregnancy from HELLP and management
stem: You are the obstetric registrar called to assess a 34-year-old G1P0 at 36 weeks gestation with 3 days of nausea, vomiting, polyuria, and progressive lethargy now confused and jaundiced. Her booking BP was 100/64. She has had two prior episodes of mild postprandial hypoglycaemia in the last 24 hours requiring oral glucose. She has no headache or visual symptoms.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.2, HR 112, BP 138/86, RR 22, SpO2 98 percent
data_table.Examination: Drowsy, jaundiced sclera, mild right upper quadrant tenderness, no peripheral oedema, asterixis present
data_table.Investigations: BSL 2.8, INR 2.4, AST 480, ALT 510, bilirubin 110, ammonia 92, creatinine 142, platelets 138, fibrinogen 1.6, urate 0.42, lactate 4.6, urine ketones positive

lead_in: Which feature most strongly favours acute fatty liver of pregnancy over HELLP syndrome in this presentation?

options.text: Elevated transaminases above 300 IU/L are seen exclusively in acute fatty liver of pregnancy rather than HELLP syndrome
Hypertension above 160/110 with proteinuria is a defining feature of acute fatty liver of pregnancy in the AU criteria
The combination of hypoglycaemia, coagulopathy out of proportion to platelet count, hyperammonaemia, and elevated lactate is most consistent with AFLP
Right upper quadrant tenderness in the third trimester is far more specific for acute fatty liver of pregnancy than HELLP
Thrombocytopenia below 100 is the most specific differentiating feature of acute fatty liver of pregnancy from HELLP

subtopic_detail: Postdates pregnancy at 41+0 weeks with favourable cervix and reassuring CTG
stem: You are the antenatal clinic registrar reviewing a 32-year-old primigravida at 41+0 weeks. The pregnancy has been uncomplicated, the fetus is in cephalic presentation, and she has had reassuring CTGs at her last two appointments. Bishop score today is 8, she has no contraindications to vaginal birth, and she has read written information about postdates options. She asks what the recommended next step is.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7, HR 80, RR 16, BP 118/74, SpO2 99 percent
data_table.Pregnancy: Singleton, cephalic, EFW 50th centile, fundal height appropriate, fetal movements normal
data_table.Investigations: CTG reactive; AFI normal; group B strep swab negative; bloods within normal limits
data_table.Bishop score: 8 (cervix 2 cm dilated, soft, anterior, 80 percent effaced, head at -1)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next recommendation?

options.text: Recommend expectant management with twice weekly CTG until spontaneous labour by 43 weeks
Recommend induction of labour between 41+0 and 41+3 weeks with amniotomy plus oxytocin
Recommend immediate elective caesarean section at 41+0 weeks for postdates indication
Recommend cervical Foley balloon insertion as a mechanical ripening method tonight
Recommend a stretch and sweep at clinic today and return in seven days for review

subtopic_detail: Painful latch assessment in established breastfeeding at day 5 postpartum
stem: You are the postnatal ward registrar reviewing a 28-year-old primipara on day 5 after spontaneous vaginal birth. She is breastfeeding every two to three hours but reports sharp nipple pain throughout the feed and now has cracked nipples. The baby is alert, producing five wet nappies in 24 hours, and has lost 6 percent of birth weight. There is no maternal fever, no breast erythema, and no induration. On observation the baby latches with pursed lips and an audible click during sucking.

data_table.Breast examination: Both nipples with linear cracks at base, no erythema, no induration, no purulent discharge
data_table.Infant observation: Latch shallow with pursed lips and clicking; tongue elevated; no audible swallowing
data_table.Investigations: No swabs taken; baby afebrile and feeding

lead_in: What is the most appropriate single next step?

options.text: Commence empiric oral flucloxacillin and topical mupirocin for presumptive nipple infection
Arrange immediate referral for frenotomy to release a presumed posterior tongue tie
Refer to lactation consultant for positioning and attachment review with feed observation
Recommend cessation of breastfeeding and transition to exclusive formula bottle feeds
