Recommend nipple shields for one week to allow the cracked nipples to heal completely

subtopic_detail: Suitability for external cephalic version at 37 weeks for breech presentation
stem: You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 31-year-old primigravida at 37+0 weeks whose presentation scan today confirms a frank breech. The pregnancy is otherwise uncomplicated with a single fetus, normal liquor volume, and an anterior placenta away from the lower segment. She has had no antepartum haemorrhage, no scars on her uterus, and intact membranes. She prefers vaginal birth and asks about external cephalic version.

data_table.Pregnancy: Singleton, frank breech, EFW 50th centile, AFI 12, anterior placenta clear of lower segment
data_table.Investigations: CTG reactive; bloods within normal limits; no antepartum haemorrhage
data_table.Past history: Nil regular medication, no uterine surgery, BMI 24

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Plan elective caesarean at 39 weeks without offering external cephalic version trial
Offer external cephalic version with tocolysis and CTG monitoring in a delivery unit
Plan vaginal breech birth without offering external cephalic version this admission
Recommend moxibustion and knee-chest exercises at home with rescan in two weeks' time
Schedule repeat scan at 39 weeks to confirm presentation before any plan is offered

subtopic_detail: Sudden fresh per vaginal bleeding at ARM with confirmed vasa praevia on antenatal scan
stem: You are the obstetric registrar in birth suite with a 33-year-old multipara at 36+2 weeks admitted for planned caesarean tomorrow for known vasa praevia diagnosed on antenatal transvaginal scan. She develops fresh vaginal bleeding 50 mL after spontaneous rupture of membranes during admission. CTG shows a sinusoidal pattern with reduced variability. There is no maternal hypotension, no abdominal pain, and no uterine tenderness.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8, HR 92, RR 18, BP 116/70, SpO2 99 percent
data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender abdomen, fresh blood at the introitus 50 mL, cervix 3 cm dilated, vertex high
data_table.Investigations: CTG sinusoidal with reduced variability; group and hold valid; bloods including coagulation in progress
data_table.Antenatal scan: Confirmed vasa praevia with fetal vessels traversing the internal os 1 cm above the cervix

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next intervention?

options.text: Proceed immediately to category 1 caesarean section in theatre as a fetal emergency
Transfuse two units of O-negative red cells to the mother and reassess after 30 minutes
Start intravenous magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection before any delivery decision
Administer betamethasone 11.4 mg IM and plan caesarean in 24 hours after lung maturation
Continue intrapartum monitoring with continuous CTG and aim for vaginal birth with vacuum

subtopic_detail: Repair location for full thickness rectal mucosa injury after vaginal birth
stem: You are the obstetric registrar called to a 28-year-old primipara who has just had an instrumental vacuum birth of a 3.9 kg infant. Inspection of the perineum after delivery reveals torn external and internal anal sphincters with a 1 cm full thickness defect into the rectal mucosa. The episiotomy was mediolateral. Estimated blood loss is 350 mL. She has had spinal anaesthesia for the birth that is still effective.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7, HR 86, RR 16, BP 118/72, SpO2 99 percent
data_table.Examination: Mediolateral episiotomy with extension through both anal sphincters and into rectal mucosa; perineum well perfused
data_table.Investigations: Hb 118 g/L; coagulation within normal limits; group and hold valid
data_table.Setting: Birth suite room with spinal still effective; theatre available within 30 minutes

lead_in: Where is the most appropriate location to perform the repair?

options.text: Transfer to operating theatre for repair under regional or general anaesthesia with adequate lighting
Repair in the birth suite room with current spinal anaesthesia using bedside instruments now
Defer repair for 24 hours to allow oedema reduction and plan a planned-list theatre slot
Pack the perineum with antiseptic gauze and arrange colorectal surgeon review at next ward round
Repair only the rectal mucosa with interrupted sutures now and the sphincters in clinic later

subtopic_detail: First-line agent for anovulatory PCOS in a woman pursuing pregnancy with elevated BMI
stem: You are the GP reviewing a 29-year-old woman with established polycystic ovary syndrome who wants to conceive. Her cycles are 60 to 90 days with anovulation on luteal progesterone testing. BMI is 31. She has no pelvic pain or partner fertility concerns and her partner has a normal semen analysis. She has been trying for nine months and has not taken any prior fertility medication. There is no diabetes, no liver disease, and no contraindication to ovulation induction.

data_table.Investigations: Normal pelvic ultrasound polycystic appearance bilaterally; HbA1c 41 mmol/mol; TSH 2.1; prolactin 240 mIU/L; AMH 65 pmol/L
data_table.Examination: Mild acne and hirsutism; abdominal exam normal
data_table.Partner: Normal semen analysis; couple in a stable relationship

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line ovulation induction agent?

options.text: Letrozole 2.5 mg daily on cycle days 2 to 6 with cycle tracking and follicle monitoring
Metformin 1500 mg daily as ovulation induction monotherapy with cycle tracking and TFT review
Clomifene 50 mg daily on cycle days 2 to 6 with progressive titration each cycle if anovulatory
Gonadotrophin injections from cycle day 2 with daily ultrasound follicle and oestradiol tracking
Laparoscopic ovarian drilling as the primary fertility intervention before any pharmacological trial

subtopic_detail: Recurrent symptomatic UTI in postmenopausal woman with vaginal atrophy on examination
stem: You are the GP reviewing a 68-year-old woman who has had four culture-proven E. coli urinary tract infections in the past 12 months. She has post-coital dysuria and external dryness. She has no haematuria between infections, no flank pain, and no incontinence. Bladder scan post-void shows 25 mL residual. Examination shows a pale, smooth vaginal mucosa with loss of rugae and friability on speculum. She has had no breast cancer.

data_table.Examination: Atrophic vaginal mucosa, no prolapse, no pelvic mass, no suprapubic tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Mid-stream urine sterile today; renal tract ultrasound normal; cystoscopy report normal
data_table.Past history: Menopause at 52; no breast or endometrial cancer; not on systemic HRT

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next pharmacological intervention?

options.text: Commence daily oral trimethoprim 150 mg as long-term low-dose prophylaxis for six months
Commence daily cranberry capsule 500 mg supplement and review symptoms after three months
Commence systemic oral conjugated equine oestrogen 0.625 mg daily for symptom control
Commence vaginal oestriol 0.5 mg pessary nightly for two weeks then twice weekly thereafter
Refer for cystoscopy with bladder biopsy to exclude an underlying interstitial cystitis condition

subtopic_detail: Sudden maternal collapse with hypotension and DIC during second stage of labour
stem: You are the obstetric registrar in birth suite when a 36-year-old multipara at term in second stage suddenly becomes breathless, profoundly hypotensive, and then loses consciousness within two minutes of pushing. Saturation drops to 78 percent on air. Fresh PV bleeding ensues with non-clotting blood from her IV cannula site. Fetus is well grown with reactive CTG immediately prior. There is no history of placental abnormality, no anaphylaxis trigger, and no pulmonary embolism risk factors.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7, HR 138, RR 36, BP 70/40, SpO2 78 percent on air, GCS 8
data_table.Examination: Generalised oozing from cannula and PV; cervix fully dilated; vertex at +1; no localised wheeze; no rash
data_table.Investigations: Arterial blood gas pH 7.18 lactate 8; INR 2.4; fibrinogen 1.0 g/L; platelets 70
data_table.Setting: Birth suite; theatre and anaesthetics 2 minutes away; obstetric MET activated

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Administer intramuscular adrenaline 0.5 mg into the lateral thigh as anaphylaxis treatment first line
Activate the massive transfusion protocol and proceed to immediate operative vaginal birth
Start intravenous heparin infusion for presumed pulmonary embolism with anticoagulation as priority
Administer intramuscular oxytocin 10 units and observe for spontaneous third stage progression next
Administer high dose intravenous hydrocortisone 1 g and tranexamic acid 1 g as initial monotherapy

subtopic_detail: Distinguishing infective mastitis from breast abscess in lactating women
stem: You are the GP reviewing a 30-year-old woman who is 5 weeks postpartum, exclusively breastfeeding her first baby. She presents with 36 hours of right breast pain, redness, fevers and rigors. She started oral flucloxacillin 24 hours ago after a phone triage with the practice nurse. She remains febrile and now describes a tender lump in the upper outer quadrant that did not improve after a full breastfeed or hand expression.

data_table.Examination: Right upper outer quadrant 4 cm fluctuant tender mass with overlying erythema, no nipple discharge, lactating left breast unremarkable
data_table.Lactation: Baby feeding well from left breast, refused right breast in last 12 hours

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Switch oral antibiotic to oral cefalexin and review the response in 48 hours
Add oral metronidazole to the current flucloxacillin and continue feeding from both breasts
Cease breastfeeding from the affected breast and commence cabergoline to suppress lactation
Refer to emergency department for breast ultrasound and needle aspiration if collection confirmed
Arrange urgent surgical incision and drainage with general anaesthesia for the suspected collection

subtopic_detail: Risk-based versus universal screening approach to intrapartum GBS prophylaxis
stem: You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 32-year-old G2P1 woman at 39 weeks of gestation in early spontaneous labour. She had a vaginal swab at 36 weeks which grew group B streptococcus. Her first baby was delivered uncomplicated 3 years ago. There is no history of penicillin allergy or anaphylaxis. Her membranes ruptured 2 hours ago with clear liquor and she is 4 cm dilated with regular contractions.

data_table.CTG: Baseline 138 bpm, normal variability, accelerations present, no decelerations
data_table.Examination: Cephalic, station -1, cervix 4 cm dilated, 70 percent effaced, clear liquor
data_table.Allergy status: No known drug allergies; previous penicillin courses tolerated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate intrapartum antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin 3 g loading dose then 1.8 g every 4 hours until delivery
Intravenous cefazolin 2 g 8-hourly until delivery is the recommended first-line regimen
Intravenous clindamycin 900 mg 8-hourly until delivery is the appropriate alternative regimen
Oral amoxicillin 1 g every 6 hours until delivery is the most practical regimen now
Withhold antibiotics and re-swab now for repeat GBS PCR before any treatment decision

subtopic_detail: Use of vaginal progesterone in threatened miscarriage with previous miscarriage history
stem: You are the GP reviewing a 33-year-old woman at 8 weeks of gestation by last menstrual period with 24 hours of light vaginal bleeding and mild lower abdominal cramping. She has had two prior first-trimester miscarriages. There is no shoulder-tip pain, no syncope, and no products passed. Her observations are stable. Transvaginal ultrasound shows a viable intrauterine pregnancy with crown rump length matching dates and fetal heart pulsation 152 bpm.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.6, HR 78, BP 118/72 mmHg, SpO2 99 percent
data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender abdomen, speculum shows closed cervix with minimal blood in posterior fornix
data_table.Bloods: Quantitative beta hCG 38000 IU/L, haemoglobin 122 g/L, rhesus negative
data_table.Ultrasound: Single viable intrauterine pregnancy, crown rump length 17 mm, fetal heart rate 152 bpm, no subchorionic haematoma

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence intramuscular medroxyprogesterone 150 mg weekly until 16 weeks of gestation
Commence oral medroxyprogesterone 10 mg twice daily until 12 weeks of gestation
Reassure and arrange follow-up scan in 2 weeks without progesterone supplementation now
Commence vaginal micronised progesterone 400 mg twice daily until 16 weeks of gestation
Refer for inpatient admission and intravenous hydration with serial beta hCG monitoring

subtopic_detail: Counselling on success and risk for VBAC after one prior caesarean for non-recurring indication
stem: You are the obstetric registrar in an antenatal clinic seeing a 34-year-old G2P1 woman at 36 weeks of gestation. Her first baby was born by lower segment caesarean section at term for breech presentation. She is keen to discuss the option of vaginal birth this time. The current pregnancy is uncomplicated, the baby is cephalic with an estimated weight on the 60th centile, and there are no maternal medical comorbidities.

data_table.Obstetric history: First baby 2022, breech at term, elective LSCS, no labour, no infection, baby 3.4 kg
data_table.Current pregnancy: Cephalic, EFW on 60th centile, placenta anterior fundal, normal liquor
data_table.Examination: Symphysis-fundal height 36 cm, BP 116/72 mmHg, dipstick negative
data_table.Imaging: Anatomy and growth scan confirm normal placental position and no scar dehiscence

lead_in: Which counselling statement is most accurate?

options.text: Trial of labour is contraindicated because of the previous caesarean delivery scar status
VBAC success in this scenario is approximately 70 to 75 percent with uterine rupture risk near 0.5 percent
Induction of labour using prostaglandin pessaries is the safest path to a successful VBAC outcome
Continuous electronic fetal monitoring is unnecessary if she is admitted in established spontaneous labour
Epidural analgesia must be declined as it masks the abdominal pain of uterine rupture in labour

subtopic_detail: Antenatal planning for suspected placenta accreta spectrum disorder
stem: You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 36-year-old G4P3 woman at 28 weeks of gestation. She has had three previous caesarean sections. The mid-trimester anatomy scan reported an anterior placenta extending across the previous scar. A targeted 24-week ultrasound described loss of the retroplacental clear zone, multiple placental lacunae, and increased subplacental vascularity. She has had no bleeding and is otherwise well in the current pregnancy.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.6, HR 84, BP 116/72 mmHg, SpO2 99 percent
data_table.Imaging summary: Anterior placenta praevia covering os, loss of retroplacental clear zone, lacunae, bridging vessels, possible bladder wall invasion
data_table.Examination: Uterus appropriate size for dates, no PV bleeding, no contractions
data_table.Bloods: Haemoglobin 118 g/L, platelets 240 x10^9/L, ferritin 36 micrograms/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Plan vaginal delivery after 39 weeks with a cell-salvage trolley available in theatre
Repeat ultrasound at 36 weeks and plan caesarean section after spontaneous labour onset
Refer to a tertiary placenta accreta multidisciplinary centre for planned caesarean hysterectomy at 34 to 36 weeks
Arrange elective uterine artery embolisation now and review imaging again at 36 weeks
Discharge to a remote community hospital and plan delivery there with on-call surgical staff

subtopic_detail: Workup of cyclical dyschezia and rectovaginal nodule suggesting deep infiltrating endometriosis
stem: You are the GP reviewing a 31-year-old nulliparous woman with a 3-year history of cyclical pelvic pain, dyspareunia, and worsening cyclical dyschezia and rectal bleeding only during menstruation. She has tried two combined oral contraceptive pills with breakthrough pain. A standard transabdominal ultrasound 6 months ago was reported as normal. She is keen to preserve fertility and wants to know what to do next.

data_table.Examination: Tender posterior fornix with a palpable nodule, fixed retroverted uterus, no adnexal mass
data_table.Bowel symptoms: Cyclical rectal bleeding only with periods, no melaena, no weight loss
data_table.Bloods: Haemoglobin 118 g/L, ferritin 22 micrograms/L, CA-125 64 U/mL
data_table.Sexual history: Single partner, contraception nil currently, last STI screen normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Refer urgently for colonoscopy to exclude colorectal malignancy before any gynaecological workup
Commence empirical GnRH agonist therapy with norethisterone add-back without further imaging
Order a Mirena intrauterine device and review symptoms over the next 6 months in clinic
Request CA-125 and full blood count and review the response to a 3-month progestin trial
Refer for a specialised transvaginal ultrasound mapping for deep infiltrating endometriosis with bowel protocol

subtopic_detail: Workup and management of recurrent miscarriage with positive antiphospholipid antibodies
stem: You are the obstetric registrar in a recurrent miscarriage clinic reviewing a 34-year-old woman who has had three consecutive first-trimester miscarriages. She is otherwise well, has had no thromboembolic events, and her last pregnancy was lost at 9 weeks. She had karyotype testing on the last products of conception which was 46,XX. Her partner has a child from a previous relationship. Initial screening bloods are back.

data_table.Initial screen: TSH 2.1 mIU/L, normal renal and liver function, fasting glucose 5.0 mmol/L
data_table.Thrombophilia: Lupus anticoagulant positive on 2 occasions 12 weeks apart, anticardiolipin IgG 60 GPL units, beta-2 glycoprotein 1 IgG 55 units
data_table.Imaging: Pelvic ultrasound normal cavity, no fibroid or polyp

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan to commence in her next pregnancy?

options.text: Low-dose aspirin 100 mg daily commencing preconception plus prophylactic enoxaparin from positive pregnancy test
Warfarin INR target 2.0 to 3.0 from preconception until delivery to maintain anticoagulation
Oral prednisolone 10 mg daily from preconception until 12 weeks of gestation to suppress immune response
Intravenous immunoglobulin infusion at 6, 10 and 14 weeks of gestation as primary therapy
Hydroxychloroquine monotherapy 400 mg daily without aspirin or anticoagulation considered

subtopic_detail: Endometrial sampling threshold in heavy menstrual bleeding with failed levonorgestrel IUS
stem: You are the GP reviewing a 47-year-old G2P2 woman with heavy menstrual bleeding refractory to a levonorgestrel intrauterine system inserted 9 months ago. She has had no intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding. Her BMI is 36, she has type 2 diabetes on metformin, and she has no personal history of breast cancer. Pelvic ultrasound after IUS insertion was reported as normal endometrium with the device correctly positioned.

data_table.Examination: Threads visible at the cervix, no uterine tenderness, no adnexal masses, BMI 36
data_table.Cycle pattern: Heavy bleeding for 8 days every 23 days, soaking through pads hourly day 2 to 3
data_table.Bloods: Haemoglobin 95 g/L, ferritin 8 micrograms/L, TSH 1.8 mIU/L
data_table.Imaging: Transvaginal ultrasound 4 months ago: endometrial thickness 7 mm, no focal lesion, IUS in situ

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Remove the Mirena and trial tranexamic acid plus mefenamic acid during the next two menstrual cycles
Refer to gynaecology for direct endometrial ablation as the next definitive treatment step
Refer for total laparoscopic hysterectomy as the definitive treatment given failed IUS trial
Refer for hysteroscopy with directed endometrial biopsy to exclude endometrial hyperplasia or cancer
Order a repeat pelvic ultrasound looking for a missed submucous fibroid as the cause of failure

subtopic_detail: Gestational hypertension first-line therapy
stem: You are the obstetric registrar in the antenatal day-stay unit reviewing a 30-year-old primigravid woman at 34 weeks gestation referred for elevated blood pressure. Blood pressure has been consistently 152/96 on three readings over 90 minutes after rest. Urine dipstick is negative for protein. She reports no headache, no visual changes, no epigastric pain and feels well with normal fetal movements. CTG is reassuring. Bloods including FBC, LFTs, UEC and uric acid are within reference range, and the protein:creatinine ratio is below the pre-eclampsia threshold.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 152/96 (averaged over 3 readings), HR 84, RR 16, SpO2 99%, Temp 36.6
data_table.Examination: Fundal height appropriate; reassuring fetal movements; no peripheral oedema; reflexes normal
data_table.Investigations: FBC, LFTs, UEC, uric acid all within reference range; spot protein:creatinine ratio 18 mg/mmol; CTG reassuring

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate first-line antihypertensive?

options.text: Atenolol 50 mg daily titrated upward to BP response as first-line oral antihypertensive in the antenatal day-stay setting
Labetalol 100 mg twice daily titrated to a target around 135/85 mmHg with weekly review and serial growth scans
Perindopril 5 mg daily titrated upward to BP response as the primary oral agent for new-onset hypertension in pregnancy
Hydralazine 25 mg orally three times daily as initial outpatient antihypertensive therapy in day-stay assessment review
Indapamide 1.5 mg daily as thiazide-like diuretic antihypertensive in this new-onset late pregnancy hypertensive presentation

subtopic_detail: Magnesium sulfate for severe pre-eclampsia
stem: You are the obstetric registrar called to the birth suite. A 26-year-old primigravid woman at 36+3 weeks gestation is admitted with severe pre-eclampsia. BP is persistently 170/112 with 3+ proteinuria, severe headache and right upper quadrant pain. ALT is 88 U/L and platelets 92. Reflexes are brisk with 3 beats of clonus. She has had no seizures so far. She is being prepared for induction of labour. She has normal renal function.

data_table.Examination: Headache, RUQ tenderness, brisk reflexes, 3 beats clonus, no seizure activity; CTG reassuring
data_table.Investigations: ALT 88 U/L, AST 76 U/L, platelets 92 x 10^9/L, creatinine 76 micromol/L, urate 0.45 mmol/L, urine PCR 320 mg/mmol

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate magnesium sulfate regimen for seizure prophylaxis?

options.text: Magnesium sulfate 1 g IV loading over 5 minutes followed by 0.5 g/h IV infusion until 12 hours postpartum on labour ward
Magnesium sulfate 10 g intramuscular loading then 5 g IM every 4 hours for 24 hours postpartum using Pritchard schedule
Magnesium sulfate 8 g IV loading over 5 minutes followed by 2 g/h IV continuous infusion until 24 hours postpartum review
Magnesium sulfate 2 g IV bolus only at presentation without subsequent maintenance infusion or postpartum continuation
Magnesium sulfate 4 g IV loading over 20 minutes then 1 g/h IV infusion continued for at least 24 hours after delivery

subtopic_detail: Intrapartum chorioamnionitis
stem: You are the obstetric registrar on the birth suite caring for a 28-year-old multiparous woman at 39 weeks gestation. She has been labouring for 14 hours with spontaneous rupture of membranes 18 hours ago. Over the past 90 minutes she has developed a temperature of 38.6 degrees, maternal heart rate 118 sinus, fetal tachycardia 178, foul-smelling amniotic fluid, and uterine tenderness between contractions. Her GBS status is unknown. She has no penicillin allergy. She is not yet fully dilated and continued labour is appropriate.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 38.6, HR 118, BP 108/68, RR 22, SpO2 97%, fetal HR 178
data_table.Examination: Uterine tenderness between contractions; foul-smelling amniotic fluid; 7 cm dilated
data_table.Investigations: FBC WCC 18.2 with neutrophilia, CRP 84; blood and urine cultures sent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empiric antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Ampicillin 2 g IV every 6 hours alone as empiric monotherapy throughout the remainder of labour and immediate postpartum
Cefazolin 2 g IV every 8 hours as empiric single-agent monotherapy throughout labour and the immediate postpartum interval
Ampicillin 2 g IV 6 hourly plus gentamicin 5 mg/kg IV daily; add metronidazole 500 mg IV 12 hourly if caesarean is required
Vancomycin 25 mg/kg IV plus ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily as empiric combination directed at suspected polymicrobial uterine infection
Withhold antibiotics until amniotic fluid and blood culture microbiology results return to allow targeted antimicrobial therapy

subtopic_detail: Umbilical cord prolapse
stem: You are the obstetric registrar in the birth suite. A 32-year-old multiparous woman at 38 weeks gestation has had spontaneous rupture of membranes one minute ago. The midwife performing the post-rupture examination palpates a pulsating cord through the cervix. The cervix is 6 cm dilated, the head is high at -3 station, and the CTG immediately shows a prolonged deceleration to 60 bpm sustained over 90 seconds. The woman has had two previous uncomplicated vaginal births. The on-call anaesthetist is available and theatre staff have been called.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal HR 96, BP 122/76, fetal HR 60 sustained 90 s, then variable
data_table.Examination: Pulsating cord palpable below the presenting part; cervix 6 cm; head at -3 station; intact membranes elsewhere
data_table.Investigations: Group and hold up to date; FBC, UEC normal

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Attempt manual replacement of the cord into the uterus and continue labour towards expected vaginal delivery in birth suite
Place the woman in left lateral recumbent position and reassess the cardiotocograph trace in 10 minutes before any further action
Commence intravenous oxytocin to augment labour for rapid vaginal delivery before transferring her to operating theatre
Elevate the presenting part manually, position knee-chest or exaggerated Sims, fill the bladder, prepare for category 1 caesarean
Perform immediate fetal scalp blood sampling to assess acidosis severity before deciding on the appropriate mode of delivery

subtopic_detail: Retained placenta management
stem: You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 29-year-old primigravid woman who delivered a healthy term infant 35 minutes ago after an active third stage with intramuscular oxytocin 10 IU. The placenta has not delivered despite controlled cord traction. Estimated blood loss so far is 400 mL with ongoing trickling. BP is 108/70, HR 96. The uterus is well contracted at the umbilicus. There is no inversion. She is otherwise well, has no penicillin allergy, and an epidural is in situ and functioning.

data_table.Examination: Uterus contracted at umbilicus; ongoing trickling bleeding; no inversion; cord still externally visible; bladder catheter draining 250 mL
data_table.Investigations: Hb 116 pre-delivery; group and screen valid; FBC and coags pending
data_table.Medications: Oxytocin 10 IU IM given; epidural in situ

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Transfer to theatre for examination under anaesthesia and manual removal of placenta with broad-spectrum prophylactic antibiotics
Inject 20 IU of oxytocin into the umbilical vein and wait a further 30 minutes for placental separation while observing for ongoing bleeding
Continue controlled cord traction with vigorous abdominal fundal pressure to expel the placenta from below over the next several minutes
Wait a further 60 minutes for spontaneous placental separation before considering any active intervention or transfer to operating theatre
Administer carboprost 250 mcg intramuscularly as the principal pharmacological intervention for the retained placenta in this stable patient

subtopic_detail: Shoulder dystocia - HELPERR algorithm
stem: You are the obstetric registrar called urgently to a birth suite. A 33-year-old multiparous woman with gestational diabetes (HbA1c 6.5%) at 40 weeks gestation has just delivered the head of a baby estimated at 4.3 kg at term ultrasound, but the head has retracted against the perineum (turtle sign) and the anterior shoulder is impacted behind the symphysis pubis. Routine downward traction has not resolved the impaction. There is no umbilical cord around the neck.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal HR 102, BP 124/78; fetal HR not currently available with delivery in progress
data_table.Examination: Turtle sign positive; anterior shoulder impacted behind symphysis; perineum intact at this point with no episiotomy
data_table.Investigations: Group and hold valid; HbA1c 6.5% at booking
data_table.Medications: Oxytocin infusion as augmentation; epidural in situ

lead_in: Which manoeuvre is the most appropriate FIRST step within the HELPERR algorithm?

options.text: Immediately perform symphysiotomy to disimpact the shoulder as the initial obstetric manoeuvre attempted in this emergency
Cleidotomy (deliberate fracture of the fetal anterior clavicle) as the initial manoeuvre to disimpact the shoulder from below the symphysis
Apply heavy fundal pressure to expel the baby through the obstructed pelvic outlet as the first step in this dystocic delivery sequence
Perform internal rotation manoeuvres such as Wood's screw or Rubin as the first step in this established shoulder dystocia in the birth suite
Call for help, then hyperflex the maternal hips onto her abdomen (McRoberts) and add suprapubic pressure if shoulder remains impacted

subtopic_detail: Endometrial cancer initial workup and staging
stem: A 62-year-old postmenopausal woman is referred to your gynaecology outpatient clinic with three episodes of vaginal bleeding over the past two months. She had menopause at 51 and has been on no hormone therapy. BMI is 34 with a history of type 2 diabetes. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an endometrial thickness of 14 mm with a heterogeneous appearance. Endometrial pipelle biopsy in clinic reveals grade 2 endometrioid adenocarcinoma. She has no symptoms of metastatic disease. Examination is unremarkable apart from cervix appearing normal.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft, no masses; cervix normal on speculum; bimanual examination unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: TVUS endometrial thickness 14 mm, heterogeneous; pipelle biopsy: grade 2 endometrioid adenocarcinoma; CA-125 pending

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next imaging investigation for staging?

options.text: Whole-body 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose PET-CT as the principal first-line staging investigation prior to discussion at gynaecology oncology MDM
Pelvic MRI with contrast to assess myometrial invasion and cervical involvement plus CT chest abdomen pelvis for distant disease assessment
Abdominal ultrasound only as primary imaging with onward referral to the gynaecological oncology multidisciplinary team review meeting
Hysteroscopy with directed biopsy and dilatation and curettage to confirm histology and grade before any further imaging steps are taken
Plain chest x-ray only to exclude metastatic disease before referral for surgical planning and definitive operative staging procedure

subtopic_detail: GBS intrapartum chemoprophylaxis
stem: A 29-year-old woman gravida 2 para 1 at 39 weeks and 2 days gestation presents to your birth suite in spontaneous labour with regular painful contractions every 3 minutes and a cervix dilated to 5 cm. Her routine vaginal-rectal culture at 36 weeks was positive for group B Streptococcus. She has no allergies. Her membranes are still intact and the cardiotocograph is reassuring. She had an uncomplicated previous vaginal birth. She received no antenatal antibiotics. The midwife seeks your antibiotic order.

data_table.Examination: 5 cm dilated; membranes intact; vertex; CTG reassuring
data_table.Investigations: GBS LVS positive at 36 weeks; FBC and group and screen normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate intrapartum chemoprophylaxis?

options.text: Intravenous ampicillin 2 g loading then 1 g four-hourly until delivery as the recommended first-line agent for intrapartum chemoprophylaxis in penicillin-tolerant women
Oral amoxicillin 1 g eight-hourly until delivery as a simpler regimen that avoids intravenous access in low-risk women with intact membranes still in labour
Intravenous clindamycin 900 mg eight-hourly as primary chemoprophylaxis to cover possible undocumented penicillin allergy in a woman without recorded allergies today
Intravenous benzylpenicillin 3 g loading dose then 1.8 g four-hourly until delivery according to current recommended Australian intrapartum chemoprophylaxis dosing
Withhold antibiotics until membrane rupture occurs given intact membranes are protective and there is no current acute risk factor for early-onset neonatal sepsis today

subtopic_detail: PCOS Rotterdam diagnosis
stem:
A 24-year-old woman attends your general practice clinic with a four-year history of irregular menstrual cycles of variable length up to 90 days and increasing facial hirsutism. She has gained 6 kg in two years and is not currently using contraception. She is not seeking pregnancy at present. Her examination shows BMI 28 with mild upper-lip and chin terminal hair.

Her bloods show normal prolactin, normal TSH, normal 17-hydroxyprogesterone and elevated free androgen index. Pelvic ultrasound demonstrates a single ovary with 14 follicles measuring 2 to 9 mm.

data_table.Examination: BMI 28; mild facial hirsutism; no acanthosis nigricans; no virilisation
data_table.Investigations: TSH 1.6; prolactin 320; 17-OHP normal; FAI elevated; ovary 14 follicles 2-9 mm

lead_in: Does this presentation meet diagnostic criteria for polycystic ovary syndrome?

options.text: No; without prior progestogen-induced withdrawal bleed challenge testing oligo-ovulation cannot be confirmed and PCOS criteria cannot yet be applied to this clinical case
No; PCOS requires the full triad of oligo-ovulation, hyperandrogenism and polycystic morphology together with exclusion of mimickers and at least one metabolic feature present
No; her ovarian morphology threshold of 14 follicles is below the current diagnostic cut-off using newer transvaginal ultrasound technology with higher resolution imaging
Yes; she meets PCOS criteria but only because AMH level above the laboratory cut-off has replaced ultrasound morphology in current diagnostic frameworks worldwide
Yes; she meets two of three Rotterdam criteria after exclusion of mimicking causes including thyroid, prolactin and adrenal cortical disorders biochemically today

subtopic_detail: Hyperemesis gravidarum management
stem:
A 24-year-old woman gravida 1 at 8 weeks gestation by certain dates presents to your emergency department after five days of inability to tolerate oral fluids with vomiting more than ten times daily. She has lost 4.2 kg from her booking weight three weeks ago and reports dizziness and orthostatic symptoms. Examination shows dry mucous membranes and tachycardia. Her urine ketones are 3+ and serum sodium is 132 mmol/L.

Routine antenatal bloods include normal TSH, normal LFTs and a viable intrauterine pregnancy on bedside ultrasound. She has had no improvement on oral pyridoxine and doxylamine over three days.

data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes; postural BP drop 18 mmHg; weight loss 4.2 kg (5.6%)
data_table.Investigations: Urine ketones 3+; Na 132, K 3.4, Cr 76; TSH 1.2; viable 8/40 IUP on USS
data_table.Medications: Doxylamine 25 mg + pyridoxine 25 mg nocte (3 days, no relief)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next pharmacological step?

options.text: Admit for intravenous Hartmann's resuscitation, intravenous metoclopramide 10 mg eight-hourly and add intravenous thiamine 100 mg before any dextrose-containing fluids
Add ondansetron 8 mg oral wafer eight-hourly to her current oral antiemetics and discharge home with general practice follow-up scheduled within 48 hours
Commence intravenous 5% dextrose with potassium replacement before any thiamine to provide immediate caloric and electrolyte support in starvation ketosis
Commence corticosteroid intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg six-hourly as first-line antiemetic for refractory hyperemesis at her current gestation today
Order an urgent ultrasound to exclude gestational trophoblastic disease as the cause of severe vomiting before any pharmacological escalation in management is undertaken

subtopic_detail: Ectopic methotrexate eligibility
stem:
A 28-year-old woman gravida 2 para 1 attends your early pregnancy assessment clinic with mild right iliac fossa pain and a serum beta-hCG of 2400 IU/L two days ago that has now risen to 2860 IU/L. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an empty uterus with no intrauterine sac, a 22 mm right adnexal mass with no fetal heart activity and no free fluid.

She is haemodynamically stable, has no pain currently, and her renal and liver function are normal. She has no contraindication to methotrexate and is keen to avoid surgery if possible. Her partner can drive her in for serial reviews easily.

data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender abdomen now; mild right iliac fossa tenderness on deep palpation
data_table.Investigations: bHCG 2860 (was 2400 over 2 days); 22 mm right adnexal mass, no FH, no free fluid; Hb 128; LFTs normal; eGFR 92

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management option to offer her?

options.text: Expectant management with serial beta-hCG monitoring every 48 hours given mild symptoms and a stable haemodynamic profile with reassuring ultrasound findings today
Single-dose intramuscular methotrexate 50 mg per square metre with weekly serum beta-hCG measurement on days 4 and 7 then weekly to non-pregnant
Laparoscopic salpingectomy as first-line definitive management given any tubal ectopic carries an unacceptable risk of rupture with conservative non-surgical approaches
Laparoscopic salpingostomy with conservation of the affected tube and intraoperative methotrexate instillation to reduce persistent trophoblast risk after surgery completes
Oral mifepristone 200 mg followed by misoprostol 800 micrograms vaginally as a non-surgical alternative for tubal ectopic pregnancy with rapid effective resolution today

subtopic_detail: Placenta praevia mode of delivery
stem:
A 32-year-old woman gravida 3 para 2 at 35 weeks and 4 days gestation is admitted to your antenatal ward with a small painless fresh red vaginal bleed that has now ceased. Her 32-week placental localisation transabdominal scan and confirmatory transvaginal scan showed a placenta praevia with its lower edge covering the internal cervical os. She has had two previous caesarean sections.

Her bleeding has settled, the fetus is reactive on cardiotocography and her observations remain stable. The Hb has dropped from 116 to 109 g per litre since admission and she remains rhesus positive.

data_table.Examination: Soft uterus; no tenderness; fundal height 36 cm; CTG reactive
data_table.Investigations: Hb 109 (admission 116); blood group O Rh+; placenta covering os on TVS 32/40; FH 152 reactive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate definitive plan for this pregnancy?

options.text: Proceed to immediate emergency caesarean tonight because of the antepartum haemorrhage event despite cessation of bleeding and reassuring fetal heart rate tracing
Plan vaginal trial of labour at 39 weeks given resolution of bleeding and confidence that the placental edge will retract upward with further uterine growth before labour
Plan elective caesarean section at 36 to 37 weeks after antenatal corticosteroids, with imaging review for placenta accreta spectrum due to prior caesareans
Plan induction of labour at 38 weeks with continuous cardiotocography and full neonatal team in attendance in an obstetric theatre with surgical backup standing ready
Discharge home with daily fetal movement monitoring and return precautions; plan caesarean at 39 weeks if no further bleeding events occur over the following weeks

subtopic_detail: PPROM antibiotics and timing
stem:
A 27-year-old woman gravida 2 para 1 at 31 weeks and 2 days gestation presents to your birth suite with a sudden gush of clear fluid two hours ago that continues to leak. Speculum examination confirms pooling of amniotic fluid and a closed cervix. The fetus is in cephalic presentation with reassuring cardiotocography. She is afebrile with no abdominal tenderness, fetal heart rate 142 with normal variability, and no contractions.

Routine bloods show WCC 9.4 and CRP 8. Her group B Streptococcus status from a recent swab is negative. She has no penicillin allergy or relevant medical history.

data_table.Examination: Speculum: pooling of clear amniotic fluid; closed cervix; non-tender uterus
data_table.Investigations: WCC 9.4; CRP 8; GBS negative; CTG 142 reactive; vaginal swab pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management plan?

options.text: Discharge home with daily community midwifery review, oral amoxicillin and salbutamol nebulisers as needed for any contractions starting in the next 48 hours
Admit, give betamethasone and intravenous amoxicillin with clavulanic acid 1.2 g eight-hourly for 10 days for combined gram-positive and gram-negative coverage during latency observation today
Induce labour now with vaginal prostaglandin and intravenous oxytocin given preterm prelabour rupture of membranes carries an unacceptable ongoing chorioamnionitis risk
Admit, give betamethasone 11.4 mg intramuscular for two doses 24 hours apart, oral erythromycin 250 mg four times daily for 10 days and avoid digital examinations completely
Perform a digital vaginal examination now to assess cervical change in centimetres and add a single 6 g dose of magnesium sulfate intravenously for fetal lung neuroprotection

subtopic_detail: Twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome
stem:
A 31-year-old woman gravida 1 at 19 weeks gestation with a monochorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy attends your obstetric ultrasound clinic for routine fortnightly surveillance scanning. The scan shows twin A with an empty bladder visualised throughout the scan, deepest vertical pool of amniotic fluid 1.4 cm, and small bladder. Twin B has deepest vertical pool 9.8 cm, distended bladder, and visible cardiac dilatation.

Both fetuses have normal umbilical artery Doppler waveforms at this time. Maternal blood pressure and observations are normal. There are no maternal symptoms of preterm labour.

data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender uterus; fundal height 24 cm
data_table.Investigations: Twin A DVP 1.4 cm; Twin B DVP 9.8 cm with distended bladder; UA Dopplers normal both

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Plan elective delivery within 48 hours to remove both twins from the abnormal placental environment causing the syndrome with neonatal intensive care for the preterm pair
Continue fortnightly surveillance unchanged and reassess fluid discrepancy and bladder visibility in two weeks before deciding on any escalation in monitoring or referral
Perform a single therapeutic amnioreduction of 1.5 litres from the recipient sac today as first-line definitive treatment without further specialist fetal medicine referral
Recommend selective fetal reduction of the smaller twin by bipolar cord coagulation to preserve outcomes for the recipient larger twin in this monochorionic twin scenario
Refer urgently to a fetal medicine centre for evaluation and consideration of fetoscopic laser ablation of communicating placental anastomoses as treatment of choice now

subtopic_detail: Vasa praevia recognition and delivery
stem: A 32-year-old G2P1 is brought to the birth suite at 36+2 weeks gestation reporting a small painless gush of fresh red vaginal blood that began shortly after spontaneous rupture of membranes 20 minutes ago. Her morphology scan at 20 weeks reported a succenturiate placental lobe with the main placenta posterior, no praevia. She is not contracting. The midwife places her on continuous CTG which shows a sinusoidal baseline at 130 bpm with no accelerations. The presenting part is high. She is otherwise well, with no history of trauma.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal HR 96, BP 118/72, SpO2 99% room air, Temp 36.8
data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender abdomen; presenting part high; no contractions palpable; small amount of fresh red blood at introitus
data_table.Investigations: Bedside USS: posterior placenta with succenturiate lobe; CTG: sinusoidal pattern baseline 130 bpm

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Augment labour with controlled artificial rupture and an oxytocin infusion targeting active phase
Proceed immediately to category 1 caesarean section with neonatal team in attendance for resuscitation
Perform a careful digital vaginal examination first to assess cervical dilatation and exclude cord prolapse
Commence intravenous nifedipine tocolysis and a single dose of betamethasone before planning delivery
Start intravenous magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection and arrange repeat ultrasound now

subtopic_detail: Acute fatty liver of pregnancy vs HELLP
stem: A 34-year-old primigravida is admitted at 34+5 weeks gestation with 48 hours of progressive nausea, polydipsia, and right upper quadrant pain. She has had no headaches or visual disturbance. On arrival she is mildly jaundiced and lightly drowsy. Bloods on the labour ward triage show ALT 320, total bilirubin 60, INR 1.9, fibrinogen 1.4 g/L, platelets 110, creatinine 130, ammonia 80, capillary glucose 2.6 mmol/L, and lactate 4.2. The midwife notes the fetal heart rate is 150 bpm with reduced variability on the CTG.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 108, BP 138/86, SpO2 98% room air, Temp 36.6
data_table.Examination: Mild scleral icterus; tender right upper quadrant; no peripheral oedema; drowsy but rousable
data_table.Investigations: ALT 320, bilirubin 60, INR 1.9, fibrinogen 1.4 g/L, platelets 110, creatinine 130, ammonia 80, glucose 2.6 mmol/L, lactate 4.2

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Treat as severe HELLP with intravenous magnesium sulfate and expectant management until 36 weeks
Stabilise with glucose, correct coagulopathy with fresh frozen plasma and cryoprecipitate, then proceed to expedited delivery
Commence high-dose intravenous N-acetylcysteine as an antidote and admit to the obstetric ward for serial bloods
Initiate urgent therapeutic plasma exchange and continue expectant management with twice daily CTG
Administer intravenous betamethasone for fetal lung maturation and plan delivery in 48 hours

subtopic_detail: Cord prolapse manual elevation
stem: A 31-year-old G3P2 at 38+1 weeks gestation is in early labour at 4 cm dilation on the birth suite. Spontaneous rupture of membranes occurs and the midwife immediately calls you because the CTG drops from a baseline of 140 bpm to a sustained 70 bpm. On vaginal examination you palpate a pulsating loop of cord through the cervix. The presenting part is a high vertex. The woman is in pain but cooperative. The operating theatre is 3 minutes away and the anaesthetic team is on the unit.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal HR 92, BP 118/72, SpO2 99% room air, Temp 36.7
data_table.Examination: Cervix 4 cm dilated; pulsating cord palpable through the cervix; presenting part high vertex
data_table.Investigations: CTG: sustained fetal bradycardia 70 bpm; presentation vertex

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate next step?

options.text: Apply gentle outward traction on the cord and place warm saline soaks until theatre is ready
Insert an oxytocin infusion to expedite vaginal delivery in this multiparous woman with a vertex presentation
Place the woman in the knee-chest position with manual elevation of the presenting part and call category 1 caesarean
Perform an immediate ventouse-assisted vaginal delivery as the head is engaged and the cervix is dilating
Fill the bladder with 500 mL of warm saline as the sole manoeuvre and prepare for elective caesarean

subtopic_detail: Postpartum thyroiditis recognition
stem: A 31-year-old woman returns to her general practice 9 weeks after the birth of her second baby with anxiety, palpitations, sweating, and 3 kg weight loss despite a normal appetite. She breastfeeds 8 times per day and her baby is thriving. She has no goitre or eye signs. She is taking no medications. Her thyroid function tests show TSH less than 0.01 mIU/L, free T4 30 pmol/L, free T3 8 pmol/L. Anti-TPO antibodies are strongly positive. A radioactive iodine uptake scan performed off breastfeeding milk donation shows reduced uptake throughout the gland.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 104, BP 132/78, SpO2 99% room air, Temp 36.9
data_table.Examination: Fine resting tremor; warm peripheries; no goitre; no ophthalmopathy; no pretibial myxoedema
data_table.Investigations: TSH < 0.01 mIU/L, fT4 30 pmol/L, fT3 8 pmol/L, anti-TPO positive, low-uptake scan

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence carbimazole 15 mg daily and titrate to maintain free T4 in the upper normal range
Refer urgently for radioactive iodine ablation while ceasing breastfeeding for 6 weeks
Initiate levothyroxine 50 micrograms daily and titrate to normalise TSH within 6 weeks
Commence propranolol 20 mg three times daily for symptoms and repeat thyroid function tests in 6 weeks
Refer to a thyroid surgeon for total thyroidectomy to prevent recurrence in future pregnancies

subtopic_detail: Postmenopausal bleeding workup
stem: A 64-year-old woman attends her general practice with a 4 week history of intermittent fresh red vaginal bleeding, 13 years after her last menstrual period. She has never had hormone replacement therapy. Her body mass index is 34 kg/m^2 and she has type 2 diabetes treated with metformin. She had two uncomplicated vaginal deliveries and her cervical screening test 2 years ago was HPV negative. There is no family history of breast or gynaecological malignancy.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 76, BP 138/82, SpO2 99% room air, Temp 36.6
data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender abdomen; speculum: small amount of fresh blood at the cervical os, cervix benign in appearance; bimanual: bulky retroverted uterus, no adnexal mass
data_table.Investigations: Recent cervical screening test HPV negative; BMI 34; HbA1c 7.4 percent

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Reassure her that this is likely vaginal atrophy and prescribe topical oestrogen with review in 6 weeks
Arrange transvaginal ultrasound to measure endometrial thickness, with hysteroscopy and biopsy if thickness exceeds 4 mm
Send a serum CA-125 and arrange contrast computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis as primary workup
Repeat the cervical screening test for HPV and reflex liquid-based cytology as primary investigation
Refer directly for magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis before any other investigation is performed

subtopic_detail: Mirror syndrome recognition
stem: A 27-year-old G2P1 is admitted at 29+0 weeks gestation with progressive generalised oedema over 5 days, breathlessness on minimal exertion, and a 6 kg weight gain. A fetal medicine ultrasound that morning confirms severe fetal hydrops with ascites, pleural effusions, and scalp oedema. Her blood pressure is 152/96, urinalysis shows 3+ protein, platelets are 95, and uric acid is elevated. She has not received antenatal steroids in this pregnancy. The cause of fetal hydrops remains under investigation, but the fetus has known severe anaemia.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal HR 102, BP 152/96, SpO2 95% on 2 L nasal prongs, RR 24, Temp 36.8
data_table.Examination: Maternal facial puffiness and pitting peripheral oedema; bibasal crackles; fundus consistent with dates plus polyhydramnios
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 95, uric acid raised, ALT mildly raised, urine PCR 350 mg/mmol; fetal ultrasound: severe hydrops with ascites and pleural effusions

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Initiate intravenous magnesium sulfate and oral methyldopa, and continue conservative management until 34 weeks
Plan urgent caesarean delivery within 6 hours and forgo antenatal corticosteroids because of maternal compromise
Treat hypertension, administer antenatal corticosteroids and magnesium sulfate, then deliver within 24 to 48 hours
Perform intrauterine transfusion immediately and continue antenatal monitoring without planning delivery
Commence intravenous furosemide and fluid restriction as the primary intervention for the maternal oedema

subtopic_detail: Placental abruption with coagulopathy
stem: A 35-year-old G4P3 at 36+4 weeks gestation is brought by ambulance after sudden severe abdominal pain following a motor vehicle collision. She has had minimal vaginal bleeding. Her abdomen is tense and tender with frequent uterine contractions on palpation. The CTG shows persistent fetal bradycardia at 80 bpm with reduced variability. Initial bloods show haemoglobin 88, platelets 110, fibrinogen 1.0 g/L, INR 1.6. Two large bore intravenous lines are placed and crystalloid started.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 132, BP 86/52, SpO2 97% on 6 L mask, RR 26, Temp 36.4
data_table.Examination: Tense tender uterus with frequent contractions; minimal vaginal bleeding; CRT 4 s; pallor
data_table.Investigations: Hb 88, platelets 110, fibrinogen 1.0 g/L, INR 1.6; CTG: persistent fetal bradycardia 80 bpm

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Augment labour with an oxytocin infusion to expedite vaginal delivery in this multiparous woman with prior births
Activate the massive transfusion protocol with early fibrinogen replacement and proceed to category 1 caesarean delivery
Wait for cross-matched packed red cells before any intervention and treat with crystalloid alone in the meantime
Administer fresh frozen plasma as the sole blood product to correct the coagulopathy before delivery
Give intravenous tranexamic acid as a single agent and continue conservative management for 30 minutes

subtopic_detail: Adnexal torsion in pregnancy
stem: A 28-year-old G2P1 at 17+3 weeks gestation presents to the emergency department with 6 hours of sudden severe right iliac fossa pain and three episodes of vomiting. The pain woke her from sleep and has not improved with paracetamol. Her urinary beta-human chorionic gonadotrophin confirms the pregnancy and the pregnancy is intrauterine and viable on point-of-care ultrasound. A formal transvaginal ultrasound shows a right ovarian mass of 8 cm with absent doppler flow, and the left ovary is normal. White cell count is 13.5 with normal C-reactive protein. Urinalysis is bland.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 110, BP 116/72, SpO2 99% room air, Temp 37.2
data_table.Examination: Tender right iliac fossa with guarding; uterus consistent with dates; no peritonitis elsewhere
data_table.Investigations: Beta-hCG positive; intrauterine viable pregnancy; right ovarian mass 8 cm with no doppler flow; left ovary normal; WCC 13.5; CRP 6

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Admit for observation with analgesia and serial ultrasound, planning intervention only if pain persists beyond 24 hours
Proceed to laparoscopic detorsion with ovarian preservation and cystectomy as indicated by intraoperative findings
Plan elective oophorectomy as definitive management because preservation of an ischaemic ovary risks thromboembolic complications
Perform transvaginal cyst aspiration under ultrasound guidance to decompress the mass and relieve symptoms
Commence nifedipine for tocolysis and admit for observation with daily fetal heart rate monitoring

subtopic_detail: Vulval lichen sclerosus management
stem: A 58-year-old postmenopausal woman is referred to a gynaecology clinic with 12 months of progressive vulval pruritus and soreness that worsens at night. She has had no postcoital bleeding. On examination there are well-demarcated white wrinkled plaques on the labia minora and perineum, with loss of the labia minora architecture and narrowing of the introitus producing a figure-of-eight appearance around the vulva and anus. A vulval punch biopsy taken at this visit confirms lichen sclerosus with no atypia. She has used emollient creams alone with no benefit.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 78, BP 132/82, SpO2 99% room air, Temp 36.7
data_table.Examination: White wrinkled vulval plaques in a figure-of-eight pattern; loss of labia minora; introital narrowing; no ulceration
data_table.Investigations: Vulval punch biopsy: lichen sclerosus, no atypia; cervical screening up to date and negative

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate management?

options.text: Topical hydrocortisone 1 percent applied twice daily for 2 weeks then as required for flares
Vaginal oestrogen pessaries inserted nightly for 4 weeks then twice weekly as maintenance therapy
Topical clobetasol propionate 0.05 percent ointment with a taper over 12 weeks then maintenance plus annual review
Topical antifungal clotrimazole cream applied twice daily for 4 weeks with a planned skin biopsy if no improvement
Refer for total vulvectomy as definitive treatment to address scarring and prevent malignant transformation

subtopic_detail: Iron deficiency anaemia in pregnancy escalation
stem: A 29-year-old G3P2 at 28 weeks gestation is reviewed at antenatal clinic. She has fatigue and breathlessness on stairs. She has been taking oral ferrous sulfate 325 mg daily for 6 weeks since her booking bloods showed mild iron deficiency anaemia, but reports persistent nausea and constipation and admits she has missed doses. Her current bloods reveal further drop in haemoglobin and ferritin. She has no history of bleeding or malabsorption and is up to date with antenatal care.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 92, BP 110/68, SpO2 98% room air, Temp 36.6
data_table.Examination: Mild conjunctival pallor; symphysis-fundal height appropriate; fetal heart 142
data_table.Investigations: Hb 92 g/L, MCV 76 fL, ferritin 12 micrograms/L, CRP 3 mg/L; B12 and folate normal

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Switch to oral ferrous fumarate 200 mg three times daily and review the haemoglobin in 4 weeks for response
Arrange intravenous ferric carboxymaltose 1000 mg as a single outpatient infusion and continue antenatal care
Transfuse 2 units of red cells now given haemoglobin under 95 g/L and approaching delivery within 12 weeks
Request bone marrow biopsy through haematology to exclude underlying haemoglobinopathy and aplastic process
Recommend cessation of all iron supplementation and dietary intervention with red meat and vitamin C combinations

subtopic_detail: Gestational diabetes 75g OGTT diagnostic thresholds
stem: A 33-year-old G2P1 attends for her routine gestational diabetes screen at 26 weeks gestation. Her previous baby was 4.3 kg at 39 weeks with shoulder dystocia. Her BMI is 31. She has no family history of diabetes but was unable to attend earlier screening due to severe nausea. She underwent a fasting 75 gram oral glucose tolerance test today after an overnight fast. She is asymptomatic and has otherwise had an uncomplicated antenatal course.

data_table.Examination: Symphysis-fundal height 27 cm; fetal heart 148; appropriate growth on USS at 22 weeks
data_table.Investigations: 75g OGTT: fasting 5.3 mmol/L, 1 hour 9.8 mmol/L, 2 hour 7.6 mmol/L

lead_in: What does this OGTT result indicate?

options.text: Normal OGTT with no further glucose testing required and routine antenatal care continued to term
Gestational diabetes confirmed because the fasting and 2 hour values both meet ADIPS diagnostic thresholds
Gestational diabetes diagnosed on the basis of the elevated fasting glucose result alone meeting threshold
Impaired glucose tolerance only with planned repeat 75g OGTT performed at 34 weeks gestation for confirmation
Overt diabetes in pregnancy requiring immediate referral for insulin therapy and high-risk diabetes pregnancy clinic

subtopic_detail: Monitoring a woman receiving a magnesium sulfate infusion for seizure prophylaxis
stem: A 29-year-old woman at 34 weeks with severe pre-eclampsia started an intravenous magnesium sulfate infusion two hours ago. Her blood pressure is now controlled and she is comfortable in the birth suite.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 142/88, pulse 88, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 98% room air
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 68 micromol/L; urine output 45 mL in the past hour

lead_in: What is the most appropriate monitoring while the infusion continues?

options.text: Hourly patellar reflexes, respiratory rate and urine output
Six-hourly serum magnesium levels with hourly blood pressure
Continuous cardiotocography with four-hourly maternal observations
Hourly serum magnesium levels until the infusion is ceased
Twelve-hourly platelet count with four-hourly respiratory rate

subtopic_detail: Active management of third stage and PPH prevention
stem: A 31-year-old G2P1 has just delivered a 3.8 kg baby vaginally at 39+5 weeks gestation in the birth suite after a 7 hour uncomplicated labour. The baby is on her chest and well. Her antenatal course was unremarkable, with no known coagulopathy and a baseline haemoglobin of 124 g/L. She has had one previous uncomplicated vaginal birth. She has no contraindications to oxytocic agents and no allergies. The placenta has not yet been delivered and there is minimal bleeding so far.

data_table.Examination: Uterus contracting; minimal blood loss approximately 100 mL so far; placenta undelivered
data_table.Investigations: Hb 124 g/L (booking); coagulation screen normal; group and screen on file

lead_in: What is the most appropriate intervention for the third stage?

options.text: Wait for spontaneous placental delivery without uterotonic and clamp the cord after the placenta has emerged fully
Intramuscular ergometrine 250 micrograms given alone with subsequent controlled cord traction once contracting
Intramuscular oxytocin 10 units within one minute of birth followed by controlled cord traction once the uterus contracts
Intravenous carboprost tromethamine 250 micrograms as routine prophylaxis with delayed cord clamping for 60 seconds
Sublingual misoprostol 600 micrograms alone with immediate cord clamping and assisted delivery of the placenta

subtopic_detail: Twin chorionicity dating-scan timing
stem: A 32-year-old G1 woman is found to have a twin pregnancy at her first booking visit, where her transvaginal ultrasound today demonstrates two live fetuses at 9+0 weeks gestation. She is otherwise well, IVF-conceived after a fresh single embryo transfer, and asks about her care plan. There are no fetal anomalies seen so far. She has no other medical conditions and is on standard antenatal vitamins. She is keen to optimise outcomes for her twins.

data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender abdomen consistent with early pregnancy
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal USS today: two viable intrauterine sacs at 9+0 weeks, single embryo transferred; chorionicity not yet documented

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in confirming chorionicity?

options.text: Schedule a repeat dating ultrasound between 11 and 13+6 weeks gestation to identify the lambda or T sign reliably
Send urgent chorionic villus sampling to determine zygosity and chorionicity together by genetic analysis today
Defer chorionicity assessment to the morphology scan at 19 to 20 weeks gestation when fetal anatomy is reviewed
Assume dichorionic-diamniotic from the IVF single embryo transfer history and proceed with usual antenatal care
Determine chorionicity at the next ultrasound by counting placental masses alone without reference to inter-twin membrane

subtopic_detail: HELLP syndrome timing of delivery
stem: A 26-year-old G2P1 at 31+4 weeks gestation is admitted with right upper quadrant pain, malaise, and a blood pressure of 158/104. Today's bloods show worsening haemolysis, transaminitis, and falling platelets compared with yesterday. She has received one dose of betamethasone yesterday and her second dose is due in 12 hours. The fetus is appropriately grown and the CTG is reassuring. Magnesium sulfate has been started for seizure prophylaxis. The intensive care and neonatology teams are on standby.

data_table.Examination: Tender right upper quadrant; hyperreflexia; abdomen soft; fetal heart 142 reassuring
data_table.Investigations: Hb 96 g/L, platelets 68 x10^9/L (yesterday 102), ALT 220 U/L (yesterday 142), AST 232 U/L, LDH 720 U/L, haptoglobin low; Cr 92 micromol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate timing of delivery decision?

options.text: Plan delivery within 24 to 48 hours after completion of the corticosteroid course assuming continued stability
Defer delivery until 34 weeks given fetal wellbeing reassuring; treat with high-dose corticosteroid pulses for HELLP
Deliver by category 2 caesarean section now without waiting for the second corticosteroid dose to be administered
Commence prostaglandin induction of labour and aim for vaginal birth over the next 12 to 24 hours of admission
Transfuse platelets prophylactically to a target of 100 x10^9/L and continue conservative inpatient management

subtopic_detail: PROM at term latency management
stem: A 28-year-old G1 woman at 38+5 weeks gestation presents to the birth suite reporting a clear gush of fluid 14 hours ago, with continued damp pads since. She is not contracting. Her group B streptococcus swab is negative and her antenatal course has been uncomplicated. The fetus is cephalic, the CTG is reassuring, and there are no signs of infection. She has been listening to her body and wonders if she should keep waiting or be induced. She has no contraindications to induction.

data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender uterus; cephalic; pool of clear fluid in posterior fornix on speculum; no obvious meconium; fetal heart 140 reassuring
data_table.Investigations: GBS swab at 36 weeks negative; FBC unremarkable; CTG reassuring

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Expectant management with no specific time frame and reassessment only if maternal observations deteriorate further
Immediate category 2 caesarean section because of duration of ruptured membranes exceeding the 12-hour threshold
Discharge home to await spontaneous labour with planned return in 72 hours regardless of new symptoms or labour status
Offer induction now with oxytocin titration; continue maternal and fetal monitoring, and antibiotics if not in labour by 24 hours
Vaginal misoprostol 50 micrograms every 4 hours up to 6 doses for cervical priming despite reassuring fetal status

subtopic_detail: Endometriosis stepwise treatment after first-line failure
stem: A 28-year-old woman presents to a gynaecology clinic with 4 years of progressive dysmenorrhoea, deep dyspareunia, and chronic non-cyclical pelvic pain. She has tried 9 months of combined oral contraceptive pill continuous regimen with partial relief, and 6 months of NSAIDs around her period, with continued symptoms restricting work. A recent specialised pelvic ultrasound demonstrates a 3 cm right ovarian endometrioma and posterior compartment deep infiltrating endometriosis. She wishes to maintain fertility options for future pregnancy and is uncertain about surgery. The MDT has reviewed her case.

data_table.Examination: Tender posterior fornix; right adnexal tenderness; nodularity at uterosacral palpation
data_table.Investigations: TVUS: 3 cm right endometrioma, kissing ovaries pattern, posterior DIE; AMH 19 pmol/L; pregnancy test negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next management step?

options.text: Switch to depot medroxyprogesterone acetate 150 mg intramuscular every 12 weeks as long-term suppression
Begin tamoxifen 20 mg daily as an alternative endocrine modulator targeting endometriotic implants and pain reduction
Refer to assisted reproduction for in vitro fertilisation now without further suppression or symptom-directed therapy
Proceed to laparoscopic excision of endometriosis and ovarian cystectomy after detailed informed consent and fertility counselling
Commence a 6-month GnRH agonist trial with bone-protective add-back tibolone and reassess pain on completion

subtopic_detail: Ectopic pregnancy diagnostic threshold hCG and transvaginal ultrasound
stem: A 28-year-old G2P0 with one previous tubal ectopic 18 months ago, treated medically with methotrexate, presents to the early pregnancy assessment unit at 6 weeks 4 days by LMP with 2 days of left iliac fossa pain and minimal dark vaginal bleeding. She is haemodynamically stable. Quantitative serum beta-hCG today is 2840 IU/L. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an empty uterus with a thin endometrium, no gestational sac, no pseudosac, and a 14 mm complex adnexal mass adjacent to the left ovary with a small amount of free fluid in the pouch of Douglas. Both ovaries are visualised separately.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft with left iliac fossa tenderness, no rebound, cervical motion tenderness on bimanual, no adnexal mass clinically
data_table.Investigations: Serum beta-hCG 2840 IU/L; Hb 124 g/L; group A positive. TVUS: empty uterus, left adnexal complex mass 14 mm separate from ovary, small free fluid

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Discharge with safety-netting and review in 7 days to repeat serum beta-hCG and transvaginal ultrasound assessment
Schedule diagnostic laparoscopy in the next available elective list within two weeks for definitive visualisation
Repeat serum beta-hCG in 48 hours and re-image only if values rise less than expected before considering intervention
Single-dose intramuscular methotrexate 50 mg per square metre immediately without further imaging or assessment of suitability
Diagnose ectopic pregnancy and admit for treatment selection based on size, hCG level, symptoms, and patient preference

subtopic_detail: Vaginal discharge differential and bacterial vaginosis treatment
stem: A 27-year-old woman presents to general practice with a 1-week history of malodorous greyish vaginal discharge worse after intercourse. She denies vulval itch, dysuria, or pelvic pain. She has a regular male partner of 18 months, uses combined oral contraception, and is up to date with cervical screening (HPV negative 6 months ago). Speculum examination shows thin homogenous grey discharge coating the vaginal walls and a normal-appearing cervix. Vaginal pH on litmus is 5.2. The whiff test with 10 percent potassium hydroxide produces a strong fishy odour.

data_table.Examination: Vulva normal, vagina with thin grey homogenous discharge coating walls, no erythema, cervix normal, bimanual non-tender, no adnexal masses
data_table.Investigations: Vaginal pH 5.2; whiff test positive; saline microscopy shows clue cells with absence of lactobacilli

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

options.text: Oral metronidazole 2 g as a single dose for both the patient and her regular male partner taken simultaneously
Empirical oral azithromycin 1 g single dose plus ceftriaxone 500 mg intramuscularly for presumed chlamydia and gonorrhoea
Reassurance that the symptoms reflect physiological discharge variation with watchful waiting for 6 weeks before any treatment
Oral metronidazole 400 mg twice daily for 7 days with abstinence from alcohol during and 24 hours after treatment
Oral fluconazole 150 mg as a single dose with planned telephone review in two weeks for confirmation of symptom resolution

subtopic_detail: Umbilical cord prolapse acute management
stem: A 31-year-old G3P2 at 38 weeks 4 days with a transverse-lying second twin (cephalic first twin delivered uneventfully 12 minutes ago) is being prepared for vaginal delivery of the second twin in the birth suite. Her membranes have just ruptured spontaneously with a large gush of clear fluid. The midwife calls you urgently because the cardiotocograph shows a sudden prolonged deceleration to 70 bpm with no recovery for 90 seconds, and she has palpated a pulsating loop of umbilical cord protruding from the introitus. The woman is in lithotomy position with an epidural in situ. Theatre is two floors away.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal HR 92, BP 122/76, SpO2 99%; fetal HR 70 bpm prolonged deceleration
data_table.Examination: Visible pulsating cord at introitus, presenting part high and transverse, cervix fully dilated, epidural functioning
data_table.Investigations: Earlier USS at admission: twin 2 transverse, EFW 2.9 kg, posterior placenta, normal AFI

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Knee-chest position with manual elevation of the presenting part and transfer to theatre for category-1 caesarean section
Internal podalic version and breech extraction of the second twin by the most senior accoucheur available in the room
Resume continuous fetal monitoring while encouraging maternal pushing for two more contractions before reassessing presentation
Replace the cord into the vagina and apply warm saline-soaked gauze while awaiting senior obstetric review in the next 15 minutes
Administer subcutaneous terbutaline 250 micrograms and bladder filling with 500 mL warm saline while planning vaginal delivery

subtopic_detail: Severe ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome inpatient management
stem: A 32-year-old woman presents to the emergency department 7 days after transvaginal oocyte retrieval for IVF (her first cycle for unexplained infertility). She has 4 days of progressive abdominal distension, nausea, vomiting, reduced urine output, and shortness of breath when lying flat. She has gained 4 kg since the day of retrieval. The retrieval recovered 28 oocytes and embryo transfer was deferred 'for medical reasons'. She has no chest pain or unilateral leg swelling. Her partner is in the room.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 112, BP 96/58, RR 22, SpO2 95% air, T 36.8, weight 74 kg (up from 70 kg)
data_table.Examination: Tense ascitic abdomen with shifting dullness, JVP not seen, reduced air entry both bases, no calf tenderness, urine output 18 mL/h on catheter
data_table.Investigations: Hb 168 g/L, Hct 0.50, WCC 18.4, platelets 412, sodium 132 mmol/L, potassium 4.2, urea 11.4, creatinine 124, albumin 26 g/L, LFT mildly raised, CXR small bilateral pleural effusions, USS bilaterally enlarged ovaries 11 cm with multiple cysts, large ascites
data_table.Medications: Triggered with hCG 5000 units 8 days ago; nil regular medications

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence intravenous furosemide 40 mg twice daily to remove ascitic fluid and relieve respiratory compromise more rapidly
Bilateral percutaneous ovarian aspiration in interventional radiology to decompress the enlarged ovaries and reduce VEGF release
Admit for intravenous crystalloid resuscitation, prophylactic enoxaparin 40 mg daily, and therapeutic paracentesis if tense ascites compromises breathing
Schedule urgent embryo transfer in the next 48 hours to avoid wasting the IVF cycle while supportive care continues
Discharge home with oral fluid restriction to 1 litre per day and outpatient telephone review at 48 hours by the fertility unit

subtopic_detail: Antenatal iron deficiency anaemia oral versus intravenous iron
stem: A 29-year-old G2P1 at 26 weeks gestation attends her routine antenatal visit. She is asymptomatic and feels fetal movements well. Her booking bloods showed Hb 112 g/L and ferritin 24 micrograms/L; she was started on oral ferrous sulfate 325 mg daily 8 weeks ago. Today's repeat shows Hb 105 g/L and ferritin 16 micrograms/L. She reports persistent nausea and constipation that she attributes to the oral iron and admits she takes the tablet only every second day to tolerate it. There is no obvious source of bleeding and she has had a normal cervical screen 12 months ago.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 84, BP 112/72, SpO2 99% air, T 36.6, weight 73 kg, BMI 27
data_table.Examination: No pallor, no koilonychia, fundal height appropriate, fetal heart 142 bpm, no peripheral oedema, no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Hb 105 g/L, MCV 78 fL, ferritin 16 micrograms/L, transferrin saturation 12 percent, CRP 4 mg/L, B12 and folate normal, normal renal and liver function
data_table.Medications: Ferrous sulfate 325 mg PO alternate days (per self), pregnancy multivitamin, folic acid 500 micrograms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange a single intravenous infusion of ferric carboxymaltose 1000 mg in the day procedure unit with 30 minutes post-infusion observation
Increase ferrous sulfate to 325 mg orally three times daily for 4 weeks then repeat full blood count and ferritin to assess response
Order a transfusion of 2 units of packed red cells in the day infusion centre with type and crossmatch performed beforehand
Subcutaneous erythropoietin 50 units per kilogram three times weekly for 4 weeks to stimulate erythropoiesis as iron stores recover
Switch to oral elemental iron 60 mg daily with vitamin C and a 6-week course of laxatives to address constipation while continuing dietary advice

subtopic_detail: Lactational mastitis with continued breastfeeding
stem: A 32-year-old woman 3 weeks postpartum after an uncomplicated term vaginal birth attends her GP with a 24-hour history of left breast pain, redness over the upper outer quadrant, fevers and flu-like myalgias. She is breastfeeding her baby on demand and has no nipple cracking, no abscess felt, and no overlying skin necrosis. The baby is feeding eagerly and weight gain has been good. She has no penicillin allergy.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 96, BP 118/72, RR 14, SpO2 99% air, T 38.6, weight 68 kg
data_table.Examination: Left upper outer quadrant tender wedge of erythema 6 cm, warm, no fluctuance, no nipple cracks, contralateral breast normal, no axillary adenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Not yet performed; baby feeding well

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence empirical intravenous vancomycin in the day infusion unit and arrange daily review until clinical improvement is documented
Continue regular breastfeeding from both breasts plus paracetamol and ibuprofen, and reassess in 24 hours without commencing any antibiotic therapy
Continue breastfeeding from the affected side with warm compresses and analgesia plus oral flucloxacillin 500 mg four times daily for 5 to 7 days
Refer same day for ultrasound and incision and drainage as a presumed mastitis-associated abscess in the day surgery list
Cease breastfeeding from the affected side temporarily and switch to formula feeding while taking oral flucloxacillin 500 mg four times daily for 5 days

subtopic_detail: Postpartum endometritis empirical broad-spectrum antibiotic choice
stem: A 34-year-old G3P3 is reviewed on the postnatal ward 4 days after a category-2 emergency caesarean section at 39 weeks for prolonged second stage and fetal distress. Membranes had been ruptured for 22 hours and she received intrapartum cefazolin. Since yesterday she has fever, lower abdominal pain, and offensive lochia with increased volume. Her lochia smells foul. She is breastfeeding without difficulty. She has no chest, urinary or wound signs. The caesarean wound looks clean and dry.
