data_table.Vital signs: HR 110, BP 108/68, RR 18, SpO2 98% air, T 38.8, weight 76 kg
data_table.Examination: Soft non-distended abdomen, tender uterus above the umbilicus with bulky fundus, offensive purulent lochia on speculum, no cervical motion tenderness suggestive of PID, wound clean
data_table.Investigations: WCC 16.4, CRP 138, normal Hb, urine dip clean, blood cultures sent, MSU sent. USS abdomen pending (retained products query)
data_table.Medications: Paracetamol 1 g QID; PRN ibuprofen; LMWH prophylaxis as per protocol

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Intravenous cefazolin 2 g eight-hourly for 5 days plus oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 14 days to cover anaerobes and atypicals
Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg twice daily for 7 days with outpatient follow-up phone call in 48 hours
Intravenous meropenem 1 g eight-hourly as monotherapy until afebrile then step down to oral cefalexin to complete a 14-day course
Intravenous ampicillin 2 g six-hourly plus gentamicin 5 mg/kg daily plus metronidazole 500 mg twelve-hourly until afebrile for 24 to 48 hours
Intravenous clindamycin 600 mg eight-hourly as monotherapy with daily review for clinical improvement before any de-escalation step

subtopic_detail: Primary genital herpes in pregnancy delivery mode and neonatal prevention
stem: A 27-year-old G1P0 at 37 weeks 4 days presents to the day assessment unit reporting 24 hours of painful vulval ulceration, dysuria, headache and malaise. She has no past history of genital herpes. Her current partner has cold sores but no known genital lesions. Examination shows multiple tender shallow ulcers on the labia minora with inguinal lymphadenopathy. PCR swabs are taken and confirm primary genital HSV-2 infection 24 hours later (she has been admitted overnight). Membranes are intact, cervix is closed, no contractions, fetal CTG reassuring.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal HR 92, BP 118/72, T 38.0, SpO2 99%; fetal HR 142 reactive
data_table.Examination: Multiple painful vulval ulcers, bilateral tender inguinal nodes, no cervical lesions, intact membranes, cervix closed
data_table.Investigations: HSV-2 PCR positive, HSV-1 PCR negative; HSV serology IgG negative day 1 (consistent with primary infection), pending convalescent titre
data_table.Medications: Paracetamol; topical lidocaine 5 percent gel; no other regular medication

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan for delivery?

options.text: Discharge home with reassurance, advise pelvic rest and review only if labour starts or membranes rupture as no specific intervention is indicated
Plan for elective vaginal birth at term with intrapartum intravenous aciclovir during labour and neonatal aciclovir prophylaxis for the baby after birth
Commence oral valaciclovir 500 mg twice daily and plan elective caesarean section before 39 weeks if she remains undelivered to minimise vertical transmission
Defer any antiviral therapy until the start of labour then administer aciclovir 800 mg orally five times daily for the duration of active labour only
Plan vaginal birth but avoid invasive fetal monitoring with a scalp electrode and instrumental delivery to minimise neonatal exposure to ulcerative lesions

subtopic_detail: Routine RhD-negative anti-D prophylaxis schedule
stem: A 26-year-old woman attends her first antenatal visit at 11 weeks in her first pregnancy. Her blood group is O RhD-negative with no atypical antibodies, and her partner is RhD-positive. She is well, with no bleeding or trauma so far in pregnancy. She asks how anti-D immunoglobulin will be given.

data_table.Examination: Uterus not palpable abdominally, no bleeding or bruising
data_table.Investigations: Blood group O RhD-negative, indirect Coombs negative, antibody screen negative
data_table.Medications: Pregnancy multivitamin with iodine and folic acid

lead_in: What is the most appropriate routine schedule for prophylactic anti-D immunoglobulin?

options.text: Routine intramuscular doses at 28 and 34 weeks gestation, plus a postnatal dose if the baby is RhD-positive
Defer all anti-D until after delivery and rely on universal postnatal cord blood typing to determine treatment in any future pregnancy
Withhold all routine antenatal prophylaxis and only treat postnatally if the baby is confirmed to be RhD-positive at delivery
Monthly intramuscular anti-D injections from 20 weeks gestation through to delivery to ensure ongoing antibody cover for the fetus
A single intramuscular dose at 28 weeks gestation only if maternal antibody screening remains negative at that visit

subtopic_detail: Combined hormonal contraception eligibility in migraine with aura
stem: A 24-year-old nulliparous woman attends for contraception. She has migraine with visual aura preceding her headaches about twice a month, controlled with rizatriptan. She is a non-smoker, normotensive, and has no other vascular risk factors. She would prefer a method that does not require daily pill-taking.

data_table.Examination: Unremarkable, no neurological deficits between attacks
data_table.Investigations: Nil indicated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate contraceptive recommendation?

options.text: Combined oral contraceptive pill containing 30 mcg ethinylestradiol and levonorgestrel
Combined oral pill but only on cycle days one through twenty-one each month
Levonorgestrel intrauterine system as a first-line long-acting reversible method
Combined contraceptive vaginal ring inserted three weeks of every four-week cycle
Combined transdermal patch applied weekly with one patch-free week each month

subtopic_detail: Emergency contraception choice within 120 hours of unprotected sex
stem: A 22-year-old woman presents 78 hours after a single episode of unprotected vaginal intercourse on day 14 of a regular 28-day cycle. She is not currently using any contraception and does not wish to be pregnant. She has no contraindications to copper or hormonal contraception and is happy with whichever option is most effective.

data_table.Examination: Unremarkable, no pelvic tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Urine beta-hCG negative

lead_in: What is the most effective emergency contraception option to offer?

options.text: Yuzpe regimen of high-dose combined oral contraceptive tablets in two divided doses
Levonorgestrel intrauterine system inserted today as both emergency and ongoing contraception
Copper intrauterine device inserted today and retained for ongoing contraception
Oral ulipristal acetate 30 mg taken now as a single dose with food in clinic today
Oral levonorgestrel 1.5 mg taken now as a single dose within the next hour

subtopic_detail: Recurrent miscarriage workup after three consecutive losses
stem: A 33-year-old woman presents for review after her third consecutive first-trimester miscarriage. Her three losses all occurred between 8 and 11 weeks gestation with no live births. She is otherwise well, with regular menstrual cycles and no medical history of note. She and her partner are non-consanguineous.

data_table.Examination: Normal general and pelvic examination
data_table.Investigations: Routine antenatal bloods normal in last pregnancy; not yet investigated for cause

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial investigation panel?

options.text: Antiphospholipid antibodies, parental karyotype, pelvic ultrasound and thyroid function
Day 21 progesterone with serial luteinising hormone tracking across two ovulatory cycles
Endometrial biopsy for chronic endometritis and infectious screen including TORCH panel
Routine factor V Leiden, prothrombin gene and MTHFR thrombophilia screen as initial workup
Repeat saline-infusion sonohysterography only after a fourth consecutive pregnancy loss occurs

subtopic_detail: Initial female subfertility investigation pathway
stem: A 30-year-old woman attends with her partner after 14 months of regular unprotected intercourse without conception. Her cycles are regular at 28 to 30 days with no intermenstrual bleeding or significant dysmenorrhoea. Her partner has fathered a child in a previous relationship 4 years ago and is well.

data_table.Examination: Normal abdominal and pelvic examination, no thyroid or hirsutism findings
data_table.Investigations: No fertility investigations performed yet

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line female investigation?

options.text: Mid-luteal day 21 progesterone level taken in a typical 28-day cycle to confirm ovulation
Postcoital cervical mucus test taken in clinic 6 to 12 hours after intercourse at midcycle
Anti-mullerian hormone level for ovarian reserve assessment as the initial fertility investigation
Diagnostic laparoscopy and dye to assess for pelvic adhesions and unsuspected endometriosis
Hysterosalpingo-contrast sonography of the uterine cavity and fallopian tubes as initial test

subtopic_detail: PCOS management in a woman not seeking pregnancy
stem: A 23-year-old woman presents with cycles every 45 to 80 days, facial and chin hirsutism, and 6 kg weight gain over 12 months. She is not currently sexually active and does not wish to conceive in the next several years. Pelvic ultrasound shows polycystic ovarian morphology bilaterally and biochemistry confirms hyperandrogenism with normal thyroid and prolactin.

data_table.Examination: Modified Ferriman-Gallwey score 12, no acanthosis nigricans, no virilisation
data_table.Investigations: Total testosterone 3.4 nmol/L (elevated), free androgen index elevated, TSH normal, prolactin normal, fasting glucose 5.4, HbA1c 5.6

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacological treatment?

options.text: Combined oral contraceptive pill alongside lifestyle and weight-management advice
Metformin 500 mg twice daily titrated up to 1500 mg as first-line monotherapy
Spironolactone 100 mg daily monotherapy without reliable contraception in place
Clomifene citrate for cycle regulation taken on cycle days two through six monthly
Cyclical progestogen withdrawal alone every 90 days to induce a regular monthly bleed

subtopic_detail: Australian cervical screening program HPV-based primary screening
stem: A 26-year-old woman attends for her first cervical screening test. She is sexually active with two lifetime partners and has had HPV vaccination as a teenager. She has never had any abnormal screening result and is in a stable relationship. She has no abnormal bleeding or discharge.

data_table.Examination: Normal pelvic and speculum examination, cervix appears healthy
data_table.Investigations: First cervical screening test today

lead_in: What is the most appropriate cervical screening test and follow-up interval?

options.text: HPV-based screening only after the next pregnancy or after age 30 years if no pregnancy occurs
HPV-based primary screening test, repeated every 5 years if oncogenic HPV is not detected
Conventional Pap cytology, repeated every 2 years if cytology shows no intraepithelial lesion
HPV-based primary screening test, repeated every 3 years irrespective of the result obtained
Colposcopy and biopsy at the first visit to baseline this woman with prior HPV exposure

subtopic_detail: Endometrial hyperplasia with atypia management
stem: A 56-year-old postmenopausal woman with a BMI of 34 presents with three episodes of vaginal bleeding over the past 4 months. Transvaginal ultrasound shows endometrial thickness of 14 mm with heterogeneous echotexture. Hysteroscopy and biopsy report endometrial hyperplasia with atypia. She has completed her family and has no comorbidities prohibiting surgery.

data_table.Examination: Atrophic vagina, small uterus, no palpable adnexal mass
data_table.Investigations: Endometrial thickness 14 mm; biopsy: complex hyperplasia with atypia

lead_in: What is the most appropriate definitive treatment?

options.text: Total hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy as the recommended treatment for this lesion
Oral medroxyprogesterone acetate 20 mg daily with surveillance biopsies every 6 months
Repeat endometrial biopsy in 3 months without intervening treatment to confirm persistence
Levonorgestrel intrauterine system in situ as long-term endometrial suppressive therapy
Endometrial ablation under hysteroscopic vision with annual follow-up biopsy thereafter

subtopic_detail: Symptomatic uterine fibroid first-line medical therapy
stem: A 38-year-old G2P2 woman with heavy menstrual bleeding, cycle length 28 days, and ferritin 12 mcg/L attends for management. Pelvic ultrasound shows three intramural fibroids each under 4 cm with normal cavity contour and a uterus equivalent to 10-week size. She has completed her family but does not wish to undergo a major surgical procedure. She has no contraindications to hormonal therapy.

data_table.Examination: Bulky uterus equivalent to 10 weeks; no adnexal mass
data_table.Investigations: Hb 102 g/L, ferritin 12 mcg/L, fibroid total volume small, cavity normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line medical management?

options.text: Uterine artery embolisation performed by interventional radiology as the first-line uterus-conserving option
Combined oral contraceptive pill in extended-cycle regimen with quarterly hormone-free intervals
Hysterectomy as the definitive curative procedure for symptomatic intramural fibroids in this case
Levonorgestrel intrauterine system after exclusion of intracavitary distortion of the cavity
Gonadotrophin-releasing hormone agonist depot for 6 months alongside menopausal-symptom add-back therapy

subtopic_detail: Hyperemesis gravidarum admission and inpatient management
stem: A 28-year-old G1P0 woman at 9 weeks gestation presents to the emergency department with 5 days of relentless vomiting more than 10 times per day. She has lost 5 percent of her pre-pregnancy weight and cannot tolerate oral fluids. Urinalysis shows 3+ ketones. Her PUQE-24 score is 14. She is dizzy on standing and has not slept overnight due to vomiting.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 96/58 supine to 84/52 standing, HR 108, T 36.6
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes, sunken eyes, reduced skin turgor, no abdominal tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Urine ketones 3+, Na 134, K 3.2, urea 6.8, creatinine 88, TSH 0.4, beta-hCG 56000
data_table.Medications: Pyridoxine and doxylamine tried at home with no benefit

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial inpatient management bundle?

options.text: Discharge with oral pyridoxine-doxylamine titration and outpatient ketone monitoring by GP daily
Admit with IV thiamine, IV normal saline with potassium, and ondansetron orally dispersible or intravenous
Admit and commence IV 5 percent dextrose first to correct presumed hypoglycaemia before any other agent
Admit with IV corticosteroid pulse (methylprednisolone) as the first-line antiemetic for refractory cases
Admit with oral metoclopramide as the initial antiemetic and oral hydration trial over six hours

subtopic_detail: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy delivery timing by bile acid
stem: A 31-year-old G2P1 woman at 35+0 weeks reports relentless palmar and plantar itching, worse at night, for the past 10 days with no rash. Her previous pregnancy was uncomplicated. CTG today is reactive and growth scan a week ago showed normal interval growth and Doppler. She is otherwise well with no jaundice.

data_table.Examination: Excoriations on palms and soles, no jaundice, soft abdomen, normal fundal height
data_table.Investigations: Total bile acids 108 micromol/L, ALT 96 U/L, bilirubin 14 micromol/L, normal viral hepatitis screen

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan for delivery timing?

options.text: Continue ursodeoxycholic acid and plan elective caesarean section at 39 weeks gestation
Await spontaneous labour with twice-weekly CTG and growth scans every two weeks
Discharge home for outpatient weekly bile-acid trend with admission only if levels exceed 200
Plan induction of labour at 36 weeks given bile acids over 100 micromol/L threshold
Increase ursodeoxycholic acid to maximum dose and reassess bile acids in 7 days' time

subtopic_detail: Significant varicella exposure in non-immune pregnant woman
stem: A 28-year-old woman at 27 weeks gestation in her first pregnancy presents 36 hours after caring for her 4-year-old nephew who developed a vesicular varicella rash during the visit. She has no prior history of chickenpox or vaccination and is uncertain whether she had the disease as a child. She has no rash herself and is feeling well. She has no chronic medical conditions.

data_table.Examination: No rash on skin or mucosa; no respiratory symptoms; uterus appropriate for gestation
data_table.Investigations: Varicella zoster IgG sent today; result pending. No PCR samples available yet

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Commence prophylactic oral aciclovir today and continue to 14 days post-exposure
Reassure as antenatal varicella exposure rarely affects the fetus and require no specific action
Give live attenuated varicella vaccine today to provide rapid post-exposure protection
Admit and commence intravenous aciclovir empirically until IgG confirms her immune status
Await urgent varicella IgG result, then give VZIG within 96 hours if IgG is negative

subtopic_detail: Postnatal hypertension antihypertensive choice in breastfeeding mother
stem: A 32-year-old woman who developed pre-eclampsia at 36 weeks delivered 6 days ago after a successful induction. She has been on oral labetalol 200 mg three times daily but reports persistent fatigue and slow heart rate. Today her clinic BP is 152/98 with no proteinuria, headache, or visual disturbance. She is exclusively breastfeeding her newborn.

data_table.Examination: Brisk reflexes, no clonus, no peripheral oedema, lochia normal
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 198, LFT normal, creatinine 78, urine PCR 18
data_table.Medications: Labetalol 200 mg PO three times daily, paracetamol PRN

lead_in: What is the most appropriate antihypertensive change?

options.text: Switch to oral methyldopa 250 mg three times daily to safely cover the breastfeeding period
Switch to oral atenolol 25 mg daily for ease of dosing and convenience for the patient
Continue current labetalol dose unchanged and recheck blood pressure in 1 week clinic
Switch labetalol to enalapril 5 mg daily titrated to blood pressure target
Add nifedipine modified-release 30 mg daily to current labetalol as combination therapy

subtopic_detail: Maternal pulmonary hypertension preconception counselling
stem: A 29-year-old woman with idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension on macitentan and tadalafil attends preconception clinic to discuss starting a family with her partner. Her NYHA functional class is II and right heart catheter at the last review showed mean PAP 38 mmHg with preserved RV function. She is currently using condoms only and asks about pregnancy.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 108/68, HR 84, SpO2 96 percent on room air, BMI 25
data_table.Examination: RV heave, loud P2, no peripheral oedema, NYHA II
data_table.Investigations: Echo PASP 60 mmHg, RV function preserved, six minute walk 380 m
data_table.Medications: Macitentan 10 mg daily, tadalafil 40 mg daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate counselling and management plan?

options.text: Counsel that pregnancy is contraindicated and offer effective contraception with a long-acting method
Recommend assisted reproduction with donor egg and surrogacy as her preferred path to parenthood
Counsel that pregnancy is acceptable provided delivery is planned by elective caesarean section
Plan pregnancy with cessation of pulmonary vasodilators and serial echocardiography monitoring
Plan pregnancy and continue current PAH therapy unchanged through the entire pregnancy course

subtopic_detail: Obstetric anal sphincter injury repair and antibiotic prophylaxis
stem: A 25-year-old primigravida has just delivered a 3850 g infant after a 14-minute second stage. On systematic perineal examination by the registrar, you identify a tear extending through the perineal body, the external anal sphincter (more than 50 percent of its thickness) and into the internal anal sphincter, with intact rectal mucosa. Bleeding is controlled with pressure. She is comfortable with her epidural still functioning.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/72, HR 86, T 37.0, blood loss 350 mL
data_table.Examination: 3c tear by Sultan classification; rectal mucosa intact; sphincter ends retracted
data_table.Investigations: Hb 110 g/L on FBC done after delivery

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Pack the wound with gauze and arrange repair in the morning by the rostered consultant
Apply absorbable sutures to skin only and arrange outpatient anorectal physiotherapy review
Transfer to theatre for repair under regional anaesthesia with IV antibiotic cover
Repair on the labour bed under top-up epidural with absorbable monofilament suture
Refer for primary defunctioning colostomy as the safest initial surgical management option

subtopic_detail: Twin-twin transfusion syndrome diagnosis and referral
stem: A 30-year-old G1P0 with a monochorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy at 19 weeks is reviewed in maternal-fetal medicine. Her surveillance scan shows twin 1 with deepest vertical pocket 1 cm and twin 2 with deepest vertical pocket 9 cm; bladders of both fetuses are visible and Doppler studies are normal. Both fetuses are appropriately grown. The couple ask about management options.

data_table.Examination: Fundal height 22 cm
data_table.Investigations: MCDA twins; DVP twin 1 = 1 cm; DVP twin 2 = 9 cm; both bladders seen; normal Dopplers

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Expectant management with twice-weekly ultrasound surveillance and Doppler until delivery
Administer maternal indometacin to reduce polyhydramnios in the recipient sac as a temporising measure
Urgent referral to a fetal therapy centre for fetoscopic laser ablation as first-line treatment
Schedule serial amnioreduction of the polyhydramniotic sac every two weeks until 26 weeks gestation
Selective fetal reduction of the donor twin by intracardiac potassium chloride injection now

subtopic_detail: Cervical insufficiency with funnelling in second trimester
stem: A 31-year-old G3P0 woman at 19 weeks gestation presents with painless pelvic pressure for 24 hours. Her two previous pregnancies ended at 22 and 23 weeks with painless cervical dilatation. Today transvaginal ultrasound shows a closed external os with cervical length 8 mm and funnelling halfway down the canal. Membranes are intact. There is no bleeding or signs of chorioamnionitis.

data_table.Examination: Soft uterus, no tenderness, no bleeding, closed external os on speculum
data_table.Investigations: TVUS: CL 8 mm, T-shape funnelling; FBC normal; CRP 5; high vaginal swab pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence weekly intramuscular 17-hydroxyprogesterone caproate alone without cervical intervention
Discharge home with antibiotics and review with repeat transvaginal scan in two weeks' time
Insert pessary today as the primary intervention to support the cervix mechanically until viability
Strict bed rest until 24 weeks gestation with weekly cervical length surveillance ultrasounds
Insert McDonald cerclage today after multidisciplinary counselling and exclusion of infection

subtopic_detail: Refractory atonic postpartum haemorrhage second-line uterotonic
stem: A 28-year-old G2P2 woman has delivered a 3.9 kg boy vaginally 25 minutes ago after an oxytocin-augmented labour. Estimated blood loss is now 1500 mL with ongoing brisk bleeding from an atonic uterus that softens between bimanual compression. She has received oxytocin 10 IU IM, then 40 IU in 1000 mL crystalloid infusion, IV ergometrine 250 mcg and tranexamic acid 1 g. Her BP is falling and uterus remains soft. She has no history of asthma or significant hypertension.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 88/52, HR 124, T 36.6, SpO2 98 percent on 6 L oxygen via mask
data_table.Examination: Uterus soft on bimanual compression, no genital tract lacerations on inspection
data_table.Investigations: Hb 78 g/L on point-of-care; 4 units RBC + FFP ordered
data_table.Medications: Already received oxytocin, ergometrine and tranexamic acid

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next uterotonic step?

options.text: Insert intrauterine balloon tamponade as the next step without further pharmacological therapy
Repeat intravenous ergometrine 250 mcg now, then reassess uterine tone in five minutes
Sublingual misoprostol 800 mcg as the priority next-line uterotonic over other agents
Intramuscular carboprost 250 mcg every 15 minutes up to a maximum of 8 doses total
Repeat intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g now while waiting for blood products to arrive

subtopic_detail: Complete hydatidiform mole - diagnosis and surveillance
stem: A 30-year-old G2P1 woman presents at an estimated 10 weeks gestation with vaginal bleeding for three days and severe nausea and vomiting that has limited oral intake to sips. She has no abdominal pain. Speculum examination shows the cervical os closed with a small amount of dark blood. The uterus is palpable to the umbilicus and feels boggy. She had a normal first pregnancy and delivery two years ago and her booking bloods are otherwise unremarkable.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.6, HR 104, BP 138/86, RR 18, SpO2 98 percent room air
data_table.Examination: Uterus palpable to umbilicus, boggy, non-tender. No adnexal mass on bimanual
data_table.Investigations: Quantitative beta-hCG 460000 IU/L, TSH 0.04 mIU/L, free T4 28 pmol/L, FBC and UEC unremarkable, transvaginal ultrasound shows snowstorm appearance with multiple cystic spaces and no fetal parts, bilateral theca lutein cysts

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Misoprostol vaginally to achieve medical evacuation of the molar tissue followed by structured surveillance beta-hCG weekly for 6 weeks of follow up
Repeat transvaginal ultrasound and beta-hCG in 2 weeks before any planned intervention to confirm the diagnosis with serial assessment of clinical status
Hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy to remove the theca lutein cysts and definitively prevent malignancy in a young woman who has completed her family
Suction curettage under anaesthesia with histopathology and post-evacuation serial weekly serum beta-hCG until three undetectable values then monthly for 6 months
Single-agent intramuscular methotrexate 50 mg per square metre as primary chemotherapy and avoid all surgical evacuation in a haemodynamically stable patient today

subtopic_detail: Twin pregnancy - chorionicity determination
stem: A 27-year-old G1 woman attends for her 12-week dating scan after a spontaneous conception. She is excited to learn she has a twin pregnancy. She is otherwise well with no significant medical history and has been taking pre-pregnancy folic acid. The sonographer notes two distinct fetal poles each with normal early structures and clear cardiac activity. She asks how the type of twins will affect her care plan.

data_table.Examination: Uterus palpable just above pubic symphysis
data_table.Investigations: Crown-rump length consistent with 12+1 weeks both twins. Single placental mass, T-sign at membrane-placental junction, thin intertwin membrane
data_table.Medications: Pregnancy multivitamin with iodine and folic acid

lead_in: Which feature on this scan most reliably establishes chorionicity?

options.text: Crown-rump length concordance between the two fetuses regardless of placental morphology or membrane appearance
Number of yolk sacs visible on first trimester ultrasound is the gold standard for chorionicity assignment after 12 weeks
Two separate placental discs on second trimester anatomy scan confirm dichorionic pregnancy more reliably than first trimester signs
Fetal sex discordance on cell-free fetal DNA testing is the only reliable non-ultrasound method for chorionicity determination
T-sign at the membrane-placental junction with a thin intertwin membrane indicates monochorionic-diamniotic pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Maternal priorities immediately after a shoulder dystocia is relieved
stem: A baby is born after an impacted anterior shoulder was freed by an internal rotational manoeuvre. The baby is vigorous and with the mother, and oxytocin has been given for the third stage.

data_table.Birth: Birth weight 4.4 kg, head to body interval four minutes
data_table.Mother: Pulse 104 /min, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, placenta not yet delivered

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step for the mother?

options.text: Examine the perineum and anus, and watch closely for heavy bleeding
Move her to theatre for examination under regional anaesthesia straight away
Arrange a pelvic x-ray to exclude separation of the pubic symphysis
Give tranexamic acid and cross match four units of red cells now
Repair any tear only after a bladder scan in six hours from now

subtopic_detail: Severe pre-eclampsia - magnesium sulfate prophylaxis
stem: A 28-year-old G1 woman is admitted at 36+0 weeks gestation with a 3-day history of frontal headache, intermittent visual scotomata and worsening epigastric pain. Her booking blood pressure was normal. She has no significant past medical history. She is not yet in labour. The obstetric registrar has reviewed her and decided to induce labour after stabilisation.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 168/112 confirmed on repeat, HR 96, T 36.8, SpO2 99 percent
data_table.Examination: Brisk reflexes with clonus 3 beats bilaterally, mild peripheral oedema, gravid uterus, no abdominal tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Urine ACR 60 mg/mmol, platelets 142, ALT 92, creatinine 88, uric acid 0.42, CTG reassuring

lead_in: Which intervention is most appropriate to add now for maternal safety?

options.text: Intravenous hydralazine 5 mg bolus repeated every 20 minutes to a maximum of three doses with continuous fetal monitoring throughout administration
Oral nifedipine immediate release 20 mg as a stat dose and continued routine antenatal monitoring on the ward with 4-hourly observations
Intramuscular betamethasone 11.4 mg as fetal lung maturation steroid at 36 weeks gestation prior to planned induction of labour
Furosemide 20 mg intravenously to address peripheral oedema and reduce preload while titrating antihypertensive therapy in this hypertensive emergency
Magnesium sulfate 4 g intravenous loading dose over 20 minutes followed by 1 g per hour infusion for at least 24 hours with deep tendon reflex monitoring

subtopic_detail: Polyhydramnios at 32 weeks - workup
stem: A 33-year-old G2P1 woman attends for a growth scan at 32+1 weeks gestation arranged because her fundal height is measuring 38 cm. The pregnancy has otherwise been uncomplicated. Her previous pregnancy was a normal vaginal delivery at term. Her oral glucose tolerance test at 28 weeks was normal. She denies reduced fetal movements and has no abdominal pain or contractions. Booking serology was unremarkable.

data_table.Examination: Fundal height 38 cm (expected 32 cm), longitudinal lie, cephalic presentation, soft uterus, no tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Amniotic fluid index 32 cm (above 95th centile), estimated fetal weight 50th centile, normal fetal anatomy, normal Doppler, normal placenta, normal cervical length

lead_in: Which investigation is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure and rescan in 4 weeks with no further investigation, since the OGTT at 28 weeks was normal and the baby is structurally normal on ultrasound today
Repeat oral glucose tolerance test now and arrange detailed fetal anatomy review including the stomach bubble, swallowing assessment and cardiac views
Therapeutic amnioreduction at 32 weeks to relieve uterine distension and reduce risk of preterm labour, with cytogenetic karyotype of the amniotic fluid sample obtained
Commence oral indometacin 100 mg per day to reduce fetal urine output and decrease amniotic fluid volume while awaiting further investigations to be arranged
Admit for continuous CTG monitoring and induce labour at 32 weeks to avoid further complications related to ongoing polyhydramnios in late preterm pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Postpartum VTE prophylaxis - risk stratification
stem: A 36-year-old G3P3 woman is reviewed on the postnatal ward 12 hours after an emergency caesarean section for failure to progress at 9 cm dilatation. She had a long induction of labour. Her BMI is 34 and her age is 36. She has no personal or family history of venous thromboembolism. The baby was 4.0 kg with normal Apgar scores and is now feeding well. She is mobilising slowly with patient-controlled analgesia.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.0, HR 92, BP 122/76, SpO2 98 percent room air
data_table.Examination: Caesarean wound dry and intact, fundus firm 1 cm below umbilicus, calves soft non-tender, no oedema disproportionate
data_table.Investigations: Hb 102 (was 118 antenatal), platelets 220, creatinine 64, fibrinogen 4.2
data_table.Medications: Paracetamol, ibuprofen, oxycodone PCA, oxytocin completed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate VTE prophylaxis plan?

options.text: Mechanical prophylaxis only with graduated compression stockings, since pharmacological prophylaxis is contraindicated within 24 hours of obstetric surgery
Subcutaneous enoxaparin 40 mg daily for 10 days postpartum together with graduated compression stockings and a structured early mobilisation plan
Subcutaneous enoxaparin 40 mg daily continued for 6 weeks postpartum to cover the entire puerperal hypercoagulable period regardless of additional risk factors
Oral rivaroxaban 10 mg daily for 10 days as a more convenient alternative to subcutaneous low molecular weight heparin in the postpartum period after discharge
No pharmacological prophylaxis indicated in an otherwise well postpartum woman with no personal history of VTE, since BMI and operative birth alone do not justify treatment

subtopic_detail: HRT initiation - regimen choice in perimenopausal woman
stem: A 49-year-old woman presents to her general practice with 8 months of frequent hot flushes, drenching night sweats and irregular periods with cycles ranging from 21 to 45 days. Her last period was 6 weeks ago. She has had no abnormal bleeding between periods. Her BMI is 26, she does not smoke, blood pressure is 122/76 and she has no personal or family history of breast cancer or venous thromboembolism. She has an intact uterus and prefers reliable contraception alongside symptom relief.

data_table.Examination: No abdominal mass, no breast lump, vaginal examination unremarkable, cervical screening up to date
data_table.Investigations: FSH 18 IU/L, estradiol 200 pmol/L, TSH 1.8, fasting glucose 4.8, lipids favourable

lead_in: What is the most appropriate menopausal hormone therapy regimen?

options.text: Continuous combined oral estradiol 1 mg with medroxyprogesterone 5 mg daily started today with the simplest single daily tablet regimen for compliance benefit
Estradiol only patch 50 micrograms twice weekly with no progestogen, since the patient still has endogenous progesterone production from her own ovaries during cycles
Transdermal estradiol patch 50 micrograms twice weekly plus levonorgestrel intrauterine device for endometrial protection and effective contraception together
Combined oral contraceptive pill containing ethinylestradiol 30 micrograms plus levonorgestrel 150 micrograms with continuation past 50 years if symptoms persist
Sequential conjugated equine oestrogen 0.625 mg with norethisterone 1 mg for 12 days each month plus condoms for contraception, avoiding any hormonal contraceptive option

subtopic_detail: Asherman syndrome - investigation of secondary amenorrhoea
stem: A 32-year-old G2P1 woman attends the gynaecology clinic with 8 months of secondary amenorrhoea following a uterine evacuation for retained products of conception 10 months ago after a missed miscarriage at 11 weeks. She has not been using contraception. She had previously regular cycles. She denies hot flushes, weight changes, headaches, galactorrhoea or hirsutism. She is keen for another pregnancy. Her general health is otherwise unremarkable.

data_table.Examination: No goitre, no galactorrhoea, no hirsutism, normal external genitalia, bimanual unremarkable, no acanthosis
data_table.Investigations: Beta-hCG negative, FSH 6 IU/L, LH 5 IU/L, estradiol 280 pmol/L, prolactin 280 mIU/L, TSH 1.6, AMH 12 pmol/L

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: MRI pituitary to exclude a microadenoma as the underlying cause of her secondary amenorrhoea despite a normal serum prolactin level on screening tests done today
Day 21 progesterone level to confirm ovulatory cycles after which she should be referred for tubal patency testing if amenorrhoea persists beyond 3 further months
Empirical 12-week course of cyclical oral oestrogen 2 mg with sequential progestogen with reassessment after 3 months for resumption of menses before further investigation
Saline infusion sonohysterography or hysteroscopy as the investigation of choice for suspected intrauterine adhesions following uterine instrumentation in pregnancy loss
Diagnostic laparoscopy with chromopertubation to assess for adhesion formation involving the fallopian tubes and ovaries following the previous miscarriage event 10 months ago

subtopic_detail: Vulval lichen sclerosus - diagnosis and treatment
stem: A 58-year-old postmenopausal woman presents with 12 months of progressive vulval itch, soreness and recurrent splitting at the introitus during intercourse. She has been using over-the-counter clotrimazole intermittently without lasting benefit. Examination reveals pale porcelain-white plaques over the labia minora and clitoral hood with loss of architecture, fusion of the prepuce over the clitoris and a small fissure at the posterior fourchette. There is no ulceration or palpable nodule.

data_table.Examination: Pale porcelain-white labial plaques, fused clitoral hood, narrowed introitus, posterior fourchette fissure, no ulceration, no palpable mass, no inguinal lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Vulval swab no growth, urinalysis unremarkable
data_table.Medications: Nil topical apart from clotrimazole previously

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Continue topical clotrimazole 1 percent twice daily for 4 weeks before further specialist review since chronic vulvovaginal candidiasis remains the most likely diagnosis here
Initial vulval biopsy of representative pale plaque area followed by ultra-potent topical clomethasone propionate ointment 0.05 percent nightly for 4 weeks with planned taper
Wide local surgical excision of the affected vulval tissue with primary closure as first-line treatment for vulval lichen sclerosus given the visible architectural change and fusion
Vaginal oestrogen pessary 10 micrograms estradiol twice weekly for 6 weeks as primary therapy for atrophic vulvovaginitis given postmenopausal age and dyspareunia symptoms
Oral fluconazole 150 mg single dose for chronic vulvovaginal candidiasis with empirical management and review in 4 weeks if symptoms persist after a single weekly dose course

subtopic_detail: Induction of labour - choice based on Bishop score
stem: A 32-year-old G1 woman at 41+3 weeks gestation attends the day assessment unit for induction of labour following post-dates pregnancy. She has been counselled regarding the increased risks beyond 41 weeks and consented. Antenatal care has been uneventful with a normal CTG and biophysical profile today. Membranes are intact. Her booking BMI was 24 and the baby is in a cephalic presentation on the scan today.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 116/72, HR 78, T 36.6, CTG reactive with normal baseline 135
data_table.Examination: Cervix 1 cm dilated, 30 percent effaced, soft, mid position, vertex at -2 station (Bishop score 4)
data_table.Investigations: Group B Streptococcus screen negative at 36 weeks, ultrasound estimated fetal weight 3.6 kg, normal liquor

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step for induction of labour?

options.text: Intravenous oxytocin titrated infusion starting at 1 milli-unit per minute and doubling every 30 minutes with continuous CTG monitoring without prior cervical ripening method first
Artificial rupture of membranes alone with planned reassessment in 4 hours and oxytocin commencement at that time if regular contractions have not yet been established
Membrane sweep at clinic visit then a further week of expectant management with twice-weekly CTG monitoring before reassessing the need for active induction of labour
Misoprostol 200 micrograms orally with planned repeat doses 4 hourly without continuous monitoring required given the previous uneventful antenatal course and the cervix score
Cervical ripening with prostaglandin E2 vaginal gel or balloon catheter, repeat Bishop assessment in 6 hours and progression to artificial rupture of membranes plus oxytocin when favourable

subtopic_detail: Postpartum contraception in a breastfeeding woman
stem: You are the GP registrar reviewing a 32-year-old G2P2 at her 6-week postnatal check after a normal vaginal birth. She is exclusively breastfeeding her infant on demand. She has migraines without aura and a BMI of 27. She wants reliable, reversible contraception with the option to conceive again in 18 months. She finds taking daily medication unreliable. Pap history is up to date, blood pressure is normal and there is no history of venous thromboembolism. She declines any method that may reduce her milk supply.

data_table.Examination: Uterus involuted, perineum healed, breasts soft with established feeding, no abdominal mass
data_table.Investigations: Not required

lead_in: Which contraceptive option is most appropriate?

options.text: Combined oral contraceptive pill containing ethinylestradiol 30 micrograms and levonorgestrel 150 micrograms, commenced today with backup condoms for the first 7 days
Lactational amenorrhoea method counselling alone, with the patient relying on exclusive breastfeeding and amenorrhoea while introducing solid foods at 6 months
Levonorgestrel intrauterine device inserted today after pregnancy is excluded by history and examination, providing 5 years of contraception with no impact on breastfeeding
Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate 150 mg intramuscular every 12 weeks, starting today, with counselling about potential weight gain and delayed return of fertility after stopping
Progestogen only pill containing norethisterone 350 micrograms taken at the same time each day with a 3-hour window, beginning today before resuming sexual activity

subtopic_detail: Hyperemesis gravidarum - pharmacological escalation
stem: You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 27-year-old G1P0 at 9+4 weeks gestation in the ED with 2 weeks of intractable vomiting and inability to tolerate oral fluids over the past 36 hours. She is exhausted and tearful. She has lost 4 kg from her booking weight and the pregnancy is otherwise progressing normally on ultrasound. She has tried lifestyle measures including small frequent meals, dry toast and ginger without benefit. There is no prior history of bulimia or hyperemesis.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.5, HR 112, BP 102/64 lying, BP 88/52 standing, weight 58 kg from 62 kg booking
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes, capillary refill 3 seconds, no peritonism, no thyroid signs, no goitre, fetal heart 152
data_table.Investigations: Urine ketones 3+, Na 132 K 3.4 Cl 92 HCO3 30 urea 7.8 creatinine 78, beta-hCG 89000, TSH 0.3 free T4 18, viability ultrasound singleton 9+4

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Discharge home with oral pyridoxine 25 mg three times daily and doxylamine 12.5 mg at night, advising small frequent meals and review in 48 hours by the antenatal clinic
Commence oral prednisolone 50 mg daily as first-line therapy for refractory hyperemesis, supported by oral pyridoxine and doxylamine continued at the previously trialled doses
Commence intravenous 5% dextrose infusion at 100 mL/hour for caloric support, withhold electrolytes until biochemistry is reviewed in the morning, and arrange thyroid imaging tomorrow
Admit for intravenous Hartmann solution rehydration, give intravenous thiamine before any dextrose, and commence regular ondansetron 4 to 8 mg eight hourly with metoclopramide if needed
Arrange urgent referral for medical termination given the severity of symptoms and risk of Wernicke encephalopathy if vomiting continues despite supportive measures over coming weeks

subtopic_detail: Primary postpartum haemorrhage from uterine atony
stem: You are the obstetric registrar called to the delivery suite minutes after a 31-year-old G3P3 has delivered a 4.2 kg infant by spontaneous vaginal birth following a labour augmented with oxytocin for 12 hours. The placenta delivered intact 8 minutes ago. The midwife reports brisk ongoing vaginal bleeding estimated at 700 mL within the last 5 minutes. The woman is now feeling lightheaded. Active management of the third stage with prophylactic oxytocin 10 IU was given at delivery.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8, HR 122, BP 92/58, SpO2 99%, capillary refill 3 seconds
data_table.Examination: Uterus soft and boggy palpable above the umbilicus, no perineal or vaginal trauma seen, placenta inspected and complete, IV access bilateral 16G
data_table.Investigations: Hb 102 (booking 128), platelets 184, INR 1.0, group and hold sent, cross-match in progress

lead_in: After bimanual uterine massage and a further oxytocin infusion is started, what is the most appropriate next pharmacological agent?

options.text: Misoprostol 800 micrograms per rectum administered as a single dose, repeated in 30 minutes if bleeding continues with ongoing intravenous oxytocin infusion in the background
Transfer immediately to theatre for examination under anaesthesia and possible hysterectomy without further uterotonic given the rapid blood loss and risk of further coagulopathy
Intramuscular carboprost 250 micrograms repeated every 15 minutes to a maximum of 8 doses, omitting ergometrine because oxytocin is still infusing and uterotonic doubling is unnecessary
Insert a Bakri intrauterine balloon under sterile conditions before any second uterotonic, instil 500 mL of warm saline and continue oxytocin infusion as the only pharmacological cover
Intramuscular ergometrine 250 micrograms repeated at 5 minutes if needed, with concurrent administration of intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g over 10 minutes

subtopic_detail: Abnormal cervical screening result triage
stem: You are the GP reviewing a 34-year-old woman whose 5-yearly Cervical Screening Test result has returned. The sample is reported as oncogenic HPV positive (not 16 or 18) with reflex liquid-based cytology showing low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion. She is not pregnant, has not had a prior abnormal screen, and uses the etonogestrel implant for contraception. She has no abnormal bleeding and has had only one lifetime partner. She is anxious and asks what should happen next.

data_table.Examination: Speculum unremarkable at previous screening visit, cervix appeared healthy with no overt lesion
data_table.Investigations: CST: oncogenic HPV not 16/18 positive, LBC LSIL, prior screen 5 years ago HPV negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer for colposcopy as soon as possible because any oncogenic HPV plus cytological abnormality on the same sample requires immediate visualisation of the cervix
Repeat a Cervical Screening Test in 12 months to determine whether the HPV infection has cleared, with referral for colposcopy only if a follow-up oncogenic HPV result is detected
Recall in 5 years as per routine screening interval because cytology only shows low-grade changes and the woman is not immunocompromised and has no symptomatic concerns at presentation
Arrange HPV vaccination today as catch-up therapy to enhance clearance of the current infection, then repeat the Cervical Screening Test in 6 months to confirm resolution
Refer for diagnostic loop electrosurgical excision procedure given a high-grade lesion is possible on histology despite the cytological report, removing the risk of progression to cancer

subtopic_detail: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes - latency management
stem: You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 27-year-old G2P1 at 31+4 weeks with a sudden gush of clear fluid an hour ago. She is not contracting. The fetus is in cephalic presentation. There is no per vaginum bleeding and no fever or abdominal tenderness. CTG is reactive at 142 with normal variability. Ultrasound shows oligohydramnios with normal Doppler indices and an estimated fetal weight of 1750 g. She has had no previous preterm birth.

data_table.Examination: Sterile speculum confirms pooling of clear fluid in posterior fornix and no visible cervical dilation, abdomen soft and non-tender, fundal height 31
data_table.Investigations: WCC 9.8, CRP 4, GBS culture negative at 28 weeks, urine MCS pending, CTG reactive, ultrasound oligohydramnios EFW 1750 g

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Discharge home with twice weekly antenatal review, oral amoxicillin clavulanate 875/125 mg twice daily for 7 days as latency prophylaxis, and home temperature monitoring
Proceed to immediate induction of labour with oral misoprostol given the risk of intra-amniotic infection, with prophylactic antibiotic cover at the onset of contractions for group B streptococcus
Commence intravenous magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection at 4 g loading dose then 1 g per hour and arrange caesarean section within 4 hours under epidural anaesthesia

Admit for inpatient monitoring, give intramuscular betamethasone 11.4 mg now then in 24 hours, commence oral erythromycin 250 mg six hourly for 10 days, and plan expectant management until 34 weeks unless complications occur
Commence nifedipine tocolysis to gain 48 hours for corticosteroid effect then plan delivery at 33 weeks, withholding antibiotics in the absence of clinical signs of chorioamnionitis

subtopic_detail: Obstetric cholestasis - bile acids and delivery timing
stem: You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 33-year-old G2P1 at 36+1 weeks referred from her midwife for 2 weeks of intense generalised pruritus worse at night on the palms and soles, with no rash. There is no abdominal pain, no jaundice and no urinary symptoms. The first pregnancy was uncomplicated. She is otherwise well. The fetus is growing on the 50th centile. CTG is reactive. The previous baby was born by spontaneous vaginal birth at 39 weeks.

data_table.Examination: Excoriations over wrists and shins, no rash, no jaundice, fundus 36 weeks, fetal heart 138, no abdominal tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Bile acids 60 micromol/L, ALT 110, AST 98, GGT 22, bilirubin 12, INR 1.0, hepatitis serology negative, ultrasound liver normal architecture, fetal growth 50th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence oral ursodeoxycholic acid 500 mg twice daily, monitor bile acids weekly, give intramuscular betamethasone if delivery is anticipated below 37 weeks, and plan delivery at 37 to 38 weeks
Reassure and continue routine antenatal care to 40 weeks with weekly liver function tests because bile acids below 100 are considered low risk and do not require modification of delivery timing
Commence intravenous vitamin K and arrange immediate induction of labour with prostaglandin gel given the stillbirth risk, without trial of pharmacological symptom control beforehand
Prescribe oral chlorphenamine 4 mg three times daily for pruritus, repeat bile acids in 3 weeks, and continue routine antenatal schedule with planned delivery at 40 weeks if no progression occurs
Admit for daily CTG monitoring with intravenous N-acetylcysteine to support hepatic recovery and continue expectant management until spontaneous labour at term without intervention

subtopic_detail: Suspected ovarian torsion in an adolescent
stem: You are the gynaecology registrar called to ED to assess a 14-year-old girl with 6 hours of severe sudden-onset right iliac fossa pain, two episodes of vomiting and one syncopal episode at home. Menarche was 12 months ago. She is sexually inexperienced. Pain came on after a netball match. There has been no diarrhoea. The pain is now constant with intermittent severe peaks. Beta-hCG is negative. She is otherwise well and has no significant past medical history.

data_table.Examination: Severe tenderness right iliac fossa with voluntary guarding, palpable fullness right adnexa on gentle abdominal palpation, no peritonism elsewhere
data_table.Investigations: Beta-hCG negative, WCC 12.4 neutrophils 9.8 CRP 18, urine MCS pending, transabdominal ultrasound 8 cm right ovarian cyst with absent venous Doppler flow and reduced arterial flow

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Admit for observation, give intravenous fluids and morphine, repeat ultrasound in 12 hours, and arrange operative laparoscopy only if pain has not improved by the following morning ward round
Arrange contrast CT abdomen and pelvis to exclude appendicitis and confirm the diagnosis before any operative intervention is undertaken in an adolescent without prior surgery
Arrange urgent diagnostic and operative laparoscopy now with detorsion and ovarian conservation as the primary aim, even if the ovary appears dusky on initial inspection at theatre
Commence intravenous ceftriaxone and metronidazole empirically for tubo-ovarian abscess, admit for observation, and reassess clinically after the first dose of antibiotics has been completed
Discharge home with simple analgesia and gynaecology outpatient follow-up in 1 week given the negative beta-hCG and ability to attend the local clinic with carer support if pain returns

subtopic_detail: Heavy menstrual bleeding - first-line medical management
stem: You are the GP reviewing a 38-year-old G2P2 with 9 months of progressively heavy regular periods. She passes clots, soaks pads hourly on the heaviest 2 days, and has had 3 days off work over the last cycle. She is otherwise well, has no postcoital or intermenstrual bleeding and is not planning further pregnancies but does not wish for a surgical procedure today. Cervical screening is up to date. She is not on any anticoagulant. She is concerned about feeling persistently tired.

data_table.Examination: Pelvic examination normal, no palpable adnexal mass, cervix appears healthy, no abdominal mass, conjunctival pallor
data_table.Investigations: Hb 102, ferritin 14, TSH 1.8, beta-hCG negative, transvaginal ultrasound uterus 8 x 5 x 4 cm with single 2 cm intramural fibroid, endometrium 8 mm

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line therapy?

options.text: Insert a levonorgestrel intrauterine device at today's visit after confirming pregnancy is excluded, providing 5 years of contraception and substantially reducing menstrual blood loss
Prescribe oral tranexamic acid 1 g three times daily for the first 4 days of each cycle, combined with high-dose oral iron supplementation to address the anaemia and ongoing blood loss
Refer for endometrial ablation as definitive day-case treatment, accepting that future pregnancy is contraindicated and that long-term contraception is still needed after the ablation procedure
Commence GnRH analogue depot injection 3.75 mg monthly with add-back tibolone for 6 months as a bridge to surgical management of the intramural fibroid identified on ultrasound
Refer for hysterectomy through the public gynaecology service, with iron infusion now to correct the anaemia before any operative intervention is planned at the next available list

subtopic_detail: Reduced fetal movements at term - investigation pathway
stem: You are the midwifery group practice on-call obstetric registrar called by a 29-year-old G1P0 at 38+2 weeks who reports a 24-hour reduction in fetal movements compared with her usual pattern. She has had no bleeding or fluid loss. She is in good general health, has no medical complications, and the pregnancy has been low risk. She first noticed concern this afternoon, ate a sugary drink and lay on her left side as advised but movement remains less than baseline. She lives 20 minutes from the hospital.

data_table.Examination: Fundus 38, cephalic presentation engaged, fetal heart heard at 138 by Doppler at home (midwife visit)
data_table.Investigations: Anomaly scan at 19 weeks normal, GBS culture negative at 36 weeks, prior growth scans showed AGA

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Advise her to monitor at home for another 4 hours, drink another cold sweet drink, and call back if no improvement, with a same-day midwife home visit booked as a contingency
Book the woman for routine antenatal appointment in 2 days to assess fundal height and fetal movements at the same time, reassuring her that this often resolves spontaneously in nulliparous women
Arrange formal kick counting using the Cardiff Count to Ten chart over the next 12 hours, with admission only if fewer than 10 movements are felt in the next observation period
Advise her to come into the birth suite immediately for cardiotocograph and clinical assessment, with consideration of growth ultrasound if movements remain abnormal after CTG review
Proceed directly to category 2 caesarean section under spinal anaesthesia given the term gestation and history of reduced fetal movements over the preceding 24 hour period

subtopic_detail: Severe-range postpartum hypertension
stem: You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 32-year-old woman on day 1 postpartum after an uncomplicated spontaneous vaginal birth at 39+2 weeks. Her antenatal blood pressures were normal. She had no proteinuria documented at booking or in labour. Overnight she developed a severe occipital headache that did not respond to oral paracetamol and is photophobic. The midwife has just called you because her last three blood pressure recordings have all read above 160/110. She is breastfeeding her healthy term baby.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 168/112 mmHg confirmed on manual cuff, HR 92 bpm, RR 18, SpO2 99% on room air, T 36.8°C
data_table.Examination: Hyperreflexic at the patellae, no clonus, no focal neurology, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis 2+ protein, platelets 188 x10^9/L, ALT 28 U/L, creatinine 72 micromol/L, urate 0.38 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate antihypertensive therapy?

options.text: Oral methyldopa 250 mg three times daily commenced as outpatient therapy on discharge tomorrow
Oral nifedipine immediate-release 10 mg with blood pressure reassessment in 30 minutes
Intravenous magnesium sulfate 4 g loading dose alone with no antihypertensive agent yet
Oral sublingual nifedipine immediate-release 20 mg crushed under the tongue urgently
Oral atenolol 50 mg once daily commenced today and continued through breastfeeding

subtopic_detail: Breech at term
stem: You are the obstetric registrar in an antenatal clinic seeing a 28-year-old gravida 2 para 1 at 36+2 weeks gestation. Her previous pregnancy was a spontaneous vaginal birth at term. A growth scan today confirms a frank breech presentation, an anterior placenta, normal liquor volume and an estimated fetal weight on the 50th centile. She has no antepartum bleeding, no contractions, and no contraindications to vaginal birth. She asks about her options to avoid an elective caesarean.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/72 mmHg, HR 78 bpm, RR 16, T 36.7°C
data_table.Examination: Symphysio-fundal height 35 cm, fetal head palpable in the fundus, fetal heart rate 138 bpm by auscultation
data_table.Investigations: Anti-D negative at booking, group B streptococcus swab pending, recent normal full blood count

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Offer external cephalic version from 37 weeks gestation under tocolysis with continuous fetal cardiotocography monitoring
Book a category 4 elective lower segment caesarean section for 39 completed weeks gestation under spinal anaesthesia
Plan a vaginal breech birth with epidural analgesia attended by an experienced obstetrician at 39 weeks gestation
Begin moxibustion at the BL67 acupressure point twice daily for two weeks and review presentation at 38 weeks
Reassure that breech presentations spontaneously revert and review again at 39 weeks for a repeat presentation scan

subtopic_detail: Adolescent heavy menstrual bleeding
stem: You are the GP seeing a 15-year-old girl who reports heavy menstrual bleeding since menarche at age 12. Her cycles last 8 to 10 days, flood through tampons and pads every two hours on the heaviest days, and she has missed school each cycle. She is sexually inactive and uses no contraception. She has not had previous investigations. She has otherwise been well, plays netball weekly and has no history of bruising, epistaxis or family bleeding disorders. Her mother is in the room and is supportive.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 108/64 mmHg, HR 88 bpm, RR 16, T 36.6°C, weight 58 kg
data_table.Examination: Pale conjunctivae, no thyroid enlargement, no abdominal mass, abdomen soft and non-tender
data_table.Investigations: Hb 96 g/L, MCV 70 fL, ferritin 8 micrograms/L, beta-hCG negative, normal coagulation screen

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacological therapy?

options.text: Endometrial ablation booked through paediatric gynaecology after consent from parents
Oral combined ethinylestradiol and levonorgestrel pill cycled monthly with iron supplementation
Insertion of a levonorgestrel intrauterine system under general anaesthesia within four weeks
Oral norethisterone 5 mg three times daily continuously from day 5 to day 26 of each cycle
Oral tranexamic acid 1 g three times daily during menses with iron supplementation between cycles

subtopic_detail: Reduced fetal movements
stem: You are the obstetric registrar in the Day Assessment Unit reviewing a 34+0 weeks gravida 1 para 0 woman who self-presents with 24 hours of reduced fetal movements. She has had no antepartum bleeding, no rupture of membranes and no contractions. Her pregnancy has been uncomplicated to date with normal screening and a normal 20-week morphology scan. A growth scan two weeks ago showed an estimated fetal weight on the 30th centile with a normal umbilical artery Doppler. She is anxious and exhausted.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 124/76 mmHg, HR 86 bpm, RR 16, T 36.7°C, SpO2 99% on room air
data_table.Examination: Symphysio-fundal height 32 cm, longitudinal lie, cephalic presentation, fetal heart rate 142 bpm by auscultation
data_table.Investigations: CTG: baseline 145 bpm, variability 4 bpm for 50 of 60 minutes, no accelerations, one shallow late deceleration after a Braxton-Hicks tightening

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange immediate ultrasound assessment of growth, liquor volume and umbilical artery Doppler within 4 hours
Admit for repeat CTG in 4 hours, maternal hydration and oral mobilisation without further investigation
Discharge with kick chart, advice to return if movements decrease further and obstetric review in 7 days
Proceed directly to category 1 caesarean section within 30 minutes for non-reassuring fetal status
Administer betamethasone 11.4 mg intramuscularly and observe overnight with intermittent auscultation

subtopic_detail: Pelvic inflammatory disease with IUD
stem: You are the GP seeing a 28-year-old nulliparous woman who presents with three days of lower abdominal pain, vaginal discharge and dyspareunia. She has a copper IUD in place inserted nine months ago. She has had one new sexual partner in the last six weeks and uses no barrier contraception. She is well otherwise, working full time, and would like to keep her IUD. Examination shows lower abdominal tenderness and cervical motion tenderness, with mucopurulent cervical discharge but no peritonism.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 116/72 mmHg, HR 96 bpm, RR 16, T 38.0°C, SpO2 99% on room air
data_table.Examination: Lower abdominal tenderness without guarding, mucopurulent cervix, IUD strings visible, cervical motion tenderness, no adnexal mass
data_table.Investigations: Beta-hCG negative, vaginal swab for chlamydia and gonorrhoea pending, white cell count 13.2 x10^9/L, CRP 42 mg/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Remove the intrauterine device today and commence intramuscular ceftriaxone 500 mg with oral doxycycline and oral metronidazole 14 days
Defer all antibiotic therapy until chlamydia and gonorrhoea swab results return in two to three days then treat targeted therapy
Commence oral amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg twice daily for 14 days as monotherapy with outpatient gynaecology review
Admit for intravenous gentamicin with intravenous metronidazole and intravenous ampicillin pending swab and culture results
Give intramuscular ceftriaxone 500 mg now with oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily and metronidazole 400 mg twice daily 14 days

subtopic_detail: Selective fetal growth restriction in MCDA twins
stem: You are the maternal-fetal medicine fellow reviewing a 31-year-old gravida 2 para 1 with a monochorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy at 28+3 weeks. Surveillance ultrasound shows a fetal weight discordance of 28%. Twin A is appropriately grown on the 45th centile, while twin B is on the 4th centile. Liquor volumes are within normal range for both twins. There is no evidence of twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome. The umbilical artery Doppler in twin B shows intermittent absent end-diastolic flow.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal BP 122/76 mmHg, HR 84 bpm, T 36.8°C
data_table.Examination: Symphysio-fundal height 30 cm, fetal hearts both present and audible, no antepartum bleeding
data_table.Investigations: Estimated fetal weights twin A 1180 g, twin B 850 g, deepest vertical pocket A 4.2 cm, B 3.6 cm, MCA peak systolic velocity both within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Plan delivery now via category 1 caesarean section for both twins to prevent intrauterine death of the smaller twin
Give antenatal corticosteroids and arrange twice-weekly cardiotocography with weekly Doppler aiming delivery around 32 weeks
Proceed to selective laser photocoagulation of placental anastomoses to optimise placental flow to the smaller twin
Switch to fortnightly ultrasound and discharge home without antenatal corticosteroids until at least 34 weeks gestation
Recommend selective fetal reduction of the smaller twin to preserve the survival of the larger appropriately grown twin

subtopic_detail: Septic incomplete miscarriage
stem: You are the obstetric registrar called to ED to see a 26-year-old woman two days after a medical management of incomplete miscarriage at 9 weeks gestation. She presents with rigors, abdominal pain, foul-smelling discharge and a worsening generalised rash that began on her trunk and is spreading. She has not improved with oral paracetamol at home. She has no relevant past history. On arrival she looks unwell, clammy and confused, with a generalised macular blanching erythematous rash.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 86/48 mmHg, HR 132 bpm, RR 30, SpO2 95% on room air, T 39.8°C, lactate 4.6 mmol/L
data_table.Examination: Lower abdominal tenderness, foul-smelling brown vaginal discharge, open internal cervical os, no peritonism, generalised blanching erythroderma
data_table.Investigations: WCC 22 x10^9/L, CRP 240 mg/L, creatinine 158 micromol/L, beta-hCG 6800 IU/L, ultrasound shows retained products 28 mm

lead_in: Which combination of interventions provides the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone with metronidazole, intravenous crystalloid resuscitation and elective uterine evacuation on next list
Intravenous clindamycin and piperacillin-tazobactam, intravenous crystalloid resuscitation and urgent surgical evacuation within 4 hours
Intravenous benzylpenicillin monotherapy with intravenous crystalloid and conservative management with serial beta-hCG monitoring
Intravenous gentamicin and oral doxycycline with intravenous crystalloid resuscitation and outpatient gynaecology review in 48 hours
Intravenous methylprednisolone and intravenous hydrocortisone bolus to treat presumed adrenal crisis with supportive care

subtopic_detail: Anti-D in threatened miscarriage before 12 weeks
stem: You are the GP seeing a 27-year-old Rh-negative G2P1 woman at 9+3 weeks of pregnancy with one day of light vaginal spotting. She had a normal vaginal delivery 18 months ago with anti-D given postpartum. Today she is haemodynamically stable, the cervix is closed on speculum, and ultrasound shows a single intrauterine pregnancy with fetal heart pulsation and a small subchorionic haematoma. Her partner is also Rh-negative according to historical records.

data_table.Examination: Closed cervix, small amount of dark old blood in vault, no cervical excitation, uterus appropriate size
data_table.Investigations: Bedside US: viable intrauterine pregnancy 9+3 weeks, small subchorionic haematoma, no products in cervical canal; blood group O Rh-negative confirmed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management regarding anti-D?

options.text: Do not administer anti-D because the gestation is under 12 weeks without instrumentation
Administer 250 IU anti-D immunoglobulin intramuscularly within 72 hours of the bleeding
Confirm partner Rh-negative status on group and screen before giving any anti-D dose
Administer 625 IU anti-D immunoglobulin intramuscularly within 72 hours of the bleeding
Send a Kleihauer-Betke test now to quantify any feto-maternal haemorrhage before anti-D

subtopic_detail: Gestational thrombocytopenia versus ITP
stem: You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 32-year-old G1 woman at 34 weeks of pregnancy whose routine antenatal bloods show a platelet count of 112 x10^9/L. She is asymptomatic, blood pressure is normal and there is no rash, mucosal bleeding or splenomegaly. Her previous platelet counts during this pregnancy were 168 (booking) and 145 (28 weeks). She has no history of bleeding diathesis, no easy bruising, and is not on any medications.

data_table.Examination: Fundal height 34 cm, no bruising, no petechiae, no hepatosplenomegaly
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 112 x10^9/L, otherwise FBC normal, LFTs normal, urate normal, urine PCR negative, blood film no schistocytes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure as gestational thrombocytopenia, continue routine antenatal care, recheck at 36 weeks
Administer IV immunoglobulin 1 g/kg now to raise the platelet count before delivery onset
Commence oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily empirically for presumed immune thrombocytopenia
Arrange same-day delivery on the basis of the maternal platelet count and fetal safety risk
Plan elective caesarean section at 39 weeks because vaginal delivery is unsafe at these levels

subtopic_detail: PCOS metformin in woman seeking pregnancy
stem: You are the GP seeing a 29-year-old woman with PCOS by Rotterdam criteria who has been trying to conceive for 12 months. She has BMI 32, oligomenorrhoea (cycles every 60 to 90 days), normal day-2 FSH and TSH, and a normal hysterosalpingogram. Her partner has a normal semen analysis. She has already lost 4 kg with exercise and dietary changes over 4 months and her glucose tolerance is currently normal but with an HbA1c of 38 mmol/mol. She wants to know what to do next.

data_table.Examination: Mild acne, mild hirsutism on chin and upper lip, no acanthosis nigricans, normal pelvic examination
data_table.Investigations: Normal FSH, LH, prolactin, TSH, normal pelvic US showing polycystic ovarian morphology, HbA1c 38 mmol/mol, OGTT normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacological strategy to support conception?

options.text: Letrozole 2.5 mg from day 2 to day 6 of the cycle and monitor follicular response on US
Refer directly for IVF treatment cycle planning before any oral ovulation-induction trial
Clomifene citrate 50 mg from day 2 to day 6 of the cycle and monitor follicular response
Refer for laparoscopic ovarian drilling as second-line surgical before any oral therapy
Metformin 500 mg twice daily as monotherapy and reassess after six months of treatment

subtopic_detail: Postmenopausal genitourinary syndrome
stem: You are the GP seeing a 64-year-old woman 12 years post natural menopause complaining of urinary frequency, dysuria with sterile MSUs, recurrent post-coital spotting and superficial dyspareunia. She has tried over-the-counter vaginal moisturisers without benefit. She has a history of stage I oestrogen-receptor positive breast cancer treated 6 years ago with mastectomy and tamoxifen; tamoxifen ceased 4 years ago. She has no abnormal uterine bleeding on systematic enquiry, is not on systemic HRT, and her last cervical screening was negative HPV.

data_table.Examination: Atrophic pale vulval and vaginal mucosa, minor friable areas at the introitus, no visible lesions, no abnormal bleeding on speculum, no adnexal masses
data_table.Investigations: MSU sterile on three occasions, no haematuria on dipstick, no postmenopausal bleeding

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line therapy?

options.text: Continue lubricants and moisturisers alone and reassess in 12 months at the next visit
Refer for vaginal CO2 laser therapy as the first-line non-hormonal treatment option here
Commence oral ospemifene 60 mg daily and outpatient breast-cancer survivorship review
Commence systemic combined HRT with oestradiol patch and oral micronised progesterone capsule
Trial low-dose vaginal oestrogen after MDT agreement and informed consent counselling

subtopic_detail: Bacterial vaginosis in pregnancy
stem: You are the antenatal clinic registrar seeing a 30-year-old G2P1 woman at 18 weeks of pregnancy. She has a thin white-grey vaginal discharge with a fishy odour and no itch. She had a preterm birth at 32 weeks in her last pregnancy. Vaginal pH is 5.5 and the wet film shows clue cells. Chlamydia and gonorrhoea PCR are negative, and she has no genital herpes lesions. She is not in labour and the cervix is closed and long on speculum.

data_table.Examination: Thin homogeneous grey discharge with positive whiff test, no cervical motion tenderness, closed cervix
data_table.Investigations: Vaginal pH 5.5, clue cells on wet film, negative for trichomonas, NAAT negative for chlamydia and gonorrhoea

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Single 2 g oral dose of metronidazole on day one with no follow-up dose afterwards
Oral metronidazole 400 mg twice daily for a 5 to 7 day course in symptomatic pregnancy
Defer all treatment until after delivery because BV is self-limiting in pregnancy here
Topical clindamycin cream 2% intravaginally for seven nights with abstinence advice
Oral azithromycin 1 g as a single dose for empirical coverage of polymicrobial vaginitis

subtopic_detail: High-dose folate in women on anti-epileptic medication
stem: You are the GP seeing a 28-year-old woman with focal-onset epilepsy on lamotrigine 200 mg twice daily who is planning pregnancy. She has been seizure-free for 14 months. She has no family history of neural tube defects, takes no other medications, and is otherwise well. She is asking what folate dose to take and for how long before conceiving.

data_table.Examination: Normal general examination
data_table.Investigations: Recent serum lamotrigine within target, folate and B12 normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate folate advice?

options.text: Defer folic acid supplementation until the lamotrigine therapy is changed at preconception
Folic acid 5 mg daily started at pregnancy confirmation and continued through to 28 weeks
Folic acid 0.5 mg daily from at least one month preconception until 12 completed weeks
Cease folic acid and replace with multivitamin containing iodine 150 micrograms alone
Folic acid 5 mg daily from at least one month preconception until 12 completed weeks

subtopic_detail: Methotrexate for ectopic pregnancy
stem: You are the gynaecology registrar in EPAU reviewing a 31-year-old G2P1 woman with right iliac fossa pain and a tubal ectopic pregnancy confirmed on transvaginal ultrasound. There is no haemoperitoneum and the patient is haemodynamically stable. The ectopic mass measures 28 mm and there is no fetal cardiac activity. Her beta-hCG today is 3200 IU/L, full blood count, LFTs, and renal function are normal. She has no current breastfeeding, no pelvic inflammatory features, and is happy to attend for repeated follow-up.

data_table.Examination: Mild right iliac fossa tenderness without peritonism, soft abdomen, no cervical excitation
data_table.Investigations: Beta-hCG 3200 IU/L, Hb 124 g/L, LFTs and UEC normal; TVS: 28 mm right adnexal mass with no yolk sac, no free fluid

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management option to offer?

options.text: Expectant management with weekly serum beta-hCG until levels fall below 5 IU/L
Laparoscopic salpingectomy of the affected tube under general anaesthetic today
Single-dose IM methotrexate 50 mg/m2 with day 4 and day 7 serum beta-hCG follow up
Laparoscopic salpingostomy with conservation of the affected tube under GA today
Multi-dose IM methotrexate 50 mg/m2 every 48 hours with alternate-day folinic acid

subtopic_detail: Placenta accreta spectrum delivery planning
stem: You are the maternal fetal medicine consultant reviewing a 36-year-old G4P3 woman at 28 weeks gestation with two previous caesarean sections. The current placenta is anterior and covers the lower segment. Greyscale and colour Doppler ultrasound shows loss of the retroplacental clear zone, multiple lacunae and bridging vessels invading the bladder wall. She has no current bleeding. She lives 20 minutes from a tertiary maternity service with onsite interventional radiology and gynae-oncology.

data_table.Examination: Singleton cephalic presentation, fundal height appropriate for dates, no bleeding, no tenderness
data_table.Investigations: US 28 weeks: anterior low placenta with loss of clear zone, lacunae, bridging vessels; MRI confirms suspected placenta percreta with bladder involvement

lead_in: What is the most appropriate delivery plan?

options.text: Perform amniocentesis at 28 weeks for fetal lung maturity before timing delivery plan
Plan a trial of vaginal birth after caesarean given the two previous lower segment LSCS
Planned classical caesarean and caesarean hysterectomy at 34 to 35+6 weeks with MDT
Admit for inpatient maternal monitoring from 28 weeks until spontaneous labour onset
Plan elective lower segment caesarean section at 39 weeks with attempted placental delivery

subtopic_detail: Cervical cerclage indication
stem: You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 28-year-old G3P0 woman at 18+2 weeks of pregnancy in a high-risk antenatal clinic. Her last pregnancy ended at 21 weeks with painless cervical dilation and miscarriage, and her first pregnancy ended in a similar second-trimester loss at 22 weeks. She has no current bleeding, contractions or rupture of membranes. Transvaginal ultrasound today shows a closed external os with cervical length 22 mm and no funnelling. She has no STI infection and no other risk factors.

data_table.Examination: Cervix closed externally on speculum, no bleeding, no leaking
data_table.Investigations: TVS cervical length 22 mm, no funnelling, normal fetal anatomy, negative high-vaginal swab for chlamydia and gonorrhoea
