lead_in: What is the most appropriate intervention?

options.text: Vaginal progesterone alone until 36 weeks of gestation without any cervical cerclage now
History-indicated McDonald cervical cerclage now plus vaginal progesterone until 36 weeks
Wait for cervical length to fall below 15 mm before any cerclage or progesterone start
Place an Arabin pessary and arrange serial cervical length surveillance every two weeks
Bed rest at home and weekly cervical length scans without any other obstetric intervention

subtopic_detail: Systemic lupus erythematosus in pregnancy
stem: You are the obstetric medicine registrar reviewing a 31-year-old G2P0 woman with established SLE at her booking visit at 8 weeks of pregnancy. She has been clinically well for the last 18 months on hydroxychloroquine 400 mg daily and low-dose prednisolone 5 mg daily. She has no renal involvement, no antiphospholipid antibodies, and is anti-Ro and anti-La negative. She wants to know whether her medications should be changed and how her care plan should look.

data_table.Examination: No active rash, no joint swelling, normal cardiac and respiratory examination
data_table.Investigations: Stable mild anaemia, normal renal function, urine PCR 5 mg/mmol, low-titre ANA, no APL antibodies

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan?

options.text: Cease low-dose prednisolone because of gestational diabetes and fetal growth risk
Continue hydroxychloroquine and prednisolone, add aspirin from 12 weeks, joint MDT review
Switch hydroxychloroquine to methotrexate for better disease activity control now
Start enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneously daily for VTE and pre-eclampsia prevention
Cease hydroxychloroquine because of teratogenic concern and continue prednisolone alone

subtopic_detail: Macrosomia and mode of delivery in diabetes
stem: You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 33-year-old G2P1 woman at 38+2 weeks of pregnancy with insulin-treated gestational diabetes. Her growth scan today estimates the fetal weight at 4650 g with abdominal circumference greater than the 97th centile. She had a previous spontaneous vaginal birth at term of a 3700 g baby with no shoulder dystocia and no perineal trauma. She is otherwise well, the lie is longitudinal cephalic, and her bishop score is 4. She asks about mode of delivery.

data_table.Examination: Longitudinal cephalic, head 4/5 palpable, no contractions, no bleeding
data_table.Investigations: US EFW 4650 g (AC over 97th centile), normal liquor and Doppler, glucose log within target on insulin

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan?

options.text: Schedule symphysiotomy at the time of labour to manage the anticipated shoulder dystocia
Allow spontaneous onset of labour up to 41 weeks and plan a vaginal birth in delivery suite
Offer elective caesarean at 39+0 weeks for any insulin-treated GDM regardless of fetal weight
Offer planned caesarean section because of estimated fetal weight at least 4500 g in diabetes
Offer induction of labour at 38+3 weeks of gestation aiming for assisted vaginal birth

subtopic_detail: Group B streptococcus intrapartum prophylaxis with severe penicillin allergy
stem: You are the obstetric registrar attending the birth suite for a 30-year-old primigravida in labour at 39 weeks. Her vaginal-rectal GBS screen at 36 weeks was positive. Membranes ruptured 2 hours ago and she is now 5 cm dilated. Her booking notes record an episode of anaphylaxis after intramuscular benzylpenicillin in childhood with lip swelling, wheeze and a brief loss of consciousness. She has had no antibiotics since then. There is no other significant past history and the fetus is reassuring on CTG.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7 °C, HR 92, RR 18, SpO2 99% room air, BP 122/74
data_table.Examination: Cervix 5 cm dilated, vertex at -1 station, intact CTG reassuring, no chorioamnionitis features
data_table.Investigations: Penicillin sensitivity testing not previously performed; GBS rectovaginal swab positive at 36 weeks

lead_in: What is the most appropriate intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis?

options.text: Intravenous cefazolin 2 g loading then 1 g every 8 hours until birth as standard option
Intravenous clindamycin 600 mg every 8 hours after confirmed clindamycin susceptibility result
Intramuscular benzathine penicillin 1.2 million units single dose as soon as labour starts
Withhold intrapartum antibiotics and review the neonate clinically every 4 hours until 48 hours
Intravenous vancomycin 20 mg/kg every 8 hours until birth at the recommended infusion rate

subtopic_detail: Indications for antenatal CTG and umbilical artery Doppler in IUGR
stem: You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 32-year-old primigravida at 33+0 weeks referred from her midwife with symphysis-fundal height 27 cm against a customised growth chart 10th centile of 31 cm. She has normal blood pressure and no proteinuria. She reports normal fetal movements but feels the baby is smaller. No risk factors for placental insufficiency are identified in her booking. Australian guidelines recommend a structured response when growth restriction is suspected.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/72, HR 78, RR 16, T 36.6 °C, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Fundal height 27 cm, head presentation, cephalic, FH 142 reassuring
data_table.Investigations: Pending growth ultrasound and Doppler studies

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Continuous cardiotocography for 24 hours as a screening tool for placental insufficiency
Maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein and unconjugated oestriol to assess placental function
Magnetic resonance imaging of the fetus to characterise placental and brain morphology
Plain serial fundal height measurements weekly with no further imaging for two weeks
Ultrasound fetal biometry with amniotic fluid index and umbilical artery Doppler study

subtopic_detail: Postpartum LARC initiation timing after vaginal birth
stem: You are the postnatal ward doctor reviewing a 31-year-old woman day 1 after an uncomplicated vaginal birth of her third baby. She is fully breastfeeding and would like long-acting reversible contraception before discharge. She has no history of VTE, no liver disease and a normal cervical screen 12 months ago. Her previous contraceptive history includes a copper IUD she liked. She lives 4 hours from the nearest clinic and would prefer immediate insertion if safe.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/74, HR 78, RR 16, T 36.7 °C, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Uterus involuted to umbilicus, lochia rubra moderate, no signs of infection
data_table.Investigations: Not required for LARC selection

lead_in: What is the most appropriate contraceptive plan?

options.text: Wait until 6 weeks postpartum and offer combined oral contraception in the meantime
Lactational amenorrhoea method alone until ovulation returns and then review again later
Insert an etonogestrel subdermal implant before discharge after counselled consent today
Insert a copper IUD today on the postnatal ward as her chosen long-acting reversible method
Prescribe a combined contraceptive patch starting today and review again in two weeks at GP

subtopic_detail: Vasa praevia antenatal diagnosis and elective birth plan
stem: You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 35-year-old at 32 weeks following a third-trimester ultrasound. The scan reports a velamentous cord insertion with a fetal vessel crossing the internal cervical os, confirmed on transvaginal scan with colour Doppler. The placenta is otherwise normally located. She has had no bleeding. She is well, baby is well grown and CTG is reassuring. Her care is publicly funded at a tertiary centre with neonatal intensive care on site.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 116/72, HR 82, RR 16, T 36.6 °C, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Cephalic, no contractions, no bleeding, CTG reassuring
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound confirms a fetal vessel crossing internal os; placenta otherwise fundal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Plan vaginal birth at 39 weeks with continuous CTG and early epidural for labour
Repeat transvaginal ultrasound at 36 weeks and only consider caesarean if the vessel persists
Admit at 32 weeks for inpatient observation and elective birth at 39 weeks gestation
Admit now and plan elective caesarean at 34 to 36 weeks after antenatal corticosteroids
Discharge home with weekly outpatient ultrasound and elective caesarean at 39 weeks gestation

subtopic_detail: Management of retained placenta after vaginal birth
stem: You are the obstetric registrar called to a 28-year-old multipara 35 minutes after vaginal birth. The third stage has been actively managed with intramuscular oxytocin. The placenta has not delivered. She has had 600 mL of estimated blood loss and is haemodynamically stable. Examination reveals the placenta is palpable in the uterine cavity and the umbilical cord remains intact. She has had no neuraxial anaesthesia.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/74, HR 92, RR 16, T 36.7 °C, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Uterus firmly contracted, fundus at the umbilicus, placenta palpable in cavity, cord intact, no bleeding from uterus, perineum intact
data_table.Investigations: Hb 105 g/L, platelets 220 x10^9/L, coagulation normal, group and hold sent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Allow another 30 minutes of expectant management and recheck the placenta position after that
Apply controlled cord traction with simultaneous fundal pressure to assist delivery now
Transfer to theatre for manual removal of the placenta under regional or general anaesthesia
Inject umbilical vein oxytocin 20 units in 20 mL saline through the umbilical cord stump
Insert a Bakri intrauterine balloon to compress the lower segment and continue oxytocin infusion

subtopic_detail: Vulval lichen sclerosus maintenance and cancer surveillance
stem: You are the GP reviewing a 62-year-old postmenopausal woman six months after biopsy-confirmed vulval lichen sclerosus. Her initial 12-week course of topical clobetasol propionate produced symptom control. She is now itch-free with persisting white atrophic vulval skin and architectural change including fusion of the labia minora. There are no eroded areas, no fissures and no new pigmentation. She wants to know how often she should review the condition and whether maintenance therapy is needed.

data_table.Examination: White atrophic vulval skin, architectural change including labia minora fusion, no erosions, fissures, ulcers or new pigmentation
data_table.Investigations: Recent biopsy confirmed lichen sclerosus without atypia

lead_in: What is the most appropriate ongoing plan?

options.text: Refer for laser vulval resurfacing to reduce architectural change and prevent malignant change
Cease all topical steroid therapy permanently and review only if pruritus or symptoms recur
Switch to long-term oestrogen and progesterone hormone replacement therapy for vulval skin
Continue clobetasol propionate 0.05% twice weekly maintenance with 6 to 12 monthly clinical review
Repeat full vulval biopsy every 12 months as routine surveillance regardless of clinical features

subtopic_detail: Placenta accreta spectrum operative planning at tertiary centre
stem: You are the obstetric registrar at a tertiary maternity centre reviewing a 36-year-old G3P2 at 30 weeks. She has had two prior caesareans. Her 28-week MRI confirms an anterior placenta praevia with focal myometrial invasion through the lower segment scar and bladder serosa interruption. Vascularity into the bladder wall is reported. She is well, with no bleeding and reassuring CTG. The multidisciplinary team includes urology, interventional radiology, anaesthetics, neonatology and a dedicated obstetric blood bank.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 124/76, HR 88, RR 18, T 36.6 °C, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender uterus, no bleeding, cephalic presentation, CTG reassuring
data_table.Investigations: MRI: anterior placenta praevia with focal placenta percreta extending into bladder wall; fetal biometry on 50th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate planned mode and timing of birth?

options.text: Elective lower-segment caesarean section at 39 weeks with attempted manual placental removal
Vaginal birth at 39 weeks with senior obstetric supervision and second-line uterotonic ready
Elective classical caesarean and planned hysterectomy at 34 to 35+6 weeks at the tertiary centre
Conservative management with methotrexate after caesarean to preserve fertility and uterus
Delay caesarean to 37 weeks to allow further fetal lung maturation in a stable woman without bleeding

subtopic_detail: HELLP escalation with thrombocytopenia and transfusion thresholds
stem: You are the obstetric registrar managing a 34-year-old primigravida at 31+4 weeks with HELLP syndrome. Birth is planned by caesarean within 4 hours. Her BP is 162/108 on a labetalol infusion. She has right upper quadrant pain and gross haematuria. Her platelets are falling rapidly and her INR is rising. She has no other bleeding. She is otherwise well, has no infection and consents to all interventions. The blood bank is on standby with a massive transfusion protocol ready.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 162/108, HR 104, RR 22, SpO2 98% room air, T 37.0 °C, urine 25 mL/h
data_table.Examination: Right upper quadrant tenderness, brisk reflexes, no focal neurology, mild lower limb oedema
data_table.Investigations: Hb 92 g/L, platelets 38 x10^9/L (was 76 three hours ago), LDH 1180, AST 380, INR 1.5, fibrinogen 1.6 g/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate blood product plan immediately prior to caesarean?

options.text: Transfuse two adult therapeutic platelet units plus correct fibrinogen to above 2 g/L prior to skin incision
Withhold blood products and proceed to general anaesthesia caesarean with subsequent transfusion only
Give dexamethasone 10 mg IV every 12 hours to raise platelets above 100 before delivery is started
Transfuse four units of red cells before any other blood product or platelet transfusion is given
Commence intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g over 10 minutes and proceed without other blood products

subtopic_detail: Carriage of group B streptococcus before a planned caesarean section
stem: A 34-year-old woman attends the birth suite for her planned repeat caesarean section at 39 weeks. She is well and has had no pain or fluid loss.

data_table.Swab: Vagino-rectal swab at 36 weeks grew group B streptococcus
data_table.Examination: No contractions, membranes intact, temperature 36.7 degC

lead_in: What is the most appropriate antibiotic plan?

options.text: Give the usual single dose of surgical prophylaxis and nothing further
Give intravenous benzylpenicillin four hourly from admission until birth
Give intravenous vancomycin instead of the usual surgical prophylaxis
Give oral amoxicillin for five days beforehand to clear the carriage
Repeat the swab today and decide on antibiotics once it has grown

subtopic_detail: National Cervical Screening Program
stem: You are a general practice registrar reviewing a 32-year-old woman attending for routine preventive care. Her last cervical screening test 5 years ago detected oncogenic HPV (non-16/18) with reflex cytology showing low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion. She subsequently had a 12-month repeat test which was HPV negative. She has been in a monogamous relationship for 4 years, is up to date with the human papillomavirus vaccination, has had no abnormal bleeding, and is asymptomatic. She is requesting advice about further screening.

data_table.Examination: BMI 24 kg/m2, abdomen unremarkable, no pelvic complaints
data_table.Investigations: Five-year prior CST: HPV (non-16/18) positive, LSIL on reflex LBC; 4-year prior CST (repeat at 12 months): HPV negative

lead_in: When should her next cervical screening test be performed?

options.text: Now as a routine cervical screening test, returning her to the standard 5-yearly screening interval
In 1 year as a further surveillance test before returning to routine 5-yearly screening
In 2 years to align with the previous biennial Pap smear schedule and confirm sustained clearance
Refer to colposcopy now for direct visualisation given her prior LSIL on reflex cytology
Not require further screening as she has been vaccinated against human papillomavirus

subtopic_detail: Routine antenatal anti-D prophylaxis schedule
stem: You are the obstetric registrar in an antenatal clinic reviewing a 27-year-old RhD-negative G1P0 woman at 27+5 weeks with an uncomplicated singleton pregnancy. Booking antibody screen at 12 weeks and repeat at 27 weeks are both negative. She plans an unassisted vaginal birth at the same hospital. She has had no antenatal bleeding, no procedures and no abdominal trauma during the pregnancy.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 112/68, HR 76, SpO2 98%; symphysis-fundal height appropriate for gestation
data_table.Examination: Singleton pregnancy with cephalic presentation; fetal heart rate 142 by Doppler; abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: Indirect Coombs negative at booking and at 27 weeks; group A RhD-negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate anti-D plan?

options.text: Defer anti-D until the postnatal cord blood result confirms a RhD-positive infant
Give 625 IU intramuscular anti-D now at 28 weeks and again at 34 weeks regardless of events
Give a single 1500 IU intramuscular anti-D dose at 28 weeks with no further antenatal dose
Withhold antenatal anti-D and give only after sensitising events such as bleeding or trauma
Wait until 34 weeks and give a single antenatal anti-D dose then with postnatal follow-up

subtopic_detail: Vaginal birth after caesarean contraindicated by classical scar
stem: You are the obstetric registrar counselling a G2P1 woman at 26+0 weeks. Her first pregnancy ended in a classical (vertical upper-segment) caesarean section at 30+0 weeks for a footling breech presentation with extreme prematurity. She has no other comorbidities, a singleton cephalic pregnancy on today's ultrasound and a posterior placenta clear of the os. She has been reading about vaginal birth after caesarean and asks about her options.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/72, HR 78, SpO2 98%; afebrile; symphysis-fundal height appropriate
data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender abdomen with low transverse Pfannenstiel skin scar; uterus soft; cervix long and closed on speculum
data_table.Investigations: Ultrasound: singleton cephalic at 26 weeks, posterior placenta clear of os, normal liquor volume

lead_in: What mode of birth should be recommended?

options.text: Plan a trial of vaginal birth after caesarean from 39 weeks with continuous CTG
Offer vaginal birth after caesarean only if her cervix is favourable at 39 weeks
Plan induction of labour at 39 weeks with prostaglandins and oxytocin augmentation
Plan elective caesarean section between 36+0 and 37+0 weeks with antenatal corticosteroids
Plan external cephalic version at 37 weeks followed by elective caesarean only if breech

subtopic_detail: High-dose folate after previous neural tube defect
stem: You are the GP seeing a 28-year-old woman planning a second pregnancy. Her first child, born 3 years ago, had a myelomeningocele. She has no diabetes, no epilepsy and takes no medications. She has a normal BMI and her diet is generally adequate. She has no known coeliac disease. She is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander.

data_table.Examination: Unremarkable; cardiovascular and abdominal examination normal
data_table.Investigations: Serum B12 and ferritin normal; coeliac serology negative; HbA1c 5.0 percent

lead_in: What folate dose should be recommended for this preconception consultation?

options.text: Folic acid 0.5 mg daily starting now and continuing through the first trimester
Folic acid 0.8 mg daily commencing on confirmation of pregnancy through the first trimester
Folic acid 5 mg daily for at least 1 month preconception and through the first trimester
Folic acid 5 mg daily from the second trimester only with no preconception dosing
No folate supplementation if she eats a balanced diet that includes leafy green vegetables

subtopic_detail: Cervical screening result management with HPV other genotypes
stem: You are the GP discussing a routine cervical screening test result with a 33-year-old woman in clinic. The laboratory reports oncogenic HPV (not types 16 or 18) detected, and reflex liquid-based cytology shows low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion. She is asymptomatic, has never had abnormal screening and is not pregnant. She is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander.

data_table.Examination: Speculum examination on the day of sample was unremarkable; no contact bleeding; normal external genitalia
data_table.Investigations: Cervical screening test: HPV (not 16/18) positive; reflex LBC: low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management step?

options.text: Repeat the cervical screening test in 12 months with referral to colposcopy if persistent
Refer directly to colposcopy now given any positive HPV result and abnormal cytology
Proceed to cervical cone biopsy under general anaesthesia at the next available list
Arrange punch biopsy of the cervix in clinic without prior colposcopic assessment first
Return to routine 5-year recall because non-16/18 HPV carries minimal cancer risk overall

subtopic_detail: Gestational hypertension treatment threshold and target
stem: You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a G2P1 woman at 32+0 weeks. Her booking BP was 110/70 with normal early bloods. Today routine review documents BP 156/98 on two readings 4 hours apart with no proteinuria on dipstick or PCR, no symptoms, no headache, no visual disturbance and no epigastric pain. Fetal growth and Dopplers were normal at 28 weeks. She is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander.

data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender abdomen, fundal height appropriate, fetal heart rate 144 with reassuring CTG, no peripheral oedema, no clonus
data_table.Investigations: Urine PCR negative; FBC, LFT, urate and creatinine normal; uric acid normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate antihypertensive plan?

options.text: Methyldopa 250 mg three times daily with a target BP below 120/80 in clinic
Sublingual short-acting nifedipine 10 mg now to reduce blood pressure within minutes
Admit for intravenous magnesium sulfate loading to prevent seizures and deliver tonight
Plan immediate induction of labour at 32 weeks irrespective of corticosteroid timing
Commence oral labetalol 100 mg three times daily aiming for diastolic 80-85 mmHg

subtopic_detail: Twin chorionicity at first trimester ultrasound
stem: You are the obstetric registrar reviewing the 11+4 week dating scan of a 30-year-old G1P0. The scan reports a twin pregnancy with two separate yolk sacs, a single placental site, two distinct amniotic cavities, a thin inter-twin membrane and a T-sign at the placental junction. Both fetuses have reassuring activity and nuchal translucency within normal range. She is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander.

data_table.Examination: Soft abdomen with uterus appropriate for twin gestation; no bleeding; cervix long and closed
data_table.Investigations: Dating scan: twin pregnancy, single placental mass, thin inter-twin membrane, T-sign, two amniotic sacs, two yolk sacs, equal growth

lead_in: What surveillance plan should follow from these ultrasound findings?

options.text: Dichorionic diamniotic twin care with growth scans every 4 weeks from 24 weeks
Monochorionic diamniotic twin care with fortnightly ultrasound from 16 weeks for TTTS
Monochorionic monoamniotic care with admission and continuous CTG from 24 weeks
Perform chorionic villus sampling now to determine zygosity before further surveillance
Defer assessment of chorionicity until the morphology scan at 18-22 weeks gestation

subtopic_detail: Hyperemesis gravidarum admission and refeeding precautions
stem: You are the GP reviewing an 8-week pregnant 26-year-old woman with severe nausea and vomiting. She has been unable to keep fluids down for 24 hours and has lost 4.5 kg from a baseline of 60 kg (a 7.5 percent loss). She feels dizzy on standing and has not voided urine since this morning. She has no abdominal pain, no fever, no haematemesis and no prior bariatric surgery. She is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 112, BP 100/65 lying with 22 mmHg systolic postural drop, T 36.7 °C, SpO2 98% room air
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes, reduced skin turgor, soft non-tender abdomen, no peritonism, no organomegaly
data_table.Investigations: Urine ketones 3+; sodium 132 mmol/L, potassium 3.0 mmol/L, urea 8.4 mmol/L; LFTs and TFTs pending; quantitative beta-hCG appropriate for gestation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Oral metoclopramide 10 mg three times daily with review again in 48 hours by phone
Trial of ginger and small frequent meals with vitamin B6 25 mg three times daily
Outpatient subcutaneous ondansetron with home electrolyte and weight monitoring
Admit for intravenous thiamine 100 mg, ondansetron, crystalloid and potassium replacement
Refer to obstetrics at the next available clinic with no immediate change to therapy

subtopic_detail: Increased combined first trimester screen risk with normal NT
stem: You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 38-year-old G1P0 who has received her combined first trimester screen result at 12+3 weeks. Her nuchal translucency was normal at 2.0 mm. PAPP-A was low at the 4th centile and free beta-hCG was elevated. The combined risk for trisomy 21 is 1 in 75. The dating ultrasound showed no major structural abnormality. She is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander.

data_table.Examination: Soft abdomen; cervix long and closed; no bleeding; fetal heart present
data_table.Investigations: NT 2.0 mm; PAPP-A 4th centile; free beta-hCG elevated; combined risk 1:75 trisomy 21; no structural abnormality

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in screening or diagnosis?

options.text: Reassure her that 1 in 75 is below the threshold for further intervention and continue routine care
Amniocentesis next week for diagnostic karyotype and microarray under ultrasound guidance
Offer non-invasive prenatal testing now given normal NT to refine the risk before any invasive sampling
Return for routine 18 to 20 week morphology scan only and base decisions on the scan findings
Discuss termination of pregnancy now based on the combined screening result alone

subtopic_detail: Group B streptococcus intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis
stem: You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 32-year-old primigravida at 39+2 weeks in early spontaneous labour. Her membranes ruptured 4 hours ago and the liquor is clear. Her routine 36-week vaginal-rectal swab was positive for group B streptococcus. She has no penicillin allergy. Her observations are stable and the cardiotocograph is reassuring.

data_table.Examination: Cervix 4 cm dilated, fully effaced, vertex at -1 station, contractions every 4 minutes
data_table.Investigations: Vaginal-rectal swab at 36 weeks: GBS positive. FBC and group and screen unremarkable.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate intrapartum management?

options.text: Defer antibiotic therapy and reassess the need for prophylaxis only if maternal temperature rises above 38 °C or fetal tachycardia develops during labour progress
Commence intravenous benzylpenicillin 3 g loading dose followed by 1.8 g every 4 hours until delivery and document the time of the first dose for paediatrics
Start intravenous vancomycin 1 g 12-hourly empirically because of the rising prevalence of macrolide and lincosamide resistance in Australian GBS isolates currently
Offer a single dose of oral cefalexin 2 g now and arrange ongoing 8-hourly dosing throughout labour with neonatal observation in the maternity ward post-delivery
Recommend immediate caesarean section before active labour establishes to avoid the need for any intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis for this colonised pregnancy

subtopic_detail: First-line medical management of heavy menstrual bleeding
stem: You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 28-year-old nulliparous woman with two years of heavy menstrual bleeding. She floods through a pad every 90 minutes on her heaviest day and feels light-headed by day 3. Her cycles are regular at 28 days. She has no intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding. She would prefer to retain her fertility for the future. She has no contraindications to combined hormonal contraception.

data_table.Examination: Pale conjunctivae, abdomen soft, bimanual examination unremarkable, no adnexal mass
data_table.Investigations: Hb 96 g/L, MCV 72 fL, ferritin 7 micrograms/L, TSH 1.4 mIU/L, beta-HCG negative. Pelvic ultrasound: normal-sized uterus, no fibroids or polyps, normal endometrium 6 mm.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line medical management?

options.text: Schedule endometrial ablation at the next available list and start oral iron replacement therapy in the interim while she awaits the procedure date
Refer for outpatient hysteroscopy and dilatation and curettage as the first-line investigation and treatment before any medical therapy is initiated for this complaint
Commence cyclical norethisterone 5 mg three times daily from day 5 to day 26 of each menstrual cycle and review the response in three months from initiation
Recommend definitive laparoscopic hysterectomy as the most effective and durable treatment option for refractory heavy menstrual bleeding in a woman of her age group
Insert a 52 mg levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine device after counselling on initial irregular bleeding and start oral iron 100 mg elemental daily for the deficiency

subtopic_detail: Routine folic acid supplementation for low-risk preconception care
stem: You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 29-year-old healthy woman attending for preconception advice. She has a regular cycle, no chronic conditions and is on no regular medications. She has no personal or family history of neural tube defects. Her body mass index is 23 kg/m^2 and she does not smoke or drink alcohol. She hopes to conceive within the next six months.

data_table.Examination: Unremarkable general and pelvic examination
data_table.Investigations: Up-to-date cervical screening test negative for HPV, rubella immune, varicella immune, syphilis non-reactive, HIV negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate preconception supplementation advice?

options.text: Start folic acid 400 micrograms daily and iodine 150 micrograms daily now and continue through the first trimester of pregnancy at the same daily doses
Defer all vitamin supplementation until a positive pregnancy test and commence routine folic acid then together with a standard prenatal multivitamin preparation
Recommend high-dose folic acid 5 mg daily for at least three months before conception and continue this throughout the first trimester for routine neural tube defect prevention
Start vitamin A 10,000 international units daily, combined vitamin E and selenium and a high-dose marine omega-3 supplement during preconception planning each day
Commence elemental iron 100 mg daily plus calcium 1000 mg daily as universal preconception measures, with folic acid only added after she becomes pregnant

subtopic_detail: Gestational diabetes screening 75 g oral glucose tolerance test thresholds
stem: You are the antenatal clinic registrar reviewing a 34-year-old woman at 27+5 weeks gestation in her second pregnancy. Her first pregnancy was uncomplicated and her booking body mass index was 26 kg/m^2. She has no family history of diabetes. She fasted overnight and underwent her routine 75 g oral glucose tolerance test this morning. The fetus is appropriately grown by symphysiofundal height and ultrasound at 20 weeks was normal.

data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender uterus, fundal height 27 cm, fetal movements present
data_table.Investigations: 75 g OGTT: fasting plasma glucose 5.4 mmol/L, 1-hour 9.6 mmol/L, 2-hour 7.8 mmol/L. HbA1c 5.5%. Urinalysis negative.

lead_in: How should this result be interpreted and managed?

options.text: Results are normal; reassure her and book routine antenatal follow-up at 32 weeks with serial growth scans not currently indicated by the present screening result
Diagnose gestational diabetes, refer to the antenatal endocrinology team, commence home glucose monitoring and provide dietitian input and exercise advice this week
Repeat the 75 g oral glucose tolerance test at 32 weeks because intermediate values do not meet thresholds and confirmatory testing is needed before any diagnosis can be made
Start metformin 500 mg twice daily immediately as universal first-line pharmacotherapy and bypass dietary and lifestyle counselling at this stage of pregnancy and care
Order a subsequent HbA1c at 28 weeks and treat only if it rises above 5.7%, as glucose tolerance testing is increasingly considered less specific in pregnancy assessment

subtopic_detail: Placental abruption with maternal compromise and concealed haemorrhage
stem: You are the obstetric registrar called urgently to triage a 31-year-old multiparous woman at 34+2 weeks with sudden severe abdominal pain. She had a small painful vaginal bleed 30 minutes ago and is now pale and clammy. She has had no leaking fluid. Her booking blood pressure has been 110 to 120 systolic; she has no history of trauma. She is rhesus D positive.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.9 °C, HR 122, BP 86/52, RR 24, SpO2 99% room air, capillary refill 4 seconds
data_table.Examination: Tense, tender uterus, fundal height 36 cm, persistent firm contraction without relaxation, no urinary catheter output yet
data_table.Investigations: CTG: fetal heart rate baseline 90 bpm with late decelerations and reduced variability. FBC pending. Bedside ultrasound: posterior placenta with no praevia.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence intravenous magnesium sulfate 4 g loading dose for fetal neuroprotection and continue an ongoing maintenance infusion before any other intervention is initiated
Insert two large-bore intravenous cannulae, take group and screen with a clotting profile and admit for 24 hours of continuous fetal heart rate monitoring observation only
Administer betamethasone 11.4 mg intramuscular and tocolyse with nifedipine 20 mg orally to prolong the pregnancy to 36 weeks while monitoring blood loss carefully
Activate the massive transfusion protocol, commence intravenous resuscitation with warmed crystalloid and group O Rh-negative blood and proceed to category 1 caesarean section
Order an urgent magnetic resonance imaging of the abdomen and pelvis to formally quantify the retroplacental haematoma before deciding on the mode and timing of delivery

subtopic_detail: Shoulder dystocia initial manoeuvre
stem: You are the obstetric registrar conducting a vaginal delivery for a 32-year-old multiparous woman at 39+4 weeks. The pregnancy has been complicated by diet-controlled gestational diabetes and the estimated fetal weight at 38 weeks was 4.1 kg. After delivery of the head the chin retracts firmly against the perineum and the anterior shoulder does not deliver with routine downward traction. The time of head delivery has been noted aloud.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal: T 36.7 °C, HR 102, BP 120/78. Fetal heart rate immediately pre-event reassuring on CTG.
data_table.Examination: Turtle sign with chin retraction, head restitution incomplete, no perineal lacerations
data_table.Investigations: Not applicable in real time

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate next step?

options.text: Call for help, flatten the bed, hyperflex the maternal hips onto the abdomen and apply firm suprapubic pressure from the side of the fetal back
Apply continued strong downward axial traction on the fetal head while an assistant applies fundal pressure from above to push the anterior shoulder out
Proceed immediately to symphysiotomy under local anaesthetic to widen the maternal pelvic outlet and allow delivery of the impacted anterior shoulder rapidly
Replace the fetal head into the pelvis with Zavanelli manoeuvre and arrange immediate transfer to theatre for delivery by category 1 caesarean section as the next step
Administer intravenous oxytocin 5 international units bolus and oral nifedipine 20 mg to relax the uterus and facilitate the anterior shoulder coming under the symphysis

subtopic_detail: Postmenopausal bleeding investigation and endometrial sampling
stem: You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 62-year-old woman who reports two episodes of light vaginal bleeding over six weeks. Her last menstrual period was at age 50 and she has had no hormonal therapy. Her body mass index is 34 kg/m^2 and she has type 2 diabetes. She has had no abdominal pain or weight loss. She has no family history of gynaecological malignancy. Bimanual examination is unremarkable.

data_table.Examination: Speculum: small amount of old blood in vagina, cervix appears healthy. Bimanual: anteverted mobile non-tender uterus.
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound: endometrial thickness 9 mm, heterogeneous endometrium, no obvious focal lesion. Cervical screening up to date and negative. FBC and ferritin unremarkable.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat the transvaginal ultrasound in 8 weeks and consider further investigation only if the bleeding persists or the endometrial thickness measurement increases above 12 mm
Start systemic oral progestogen therapy with norethisterone 5 mg three times daily for three months and reassess the bleeding pattern at the end of that course
Refer for outpatient hysteroscopy with directed endometrial sampling because the endometrial thickness is above 4 mm and risk factors for endometrial carcinoma are present
Order pelvic magnetic resonance imaging now to evaluate for myometrial invasion before any histological sampling is performed and refer to gynaecological oncology
Reassure her that an endometrial thickness under 10 mm in a postmenopausal woman is reassuring and arrange a routine general practitioner review in 6 to 8 weeks

subtopic_detail: Primary postpartum haemorrhage with continued atonic bleeding after oxytocin
stem: You are the obstetric registrar called to a 28-year-old primigravida 20 minutes after a normal vaginal delivery at 40+1 weeks. Estimated blood loss is now 1300 mL and continues briskly. The placenta has been delivered intact, the perineum has no significant lacerations and the bladder is empty. She received intramuscular oxytocin 10 international units at delivery and the uterus remains poorly contracted on examination. Her booking blood pressure was 110/70 with no history of hypertension.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7 °C, HR 118, BP 92/58, RR 22, SpO2 98% room air
data_table.Examination: Soft boggy uterus above the umbilicus, bladder empty, vagina with steady fresh blood loss, no cervical or vaginal lacerations
data_table.Investigations: FBC and coagulation studies have been sent; group and screen is current

lead_in: After uterine massage, what is the most appropriate next uterotonic step?

options.text: Administer rectal misoprostol 800 micrograms with continuation of crystalloid resuscitation while awaiting return of intravenous access for ongoing fluid therapy
Activate the massive transfusion protocol and transfer to theatre immediately for examination under anaesthesia, balloon tamponade and possible B-Lynch suture insertion
Start a syntocinon infusion at 40 international units in 1000 mL of normal saline and avoid ergometrine because of her body mass index and current blood pressure measurement
Administer intramuscular carboprost 250 micrograms repeated every 15 minutes up to a maximum of 8 doses and proceed to theatre if uterine atony persists despite the doses
Give ergometrine 250 micrograms intramuscularly and intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g over 10 minutes alongside an oxytocin infusion and prepare for theatre if bleeding continues

subtopic_detail: Nausea and vomiting of pregnancy first-line
stem: You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 28-year-old G1P0 at 9 weeks gestation by her last menstrual period with three weeks of daily nausea and intermittent vomiting up to four times daily. She has lost 1 kg from her booking weight but is tolerating small sips of fluid. Her mid-stream urine ketone strip is negative. Her dating ultrasound shows a single viable intrauterine pregnancy. She is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.6 °C, HR 84, BP 112/72, RR 16, weight 64 kg (booking 65 kg)
data_table.Examination: Mucous membranes mildly dry, abdomen soft and non-tender, no thyroid enlargement
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick: ketones negative, specific gravity 1.020; beta-hCG appropriate for dates; TSH within normal range

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

options.text: Oral pyridoxine 25 mg three times daily combined with oral doxylamine 12.5 mg at night and small frequent low-fat meals with antiemetic review in one week
Oral ondansetron 8 mg three times daily as first-line monotherapy with a follow-up appointment arranged in one week to assess response and side effects
Admit for intravenous Hartmann's fluid resuscitation, thiamine cover and intravenous metoclopramide pending resolution of symptoms before discharge
Reassure her that nausea will settle by 12 weeks and provide written advice on ginger tea and acupressure bands without any pharmacological intervention
Oral promethazine 25 mg every six hours and arrange a thyroid-stimulating hormone level today to exclude hyperthyroidism as a contributing differential cause

subtopic_detail: Group B Streptococcus screening timing
stem: You are the general practice obstetric shared-care registrar reviewing a 32-year-old G2P1 at 30 weeks gestation who is asking when her swab to look for the bacteria that causes early newborn infection should be done. Her previous baby was term, healthy and did not develop early-onset sepsis. She has had no urinary tract infections this pregnancy. Her booking ultrasound was unremarkable and she is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander.

data_table.Examination: Fundal height appropriate for dates, fetal heart heard, no uterine activity
data_table.Investigations: Antenatal bloods normal, 28 week OGTT normal, current MSU pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice regarding screening timing?

options.text: Combined vaginal and rectal swab is recommended at 35 to 37 weeks gestation, with intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis offered to those who screen positive
Vaginal swab alone is recommended at 28 weeks gestation, with repeat testing at 36 weeks if the first sample returns positive on initial culture
Mid-stream urine culture alone is sufficient for screening, with vaginal swab reserved only for those whose urine sample returns culture positive for GBS
Screening is unnecessary because her previous baby did not have early-onset GBS sepsis, and intrapartum antibiotics are reserved for risk-based protocols
Combined vaginal and rectal swab is recommended at 40 weeks gestation, immediately before the onset of labour, so that the result reflects colonisation at birth

subtopic_detail: Postpartum contraception in breastfeeding
stem: You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 32-year-old non-Aboriginal woman at her 6 week postnatal visit. She is exclusively breastfeeding her healthy term baby on demand and her menses have not returned. She wants reliable contraception that does not affect her milk supply and is willing to consider any method. She has no history of venous thromboembolism, migraine with aura or breast cancer. Her blood pressure today is 116/72.

data_table.Examination: Well-healed lower segment caesarean scar, uterus involuted, no breast lumps
data_table.Investigations: Cervical screening up to date and normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line contraceptive recommendation?

options.text: Combined oral contraceptive pill containing 30 micrograms ethinylestradiol commenced today with seven days of additional condom use to provide ongoing cover
Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate 150 mg intramuscular injection now, with repeat injection every 12 weeks and no requirement for additional barrier contraception
Levonorgestrel intrauterine device inserted at this visit with no requirement for additional contraception and a string check in six weeks at her general practitioner
Lactational amenorrhoea method only, with advice to switch to another contraceptive if menses return or feeding pattern changes from full exclusive breastfeeding
Progestogen-only pill desogestrel 75 micrograms once daily started today with a 3 hour late-pill window applied if a dose is missed in error at home

subtopic_detail: Suspected endometriosis empiric trial
stem: You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 24-year-old non-Aboriginal nulliparous woman with 18 months of progressively severe dysmenorrhoea, deep dyspareunia and cyclical pelvic pain. She is sexually active in a monogamous relationship using condoms. Her cervical screening is up to date and recent pelvic ultrasound shows no endometrioma or adenomyosis. She has no contraindication to combined hormonal contraception. She is not planning pregnancy in the next two years.

data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender abdomen, bimanual exam reveals mild tenderness in posterior fornix without nodularity or fixed retroversion
data_table.Investigations: Pelvic ultrasound: no endometrioma, no hydrosalpinx, normal endometrium; FBE and ferritin normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer urgently for diagnostic laparoscopy with the option of operative excision of any endometriotic lesions identified at the same procedure
Commence regular paracetamol and oral mefenamic acid during menses only and review symptoms in three months before considering any hormonal therapy
Order serum CA-125 today and refer to gynaecology if the result is elevated above the laboratory cut-off for further evaluation including pelvic MRI
Trial continuous combined oral contraceptive pill for three to six months with regular review and refer to gynaecology if symptoms persist despite suppression
Commence intramuscular goserelin GnRH agonist therapy with hormonal add-back oestrogen-progestin therapy and review in three months for symptom response

subtopic_detail: Routine anti-D prophylaxis at 28 weeks
stem: You are the antenatal clinic registrar reviewing a 27-year-old G2P1 non-Aboriginal woman at 28 weeks gestation. She is rhesus D negative and her antibody screen is negative. Her partner is rhesus D positive. Her previous baby was rhesus D positive and she received postpartum anti-D in 2024. She is currently well with no antepartum bleeding. Her booking ultrasound and current measurements are appropriate for gestation.

data_table.Examination: Fundal height 27 cm, fetal heart heard, no uterine activity
data_table.Investigations: Blood group: O negative, indirect Coombs negative, antibody screen negative; antenatal bloods unremarkable

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Withhold antenatal anti-D because postpartum anti-D was given for the previous pregnancy and repeat the antibody screen at delivery only
Order a non-invasive prenatal test for fetal RHD status and defer prophylaxis until the result is available before issuing any anti-D immunoglobulin
Administer 625 IU intramuscular anti-D immunoglobulin today and repeat at 34 weeks gestation, then administer postpartum anti-D if the baby is rhesus D positive
Give a single 1500 IU intramuscular dose of anti-D immunoglobulin at 28 weeks only, omitting the 34 week dose given that her previous baby was unaffected
Defer prophylaxis until 36 weeks gestation and combine the routine antenatal dose with cord blood typing arrangements for delivery in the same appointment

subtopic_detail: Severe pre-eclampsia at 32 weeks
stem: You are the obstetric registrar called to assess a 29-year-old G1P0 non-Aboriginal woman at 32 weeks gestation referred from a regional clinic with new severe hypertension, headache and visual disturbance. She has had no fits. Her urine is positive for protein 3+ and her platelets are mildly reduced. The fetal heart trace is normal and there is no antepartum haemorrhage. She has had a single dose of betamethasone at the referring service one hour ago.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 168/118 repeated 165/116, HR 96, RR 18, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Headache, photophobia, brisk reflexes with two beats of clonus, no abdominal tenderness, fetal heart rate 140 with normal variability
data_table.Investigations: Urine protein 3+, platelets 118 x10^9/L, ALT 64 U/L, creatinine 78 micromol/L, normal coagulation, fundi normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Oral labetalol 200 mg, magnesium sulfate loading dose 4 g intravenous and arrange transfer to tertiary obstetric unit with maternal and fetal monitoring
Intravenous hydralazine 20 mg bolus, no magnesium until any seizure occurs, and immediate emergency caesarean section at the referring regional service today
Sublingual nifedipine 10 mg every 15 minutes until BP under 140/90 and admit for observation without magnesium sulfate or steroids
Intravenous labetalol 20 mg bolus titrated, magnesium sulfate 4 g loading then 1 g per hour, second betamethasone dose at 24 hours and transfer to tertiary unit
Intravenous furosemide 20 mg, magnesium sulfate infusion and methyldopa 250 mg three times daily without immediate intravenous antihypertensive cover

subtopic_detail: Suspected umbilical cord prolapse
stem: You are the obstetric registrar called urgently to the birthing suite for a 30-year-old G3P2 non-Aboriginal woman at 38 weeks gestation in spontaneous labour. The midwife performed artificial rupture of membranes for slow progress and immediately felt a pulsating loop of cord at the cervix. The cervix is 6 cm dilated and the presenting part is high. The cardiotocograph now shows prolonged bradycardia at 70 beats per minute. There is no antepartum haemorrhage.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal BP 122/78, HR 96, RR 18, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Cervix 6 cm dilated, vertex above ischial spines, palpable pulsating cord through cervix
data_table.Investigations: CTG fetal bradycardia 70 bpm, reduced variability

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Augment with oxytocin to speed second stage and prepare for instrumental vaginal delivery in the birthing suite under regional anaesthesia
Position in left lateral, replace the cord into the vagina warmly and arrange transfer to theatre for category 2 caesarean within 60 minutes of decision
Knee-chest or steep Trendelenburg position, elevate the presenting part manually off the cord, prepare for category 1 caesarean and call paediatrics
Insert a urinary catheter and instill 500 mL warm saline into the bladder to elevate the presenting part, then proceed to elective caesarean later today
Reassess CTG after 10 minutes in left lateral and proceed to caesarean only if bradycardia persists, otherwise continue labour with continuous monitoring

subtopic_detail: Suspected pulmonary embolism in pregnancy
stem: You are the obstetric medicine registrar reviewing a 33-year-old G2P1 non-Aboriginal woman at 26 weeks gestation with acute onset pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness for 6 hours. She has no haemoptysis and no calf swelling on examination. She has no past venous thromboembolism but had a long-haul flight returning to Australia three weeks ago. Her chest x-ray is normal. She is haemodynamically stable.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8 °C, HR 112, BP 118/72, RR 22, SpO2 95% room air
data_table.Examination: Clear chest, no calf tenderness or asymmetry, fetal heart heard, soft non-tender abdomen
data_table.Investigations: Chest x-ray clear, ECG sinus tachycardia, troponin normal, FBE normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: D-dimer level interpreted using an age-adjusted threshold to decide whether further imaging is required for diagnostic confirmation
Empirical therapeutic enoxaparin 1.5 mg/kg subcutaneous daily without imaging because pregnancy itself precludes further radiological investigation
Bilateral lower limb compression ultrasound first, and if positive for proximal deep venous thrombosis treat without further chest imaging being required
Computed tomography pulmonary angiogram as first-line imaging because it has higher sensitivity than ventilation-perfusion scan for peripheral pulmonary embolism
Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging to assess right ventricular strain and exclude pulmonary embolism without ionising radiation exposure to the developing fetus

subtopic_detail: Placenta accreta spectrum delivery planning
stem: You are the obstetric registrar at a tertiary unit reviewing a 36-year-old G4P3 non-Aboriginal woman at 32 weeks gestation. She has had three previous caesarean sections. Anterior placenta praevia was confirmed at the 20 week morphology scan and a recent dedicated tertiary ultrasound documents bridging vessels and bladder wall interruption suggestive of placenta accreta spectrum. She has had no antepartum bleeding and the fetus is appropriately grown. Her haemoglobin is 118 g/L.

data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender abdomen, fundal height appropriate, fetal heart present, no per-vaginal bleed
data_table.Investigations: Hb 118 g/L, ferritin 35 micrograms/L, blood group A positive, antibody screen negative; ultrasound features suspicious for placenta accreta spectrum

lead_in: What is the most appropriate delivery plan?

options.text: Trial of labour after caesarean at 39 weeks gestation with continuous CTG monitoring and immediate caesarean only if vaginal bleeding occurs in early labour
Planned MDT caesarean at 34 to 36 weeks after corticosteroids, with consultant obstetrician, urology, anaesthetics, blood bank cross-match and consideration of leaving placenta in situ
Defer planning until 39 weeks gestation to maximise fetal lung maturity, then perform standard elective caesarean section under spinal anaesthesia at the regional hospital
External cephalic version followed by induction of labour at 38 weeks with epidural analgesia and active management of third stage with intramuscular oxytocin
Elective caesarean at 37 weeks at the local district hospital under general anaesthesia without prior MDT planning, with on-call urology consulted only if bladder injury occurs

subtopic_detail: Gestational hypertension antihypertensive threshold
stem: You are the obstetrics registrar reviewing a 31-year-old non-Aboriginal woman in her first pregnancy at 33+4 weeks gestation in the day assessment unit with persistently elevated blood pressures detected at her community antenatal visit. She is asymptomatic with no headache, visual disturbance or epigastric pain. There is no proteinuria, normal fetal movements, and a reassuring CTG. Her booking blood pressure was 110/70 mmHg.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 152/98 mmHg (repeated 3 times at least 4 hours apart, all readings 148/96 or higher), HR 82, RR 16, T 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Symphysis-fundal height appropriate, fetal heart 142 bpm, no peripheral oedema beyond ankles, no hyperreflexia, no epigastric tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis no protein, urine protein:creatinine ratio 18 mg/mmol, FBC platelets 232 x10^9/L Hb 116 g/L, UEC creatinine 64 micromol/L, LFTs ALT 22 U/L, urate 0.30 mmol/L, CTG normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence aspirin 150 mg daily as primary prevention for pre-eclampsia, withhold antihypertensive treatment, and arrange urgent uterine artery Doppler scan within 48 hours of presentation
Admit for inpatient observation, commence intravenous hydralazine 5 mg boluses titrated to BP under 140/90 mmHg, and arrange magnesium sulfate infusion to prevent eclampsia
Withhold antihypertensive treatment, organise twice-weekly community midwife BP checks, and review in the antenatal clinic in 2 weeks for a treatment decision
Commence oral atenolol 50 mg daily, plan repeat day assessment in 1 week, and arrange a growth scan at 36 weeks given the mild blood pressure elevation noted
Commence oral labetalol 100 mg twice daily, plan day assessment review in 48 hours, and counsel on pre-eclampsia warning symptoms and self-monitoring

subtopic_detail: Antenatal corticosteroid timing in threatened preterm labour
stem: You are the obstetrics registrar reviewing a 29-year-old non-Aboriginal woman at 30+2 weeks gestation in her second pregnancy who presents to birth suite with regular painful contractions every 5 minutes and intact membranes. Her first pregnancy ended at 38 weeks with normal vaginal birth. She has not previously received corticosteroids in this pregnancy. The CTG is reassuring, and there is no antepartum haemorrhage. Speculum examination shows the cervix is 2 cm long and 2 cm dilated.

data_table.Examination: Uterine activity 3 in 10 minutes lasting 45 seconds, cervix 2 cm long and 2 cm dilated, membranes intact, fetus cephalic, fetal heart 140 bpm reactive
data_table.Investigations: FBC normal, MSU clear, fetal fibronectin positive, ultrasound estimated fetal weight 1450 g (45th centile), cervical length 18 mm

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Administer intramuscular betamethasone 11.4 mg now and again in 24 hours, commence intravenous magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection, and arrange transfer to a tertiary centre
Administer intramuscular betamethasone 11.4 mg now, withhold tocolysis and magnesium sulfate as she is over 30 weeks, and continue routine ward monitoring with CTG every 4 hours
Administer two doses of intravenous dexamethasone 6 mg 12 hours apart and arrange immediate caesarean section under regional anaesthesia given the unfavourable cervical findings noted
Commence oral nifedipine 20 mg as tocolysis, withhold corticosteroids until contractions stop, and review the cervical length and corticosteroid plan in the morning
Withhold corticosteroids as she is over 30 weeks gestation, commence vaginal progesterone 200 mg nightly, and discharge home with planned outpatient review in 1 week

subtopic_detail: Recurrent miscarriage workup
stem: You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 33-year-old non-Aboriginal woman in the early pregnancy assessment clinic after three consecutive first-trimester miscarriages. Each was confirmed as intrauterine non-viable on ultrasound between 8 and 10 weeks gestation. She has no living children, no history of stillbirth, and her partner is the same throughout. She is otherwise well, with a BMI of 24 kg/m2 and a regular 28-day cycle. There is no family history of thrombosis or autoimmune disease.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 116/72 mmHg, HR 72, RR 14, T 36.7 °C, BMI 24 kg/m2
data_table.Examination: Unremarkable systemic examination, normal pelvic examination with a normal-sized anteverted uterus
data_table.Investigations: None ordered prior to this visit

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure that three miscarriages is within statistical noise and arrange routine antenatal care at the next positive pregnancy test without specific investigations
Arrange parental karyotyping, antiphospholipid antibody screen including lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin and anti-beta2 glycoprotein I, plus pelvic ultrasound
Order an inherited thrombophilia panel including factor V Leiden, prothrombin gene mutation and protein C and S, and commence empirical aspirin 100 mg daily
Refer for in-vitro fertilisation with preimplantation genetic testing for aneuploidy on the basis that her losses are likely from fetal chromosomal abnormality
Arrange a hysteroscopy with endometrial biopsy and screen for chronic endometritis with CD138 immunohistochemistry as initial recurrent miscarriage workup measures

subtopic_detail: Type 1 diabetes preconception planning
stem: You are the obstetric medicine registrar in the joint diabetes-antenatal clinic seeing a 28-year-old non-Aboriginal woman with type 1 diabetes for 15 years who is planning her first pregnancy in the next 6 months. She uses multiple daily injections of insulin glargine and aspart and self-monitors her capillary glucose 6 times daily. She has background retinopathy and stable microalbuminuria. She takes no other medications and is not currently using contraception consistently.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 124/76 mmHg, HR 74, RR 14, T 36.6 °C, BMI 25 kg/m2
data_table.Examination: Normal cardiovascular examination, fundi show background retinopathy without proliferative changes documented last month
data_table.Investigations: HbA1c 8.2% (66 mmol/mol), urine albumin:creatinine ratio 12 mg/mmol (mild), eGFR 92 mL/min/1.73m2, TSH 1.8 mIU/L, recent retinal review documented

lead_in: What is the single best initial intervention?

options.text: Defer conception, optimise glycaemia targeting HbA1c under 6.5% with intensified insulin regimen, commence high-dose folic acid 5 mg daily, and continue effective contraception
Encourage immediate conception attempts, switch from insulin glargine to detemir as the preferred basal insulin in pregnancy, and arrange dating ultrasound at confirmation of pregnancy
Commence metformin 500 mg twice daily in addition to insulin to improve glycaemic control, arrange repeat HbA1c in 6 weeks, and start folic acid 500 micrograms daily
Refer to ophthalmology for prophylactic pan-retinal photocoagulation given the background retinopathy and high HbA1c, and defer all conception planning until that procedure has been completed
Refer to nephrology before conception for renal biopsy of the microalbuminuria, withhold pregnancy planning until biopsy is completed, and continue current insulin regimen and contraception

subtopic_detail: Monochorionic diamniotic twin surveillance for TTTS
stem: You are the maternal-fetal medicine fellow reviewing a 34-year-old non-Aboriginal woman with a monochorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy at 19+3 weeks. She has been having fortnightly scans. At her current scan there is a discordance of estimated fetal weight with one twin at the 18th centile and the other at the 62nd. Amniotic fluid deepest vertical pocket is 2.1 cm around twin A and 9.5 cm around twin B. Both bladders are visible.

data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender uterus, no contractions, fetal hearts both present
data_table.Investigations: Ultrasound DVP twin A 2.1 cm, twin B 9.5 cm, EFW twin A 18th centile, twin B 62nd centile, both bladders visible, no hydrops, cervical length 35 mm, Doppler middle cerebral artery and umbilical artery within normal range

lead_in: What is the single best next step?

options.text: Administer betamethasone for fetal lung maturation, arrange caesarean section in the next 24 hours, and admit to the antenatal ward pending neonatal team handover
Continue routine fortnightly surveillance, reassure that mild fluid discordance is common in monochorionic twins, and review with repeat scan in 2 weeks for trend assessment
Arrange immediate amnioreduction of the polyhydramniotic sac by removing 1500 mL of amniotic fluid to relieve pressure, with subsequent weekly scan follow-up
Arrange urgent referral to the fetal therapy service for assessment for fetoscopic laser ablation of placental anastomoses within the next week
Diagnose selective fetal growth restriction without TTTS, arrange weekly Doppler surveillance, and continue conservative management until 36 weeks with planned caesarean section

subtopic_detail: Painless antepartum haemorrhage at 32 weeks with low-lying placenta
stem: You are the obstetrics registrar called to triage for a 32-year-old non-Aboriginal woman in her second pregnancy at 32+4 weeks with sudden painless bright-red vaginal bleeding of around 150 mL, no contractions and good fetal movements. Her morphology scan reported a posterior placenta extending to 1 cm from the internal cervical os. She has had one previous caesarean section. The CTG is reassuring. She is haemodynamically stable.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/72 mmHg, HR 92, RR 18, SpO2 99% room air, T 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender uterus, fetus cephalic, fetal heart 142 bpm reactive, no palpable contractions, no abdominal tenderness, no signs of shock, perineum stained with bright-red blood approximately 150 mL on the pad
data_table.Investigations: FBC Hb 112 g/L platelets 215 x10^9/L, group and hold sent, fibrinogen 4.2 g/L, CTG reassuring, bedside ultrasound confirms posterior low-lying placenta within 1 cm of internal os and fetus appropriately grown

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence intravenous magnesium sulfate for tocolysis and fetal neuroprotection, administer methyldopa for the elevated maternal pulse, and review obstetric Doppler studies in 24 hours
Perform a gentle digital vaginal examination to assess cervical dilatation, send a high vaginal swab, and continue ward monitoring with CTG every 4 hours for the next 24 hours
Arrange immediate category 1 caesarean section under general anaesthesia within 30 minutes given the antepartum haemorrhage and prior caesarean section history
Discharge home with follow-up scan in 2 weeks, telephone parental education for any recurrent bleed and routine community midwife review at the next antenatal visit in a fortnight
Admit to the antenatal ward, administer betamethasone 11.4 mg IM and book Anti-D, withhold digital and speculum examination, and arrange transfer to a centre with neonatal intensive care capability

subtopic_detail: Intravenous iron in third-trimester iron deficiency anaemia
stem: You are the antenatal clinic registrar reviewing a 30-year-old non-Aboriginal G3P2 woman at 32+0 weeks gestation with fatigue and pallor on routine screening. She has been taking oral ferrous sulfate 325 mg daily since 18 weeks but stopped 4 weeks ago because of nausea and constipation. She has no haemoglobinopathy and her booking ferritin was 14 microg/L. There is no clinical bleeding and no plan for elective caesarean section. She is keen to be well before her induction date booked at 39+0 weeks.

data_table.Examination: Pale conjunctivae, no jaundice, soft uterus appropriate for gestation, fetal heart 144 bpm
data_table.Investigations: Hb 92 g/L, MCV 76 fL, ferritin 8 microg/L (deficient under 30 in pregnancy), transferrin saturation 8%, B12 and folate normal, CRP 4 mg/L, urinalysis nil

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Recommence oral ferrous sulfate 325 mg three times daily with vitamin C and review the FBC in 4 weeks, with no plan for IV iron unless oral therapy fails at the next review
Arrange intravenous ferric carboxymaltose infusion 1000 mg in day stay, recheck the FBC and ferritin in 4 weeks, and counsel that oral iron can be re-trialled postpartum if needed
Transfuse 1 unit of packed red cells given the symptomatic anaemia and short time to delivery, and counsel that iron stores will be replenished by the transfusion
Switch oral iron to ferrous fumarate 200 mg every second day with the rationale of reduced hepcidin response, and schedule routine community midwife review in 2 weeks for FBC check
Arrange erythropoiesis-stimulating agent darbepoetin 100 micrograms weekly given the poor response to oral iron and the short timeframe before her planned induction at 39 weeks

subtopic_detail: Second-trimester medical termination after fetal anomaly
stem: You are the obstetrics registrar in a tertiary maternal-fetal medicine clinic in New South Wales seeing a 34-year-old non-Aboriginal woman at 21+0 weeks gestation with a recently confirmed lethal fetal anomaly diagnosed on the morphology scan and reconfirmed by tertiary review. She and her partner request termination of pregnancy. She has had one previous uncomplicated vaginal birth. She has no medical comorbidity, no allergies and is Rh-positive. She has been counselled by the genetic counsellor and social worker.

data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender uterus consistent with dates, cervix long and closed on speculum
data_table.Investigations: Detailed morphology and tertiary review confirm lethal anomaly, FBC normal, group and hold sent, MSU clear, infection screen negative

lead_in: What is the single best management plan?

options.text: Commence vaginal misoprostol 200 micrograms every 6 hours alone without mifepristone priming and admit to the antenatal ward with intermittent CTG monitoring throughout the process
Arrange outpatient surgical dilatation and evacuation under conscious sedation in the next 48 hours, without antenatal cervical preparation, and discharge home after recovery
Admit for combined regimen: oral mifepristone 200 mg followed in 24 to 48 hours by vaginal or buccal misoprostol 400 micrograms every 3 hours, with multidisciplinary support and bereavement care
Arrange oxytocin infusion alone to induce labour in the antenatal ward and plan vaginal birth with continuous fetal heart monitoring throughout the procedure
Defer the procedure and recommend continuation of pregnancy with palliative care planning for the newborn, citing late gestation as an obstacle to safe termination of pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes at 34 weeks
stem: You are the obstetric registrar at a tertiary maternity hospital reviewing a 34+0 week gestation primigravida who presents with a 6-hour history of clear fluid loss per vaginum. Sterile speculum confirms pooling of liquor with positive nitrazine test and ultrasound shows reduced amniotic fluid index. She is afebrile with no uterine activity and the fetal heart rate trace is reassuring. Her group B streptococcus swab from 36 weeks is not yet available because of her current gestation.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8 °C, HR 78, RR 16, SpO2 99% room air, BP 118/72 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender uterus, no palpable contractions, cephalic presentation, fundal height 33 cm, no per-vaginal blood loss
data_table.Investigations: Speculum confirms pooling, nitrazine positive, ultrasound AFI 4 cm, fetal heart rate trace category 1, FBC and CRP within reference ranges, group B streptococcus swab not available, cervical length not measured

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Discharge home with twice weekly review and instructions to return if fever vaginal bleeding decreased fetal movements or rupture of fresh liquor, with planned induction of labour booked for 37+0 weeks gestation

Proceed immediately to lower segment caesarean section under spinal anaesthesia given the gestation and uncertain group B streptococcus status with a single dose of intravenous cefazolin 2 g at induction of anaesthesia

Admit for tocolysis with nifedipine, intramuscular betamethasone 11.4 mg now and in 24 hours, intravenous magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection and reassess in 48 hours before discussing planned delivery

Admit for inpatient expectant management with intravenous benzylpenicillin and oral erythromycin, 4-hourly observations, intermittent CTG and plan induction of labour by 37+0 weeks if not delivered earlier

Admit for immediate induction of labour with vaginal prostaglandin gel and intravenous oxytocin titration and intrapartum intravenous benzylpenicillin for group B streptococcus prophylaxis throughout the labour

subtopic_detail: Gestational diabetes mellitus diagnosis at 28 weeks
stem: You are the antenatal clinic registrar reviewing a 31-year-old G2P1 woman at 28 weeks' gestation. Her routine 75 g 2-hour oral glucose tolerance test results are back. She has no symptoms, has gained 11 kg this pregnancy and her body mass index at booking was 31 kg/m2. She had no GDM in her first pregnancy, which ended in a normal vaginal birth of a 3.5 kg infant. Her fetus is appropriately grown on today's growth scan with normal amniotic fluid.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7 °C, HR 76, RR 14, SpO2 99% room air, BP 116/74 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Fundal height 28 cm, cephalic presentation, fetal heart 142/min, no oedema
data_table.Investigations: 75 g OGTT fasting 5.4 mmol/L, 1 hour 11.2 mmol/L, 2 hour 8.0 mmol/L; HbA1c 5.4%, urinalysis no glucose no ketones, growth scan within reference ranges, amniotic fluid index 14 cm

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Diagnose gestational diabetes mellitus, refer to the diabetes in pregnancy multidisciplinary clinic, commence self-monitoring of capillary blood glucose four times daily and start individualised lifestyle and dietary modification
Repeat the 75 g oral glucose tolerance test in 2 weeks because the 2 hour value is below the diagnostic threshold and the fasting glucose was within the reference range at this current testing point

Reassure that the results are within normal range for the third trimester and recommend a follow-up HbA1c at 6 weeks postnatal with no further antenatal glucose testing or dietary intervention required at this stage

Commence metformin 500 mg twice daily and refer for endocrinology review in 4 weeks while continuing routine antenatal care and reserving any insulin therapy until after delivery if hyperglycaemia persists postpartum

Arrange a 100 g 3-hour oral glucose tolerance test to confirm gestational diabetes mellitus using two abnormal values out of four glucose readings as per Carpenter-Coustan diagnostic thresholds for confirmation

subtopic_detail: Postpartum endometritis empirical antibiotics
stem: You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 30-year-old woman on day 4 after an emergency lower segment caesarean section for failure to progress. She has new lower abdominal pain, foul-smelling lochia and a temperature of 38.6 °C since this morning. She is haemodynamically stable but tachycardic and uncomfortable. Her wound is intact with no discharge. There is no flank tenderness and the breasts are non-tender.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.6 °C, HR 112, RR 20, SpO2 98% room air, BP 110/68 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Tender uterus on bimanual examination palpable just above the symphysis, foul-smelling lochia, clean caesarean wound, no flank tenderness, breasts soft, calves non-tender
data_table.Investigations: FBC WCC 16.8 x10^9/L, CRP 142 mg/L, UEC creatinine 64 micromol/L, lactate 1.8 mmol/L, urinalysis no nitrites, blood cultures sent, high vaginal swab sent, group B streptococcus status from booking visit unknown

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Oral amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily and arrange community midwife review with follow-up at the postnatal clinic in 48 hours if symptoms have not settled or temperatures persist over the next observation period

Intravenous ampicillin 2 g 6 hourly, gentamicin 5 mg/kg daily and metronidazole 500 mg 12 hourly with admission for clinical reassessment at 48 hours and a switch to oral therapy 24 hours after clinical resolution

Intravenous flucloxacillin 2 g 6 hourly alone as monotherapy because the most likely organism complicating post-caesarean infection is Staphylococcus aureus from the wound site rather than the endometrial cavity

Intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g once daily alone with admission for fluid resuscitation and reassessment at 24 hours and step-down to oral cefalexin if symptoms have improved by the time of consultant ward round

Intravenous vancomycin 25 mg/kg loading and 15 mg/kg 12 hourly maintenance with intravenous metronidazole and arrange interventional radiology drainage if the bedside ultrasound shows retained products in the cavity

subtopic_detail: PCOS infertility ovulation induction first-line
stem: You are the general practice registrar in a shared-care arrangement with a fertility clinic, reviewing a 28-year-old non-Aboriginal woman who has been trying to conceive for 14 months. She has a body mass index of 27 kg/m2, oligomenorrhoea since menarche, mild facial hirsutism and a polycystic ovarian morphology on pelvic ultrasound. Her semen analysis from her partner is normal and her hysterosalpingogram shows patent fallopian tubes. Pelvic examination is unremarkable.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.6 °C, HR 72, RR 14, SpO2 99% room air, BP 116/72 mmHg, BMI 27 kg/m2
data_table.Examination: Mild upper lip and chin hirsutism, no acanthosis nigricans, no abdominal masses, normal bimanual pelvic examination
data_table.Investigations: Day 21 progesterone 3 nmol/L (anovulatory cycle), AMH 52 pmol/L, fasting insulin slightly elevated, fasting glucose 5.1 mmol/L, TSH and prolactin within reference ranges, partner semen analysis normal, hysterosalpingogram tubes patent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacological agent for ovulation induction?

options.text: Clomifene citrate 50 mg daily on cycle days 2 to 6 with luteinising hormone monitoring every cycle, escalating to clomifene 150 mg if ovulation does not occur on the lower dose after three completed treatment cycles

Metformin 500 mg three times daily as monotherapy targeting weight reduction, ovulation restoration and improved insulin sensitivity over a 6 month trial before considering any second-line ovulation induction agent

Letrozole 2.5 mg daily on cycle days 2 to 6 with follicular tracking ultrasound and progesterone check, escalating by 2.5 mg per cycle to a maximum 7.5 mg if ovulation does not occur on the lower dose

Recombinant follicle-stimulating hormone subcutaneous injection daily from cycle day 3 with serial transvaginal follicular tracking from day 8 onwards under specialist supervision in a tertiary fertility clinic

Laparoscopic ovarian drilling under general anaesthetic as a single procedure offering durable ovulation restoration with lower multiple pregnancy rates than oral ovulation induction agents in selected anovulatory women

subtopic_detail: Severe pre-eclampsia magnesium sulfate seizure prophylaxis
stem: You are the obstetric registrar at a tertiary maternity hospital reviewing a 33-year-old primigravida at 35+5 weeks gestation referred from a peripheral hospital with severe pre-eclampsia. She has a frontal headache, visual scotomata and right upper quadrant pain. Her blood pressure has been 168/110 mmHg on repeated readings and her urinalysis shows 4+ protein. The fetal heart rate trace is reassuring. She has had a single 20 mg dose of oral nifedipine 30 minutes ago with persistent hypertension.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8 °C, HR 92, RR 18, SpO2 98% room air, BP 168/110 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Awake and orientated, hyperreflexia 3+ patellar with 4-beat clonus, right upper quadrant tenderness, no peripheral oedema, no focal neurology, fundal height 36 cm
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis 4+ protein, PCR 480 mg/mmol, platelets 98 x10^9/L, ALT 142 U/L, AST 168 U/L, creatinine 92 micromol/L, urate 0.42 mmol/L, FBC otherwise within reference ranges, CTG category 1

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate medication?

options.text: Oral methyldopa 250 mg three times daily titrated to target blood pressure of 130 to 140 over 80 to 90 mmHg over the next 24 to 48 hours of admission and obstetric specialist co-management on the antenatal ward

Intravenous hydralazine 5 mg bolus repeated every 20 minutes as needed and intravenous magnesium sulfate 6 g over 20 minutes loading dose, then commence intravenous magnesium sulfate 2 g per hour maintenance infusion
