Intravenous labetalol 20 mg bolus repeated every 10 minutes to a maximum cumulative dose of 80 mg and intravenous magnesium sulfate 6 g loading then 3 g per hour maintenance with deep tendon reflex monitoring

Intravenous labetalol 20 mg bolus titrated to target 140 to 150 over 90 to 100 mmHg and intravenous magnesium sulfate 4 g over 20 minutes then 1 g per hour maintenance with hourly deep tendon reflex monitoring

Intravenous glyceryl trinitrate infusion titrated to a target mean arterial pressure of 90 mmHg and oral diazepam 10 mg for seizure prophylaxis with continuous CTG and 4 hourly observations of blood pressure

subtopic_detail: Shoulder dystocia HELPERR sequence
stem: You are the obstetric registrar covering the delivery suite when you are called urgently to a vaginal birth in progress. The midwife reports that the fetal head has delivered, restituted to face the maternal left thigh, and then retracted against the perineum with no progress over the last 60 seconds despite routine downward axial traction. The mother is a primipara at 39+3 weeks with a recent fundal growth scan estimating the fetus at 4.2 kg. She is exhausted but cooperative.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal HR 104, RR 22, SpO2 99% room air, BP 122/78 mmHg, fetal heart rate 90/min and falling
data_table.Examination: Cephalic delivery with turtle sign, head retracted against perineum, anterior shoulder lodged behind pubic symphysis, posterior shoulder not yet delivered, attempt at routine axial traction has failed
data_table.Investigations: Not applicable in the acute manoeuvre phase; documentation will follow delivery

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Apply firm sustained fundal pressure to assist anterior shoulder delivery while continuing downward axial traction on the fetal head and request another midwife to support the maternal abdomen during the manoeuvre

Apply forceps to the after-coming head and rotate the head 180 degrees to deliver the anterior shoulder while the assistant maintains continuous downward traction to dislodge the impacted shoulder from the symphysis

Proceed immediately to symphysiotomy under local anaesthetic to enlarge the pelvic outlet because the anterior shoulder is impacted behind the symphysis and time-critical fetal distress is rapidly developing

Cease all maternal effort, call the consultant obstetrician and request the operating theatre to be readied for an emergency Zavanelli manoeuvre with replacement of the head and caesarean section delivery

Call for help, perform the McRoberts manoeuvre with hyperflexion of the maternal thighs onto the abdomen and apply suprapubic pressure aimed at displacing the anterior shoulder posteriorly while continuing axial traction

subtopic_detail: Primary postpartum haemorrhage uterotonic ladder
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in the delivery suite called urgently to a 28-year-old G2P1 woman who has just delivered a 4.0 kg baby vaginally after a prolonged second stage. Estimated blood loss is now 1200 mL and ongoing. The uterus is boggy and poorly contracted on palpation. There is no retained placenta and no obvious trauma to the genital tract on rapid inspection.

She has known chronic hypertension controlled on oral labetalol. Intravenous oxytocin 10 units has already been given by the midwife as part of active management.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.9 °C, HR 118, RR 22, SpO2 99% room air, BP 102/68 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Boggy poorly contracted uterus palpable at umbilicus, ongoing per-vaginal blood loss, no genital tract trauma identified, placenta delivered intact, IV access wide bore in both antecubital fossae
data_table.Investigations: FBC pre-delivery Hb 118 g/L, blood type O Rh-positive, group and hold sent, baseline coagulation profile within reference ranges, second large-bore cannula sited

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next pharmacological step?

options.text: Commence an oxytocin infusion 40 units in 1000 mL Hartmann's at 250 mL/hour, give rectal misoprostol 800 micrograms and intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g over 10 minutes alongside ongoing bimanual uterine massage

Commence an oxytocin infusion 40 units in 1000 mL Hartmann's at 250 mL/hour, give intramuscular carboprost (15-methyl PGF2 alpha) 250 micrograms and add intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g over 10 minutes
Commence an oxytocin infusion 40 units in 1000 mL Hartmann's at 250 mL/hour, give rectal misoprostol 600 micrograms and arrange a balloon tamponade device for insertion if bleeding continues

Commence intravenous norepinephrine titrated to mean arterial pressure 65 mmHg and give intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g over 10 minutes while preparing for emergency examination under anaesthesia in theatre
Commence an oxytocin infusion 40 units in 1000 mL Hartmann's at 250 mL/hour, give intramuscular ergometrine 250 micrograms and add intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g over 10 minutes

subtopic_detail: NCSP follow-up of higher-risk HPV positive primary screening
stem: You are the general practitioner reviewing a 38-year-old woman whose 5-yearly cervical screening test has just returned. She has had three previous normal Pap smears, is not pregnant, has no abnormal bleeding and is in a stable monogamous relationship. The cervical screening test detected HPV other than 16 and 18, and the liquid-based reflex cytology was negative for intraepithelial lesion or malignancy. She is asking about what should happen next under the National Cervical Screening Program.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.6 °C, HR 70, RR 14, SpO2 99% room air, BP 118/72 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Unremarkable bimanual examination, cervix appears smooth on speculum, no contact bleeding, no discharge
data_table.Investigations: Cervical screening test HPV (not 16/18) detected, reflex liquid-based cytology negative for intraepithelial lesion or malignancy, HIV negative, no immunosuppression

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step under the National Cervical Screening Program?

options.text: Refer immediately to a gynaecologist for diagnostic colposcopy with directed biopsy regardless of cytology to confirm presence or absence of high-grade cervical intraepithelial neoplasia and exclude occult invasive disease

Repeat the cervical screening test in 12 months to assess HPV persistence; refer for colposcopy if HPV is still detected at the 12-month repeat test or if any cytology becomes pHSIL or HSIL on reflex testing

Reassure her, return her to routine 5-yearly cervical screening because the reflex cytology was negative for intraepithelial lesion or malignancy and the HPV strain detected was a lower-oncogenic-risk non-16/18 type

Arrange a self-collected vaginal swab for HPV testing within 3 months as a confirmatory specimen because of a meaningful false-positive rate on practitioner-collected primary cervical samples in the screening setting

Prescribe topical imiquimod 5% cream three nights per week for 16 weeks to assist HPV clearance and arrange a repeat cervical screening test after treatment is complete with referral if persistent positivity remains

subtopic_detail: Monochorionic-diamniotic twin surveillance for TTTS and selective growth restriction
stem: You are the obstetric registrar in a tertiary maternal-fetal medicine clinic reviewing a 31-year-old woman who is 18+0 weeks by first-trimester crown-rump length in a spontaneously conceived twin pregnancy. The dating scan at 12 weeks showed two fetuses, a single placental mass, a thin intertwin membrane with a T-sign, and concordant nuchal translucency measurements. Her routine 18-week morphology scan today shows two structurally normal fetuses but the deepest vertical pocket of amniotic fluid in twin A is 1.4 cm and in twin B is 9.2 cm; estimated fetal weights are within 12% of each other and umbilical artery Dopplers are normal.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/72 mmHg, HR 82, T 36.8 °C, fundal height 24 cm, no uterine activity
data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender abdomen, cervix long and closed on transvaginal ultrasound at 38 mm
data_table.Investigations: Routine antenatal bloods normal, 18-week scan as above, both fetuses with normal cardiac four-chamber view

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Continue routine antenatal care with the next ultrasound at 28 weeks because the discordance in fluid volumes is within physiological variation for monochorionic-diamniotic twin pregnancies at this gestation

Arrange amnioreduction of the polyhydramniotic sac as a temporising day-stay procedure and review again in two weeks to assess whether the deepest vertical pocket discordance has stabilised on serial transabdominal ultrasound scans
Administer betamethasone 11.4 mg intramuscularly now with a second dose in 24 hours and plan delivery by caesarean section once a viable gestational age beyond 24+0 weeks has been reached

Refer urgently to a fetal medicine unit for fetoscopic laser ablation of placental anastomoses and continue fortnightly monochorionic surveillance with deepest vertical pocket, growth and middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity assessment

Arrange amniocentesis of both sacs for karyotype and parvovirus B19 PCR because monochorionic twins with discordant amniotic fluid should be evaluated for chromosomal or infective causes of growth and fluid discordance

subtopic_detail: History-indicated cervical cerclage timing in recurrent mid-trimester loss
stem: You are the antenatal clinic registrar seeing a 33-year-old G4P0 at 11+5 weeks. She has had three previous pregnancies ending in painless mid-trimester losses at 19, 20 and 22 weeks, each preceded by sudden membrane rupture without contractions or bleeding. There is no history of cervical surgery, infection or trauma. She is otherwise well, takes folic acid and iodine, and dating ultrasound confirms a singleton with normal nuchal translucency. She asks what can be done in this pregnancy to reduce the risk of another mid-trimester loss.

data_table.Examination: Cervix appears closed on speculum; transvaginal length 35 mm with no funnelling
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, thyroid function and HbA1c normal; antiphospholipid screen negative on 12-week recheck after prior negative result

lead_in: What is the most appropriate intervention?

options.text: Commence vaginal progesterone 200 micrograms nightly from 16 weeks and arrange fortnightly transvaginal cervical length surveillance from 16 to 24 weeks, deferring any cerclage decision until cervical shortening below 25 mm is documented
Plan elective McDonald cervical cerclage at 12 to 14 weeks gestation under regional anaesthesia with single-dose perioperative antibiotic prophylaxis and removal at 36 to 37 weeks gestation
Arrange transabdominal cerclage at 14 to 16 weeks gestation via open laparotomy because of the failure of three previous pregnancies, accepting that delivery will require elective caesarean section
Recommend strict bed rest from 16 weeks gestation onward with hospital admission for monitoring from 18 weeks gestation until 24 weeks gestation and use of an Arabin pessary if shortening develops

Provide reassurance, schedule routine antenatal care and counsel that no specific intervention has proven benefit in this scenario given the absence of cervical shortening on her booking transvaginal scan

subtopic_detail: Vacuum versus forceps choice in delayed second stage at full station with adequate analgesia
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar called to a primiparous woman at 40+3 weeks in established second stage of labour for 2 hours and 50 minutes despite oxytocin augmentation and active pushing for 90 minutes. She has a working epidural sited 6 hours ago with bilateral T10 block. The CTG shows late decelerations with reduced variability for the last 12 minutes.

The vertex is at +2 station, occiput-anterior with no caput, no moulding and the head is fully engaged on abdominal palpation. The bladder is empty after recent catheterisation.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal BP 124/78 mmHg, HR 96, T 37.0 °C, fetal HR baseline 140 with late decelerations to 100
data_table.Examination: Vertex at +2, OA, no caput or moulding, fully dilated, membranes ruptured, clear liquor
data_table.Investigations: Fetal scalp lactate 4.1 mmol/L, maternal blood group O positive, antibody screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in delivery?

options.text: Continue active maternal pushing with directed coaching for a further 30 minutes and only escalate to instrumental delivery if the fetal heart rate trace deteriorates further or if no progress is made on the next vaginal examination

Transfer urgently to theatre for category 1 caesarean section because instrumental delivery from +2 station carries an unacceptable risk of failed instrumental delivery and neonatal injury at this advanced maternal effort point
Perform a midcavity rotational Kielland forceps delivery in the labour room with infiltration of the perineum using 1% lidocaine 10 mL prior to the application of the blades to the fetal head

Perform a Ventouse delivery with a Kiwi single-use cup using sequential pulls with contractions only, accepting up to three cup detachments before considering escalation to forceps or to theatre for trial of instrumental delivery

Perform an outlet Ventouse delivery with a soft cup in the labour room using maternal effort with each contraction and a maximum of three pulls and two cup detachments before recourse to forceps or theatre

subtopic_detail: External cephalic version offer at term for uncomplicated breech presentation
stem: You are the antenatal clinic registrar reviewing a 28-year-old G2P1 at 36+5 weeks in an uncomplicated singleton pregnancy. The first pregnancy was a normal vaginal delivery of a 3400 g infant. Examination today suggests a longitudinal lie with breech presentation, confirmed on bedside ultrasound as a frank breech with normal amniotic fluid, posterior placenta, estimated fetal weight 2900 g and reassuring umbilical artery Dopplers. She has no contraindications to vaginal delivery and is asking about her options for the rest of the pregnancy and delivery.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 116/70 mmHg, HR 78, T 36.7 °C, fundal height 34 cm, audible fetal heart 142
data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender uterus, frank breech with head palpable in fundus, cervix not assessed; no uterine activity
data_table.Investigations: 36-week ultrasound as above, group B Strep swab pending, blood group A positive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Recommend elective caesarean section at 39 weeks gestation now without further attempts at version because the Term Breech Trial established lower neonatal morbidity with planned caesarean for term breech presentation
Encourage daily moxibustion at the BL67 acupoint and knee-chest positioning exercises for 10 minutes three times daily and review at 38 weeks to reassess fetal presentation

Offer external cephalic version at 37+0 weeks in a unit with theatre and CTG facilities with tocolysis, anti-D if Rh negative, and counselling on a 50% success rate and rare risks of placental abruption or emergency caesarean

Recommend planned vaginal breech birth at the local district hospital with continuous CTG monitoring without first attempting external cephalic version because of her favourable obstetric history of one prior normal vaginal birth
Arrange weekly transvaginal cervical length scans from 37 weeks and admit for induction of labour with prostaglandin pessary at 38 weeks if cervical length is favourable for breech vaginal delivery

subtopic_detail: VBAC eligibility and risks counselling with prior lower-segment caesarean
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in clinic seeing a 32-year-old G3P2 at 30+0 weeks who is asking about a trial of vaginal birth after caesarean. Her first delivery was an uncomplicated normal vaginal birth at 39 weeks. Her second was an elective caesarean at 39+4 weeks for breech presentation; the operation note documents a low transverse uterine incision with no extension and an uncomplicated postoperative course.

The current pregnancy is uncomplicated, the fetus is cephalic with estimated weight on the 50th centile, and she lives 25 minutes from a maternity unit with 24-hour theatre, anaesthesia and on-site paediatric services.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 112/68 mmHg, HR 80, BMI 27, fundal height 30 cm
data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender uterus, cephalic presentation, regular fetal heart rate 148
data_table.Investigations: Routine antenatal bloods normal, 28-week morphology and growth normal, GBS swab pending at 36 weeks

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate counselling for planned mode of birth?

options.text: Recommend planned VBAC with continuous CTG monitoring in labour and counsel on a 0.5% uterine rupture risk, 70-75% success rate and the importance of intravenous access and group and hold on admission

Recommend elective repeat caesarean section at 39 weeks because two prior births including one caesarean meet criteria that contraindicate VBAC at any Australian metropolitan maternity unit regardless of facility level

Recommend induction of labour at 39 weeks with vaginal prostaglandin E2 and oxytocin augmentation as needed to achieve delivery before 40 weeks and minimise uterine rupture risk associated with post-dates pregnancy

Recommend VBAC at home with a private midwife and continuous Doppler auscultation every 15 minutes in active labour because her prior vaginal birth makes the rupture risk negligible and hospital transfer is feasible

Defer the decision until 38 weeks and reassess based on cervical length and Bishop score at that time, planning VBAC only if the cervix is favourable for spontaneous labour without any need for cervical ripening

subtopic_detail: Hyperemesis gravidarum admission and thiamine before glucose
stem: You are the gynaecology registrar in the emergency department reviewing a 26-year-old G2P1 at 9+0 weeks in her second pregnancy who presents with three weeks of intractable nausea, 14 vomits in the last 24 hours and inability to tolerate oral fluids. She has lost 6 kg since her booking weight 4 weeks ago (8% of pre-pregnancy body weight). Pyridoxine, doxylamine and metoclopramide tablets at home have not helped. She has not taken any thiamine supplementation. She has no fever, abdominal pain or per vaginal bleeding.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 96/58 mmHg supine, HR 112, T 36.6 °C, RR 18, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes, capillary refill 3 sec, mildly ketotic breath, soft non-tender abdomen, no localising signs
data_table.Investigations: Na 132, K 3.2, Cl 92, urea 8.6, creatinine 78, glucose 3.6 mmol/L, urinary ketones 3+, beta-hCG appropriate for 9 weeks, TFTs pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management plan?

options.text: Commence 5% dextrose 1 L over 2 hours, add ondansetron 4 mg IV every 8 hours and arrange discharge home with oral pyridoxine, doxylamine and antenatal dietitian follow-up within the next week
Administer one litre of Hartmann's solution over 1 hour, give IM metoclopramide 10 mg every 8 hours, and discharge once tolerating oral fluids without specific thiamine or potassium replacement

Admit for IV normal saline with added potassium chloride to correct dehydration, give IV thiamine 100 mg daily before any glucose-containing fluid, and use ondansetron or metoclopramide as antiemetic with pyridoxine and doxylamine continued

Admit for total parenteral nutrition via a peripherally inserted central catheter for 7 days, withhold all oral intake and stop pyridoxine and doxylamine while parenteral nutrition is in place to allow gut rest

Arrange urgent ultrasound to exclude molar pregnancy and multiple gestation, withhold antiemetics until imaging is complete and refer to early pregnancy assessment for repeat beta-hCG in 48 hours before further treatment

subtopic_detail: Antiphospholipid syndrome confirmation and aspirin plus LMWH management
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar in a preconception clinic seeing a 35-year-old woman who has had three consecutive first-trimester miscarriages at 8, 10 and 9 weeks gestation, each with documented fetal pole and absent fetal heart on follow-up ultrasound. She has no living children and no prior pregnancy losses beyond 12 weeks. She is otherwise well, takes folic acid and iodine.

Investigations after her second loss showed normal karyotype on both partners, normal pelvic ultrasound, normal thyroid function and HbA1c. Lupus anticoagulant was positive on a single sample. Repeat testing 12 weeks later again shows positive lupus anticoagulant; anticardiolipin and anti-beta-2-glycoprotein-1 antibodies are negative on both occasions.

data_table.Examination: Unremarkable; no thrombotic skin signs
data_table.Investigations: Both LA samples positive 12 weeks apart, ACL and B2GP1 negative both times, FBC and renal function normal, no prior thrombosis

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate plan once she conceives again?

options.text: Commence warfarin 5 mg daily before conception and continue throughout pregnancy with a target INR of 2.0 to 3.0 to minimise placental microthrombi formation and recurrent first-trimester loss

Confirm obstetric antiphospholipid syndrome on her recurrent loss pattern and persistent lupus anticoagulant, then once pregnancy is confirmed commence low-dose aspirin 100 mg daily and prophylactic enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneously daily

Recommend natural killer cell immunotherapy with intravenous immunoglobulin every 4 weeks from confirmation of pregnancy until 28 weeks gestation to suppress maternal alloimmune rejection of the embryo

Counsel that no specific treatment is indicated because she does not meet criteria for obstetric APS without anticardiolipin or anti-beta-2-glycoprotein-1 antibody positivity in addition to her lupus anticoagulant
Commence high-dose prednisolone 40 mg daily and aspirin 100 mg daily from a positive pregnancy test and continue at this dose until 20 weeks gestation to suppress autoimmune placental injury

subtopic_detail: Heterotopic pregnancy after IVF with intrauterine and adnexal sac
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar in the early pregnancy assessment clinic seeing a 34-year-old woman at 7+3 weeks by IVF transfer date who reports increasing right iliac fossa pain over the last 48 hours and a small amount of dark per vaginal bleeding today. She is haemodynamically stable. The pregnancy was conceived via fresh embryo transfer (two blastocysts) 51 days ago.

Transvaginal ultrasound shows an intrauterine gestational sac with a 6+5 fetal pole and cardiac activity (CRL 11 mm), free fluid in the pouch of Douglas, and a separate right adnexal complex mass measuring 28 mm with no obvious yolk sac but a hyperechoic ring surrounding a small fluid collection.

data_table.Examination: Right iliac fossa tenderness with voluntary guarding, no peritonism, closed cervix on speculum, scant dark blood
data_table.Investigations: Serum beta-hCG 24,000 IU/L, Hb 118 g/L, FBC otherwise normal, group A positive antibody negative

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence single-dose intramuscular methotrexate 50 mg/m^2 to treat the right adnexal pregnancy while observing the intrauterine pregnancy expectantly with serial beta-hCG monitoring every 48 hours and ultrasound at 1 week

Arrange repeat ultrasound and beta-hCG in 48 hours with safety-net advice for emergency presentation if pain or bleeding worsen, on the basis that the adnexal mass may represent a corpus luteum cyst rather than a coexistent ectopic pregnancy

Arrange ultrasound-guided transvaginal aspiration of the adnexal mass and instillation of potassium chloride 2 mmol into the ectopic sac, preserving the intrauterine pregnancy with no need for laparoscopic intervention

Arrange urgent laparoscopic salpingectomy of the right tubal ectopic pregnancy under general anaesthesia, manipulating the uterus minimally and counselling that the intrauterine pregnancy will most likely continue uneventfully

Plan suction evacuation of the intrauterine pregnancy in theatre followed by single-dose methotrexate 50 mg/m^2 for the ectopic pregnancy given the high risk of miscarriage of the intrauterine pregnancy after laparoscopy

subtopic_detail: NCSP management of oncogenic HPV 16/18 positive primary screening test
stem: You are the GP registrar reviewing a 32-year-old woman who had her routine Cervical Screening Test 4 weeks ago. The result reports oncogenic HPV detected, type 16, with reflex liquid-based cytology showing low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (LSIL). She has had two prior normal screening tests at age 25 and 27, is in a monogamous relationship, has never had an abnormal cervical screen and is not pregnant. She is not immunocompromised. She has no symptoms; specifically no postcoital bleeding, intermenstrual bleeding or vaginal discharge.

data_table.Examination: Speculum exam at sample collection 4 weeks ago: cervix appears macroscopically normal
data_table.Investigations: CST result as above: HPV 16 positive, reflex cytology LSIL; previous CSTs negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat the cervical screening test in 12 months because cytology shows only LSIL and most low-grade lesions regress spontaneously without colposcopy or further intervention being required for screening management

Arrange repeat cervical screening test in 6 months together with self-collected HPV swab to confirm persistence before referring her for colposcopy and biopsy at a tertiary gynaecology oncology centre
Treat empirically with a course of cervical cryotherapy in clinic to ablate any low-grade lesion, then repeat the cervical screening test in 6 months to confirm resolution of the HPV 16 infection

Arrange counselling about HPV transmission and vaccinate her with the 9-valent HPV vaccine catch-up dose series, then repeat screening in 5 years if vaccination response is documented as adequate by serology testing

Refer to colposcopy for direct visualisation of the cervix and directed biopsy as needed because oncogenic HPV type 16 detection on primary screening is a higher-risk result regardless of accompanying reflex cytology grade

subtopic_detail: Failed first-line hormonal therapy and indication for diagnostic laparoscopy with excision
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 27-year-old nulligravid woman with 4 years of cyclical pelvic pain, dysmenorrhoea, deep dyspareunia and ovulatory pain. She has had a 12-month trial of combined oral contraceptive pill taken continuously without break, with adequate compliance, and a 6-month trial of norethisterone 5 mg twice daily added subsequently. Her pain numerical rating score remains 7 to 8 out of 10 on most days with 3 to 4 days of school absence per month.

She has not yet attempted pregnancy and is not currently trying to conceive. Examination shows a tender uterosacral ligament nodule and a fixed retroverted uterus. Pelvic ultrasound shows a 3 cm left ovarian endometrioma and a hypoechoic mass at the rectovaginal septum.

data_table.Examination: Tender uterosacral nodule, fixed retroverted uterus, no palpable mass on bimanual
data_table.Investigations: Pelvic US: 3 cm left endometrioma, suspected rectovaginal deep infiltrating endometriosis; CA-125 elevated at 76; STI screen negative

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Plan diagnostic laparoscopy with excision of visible endometriotic deposits at a unit with bowel and ureteric expertise, after preoperative imaging staging and multidisciplinary planning for possible rectovaginal excision

Commence GnRH agonist (leuprorelin 3.75 mg monthly) with tibolone add-back for 12 months because medical menopause is the most effective second-line therapy and avoids surgical risk in young nulligravid women

Insert a levonorgestrel-releasing 52 mg intrauterine device as third-line hormonal therapy and review symptom response in 6 months before considering surgical investigation or referral to a tertiary endometriosis service

Recommend a definitive total laparoscopic hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy because of severity, failed medical therapy and presence of deep infiltrating disease confirmed on ultrasound and examination

Reassure her that elevated CA-125 with an endometrioma is typical and continue current hormonal therapy with the addition of regular pelvic floor physiotherapy and a multidisciplinary pain clinic referral instead of surgical management

subtopic_detail: Lichen sclerosus diagnosis and ultrapotent topical corticosteroid induction
stem: You are the GP registrar reviewing a 58-year-old postmenopausal woman with 6 months of vulval itch, soreness and dyspareunia. She has tried over-the-counter topical clotrimazole without benefit. There is no urinary or bowel symptom, and she has not noticed unusual discharge. She has a personal history of autoimmune thyroiditis. Examination shows the typical figure-of-eight white atrophic plaques involving the labia minora, clitoris and perianal region with loss of architecture and partial fusion of the clitoral hood. There are no ulcers or focal masses. The vagina is not involved.

data_table.Examination: Symmetrical figure-of-eight white atrophic plaques, loss of labia minora architecture, partial clitoral hood fusion, no ulceration
data_table.Investigations: No prior biopsy; STI swabs negative; vaginal pH and discharge normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Prescribe topical oestrogen cream nightly for 12 weeks because postmenopausal vulval atrophy is the most likely diagnosis and topical oestrogen restores vulval epithelial integrity and improves dyspareunia and itch

Commence clobetasol propionate 0.05% ointment nightly for 4 weeks, then alternate nights for 4 weeks, then twice weekly maintenance, with safety-net advice to return if any ulcer, fissure or focal mass develops

Refer urgently to gynaecology oncology for biopsy under general anaesthesia and consideration of wide local excision because of the multifocal white plaques in a postmenopausal woman that may represent VIN or invasive squamous cell carcinoma

Prescribe a 6-week course of topical hydrocortisone 1% twice daily and a vulval emollient and reassess at 6 weeks, reserving stronger topical steroids for refractory cases that have failed milder therapy

Treat empirically with oral fluconazole 150 mg once weekly for 6 weeks for presumed recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis given the unresponsiveness to topical clotrimazole and consider HRT systemic therapy

subtopic_detail: First-line management of stress urinary incontinence with supervised pelvic floor training
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar in clinic seeing a 48-year-old G3P3 with 3 years of involuntary urine loss with cough, sneeze and lifting her grandchildren. She does not get up at night to void and denies urgency, frequency, dysuria or urinary tract infections. Her BMI is 31. She is still menstruating regularly and is not on any hormonal medication. She drinks 4 cups of coffee daily.

A 3-day bladder diary shows average daily fluid intake of 2.5 L, 7 voids per day, no nocturia and 4 episodes of stress leakage with provocation. Postvoid residual on bladder scan is 35 mL. Urinalysis is unremarkable. Cough stress test reveals immediate leakage with full bladder and no urethral hypermobility on examination.

data_table.Examination: Cough stress test positive at full bladder, no demonstrable cystocele or rectocele, no urethral hypermobility, well-supported anterior vaginal wall
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis nil; PVR 35 mL; 3-day diary as above

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate first-line management?

options.text: Refer for urodynamic studies to confirm urodynamic stress incontinence before commencing any conservative therapy because the bladder diary findings are subjective and may not distinguish stress from mixed incontinence

Refer for placement of a mid-urethral retropubic mesh sling as definitive first-line surgical therapy given her relatively young age and the impact on her quality of life and ability to engage with her grandchildren

Trial oxybutynin 5 mg twice daily for 6 weeks and review symptoms with a repeat 3-day bladder diary before considering escalation to mirabegron or referral for urodynamic assessment and surgical treatment

Refer for supervised pelvic floor muscle training with a continence physiotherapist for 12 weeks, advise weight loss aiming for 5 to 10% body weight reduction and reduce caffeine intake from 4 to under 2 cups daily

Commence intravaginal oestrogen pessary nightly for 6 weeks and review, on the basis that oestrogen deficiency contributes to urethral closure failure even in still-menstruating women over 40 years of age

subtopic_detail: Recognition of absolute contraindications to systemic menopausal hormone therapy
stem:
You are the GP registrar reviewing a 52-year-old woman with 18 months of vasomotor symptoms (10 to 12 hot flushes per day, severe night sweats waking her 4 times nightly), mood changes and sleep disturbance. Her last menstrual period was 14 months ago. She has tried cognitive behavioural therapy for hot flushes, paroxetine 20 mg daily for 12 weeks (no benefit, ceased 6 weeks ago) and clonidine 50 mcg twice daily (no benefit).

She had a unilateral hormone-receptor-positive invasive ductal breast carcinoma 6 years ago treated with lumpectomy, sentinel lymph node biopsy, radiotherapy and 5 years of tamoxifen, completed 12 months ago. She has no evidence of recurrence and was discharged from oncology surveillance 6 months ago.

data_table.Examination: Unremarkable; both breasts soft with surgical scar on right; no axillary lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Last surveillance mammogram 6 months ago: normal; FSH not measured (clinically postmenopausal)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her vasomotor symptoms?

options.text: Commence transdermal oestradiol 50 micrograms patch twice weekly with cyclical micronised progesterone 200 mg orally nightly for 12 days each month and review symptom response at 12 weeks

Prescribe tibolone 2.5 mg daily because it has a lower breast cancer risk profile than combined oestrogen-progestogen and has been shown to be safe to use in breast cancer survivors with severe vasomotor symptoms

Trial venlafaxine 37.5 mg daily titrated to 75 mg daily over 2 weeks for vasomotor symptoms and refer her to a sleep psychologist for CBT-insomnia given the persistent night sweats and sleep disturbance

Refer to a specialist menopause clinic for consideration of low-dose vaginal oestrogen as systemic treatment for hot flushes because the systemic absorption from vaginal preparations is too low to affect breast cancer recurrence risk

Recommend phytoestrogens (red clover, black cohosh) at over-the-counter doses with a focus on lifestyle modification including avoiding triggers, layered clothing, weight maintenance and regular exercise as first-line for breast cancer survivors

subtopic_detail: Intrapartum GBS prophylaxis indications and antibiotic choice
stem: You are the obstetric resident on the labour ward reviewing a 28-year-old G2P1 at 39+1 weeks who presented 6 hours ago in spontaneous labour. Her routine 36-week vaginal-rectal swab grew Group B streptococcus. She is in established labour with regular contractions every 3 minutes and is now 6 cm dilated with intact membranes. Her temperature is 37.0, fetal heart rate is reassuring on intermittent auscultation, and she reports no penicillin allergy. Her previous baby was unaffected by GBS.

data_table.Examination: 6 cm cervix, fully effaced, vertex at -1 station, membranes intact, regular contractions q3 min
data_table.Investigations: 36-week LVS positive for GBS; FBC and routine antenatal bloods normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate antibiotic plan?

options.text: Administer a single oral dose of 1 g azithromycin in early labour as effective single-dose prophylaxis covering Group B streptococcus and atypical organisms, with no further antibiotic required throughout the labour course

Defer antibiotic administration until membrane rupture or until the cervix reaches 8 cm because GBS transmission risk only becomes clinically relevant in the second stage of labour with imminent delivery imminent
Commence intravenous benzylpenicillin 3 g now followed by 1.8 g every 4 hours until delivery to provide adequate intrapartum antibiotic cover for early-onset neonatal GBS sepsis prevention

Commence intravenous vancomycin 1 g over one hour every 12 hours as first-line therapy because vancomycin has superior intrapartum tissue penetration and lower neonatal nephrotoxicity than narrow-spectrum penicillins given in labour

Decline intrapartum prophylaxis because she had a healthy unaffected first baby and previously unaffected babies have established maternal immunity that durably reduces transmission risk to less than one percent during any subsequent labour

subtopic_detail: Gestational diabetes mellitus diagnostic thresholds (ADIPS 2017)
stem:
You are the antenatal care GP reviewing a 32-year-old G1P0 at 27+5 weeks. She has a BMI of 31, her mother has type 2 diabetes and she is otherwise well. Her routine 28-week 75 g oral glucose tolerance test taken this week returned a fasting plasma glucose of 5.3 mmol/L, a 1-hour value of 9.8 mmol/L and a 2-hour value of 8.2 mmol/L.

She has had no symptoms of polyuria or polydipsia. Her fundal height is 28 cm and the fetus is moving well; recent ultrasound at 22 weeks was unremarkable.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 122/78, HR 80, T 36.6, weight 86 kg, BMI 31
data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender abdomen, fundal height 28 cm, fetal heart rate 142, no oedema
data_table.Investigations: OGTT 75 g: fasting 5.3 mmol/L, 1-hr 9.8 mmol/L, 2-hr 8.2 mmol/L; HbA1c 5.6%; urinalysis no glucose, no protein

lead_in: What is the most appropriate interpretation and management?

options.text: Diagnose overt diabetes in pregnancy (not GDM) based on the 1-hour value above 9.5 mmol/L and commence basal-bolus insulin therapy immediately, deferring lifestyle modification because pharmacotherapy is required from the outset

She does not meet diagnostic thresholds for gestational diabetes because all three OGTT values are below the WHO 2013 cut-offs of 5.5 fasting, 11.1 at 1-hour and 8.5 at 2-hour; reassure and repeat routine antenatal care

She meets ADIPS criteria for gestational diabetes mellitus on the basis of the elevated fasting glucose; commence self-monitoring of blood glucose, refer to a multidisciplinary diabetes-in-pregnancy clinic and provide medical nutrition therapy

Diagnose impaired glucose tolerance only and recommend a repeat 75 g OGTT in 4 weeks to confirm persistence before committing the woman to the multidisciplinary diabetes-in-pregnancy pathway with all of its associated lifestyle interventions

Recommend a 3-day high-carbohydrate diet and repeat the OGTT to confirm because false positives are common in women with high BMI and a single high fasting value during pregnancy is unreliable as a stand-alone test

subtopic_detail: Postpartum endometritis after caesarean section
stem: You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 30-year-old G2P2 day 3 post emergency caesarean section for failure to progress at 9 cm. Her membranes were ruptured for 22 hours before delivery and she received a single dose of intravenous cefazolin at incision. Today she has a temperature of 38.6 degrees C, lower abdominal tenderness, foul-smelling lochia and uterine tenderness on bimanual examination. She is otherwise haemodynamically stable. Her FBC shows neutrophilic leucocytosis and her urine dipstick and chest examination are unremarkable.

data_table.Examination: Tender boggy uterus at umbilicus, foul-smelling lochia, CS wound clean and dry, calves soft, chest clear
data_table.Investigations: WCC 18.6 x10^9/L (neutrophils 16.0), CRP 142 mg/L, urinalysis negative, blood cultures taken, lactate 1.6 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Commence intravenous ampicillin 2 g 6-hourly plus gentamicin 5 mg/kg daily plus metronidazole 500 mg 12-hourly until clinically afebrile for 24 to 48 hours, then transition to oral amoxicillin clavulanate to complete a 7-day course

Commence oral cefalexin 500 mg 6-hourly plus doxycycline 100 mg 12-hourly for a 10-day outpatient course because oral options are equivalent in efficacy and avoid prolonged maternal hospital separation from the newborn

Administer single dose intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g and azithromycin 1 g orally as syndromic treatment for pelvic inflammatory disease and arrange outpatient gynaecology review within 7 days for clinical reassessment and follow up swabs

Treat with intravenous piperacillin tazobactam 4.5 g 8-hourly as monotherapy for 10 days regardless of clinical response, because broad-spectrum monotherapy avoids the nephrotoxicity associated with gentamicin combination regimens

Withhold antibiotic therapy pending blood culture and high vaginal swab results in 48 hours, and treat with intravenous paracetamol and uterotonic ergometrine while monitoring trends in inflammatory markers over the same time period

subtopic_detail: Routine antenatal anti-D prophylaxis scheduling
stem: You are the antenatal care GP reviewing a 24-year-old G1P0 RhD-negative woman at 27+5 weeks. Her booking blood group was confirmed Rh-negative with no atypical antibodies on the indirect antiglobulin test, and her partner is RhD-positive. The pregnancy has been uncomplicated and she has had no episodes of bleeding, abdominal trauma or invasive procedures since conception. Her routine 28-week bloods including a repeat antibody screen have been collected today.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 116/74, HR 78, T 36.7, fundal height 28 cm
data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender abdomen, fetal heart rate 144, no bleeding
data_table.Investigations: Maternal blood group O Rh-negative, indirect antiglobulin test negative, partner Rh-positive, anti-D titre not yet performed in pregnancy

lead_in: What is the recommended schedule of anti-D immunoglobulin?

options.text: Determine fetal RhD genotype by free-fetal DNA testing at 26 weeks and administer anti-D immunoglobulin only if the fetus is confirmed RhD-positive, otherwise withhold all anti-D prophylaxis throughout the pregnancy

Defer antenatal anti-D prophylaxis until 34 weeks because a single late-third-trimester dose has been shown to be non-inferior to the two-dose schedule and avoids the small risk of plasma-derived product transmission of infection

Administer a single 1250 IU intramuscular dose now at 28 weeks and do not repeat at 34 weeks because the higher-dose single regimen provides adequate prophylaxis against subsequent fetomaternal haemorrhage until birth

Withhold antenatal anti-D prophylaxis and administer only a postnatal dose within 72 hours of birth if the baby tests RhD-positive on cord blood sampling at delivery, as routine antenatal dosing is no longer recommended in low-risk pregnancies
Administer 625 IU of intramuscular anti-D immunoglobulin at 28 weeks and again at 34 weeks, with a further dose within 72 hours of birth if the baby is RhD-positive on cord blood testing

subtopic_detail: Severe pre-eclampsia at 32 weeks - magnesium and steroid timing
stem: You are the obstetric registrar admitting a 27-year-old G1P0 at 32+1 weeks who presents to triage with new severe headache, blurred vision and right upper quadrant pain. Her BP was 158/108 on arrival and a repeat at 15 minutes is 162/110. She has 3+ proteinuria on dipstick and brisk lower limb reflexes with no clonus. The CTG shows a baseline of 140 with normal variability and no decelerations. The fetus is in cephalic presentation, ultrasound at 30 weeks showed normal growth and Dopplers.

data_table.Examination: Brisk reflexes no clonus, no focal neurology, soft non-tender abdomen, fundal height 31 cm, CTG reassuring
data_table.Investigations: Urine PCR 380 mg/mmol, platelets 138 x10^9/L, ALT 92 U/L, AST 88 U/L, creatinine 78 micromol/L, Hb 124 g/L, INR 1.0

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management plan?

options.text: Commence a low-dose aspirin 150 mg daily and calcium 1.5 g daily as secondary prevention of pre-eclampsia and arrange a fortnightly outpatient growth and Doppler scan and growth scans aiming for delivery at term in this primigravida

Commence oral methyldopa 250 mg three times daily and arrange weekly outpatient antenatal review with home blood pressure monitoring, deferring magnesium and steroids until 34 weeks because expectant management is preferred at this gestation

Deliver immediately by category 1 caesarean section regardless of cervical state because severe pre-eclampsia with any HELLP feature is an absolute contraindication to attempted vaginal birth at any gestation under 37 weeks

Administer intravenous hydralazine 10 mg bolus and intravenous furosemide 40 mg now, omit magnesium because reflexes show no clonus, and arrange induction of labour over the next 12 hours regardless of fetal lung maturity at this gestation

Administer intravenous magnesium sulfate 4 g loading then 1 g/hour for seizure prophylaxis, treat her blood pressure with oral or intravenous labetalol or nifedipine to target under 160/110, give intramuscular betamethasone 11.4 mg and plan delivery within 24 to 48 hours

subtopic_detail: Symptomatic placenta praevia at 34 weeks
stem: You are the obstetric registrar called to triage to assess a 33-year-old G3P2 at 34+2 weeks who has had a sudden painless bright red vaginal bleed of approximately 200 mL while resting at home this evening. Her 20-week morphology scan identified a complete placenta praevia covering the internal os; a follow-up scan at 32 weeks confirmed the placenta still covered the os. Her previous two deliveries were by caesarean section. She is anxious but haemodynamically stable. The CTG is reassuring with no contractions felt.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft non-tender, fundal height 34 cm, cephalic presentation, sanitary pad shows fresh blood approximately 50 mL since arrival, CTG baseline 140 normal variability
data_table.Investigations: Hb 114 g/L, platelets 220 x10^9/L, group and screen, crossmatch in progress, INR 1.0, fibrinogen 4.1 g/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Reassure her and discharge home with strict bed rest and instructions to return with any further bleeding, contractions or reduced fetal movements over the coming days until the planned 36-week elective caesarean delivery

Perform a digital vaginal examination to assess cervical dilatation and the lower uterine segment placental relationship and proceed to artificial rupture of membranes if the cervix is favourable to induce labour for vaginal birth

Admit for inpatient observation with continuous CTG, two large-bore intravenous cannulas, crossmatched blood ready, intramuscular betamethasone for fetal lung maturity, no vaginal examination, and discuss timing of caesarean delivery with the consultant

Proceed immediately to category 1 caesarean section without waiting for crossmatched blood or maternal stabilisation because any antepartum haemorrhage at over 32 weeks in placenta praevia mandates immediate delivery regardless of CTG

Administer tocolytic indometacin and intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g and continue outpatient management with a daily home CTG and weekly hospital review for ongoing bleeding episodes until 37 weeks of gestation are reached

subtopic_detail: Umbilical cord prolapse - immediate management
stem: You are the obstetric registrar called urgently to the labour ward where a 26-year-old G2P1 at 38+4 weeks has just had spontaneous rupture of membranes during a routine examination. She was at 4 cm cervical dilatation with the head at -3 station. The midwife felt a pulsating cord at the introitus on the gush of liquor. The CTG had been reassuring but now shows a prolonged bradycardia of 70 bpm sustained for 2 minutes. The mother is supine on the bed. The theatre team has not been activated yet.

data_table.Vital signs: Mother: BP 124/76, HR 102, SpO2 99%, T 36.8; Fetal: HR 70 sustained 2 minutes
data_table.Examination: Cord palpable and pulsating at introitus, cervix 4 cm, head at -3 station, baseline preceding was 140
data_table.Investigations: Recent FBC and group and screen routine, no abnormalities

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Encourage rapid pushing with sustained Valsalva manoeuvres and prepare for an operative vaginal birth with rotational Kielland forceps because vaginal birth at 4 cm with a sustained bradycardia is the fastest route to delivery

Place the mother in knee-chest position or steep Trendelenburg with manual elevation of the presenting part to relieve cord compression, activate category 1 caesarean section and consider tocolysis with terbutaline 250 mcg subcutaneously en route to theatre

Reduce the cord back into the uterus manually and place a tight perineal pad over the introitus to prevent further prolapse, then continue routine labour management with intermittent auscultation over the following hours

Administer intravenous oxytocin 5 IU bolus followed by an infusion to augment contractions and accelerate cervical dilatation to enable vaginal birth, and reassess the CTG after 15 minutes of augmented contractions

Insert a 500 mL Foley catheter into the bladder and inflate the balloon to elevate the presenting part, then transfer the patient by ambulance to a tertiary maternal-fetal medicine centre for definitive operative delivery

subtopic_detail: Shoulder dystocia first-line management algorithm
stem: You are the obstetric registrar attending a vaginal birth of a 32-year-old G3P2 at 40+3 weeks. Her two previous babies weighed 3900 g and 4100 g. The current pregnancy was uncomplicated and her clinically estimated fetal weight at 39 weeks was 4000 g. After delivery of the head there is a turtle-neck sign, restitution does not occur and routine axial traction fails to deliver the anterior shoulder. The clock starts. The midwife immediately calls for senior assistance and a neonatal team.

data_table.Vital signs: Mother BP 122/76, HR 108; Fetal HR 130 prior
data_table.Examination: Head delivered, turtle-neck sign, no restitution, anterior shoulder behind pubic symphysis, perineum intact
data_table.Investigations: Bladder empty, epidural in place

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate next step after calling for help?

options.text: Perform a generous mediolateral episiotomy as the immediate first action because more vaginal space is the primary mechanical solution to shoulder dystocia regardless of the shoulder-pelvis relationship and the perineum is the rate-limiting structure

Hyperflex maternal hips onto the abdomen in McRoberts position and apply firm suprapubic pressure directed posteriorly and laterally with axial traction on the fetal head to attempt anterior shoulder release

Apply firm fundal pressure with strong downward axial traction on the head and ask the mother to push vigorously for 30 seconds to dislodge the anterior shoulder by combined uterine and maternal expulsive forces

Move directly to the Zavanelli manoeuvre by cephalic replacement and emergency caesarean section as the safest first action whenever the anterior shoulder is impacted because internal manoeuvres carry unacceptably high brachial plexus injury risk

Cut the umbilical cord and proceed with prompt vaginal extraction with traction below the horizontal because cord transection ends the time-critical hypoxia and provides immediate tactile access to the shoulder

subtopic_detail: Gestational trophoblastic neoplasia after complete mole - referral and chemotherapy
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar following a 32-year-old woman who underwent suction evacuation of a complete hydatidiform mole 9 weeks ago. Histology confirmed a complete mole with diploid 46,XX karyotype. Her serum beta-hCG fell from 92 000 IU/L pre-evacuation to 4200 at 4 weeks, 3850 at 5 weeks, 3900 at 6 weeks and now 4050 IU/L at 7 weeks post-evacuation.

She has had no abnormal vaginal bleeding and feels well. A transvaginal ultrasound today shows a 2 cm intramyometrial mass with increased vascularity. Chest X-ray is clear.

data_table.Examination: Soft abdomen, no organomegaly, normal speculum, no abnormal bleeding
data_table.Investigations: Serial b-hCG plateau over 3 weeks at 3850 to 4200 IU/L, TVS: 2 cm intramyometrial mass with high vascular flow, CXR clear, FBC/UEC/LFTs normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer urgently to a tertiary gestational trophoblastic disease service for FIGO 2000 staging, complete metastatic workup including CT chest abdomen pelvis and MRI brain, and consideration of single-agent methotrexate chemotherapy for low-risk gestational trophoblastic neoplasia

Repeat the serum beta-hCG in 4 weeks and only consider further investigation or referral if the value rises by more than 50 percent or if she develops symptoms of recurrent disease such as bleeding, dyspnoea or central neurological deficits

Arrange repeat suction curettage of the uterine cavity as definitive treatment for the intramyometrial mass without referral to a tertiary centre or chemotherapy because single-agent chemotherapy carries unacceptable bone marrow toxicity at her age

Perform a total abdominal hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy as definitive treatment of post-molar gestational trophoblastic disease because chemotherapy carries unacceptable risks of long-term secondary malignancy in young women

Commence the combination chemotherapy regimen EMA-CO (etoposide methotrexate actinomycin-D cyclophosphamide vincristine) immediately at the local oncology service as initial empirical therapy without further staging or referral to a national GTD centre

subtopic_detail: Polycystic ovary syndrome diagnosis using Rotterdam criteria
stem:
You are the GP registrar reviewing a 24-year-old nulligravid woman with 18 months of irregular cycles ranging from 45 to 90 days, troublesome facial and lower-abdominal hirsutism that she shaves twice weekly, and adult-onset acne. She is not on hormonal contraception, has had no abnormal cervical screening, and has a BMI of 31 with central distribution. She is not trying to conceive.

Targeted assessment shows total testosterone in the upper-normal range with a low SHBG and a normal free androgen index calculation aligned with that. TSH, prolactin, early-morning 17-hydroxyprogesterone, day-21 progesterone and HbA1c are normal; transvaginal ultrasound shows 14 follicles measuring 2 to 9 mm in one ovary and increased ovarian volume on the other.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 124/76, HR 78, BMI 31, waist circumference 92 cm
data_table.Examination: Modified Ferriman-Gallwey score 10, mild acanthosis nigricans at nape, mild adult acne on jawline, no Cushingoid features
data_table.Investigations: Total testosterone upper-normal with low SHBG; TSH, prolactin, 17-OHP, day-21 progesterone, HbA1c normal; TVUS 14 follicles 2-9 mm one ovary, increased ovarian volume contralaterally

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer her to a reproductive endocrinology clinic for letrozole ovulation induction immediately and counsel her about ovarian drilling as a second-line surgical option if pharmacotherapy fails to restore ovulation

Defer the diagnosis until she has undergone a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test, a 24-hour urinary free cortisol, plasma metanephrines, and a fasting lipid panel to first exclude any alternative endocrine cause for her symptoms

Diagnose polycystic ovary syndrome based on her oligomenorrhoea, clinical and biochemical hyperandrogenism and polycystic ovarian morphology, and commence a combined oral contraceptive pill with metformin as initial therapy

Commence cyproterone acetate as monotherapy at a dose of 50 mg daily for 21 days each cycle to control her hirsutism and acne and reassess after a 6-month treatment trial before considering any further interventions

Arrange a repeat transvaginal ultrasound in 3 months and a serum anti-Mullerian hormone level before any diagnosis is formalised, since polycystic ovarian morphology alone is not adequate without additional confirmatory imaging

subtopic_detail: Anti-D prophylaxis after threatened miscarriage
stem:
You are the early pregnancy assessment service registrar reviewing a 28-year-old gravida 2 para 1 woman at 9+2 weeks gestation by certain dates who has had two episodes of moderate bright red painless vaginal bleeding without clots over the last 8 hours. She is haemodynamically stable; her cervix is closed on speculum examination with a small amount of fresh blood at the os; transvaginal ultrasound shows a single live intrauterine pregnancy with crown-rump length consistent with dates, fetal heart of 162 beats per minute, and a small subchorionic haematoma.

Her blood group is O Rhesus D negative; she has no anti-D antibodies on routine antibody screen and her previous pregnancy was uncomplicated and resulted in a vaginal birth at term with appropriate postpartum anti-D administration.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/72, HR 84, SpO2 99% in air, T 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender abdomen, speculum: closed cervix with fresh blood at os, no products, no adnexal mass on bimanual
data_table.Investigations: Hb 122 g/L; group and antibody screen: O Rh D negative, antibody screen negative; beta-hCG 56,000 IU/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step regarding anti-D immunoglobulin?

options.text: Refer her urgently to maternal fetal medicine for cordocentesis to determine fetal Rhesus D status before deciding whether anti-D is needed for this episode of antenatal sensitising vaginal bleeding event today

Administer 625 IU of intramuscular anti-D immunoglobulin now as the standard antenatal sensitising-event dose and arrange a repeat antibody screen in 6 weeks to confirm there has been no sensitisation in this pregnancy

Defer the anti-D decision until a fetomaternal haemorrhage flow cytometry result is available within 24 hours and dose her anti-D based on the calculated volume of fetal red cells that have crossed the placenta today

Reassure her, document the threatened miscarriage with confirmed viability on ultrasound, and discharge with safety-net advice without administering anti-D immunoglobulin at this gestation given the clinical picture today

Administer 250 IU of intramuscular anti-D immunoglobulin now and repeat the dose if any further bleeding occurs in the next 72 hours, and arrange a Kleihauer-Betke test before each subsequent anti-D administration

subtopic_detail: Levonorgestrel-IUD insertion contraindication assessment
stem:
You are the sexual health clinic registrar consulting with a 32-year-old para 2 woman requesting a 52 mg levonorgestrel intrauterine system for both contraception and management of heavy menstrual bleeding. She has no significant past medical history; her cervical screening is current and normal; she has one stable male partner of 5 years and uses condoms intermittently. She had unprotected intercourse 5 days ago.

Her last menstrual period began 16 days ago. Bimanual pelvic examination is unremarkable. As part of pre-insertion workup, a self-collected vulvovaginal nucleic acid amplification test returns positive for Chlamydia trachomatis with the speciation of the request now confirmed by the on-site sexual health laboratory.

data_table.Examination: External genitalia normal, speculum: scant clear discharge, no cervical motion tenderness, no adnexal mass on bimanual examination
data_table.Investigations: Vulvovaginal NAAT: Chlamydia trachomatis positive; gonorrhoea NAAT negative; cervical screening current

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Proceed with same-day insertion of the levonorgestrel intrauterine system and prescribe a single oral azithromycin 1 g dose at the time of the procedure to cover the recently detected chlamydia infection during the IUD insertion

Insert the intrauterine system today and arrange a test-of-cure NAAT for chlamydia 4 weeks after the procedure to confirm clearance, without treating with oral antibiotics either before or after the insertion of the device

Defer insertion and prescribe oral azithromycin 1 g single dose for her and her partner now, then proceed with insertion at 1 week post treatment without rechecking for resolution of the chlamydia infection prior to insertion

Insert a copper intrauterine device today instead of the hormonal device since the copper device also provides emergency contraception coverage for the unprotected intercourse 5 days ago in this clinical context

Defer the intrauterine system insertion, prescribe oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days for her and contact tracing for her partner, and rebook her for the procedure once she has completed treatment and is asymptomatic

subtopic_detail: Cyclic mastalgia evaluation and first-line management
stem:
You are the GP registrar reviewing a 31-year-old para 1 woman with 6 months of bilateral breast heaviness, soreness and tenderness that begins around 7 to 10 days before each menstrual period and resolves with menses. She breastfed her child for 9 months and stopped 2 years ago. She drinks two coffees per day, exercises three times a week, and is not on hormonal contraception.

She is up to date with cervical screening and is not in a BreastScreen age group. Examination today, performed in the late luteal phase, reveals diffuse bilateral nodularity without a dominant mass, no skin changes, no nipple discharge and no axillary lymphadenopathy; her bra is supportive but not specifically fitted.

data_table.Examination: Diffuse bilateral nodularity with no dominant mass, no skin tethering or peau d'orange, no nipple discharge, no axillary lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: No imaging or bloods performed; menstrual cycle 28 days, regular

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange a bilateral diagnostic mammogram and a targeted ultrasound today and refer her urgently to a breast surgeon for a tissue diagnosis given the persistent nature of her bilateral breast symptoms over the past 6 months

Commence a combined oral contraceptive pill containing 30 microgram ethinylestradiol now as first-line therapy aimed at suppressing cyclical breast tissue stimulation and at reducing her cycle-related breast tenderness

Recommend a strict caffeine-free diet, a low-fat diet under 15 percent of total energy and high-dose vitamin E 1000 IU daily as evidence-based interventions for cyclic mastalgia to use throughout her menstrual cycle each month

Reassure her, advise a professionally fitted supportive bra including a sports bra at night during the symptomatic week and regular simple analgesia, and review at 3 months with a symptom diary linking pain to her cycle

Commence oral tamoxifen 10 mg daily for a 6-month course and refer her to a breast clinic for a discussion of danazol if the first-line treatment fails to provide adequate symptom control over the trial period

subtopic_detail: Vasa praevia recognition at second trimester scan
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 33-year-old primigravid woman at 21+0 weeks gestation referred from a private radiology practice after her morphology scan. The transabdominal scan demonstrates a normally grown singleton fetus with normal anatomy, a posterior fundal placenta, and a velamentous cord insertion with two unprotected fetal vessels coursing within the membranes across the internal cervical os. Transvaginal imaging confirms type 1 vasa praevia (velamentous cord insertion) with the aberrant vessels within 1 cm of the internal os.

She is well, asymptomatic, with no bleeding, no contractions and a normal cervical length of 36 mm. Her IVF cycle used a single-embryo transfer and she had no first-trimester bleeding episodes.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 110/68, HR 78, SpO2 99% in air, T 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender uterus, no bleeding, no contractions; speculum: closed cervix, no discharge or bleeding
data_table.Investigations: Morphology scan: singleton, posterior placenta, velamentous insertion, type 1 vasa praevia, cervical length 36 mm, normal Doppler

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Reassure her that vasa praevia diagnosed in the second trimester resolves spontaneously by term in around 80% of cases, plan a vaginal delivery at term with continuous CTG monitoring and discharge her from the high-risk obstetric clinic now

Arrange an immediate cervical cerclage at 22 weeks gestation and bed rest for the remainder of the pregnancy followed by induction of labour at 39 weeks once fetal maturity has been clinically confirmed at term

Arrange a follow-up transvaginal ultrasound at 32 weeks, plan elective caesarean section between 34+0 and 36+0 weeks with antenatal corticosteroids beforehand, and counsel about inpatient admission from 30 to 32 weeks for monitoring

Plan elective caesarean section at 39+0 weeks gestation with continuous CTG monitoring from 36 weeks and admission to the labour ward at 38 weeks for daily fetal surveillance with paper trace and ultrasound assessment

Offer termination of pregnancy at 22 weeks given the high perinatal mortality associated with undiagnosed vasa praevia and the diagnostic certainty achieved by the morphology ultrasound on the transabdominal and transvaginal scans

subtopic_detail: Postpartum thyroiditis recognition in transient hypothyroid phase
stem:
You are the GP registrar reviewing a 34-year-old para 1 woman 5 months postpartum who reports 6 weeks of progressive fatigue, intolerance of cold, weight gain of 3 kg above her usual postpartum weight despite reduced appetite, constipation, and a low mood that has not responded to a structured exercise plan. She had a euthymic pregnancy on no thyroid medications, an uncomplicated vaginal birth at 39+5 weeks, and is exclusively breastfeeding with no infant feeding concerns.

Her Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale today is 9 (cut-off 13). Examination is bland; she has mild non-tender diffuse goitre, no proptosis, no tremor, and her DTRs show a delayed relaxation phase bilaterally.

data_table.Examination: Mild diffuse non-tender goitre, no proptosis, no fine tremor, dry skin, delayed ankle reflex relaxation phase bilaterally
data_table.Investigations: TSH 14.2 mIU/L (RR 0.4-4.0), free T4 9.6 pmol/L (RR 10-22), anti-TPO antibodies positive at high titre, free T3 4.0 pmol/L (RR 3.5-6.5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence oral propranolol 20 mg three times daily and arrange a thyroid uptake scan in 4 weeks to assess for subacute or postpartum thyroiditis in the thyrotoxic phase and to plan ongoing therapy from there

Commence oral levothyroxine at 50 micrograms daily, recheck thyroid function in 6 to 8 weeks, plan to taper and trial cessation around 12 months postpartum, and counsel about lifelong hypothyroidism risk and recurrence

Refer her to a perinatal mental health service for an antidepressant trial of sertraline 50 mg daily for postnatal depression and recheck thyroid function only if she does not improve over a 4 to 6 week monitored treatment course

Refer her urgently to an endocrinologist for a radioactive iodine uptake scan to differentiate between postpartum thyroiditis and Graves disease before initiating any thyroid hormone replacement therapy in this woman

Repeat thyroid function tests in 6 weeks without treatment and counsel her that the changes are likely physiological postpartum and very likely to normalise spontaneously without need for any thyroid hormone replacement therapy

subtopic_detail: Choice between vacuum and forceps for instrumental delivery
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar called to the birth suite for a 28-year-old primigravid woman at 39+4 weeks gestation in the second stage of labour. She has been actively pushing for 90 minutes after a 60-minute passive descent phase with adequate uterine contractions, an effective epidural and reassuring CTG. The presenting head is at +2 station, occiput-anterior position, with no caput or moulding, the bony skull is at the level of the ischial spines plus 2 cm and zero-fifths palpable abdominally.

The bladder is empty after a recent in-out catheter. Her membranes are ruptured with clear liquor. She and her partner are tiring and asking for help to complete the birth in a controlled and safe way.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 124/78, HR 96, T 37.0 degrees C; CTG: baseline 140 bpm, normal variability, no decelerations
data_table.Examination: Cervix fully dilated, vertex OA, station +2, no caput or moulding, zero-fifths palpable abdominally, intact perineum
data_table.Investigations: Latest VBG: pH 7.34, BE -3.2, lactate 1.8 mmol/L (cord gas not yet)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate choice of instrument for an instrumental vaginal delivery in this setting?

options.text: Augment her labour with intravenous syntocinon at 12 mU/min for a further 60 minutes of active pushing before considering any instrumental or operative intervention, given her reassuring fetal heart trace

Proceed to a Kielland rotational forceps delivery to rapidly complete the second stage of labour, given her primiparity and the duration she has already spent actively pushing without effective progression of descent

Proceed to Neville-Barnes outlet forceps delivery with infiltration of pudendal block local anaesthesia and a generous mediolateral episiotomy to minimise the risk of any obstetric anal sphincter injury during her birth

Proceed to a low-station vacuum-assisted delivery using a soft cup, applying axial traction with each contraction and aborting after three pulls without descent or three cup detachments per consensus criteria

Proceed to category 2 caesarean section for failure to progress in the second stage of labour given the duration of active pushing and the maternal exhaustion now interfering with effective bearing-down efforts

subtopic_detail: Acute fatty liver of pregnancy versus HELLP using Swansea criteria
stem:
You are the obstetric medicine registrar called to ED for a 32-year-old primigravid woman at 34+5 weeks gestation with 5 days of malaise, anorexia and right upper quadrant discomfort, now with 24 hours of polyuria and polydipsia, mild jaundice and confusion. She has had a normal pregnancy and her booking BP was 110/68. Today her BP is 138/86. She is hypoglycaemic at the bedside, oliguric and has marked coagulopathy with a prolonged INR without thrombocytopenia.

Liver biochemistry shows a moderate hepatocellular transaminase rise with significant hyperbilirubinaemia and a raised ammonia. Urate is markedly elevated. CTG is reassuring; ultrasound shows a bright liver with no biliary dilatation and the fetus is appropriately grown.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 138/86, HR 110, T 37.0 degrees C, SpO2 98% in air, urine output 18 mL/hour
data_table.Examination: Drowsy with mild asterixis, scleral icterus, tender right upper quadrant, no peripheral oedema beyond mild ankle swelling
data_table.Investigations: BGL 2.4 mmol/L, ALT 312 U/L, AST 286 U/L, bilirubin 88 micromol/L, ALP 220 U/L, urate 0.52 mmol/L, ammonia 92 micromol/L, INR 2.1, platelets 168 x10^9/L, fibrinogen 1.4 g/L, WCC 18.4 x10^9/L, creat 132 micromol/L, urine protein PCR 28 mg/mmol; liver ultrasound: bright echotexture, no dilated ducts

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence ursodeoxycholic acid 15 mg/kg/day and rifaximin 550 mg twice daily for presumed intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy and arrange induction of labour at 37+0 weeks in line with cholestasis-of-pregnancy guidance

Arrange a percutaneous liver biopsy to differentiate acute fatty liver of pregnancy from autoimmune hepatitis or acute viral hepatitis before deciding whether to deliver and to guide subsequent immunosuppressive therapy choice

Stabilise with 10% dextrose infusion, correct coagulopathy with fresh frozen plasma and cryoprecipitate, give betamethasone if not already given, contact ICU and plan urgent delivery within 24 hours after maternal stabilisation

Commence intravenous magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis and intravenous labetalol for tight blood pressure control, expect this to be HELLP syndrome, and continue conservative inpatient management to maximise the gestational age at delivery

Transfer her to a quaternary liver transplant centre for assessment of urgent transplantation as the primary therapy and recommend continuation of the pregnancy until transplant assessment is completed prior to any delivery

subtopic_detail: GDM diagnosis on 75g OGTT with ADIPS thresholds
stem:
You are the antenatal GP reviewing a 32-year-old G1P0 woman at 26 weeks gestation with results from her routine 75 g oral glucose tolerance test today. She is asymptomatic, pre-pregnancy BMI was 24, weight gain so far is 7 kg, has no family history of diabetes, is of Anglo-Australian background, and had a normal early pregnancy HbA1c of 5.2 percent at booking.

Her pregnancy has otherwise been uncomplicated with normal morphology scan and appropriate fundal height. She has no glycosuria on dipstick today. She takes only pregnancy multivitamins and no medications that affect glucose metabolism.

data_table.Investigations: 75 g OGTT - fasting glucose 5.3 mmol/L, 1-hour 10.2 mmol/L, 2-hour 8.4 mmol/L; booking HbA1c 5.2%; urine dipstick negative for glucose, ketones and protein

lead_in: What is the most appropriate diagnosis and initial management plan?

options.text: Diagnose gestational diabetes mellitus on the abnormal fasting and 1-hour values, refer to the diabetes-in-pregnancy multidisciplinary clinic, commence dietary advice and home blood glucose monitoring with targets fasting under 5.0 and 2-hour postprandial under 6.7 mmol/L

Diagnose overt diabetes in pregnancy on the basis of two abnormal OGTT values, commence metformin 500 mg twice daily immediately, refer urgently to obstetric medicine and arrange fetal echocardiography for screening of congenital cardiac anomalies

Reassure the patient that her test is within the normal range as only the fasting glucose is above 5.1 and a single abnormal value does not establish a diagnosis of gestational diabetes mellitus in Australia or internationally

Repeat the 75 g OGTT in 4 weeks because borderline elevations at 26 weeks may resolve as pregnancy progresses and the patient has no risk factors for gestational diabetes including normal BMI and no family history

Commence metformin 500 mg twice daily as first-line therapy without dietary trial because two abnormal values predict failure of lifestyle therapy alone and pharmacotherapy should not be delayed in pregnancy where the fetus is at risk

subtopic_detail: Tubal ectopic pregnancy single-dose methotrexate eligibility
stem:
You are the emergency gynaecology registrar reviewing a 30-year-old G2P0 woman 6 weeks and 2 days from last menstrual period with intermittent right pelvic pain over 48 hours and minimal brown PV spotting. She is haemodynamically stable, the abdomen is soft with mild right iliac fossa tenderness only on deep palpation, no rebound, and the cervix is closed on speculum.

Transvaginal ultrasound shows an empty uterus with thin endometrium, a right adnexal mass measuring 2.8 cm with no fetal pole and no fetal cardiac activity, and no free fluid in the pouch of Douglas. She has no prior abdominal surgery, normal liver and renal function, no breastfeeding, and is reliable for outpatient follow-up. She prefers fertility-sparing management if safe.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/72, HR 86, T 36.7, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Soft abdomen, mild RIF tenderness, no rebound, no guarding, closed cervix, no cervical excitation
data_table.Investigations: Serum bHCG 2840 IU/L, Hb 128, WCC 7.4, platelets 240, Cr 64 (eGFR >90), AST 22, ALT 19, blood group O Rh+, urine bHCG positive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Single-dose intramuscular methotrexate 50 mg/m squared with day-4 and day-7 bHCG monitoring, expecting >=15 percent fall between day 4 and day 7, and arranging weekly bHCG until non-pregnant levels are confirmed

Expectant management with serial bHCG every 48 hours and weekly transvaginal ultrasound, accepting that intervention will only be required if bHCG plateaus or rises or if the patient develops worsening pain or instability

Urgent laparoscopic salpingectomy of the affected right fallopian tube as definitive surgical management with intraoperative tubal exploration to confirm diagnosis and histopathological assessment of the removed specimen postoperatively

Urgent laparoscopic salpingostomy to preserve the affected fallopian tube with intra-operative methotrexate as required and weekly bHCG follow-up to detect persistent trophoblast, since fertility preservation is the patient's priority

Two-dose intramuscular methotrexate 50 mg/m squared regimen given on day 1 and day 4 as a more effective protocol with the same follow-up schedule of day-4 and day-7 bHCG measurements as the single-dose protocol used in Australia

subtopic_detail: First-line manoeuvre for shoulder dystocia using HELPERR mnemonic
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar attending the spontaneous vaginal birth of a 30-year-old G2P1 woman at 39 weeks and 4 days gestation in active second stage. The fetal head has delivered at 03:14 but immediately retracts against the perineum (turtle sign), and routine gentle downward axial traction by the accoucheur over the next 30 seconds fails to deliver the anterior shoulder.

There is no cord around the neck visible, the woman is on the labour bed in a semi-recumbent position, and the team has been called for assistance. The estimated fetal weight today is 3.9 kg.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal BP 122/76, HR 96; fetal heart rate prior to delivery of head 140-150 with normal variability
data_table.Examination: Turtle sign visible on perineum, anterior shoulder not delivered after gentle downward axial traction, time of head delivery 03:14, no obvious cord around neck
data_table.Investigations: Estimated fetal weight 3.9 kg on third-trimester scan; no maternal diabetes; previous birth weight 3.4 kg uncomplicated vaginal birth

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first manoeuvre?

options.text: Generous mediolateral episiotomy with sharp scissors immediately to widen the vaginal outlet, before any positional change, as this provides additional room for internal manoeuvres and reduces the risk of severe perineal laceration during further attempts

McRoberts manoeuvre by hyperflexion and abduction of the maternal hips against the abdomen combined with steady suprapubic pressure applied by a second clinician to dislodge the anterior shoulder from behind the symphysis pubis

Woods corkscrew manoeuvre by rotating the posterior shoulder 180 degrees anteriorly to dislodge the impacted anterior shoulder, performed before any external manoeuvres because the impacted shoulder is unlikely to release with positional change alone

Delivery of the posterior arm by sweeping it across the fetal chest and out of the vagina to reduce the bisacromial diameter and free the anterior shoulder from behind the symphysis pubis without need for external manoeuvres first
