Zavanelli manoeuvre with replacement of the fetal head into the vagina to allow caesarean delivery, with concurrent tocolysis using a single dose of terbutaline 250 mcg subcutaneously to relax the uterus during the manoeuvre

subtopic_detail: Intrapartum GBS prophylaxis at preterm with unknown maternal carriage
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 30-year-old G2P1 woman at 33+0 weeks gestation in spontaneous preterm labour. SROM occurred 2 hours ago with clear liquor. Contractions are 3 in 10 minutes, cervix is 4 cm dilated and 80 percent effaced. The 28-week swab was not done as planned and her 36-week LVS for GBS has not yet been collected.

Fetal heart rate is reassuring on CTG. Fetal lung maturity has not been induced. There is no maternal fever, no offensive discharge, no allergies and no antibiotic exposure in the previous 4 weeks. Tocolysis with nifedipine is being commenced to allow steroids and magnesium for neuroprotection.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal T 36.8, HR 92, BP 118/72; CTG: baseline 140 with normal variability, accelerations present, no decelerations
data_table.Examination: Cervix 4 cm dilated 80% effaced, vertex at -2 station, intact membranes ruptured 2 hours ago (clear liquor), no clinical chorioamnionitis
data_table.Investigations: FBC, CRP normal; bHCG previously confirmed; GBS swab not collected; no penicillin allergy; not previously colonised in last pregnancy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate antibiotic plan?

options.text: Withhold antibiotics until the result of an urgent GBS swab and avoid empirical treatment to limit unnecessary intrapartum antibiotic exposure and the risk of antimicrobial resistance and altered neonatal microbiome

Commence intravenous benzylpenicillin 3 g loading dose followed by 1.8 g every 4 hours until birth as intrapartum group B streptococcus prophylaxis given preterm labour and unknown maternal GBS carriage status

Commence intravenous erythromycin 250 mg every 6 hours as antibiotic of choice for preterm prelabour rupture of membranes only, which doubles as group B streptococcus prophylaxis throughout the duration of labour in this presentation

Commence intravenous cefazolin 2 g loading dose then 1 g every 8 hours as first-line group B streptococcus prophylaxis throughout labour because it provides equivalent neonatal protection with broader spectrum than penicillin alone

Commence oral amoxicillin 500 mg every 8 hours during labour as adequate intrapartum group B streptococcus prophylaxis for the duration of established labour up to the birth of the baby in normal vaginal birth

subtopic_detail: Hyperemesis gravidarum with dehydration and electrolyte disturbance requiring admission
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in the early pregnancy assessment unit reviewing a 26-year-old G1P0 woman at 9 weeks gestation by certain LMP with confirmed intrauterine singleton on prior scan. She has had persistent vomiting more than 10 times daily for 4 days, is unable to tolerate even sips of water, has lost 4.5 kg (6 percent of pre-pregnancy weight), and feels light-headed on standing.

She has tried oral ondansetron wafers and dietary modification at home without effect. Urine on arrival shows ketones ++++. There is no fever, abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding or thyroid symptoms, and her TSH on screening was 1.4.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 105/65 lying, 88/52 standing with HR 122, T 36.7, RR 18, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes, capillary refill 3 sec, soft abdomen with no peritonism, no goitre, no thyroid signs
data_table.Investigations: Na 131, K 3.2, Cl 86, HCO3 28, urea 8.4, Cr 88, ALT 42, urine ketones ++++, beta-hCG appropriate for gestation, USS confirms viable IUP

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Admit for IV rehydration with Hartmann solution, IV ondansetron 4 mg 8-hourly, IV thiamine 100 mg before any glucose-containing fluid, potassium replacement and recheck electrolytes in 6 hours with daily ketone monitoring

Discharge home with oral metoclopramide 10 mg 8-hourly and oral pyridoxine 25 mg 8-hourly with advice to sip clear fluids and review GP in 24 hours, with safety net advice to return if symptoms or weight loss progress

Commence oral prednisolone 40 mg daily for 1 week then taper as first-line therapy for refractory hyperemesis given her failed home antiemetic therapy, with admission only if symptoms have not resolved after the steroid course

Admit for IV haloperidol 1 mg 8-hourly as third-line antiemetic monotherapy because of failure of first-line oral therapies, with no role for hydration as the patient is otherwise stable apart from intermittent vomiting symptoms

Commence total parenteral nutrition via central line within the first 24 hours of admission to provide complete nutritional support, with concurrent ondansetron 8 mg every 8 hours and weight gain targets reviewed daily by dietetics

subtopic_detail: Low-dose vaginal oestrogen for urogenital atrophy after early breast cancer
stem:
You are the GP reviewing a 56-year-old woman with troublesome vaginal dryness, dyspareunia significantly affecting her relationship, and three culture-confirmed urinary tract infections over the past 6 months attributed to urogenital atrophy. She completed treatment for ER-positive early breast cancer 8 years ago (lumpectomy, radiotherapy, 5 years of tamoxifen) and is currently on no breast cancer therapy with no recurrence on annual surveillance.

She has trialled non-hormonal vaginal lubricants and moisturisers consistently over the past 6 months without benefit. She does not have significant systemic vasomotor symptoms and is otherwise well.

data_table.Examination: Atrophic vaginal mucosa with thinning of rugae, pale and friable epithelium, no obvious lesion, no pelvic mass; breast examination unchanged from baseline
data_table.Investigations: Recent surveillance mammogram normal, no current oncological therapy, eGFR >90, vaginal pH 6.5, urine culture pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence systemic combined hormone therapy with oral conjugated equine oestrogen 0.625 mg plus medroxyprogesterone acetate 2.5 mg daily for symptom control of both urogenital and vasomotor symptoms, with annual mammogram surveillance

Continue intensive non-hormonal lubricants and moisturisers with sexual health counselling and referral to a pelvic floor physiotherapist for assessment of pelvic floor function, with reassurance that hormonal therapy is not safe

Trial low-dose vaginal oestradiol pessary 10 mcg twice weekly in consultation with her breast oncology team, with patient counselling regarding the small but uncertain risk and the option to reassess after 3 to 6 months of therapy

Commence ospemifene 60 mg daily as a selective oestrogen receptor modulator with vaginal trophic effect and no systemic oestrogenic activity, providing an effective alternative to vaginal oestrogen in breast cancer survivors

Commence intravaginal DHEA (prasterone) 6.5 mg daily as a tissue-specific androgenic precursor with minimal systemic effect, since the intravaginal route bypasses systemic exposure and is therefore safer in breast cancer survivors

subtopic_detail: Direct colposcopy referral for HPV 16 positive on routine cervical screening
stem:
You are the GP reviewing the results of a 30-year-old woman's first cervical screening test (CST) performed 4 weeks ago. She is asymptomatic with no intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding, no abnormal discharge, and a macroscopically normal cervix on speculum at the time of collection. Her result shows HPV detected, type 16 positive, and reflex liquid-based cytology (LBC) reports negative for intraepithelial lesion or malignancy (NILM).

Her last sexual partner change was 6 months ago, she has been with her current partner for 4 months, and her vaccination history includes HPV vaccination at age 13 (Gardasil 4-valent, completed). She has no comorbidities and is on no medications.

data_table.Examination: Cervix macroscopically normal at the time of CST collection, no contact bleeding, no visible lesion or polyp, no adnexal mass on bimanual examination
data_table.Investigations: CST: HPV detected, type 16 positive; reflex LBC negative for IEL or malignancy; urine bHCG negative; no other recent investigations available

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat the cervical screening test in 12 months to assess HPV persistence and reflex cytology, with continued routine screening pathway if HPV has cleared spontaneously between now and the recommended follow-up interval

Repeat the cervical screening test in 5 years as part of the routine screening interval, with normal further screening if no new symptoms develop in the interim and continuation of current sexual health and contraceptive practices

Commence topical imiquimod 5 percent cream three times per week for 12 weeks for HPV clearance, with cervical screening repeated after completion of treatment to assess for clearance of the underlying HPV 16 infection

Refer to a gynaecology colposcopy clinic for colposcopic assessment now, since HPV 16 or 18 detection on cervical screening warrants colposcopy regardless of reflex cytology result due to the higher risk of high-grade dysplasia

Perform an endometrial pipelle biopsy in the GP rooms to exclude endometrial pathology associated with the abnormal cervical screening test before referral for further specialist gynaecology assessment and ongoing management plan

subtopic_detail: Threatened miscarriage at 8 weeks expectant management
stem:
You are the early pregnancy assessment service registrar reviewing a 30-year-old G2P1 woman at 8 weeks gestation by certain last menstrual period and a recent dating scan, who presents with 12 hours of light fresh vaginal spotting and mild lower abdominal cramping. She has had no passage of clots or tissue, no dizziness, no shoulder tip pain and her previous pregnancy was uncomplicated.

She is rhesus D positive. Her observations are normal and abdominal examination is unremarkable. Speculum examination shows a small amount of fresh blood in the vault and a closed cervical os with no products of conception visible.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7, HR 84, BP 116/72, RR 14, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Closed cervical os with light fresh blood in the vault, uterus consistent with dates, no adnexal tenderness, no peritonism on abdominal exam, bimanual examination unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound: intrauterine gestational sac with single live fetal pole, crown-rump length consistent with 8 weeks 0 days, fetal heart rate 162 beats per minute, no subchorionic haematoma; beta-hCG 56000 IU/L; blood group O positive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Commence intramuscular methotrexate 50 mg per square metre body surface area today to terminate the pregnancy because the bleeding represents an inevitable miscarriage which will be safer to complete medically than to await expectant resolution

Arrange suction dilatation and curettage in theatre today to evacuate the uterine contents to reduce the risk of haemorrhage, infection and ongoing miscarriage symptoms, given the bleeding and the documented intrauterine gestational sac on ultrasound

Admit overnight for observation, intravenous fluid maintenance, fasting from midnight and consent for emergency theatre in case of progression to incomplete miscarriage with heavy bleeding overnight, with morning gynaecology team reassessment

Prescribe vaginal micronised progesterone 400 mg twice daily as ovulation-induction support, advise prolonged bed rest at home with no work for two weeks, and arrange repeat early pregnancy ultrasound in three days for reassurance

Reassure that the live intrauterine pregnancy carries a high likelihood of progressing, provide written return precautions for heavy bleeding or severe pain, advise against intercourse for 7 days, and arrange repeat transvaginal ultrasound in 7 to 10 days for reassessment

subtopic_detail: Tubal ectopic pregnancy single-dose methotrexate criteria
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 28-year-old G2P0 woman with 6 weeks 2 days amenorrhoea, mild left-sided abdominal pain for 2 days, and one episode of light brown vaginal spotting today. Her observations are stable. She had a normal full blood examination, baseline liver and renal function are normal, and she has no known medical comorbidity, no breastfeeding, no immunosuppression and no known peptic ulcer disease.

She is rhesus D positive and has full insight into the diagnosis and treatment options. She has a partner and can attend follow-up scans and blood tests reliably for at least the next two weeks.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8, HR 78, BP 122/72, RR 14, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Soft abdomen, mild left iliac fossa tenderness, no rebound or guarding, no cervical motion tenderness, closed cervical os with no products of conception
data_table.Investigations: Beta-hCG 1850 IU/L; transvaginal ultrasound: empty uterus, 22 mm left adnexal mass with no fetal cardiac activity, no free fluid in pouch of Douglas; Hb 128, normal LFTs and renal function

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Administer single-dose intramuscular methotrexate 50 mg per square metre body surface area today, arrange beta-hCG measurement on days 4 and 7, and counsel on avoidance of alcohol, folic acid, NSAIDs and conception for 3 months

Proceed to laparoscopic salpingectomy this evening regardless of haemodynamic stability because all tubal ectopic pregnancies require definitive surgical management to reduce future recurrence and persistent trophoblast risk in the contralateral fallopian tube

Adopt expectant management with weekly beta-hCG monitoring until resolution because the beta-hCG is below 1000 and the ectopic mass measures less than 30 mm on transvaginal ultrasound with no haemorrhage, avoiding the toxicity of methotrexate completely

Insert misoprostol 800 micrograms per vagina now for medical termination of the ectopic pregnancy, with mifepristone 200 mg orally 48 hours later, and arrange beta-hCG monitoring weekly until resolution to baseline

Admit for observation with intravenous fluids, fasting from midnight, and laparoscopic salpingostomy in the morning if there is no clinical improvement overnight, with intraoperative methotrexate flush if any persistent trophoblastic tissue is identified

subtopic_detail: PCOS letrozole first-line ovulation induction
stem: You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 28-year-old woman with 18 months of primary subfertility. She has cycles of 35 to 90 days, mild hirsutism, a BMI of 29, and ultrasound showing polycystic ovarian morphology bilaterally. Her partner's semen analysis is normal, her tubes are patent on hysterosalpingography, day 21 progesterone is consistently low, thyroid function and prolactin are normal, and she has had ongoing dietary support with structured exercise for 12 months without conceiving. She is non-smoker, non-diabetic and rubella immune. She has no contraindications to letrozole or clomifene.

data_table.Examination: Mild upper-lip and chin hirsutism, no acanthosis nigricans, normal pelvic exam
data_table.Investigations: Pelvic ultrasound polycystic ovaries bilaterally, no endometrial pathology; HSG patent tubes; partner semen analysis normal; HbA1c 5.4%, TSH 1.8, prolactin normal, fasting cholesterol panel normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacological therapy for ovulation induction?

options.text: Commence subcutaneous follicle-stimulating hormone gonadotropin injections from day 2 of the cycle with serial transvaginal ultrasound follicle tracking and a triggering dose of human chorionic gonadotropin once the lead follicle reaches 18 mm in diameter

Letrozole 2.5 mg orally daily from cycle days 2 to 6 with serial follicle tracking and timed intercourse, escalating to 5 mg in the next cycle if no ovulation is achieved, with maximum dose 7.5 mg daily for a maximum of 5 to 6 cycles

Metformin 500 mg three times daily for 6 months as monotherapy, with avoidance of clomifene or letrozole because metformin alone in normoglycaemic women with polycystic ovarian syndrome is sufficient to restore ovulation and achieve conception

Refer immediately for in vitro fertilisation with intracytoplasmic sperm injection as first-line management of subfertility in polycystic ovarian syndrome to maximise success rates given the long duration of infertility and the age of the woman

Clomifene citrate 50 mg orally daily from cycle days 2 to 6 with serial follicle tracking and timed intercourse, escalating to 100 mg in the next cycle if anovulatory, with up to 6 ovulatory cycles before escalating to second-line therapy

subtopic_detail: Postpartum levonorgestrel IUD 4 weeks postnatal in a breastfeeding woman
stem: You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 32-year-old G3P3 woman 4 weeks following an uncomplicated normal vaginal delivery of a term healthy infant. She is exclusively breastfeeding, has resumed sexual activity this week using condoms, and explicitly wants long-acting reversible contraception with a 5-year horizon and minimal day-to-day involvement. She has no history of pelvic infection, no abnormalities of the uterus on her recent postnatal examination, and is happy with vaginal insertion. She has no contraindications to progestogens and no migraine with aura. Her partner is supportive and she has age-appropriate completed family discussions.

data_table.Examination: Uterus well involuted, no tenderness, normal-looking cervix on speculum, lochia minimal, perineum healed
data_table.Investigations: Hb 132, postnatal urinalysis normal, no current STI symptoms

lead_in: Which contraceptive option is the most appropriate to offer at this consultation?

options.text: Recommend continued lactational amenorrhoea method alone for the first 6 months postpartum with exclusive breastfeeding and amenorrhoea, deferring all other contraceptive methods until weaning is established and a return to the GP at that time

Commence the combined oral contraceptive pill containing ethinylestradiol 30 micrograms with levonorgestrel 150 micrograms today with quick-start instructions, plus condoms for 7 days as additional precaution while the pill becomes effective

Offer levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine device insertion today as outpatient procedure in the practice, confirm she is not at risk of current pregnancy, provide written information and arrange a 6-week post-insertion check by phone or in person

Refer for laparoscopic tubal ligation as the most appropriate definitive long-acting contraception for a multiparous woman who states she has completed her family, with day-surgery booking and preoperative counselling on regret and reversibility

Prescribe progestogen-only oral contraceptive desogestrel 75 micrograms taken at the same time each day with a 12-hour late window for missed doses, with condom backup for the first 48 hours after starting and a 6-week phone review

subtopic_detail: VBAC counselling for prior single low transverse caesarean
stem: You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 33-year-old G2P1 woman at 36 weeks gestation in a tertiary centre antenatal clinic for mode of birth discussion. Her first pregnancy was complicated by breech presentation managed with an elective lower segment caesarean at 39 weeks; the operation was uncomplicated and recovery uneventful. The current pregnancy has been uncomplicated, the fetus is cephalic, growth is appropriate, the placenta is normally sited, and there are no contraindications to vaginal birth. She wants to understand her options for this delivery and is open to either elective repeat caesarean or planned vaginal birth after caesarean.

data_table.Examination: Symphysis-fundal height appropriate, cephalic presentation, well engaged, no scar tenderness, uterus soft and non-irritable
data_table.Investigations: Recent growth ultrasound at 34 weeks with estimated fetal weight on the 55th centile, anterior placenta away from scar, normal liquor volume; bloods unremarkable; CTG normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate counselling and management plan?

options.text: Recommend mandatory elective repeat lower segment caesarean section at 39 plus 0 weeks gestation to all women with a previous caesarean delivery to avoid the risks of uterine rupture and emergency caesarean associated with planned vaginal birth after caesarean

Offer planned home waterbirth supervised by midwifery group practice for vaginal birth after caesarean given her low-risk antenatal course and previous normal recovery from caesarean, with ambulance transfer arrangement to the tertiary hospital

Plan induction of labour with prostaglandin E2 vaginal gel at 38 weeks gestation in all women planning vaginal birth after caesarean to optimise success rates by avoiding the risks associated with spontaneous post-term labour or a prolonged latent phase

Discuss planned vaginal birth after caesarean with quoted success rate of 72 to 75% in appropriate candidates and uterine rupture risk of 0.5%, plan for spontaneous labour with continuous CTG monitoring and IV access at a centre with immediate access to theatre

Offer elective repeat caesarean section at 37 plus 0 weeks gestation given the maternal preference for a planned approach and the avoidance of intrapartum monitoring, with antenatal corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity prior to the procedure

subtopic_detail: Severe pre-eclampsia magnesium sulfate seizure prophylaxis and BP control
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar called to the assessment unit to see a 34-year-old G1P0 woman at 34 weeks gestation with a 3-day history of escalating headache, blurred vision and right upper quadrant pain. She has had antenatal care including a normal morphology scan and her blood pressure has been climbing over the last 2 weeks. She has had no seizure activity.

Her fetus is reactive on CTG with normal liquor and growth on recent ultrasound. She has no allergies, no asthma and no significant past history. The neonatal team has been contacted and a single antenatal corticosteroid course was given at 32 weeks for prior threatened preterm labour.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 168/108 confirmed on repeat in two arms, HR 96, RR 18, SpO2 98% room air, reflexes 3+ with sustained clonus at the right ankle
data_table.Examination: Right upper quadrant tenderness, no peripheral oedema, no neurology focal deficit, fetus active, fundal height appropriate
data_table.Investigations: Urine PCR 350 mg/mmol, Hb 116, platelets 92, ALT 110, urate 0.42, creatinine 88, LDH 540, normal coags, CTG reactive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Commence oral nifedipine slow-release 30 mg twice daily, observe for 6 hours in the assessment unit and admit if her blood pressure does not respond to two doses, with arrangement of repeat bloods and CTG monitoring in the morning

Arrange immediate emergency caesarean section without prior maternal stabilisation, given the severe blood pressure readings, the symptoms of headache and right upper quadrant pain, and the platelet count of 92 with deranged liver function

Administer intravenous phenytoin loading dose 18 mg/kg over 30 minutes for seizure prophylaxis with continuous cardiac monitoring, and commence labetalol infusion at 20 mg/hour to control her blood pressure to a target below 160/110

Commence diazepam 10 mg intravenously now for seizure prophylaxis, continue antenatal corticosteroids with a repeat dose of betamethasone 11.4 mg intramuscularly, and admit to the ward for serial maternal observations and 4-hourly bloods

Commence magnesium sulfate 4 g IV loading dose over 15 minutes then 1 g/hour infusion for seizure prophylaxis, give IV labetalol 20 mg bolus repeated as needed for blood pressure target below 160/110, admit to the high-dependency unit and plan delivery within 24 to 48 hours

subtopic_detail: Endometriosis empirical COCP trial then diagnostic laparoscopy
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 28-year-old nulliparous woman with 18 months of progressive cyclical pelvic pain, deep dyspareunia and dysmenorrhoea unresponsive to escalating doses of paracetamol and ibuprofen. She is not currently trying to conceive and uses condoms for contraception. There is no abnormal vaginal discharge, no urinary symptoms, and she has had a negative chlamydia and gonorrhoea screen 3 months ago.

Speculum and bimanual examination today are unremarkable. Transvaginal ultrasound shows no endometrioma, no obvious deep infiltrating endometriosis nodule and a normal uterus. She is interested in symptom management but does not wish to conceive in the next 12 months.

data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender abdomen, bimanual exam unremarkable, no adnexal mass or tenderness, normal cervix on speculum exam
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound: normal uterus, no endometrioma, no deep infiltrating endometriosis nodule, ovaries of normal volume; recent chlamydia and gonorrhoea NAAT negative; cervical screening up to date and negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence empirical combined oral contraceptive pill taken continuously without a withdrawal week for 3 months as a therapeutic trial for suspected endometriosis, with planned review and consideration of diagnostic laparoscopy if symptoms fail to improve substantially

Refer for diagnostic and operative laparoscopy as first-line management for all women with symptoms suggesting endometriosis, given the limitations of transvaginal ultrasound in identifying superficial peritoneal disease and the gold-standard role of laparoscopy

Arrange a contrast pelvic magnetic resonance imaging to characterise deep infiltrating endometriosis prior to commencing any therapy, with planned multidisciplinary case conference to map disease distribution before considering hormonal management options

Commence gonadotropin-releasing hormone analogue therapy with goserelin 3.6 mg subcutaneously monthly with add-back hormone therapy to minimise bone density loss and vasomotor symptoms, with planned 6-month course as first-line medical management

Prescribe oxycodone immediate release 5 mg orally up to four times daily as required for chronic cyclical pelvic pain with planned chronic pain clinic referral for opioid stewardship and review of escalation criteria for intervention

subtopic_detail: MCDA twin selective IUGR type II reversed end-diastolic flow delivery timing
stem:
You are the maternal fetal medicine fellow reviewing a 30-year-old G1P0 woman at 34 plus 2 weeks gestation with a monochorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy. Twin A has been growing on the 50th centile throughout pregnancy. Twin B has been on the 5th centile since 28 weeks with an estimated fetal weight discrepancy of 28% compared to twin A. Today twin B has intermittently reversed end-diastolic flow in the umbilical artery.

There is no evidence of twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome (deepest vertical pockets normal in both sacs) and no evidence of fetal anaemia on middle cerebral artery Doppler. Both fetuses have reactive CTGs at this time.

data_table.Examination: Symphysis-fundal height appropriate for gestation, no tenderness, no contractions, normal abdominal examination, fetal heart auscultation audible from both sacs
data_table.Investigations: MCDA twins; growth scan today: twin A 2350 g (50th centile), twin B 1690 g (less than 5th centile); twin B umbilical artery Doppler with intermittent reversed end-diastolic flow consistent with type II selective IUGR; twin A umbilical Doppler normal; both MCA peak systolic velocities normal; deepest vertical pocket twin A 5 cm, twin B 3 cm; both CTGs reactive; betamethasone given at 32 weeks for prior threatened preterm labour

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Plan elective lower segment caesarean section within 24 hours with neonatal team standby for a high-risk preterm twin delivery, repeat magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection at 34 weeks, and admit to the fetal medicine ward for monitoring overnight

Continue weekly outpatient surveillance with growth scans, umbilical artery and ductus venosus Doppler, and twice-weekly CTG monitoring with delivery deferred until 37 weeks gestation to maximise fetal lung maturity prior to elective delivery of the twins

Offer fetoscopic laser ablation of placental anastomoses to selectively reduce twin B given the marked growth discrepancy and abnormal Doppler, to protect the larger twin A from neurological injury associated with intrauterine demise of the smaller twin

Arrange intrauterine red cell transfusion to twin B given the abnormal umbilical artery Doppler suggestive of fetal anaemia and growth restriction, with cross-matched O negative blood and ultrasound-guided percutaneous umbilical sampling immediately

Administer a single intramuscular betamethasone rescue dose given that the previous course was given more than 2 weeks ago, and plan delivery at 36 plus 0 weeks gestation if the umbilical Doppler does not deteriorate further on weekly review

subtopic_detail: Heavy menstrual bleeding first-line management
stem:
A 41-year-old woman attends your general practice with a 2-year history of heavy menstrual bleeding causing her to miss work for 1 to 2 days each month. Periods are predictable every 28 days but soak through pads hourly for the first 2 days. She has 2 children and her family is complete. There is no intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding. Pelvic examination is normal.

Cervical screening is up to date and unremarkable. Transvaginal ultrasound shows a uniform endometrium 6 mm thick with no fibroids or polyps. She would like a long-term solution and is open to hormonal therapy.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 124/76 mmHg, HR 78 bpm, BMI 27 kg/m2
data_table.Examination: Pelvic exam normal, no adnexal masses
data_table.Investigations: Hb 108 g/L, ferritin 12 micrograms/L, thyroid function normal, beta-hCG negative, TVUS endometrium 6 mm uniform

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line management?

options.text: Referral for total laparoscopic hysterectomy as definitive treatment given her completed family
Combined oral contraceptive pill 30 micrograms ethinylestradiol with norethisterone continuously
Tranexamic acid 1 g orally three times daily on heavy days only as a non-hormonal option
Referral for endometrial ablation as definitive treatment with preservation of the uterus
Insertion of a 52 mg levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system with oral iron supplementation

subtopic_detail: Severe pre-eclampsia BP control choice
stem: You are the obstetric registrar called urgently to the birth suite to review a 34-year-old primigravida at 33+2 weeks gestation with persistent severe hypertension despite oral labetalol 200 mg given 30 minutes ago. She reports a severe frontal headache and one episode of vomiting. Reflexes are brisk with 3 beats of clonus. Urine dipstick shows 4+ protein. Fetal CTG is reassuring. Intravenous access is established. The consultant is en route. The midwife has prepared the typical antihypertensive options for severe pre-eclampsia.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 178/116 mmHg (confirmed on 2 readings), HR 92 bpm, RR 18, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Brisk reflexes, 3 beats clonus, no focal deficit, fundoscopy normal, mild facial oedema
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 142 x10^9/L, ALT 64 U/L, creatinine 78 micromol/L, uric acid 0.48 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate antihypertensive intervention?

options.text: Hydralazine 5 mg intravenously over 2 minutes, repeat after 20 minutes if target not reached
Sublingual nifedipine 10 mg capsule punctured for rapid release with 5-minute reassessment
Sodium nitroprusside infusion titrated to systolic blood pressure under 130 mmHg
Captopril 25 mg orally to address renin-angiotensin contribution to placental hypertension
Furosemide 40 mg intravenously to reduce intravascular volume and lower blood pressure

subtopic_detail: Shoulder dystocia manoeuvre sequence
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar at a regional hospital. A multiparous woman at 39+6 weeks is delivering. The head has been born but turtle sign is observed and routine downward traction has failed to deliver the anterior shoulder. The midwife has called for help. The clock has been started. The maternal head-of-bed has been flattened and her position has been adjusted with thighs flexed onto her abdomen.

Suprapubic pressure has been applied for 30 seconds without success. The estimated time since head delivery is 1 minute 20 seconds. No episiotomy was performed.

data_table.Examination: Head delivered, restitution complete, anterior shoulder impacted on symphysis, no cord prolapse
data_table.Investigations: Estimated fetal weight at last antenatal review 4150 g

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next manoeuvre?

options.text: Cease attempts and prepare for an immediate caesarean section in the operating theatre
Apply fundal pressure to push the anterior shoulder past the symphysis during traction
Perform symphysiotomy under local anaesthesia to widen the pelvic outlet immediately
Continue applying downward traction with greater force while the McRoberts position is maintained
Internal rotational manoeuvre to deliver the posterior shoulder by reaching in and rotating 180 degrees

subtopic_detail: VBAC counselling
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar counselling a 34-year-old woman at 30 weeks in her second pregnancy. Her first birth 3 years ago was a lower-segment caesarean section for breech presentation at 39 weeks, with no complications and good wound healing documented. This pregnancy has been low risk with normal growth and a cephalic presentation at the most recent scan. She has no medical comorbidities.

She has read about vaginal birth after caesarean online and asks you to explain the absolute risk of uterine rupture during a trial of labour. The hospital has on-site theatre and obstetric cover 24 hours a day.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/72 mmHg, HR 80 bpm, BMI 26 kg/m2
data_table.Examination: Symphysis fundal height 30 cm, cephalic presentation, well-healed Pfannenstiel scar
data_table.Investigations: Anomaly scan normal, glucose tolerance test normal, group B streptococcus screening pending

lead_in: Which figure most accurately reflects the absolute risk of symptomatic uterine rupture for her?

options.text: Approximately 5% in a planned vaginal birth after caesarean with one prior lower-segment scar
Approximately 0.5% in a planned vaginal birth after caesarean with one prior lower-segment scar
Approximately 0.01% in a planned vaginal birth after caesarean with one prior lower-segment scar
Approximately 10% in a planned vaginal birth after caesarean with one prior lower-segment scar
Approximately 2% in a planned vaginal birth after caesarean with one prior lower-segment scar

subtopic_detail: Acute fatty liver of pregnancy
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar called to the antenatal ward for a 28-year-old primigravida at 36+1 weeks. She has had 5 days of nausea, vomiting, anorexia, and right upper quadrant discomfort. Today she has become drowsy and developed mild jaundice. There is no headache, visual disturbance, or epigastric pain. Her blood pressure is mildly elevated but her reflexes are normal and there is no clonus.

Urine dipstick shows 1+ protein and 2+ ketones. The fetal CTG is reassuring. She has no known liver disease. The consultant is en route. Her admission bloods have just returned.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 138/86 mmHg, HR 110 bpm, RR 24, Temp 37.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Mildly drowsy, jaundiced sclerae, RUQ tender, no asterixis, no focal deficit, fundal height 35 cm
data_table.Investigations: Bilirubin 78 micromol/L, ALT 320 U/L, AST 290 U/L, INR 1.9, glucose 2.4 mmol/L, ammonia 110 micromol/L, urate 0.58 mmol/L, platelets 168 x10^9/L, creatinine 124 micromol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence intravenous magnesium sulfate and antihypertensives for severe pre-eclampsia and continue expectant care
Arrange urgent delivery by caesarean section after correction of coagulopathy and hypoglycaemia
Treat for viral hepatitis with supportive care while awaiting serology and avoid early delivery
Administer ursodeoxycholic acid orally and arrange outpatient hepatology review for intrahepatic cholestasis
Arrange transjugular liver biopsy to confirm the diagnosis before considering delivery

subtopic_detail: Whether to swab at 36 weeks after streptococcal bacteriuria
stem: A 26-year-old woman in her first pregnancy attends her 36 week visit. A urine sample sent earlier in the pregnancy for frequency was treated with an oral antibiotic.

data_table.Urine at 19 weeks: Group B streptococcus, pure growth above the significant threshold
data_table.Today: Well, no symptoms, no allergies, cervix long and closed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan?

options.text: Omit the swab; she already qualifies for antibiotics once labour starts
Swab her now and give antibiotics in labour only if it grows again
Swab her now and repeat the urine culture before making any plan
Treat her again with an oral antibiotic now to reduce carriage at birth
No swab and no antibiotics, since the bacteriuria was treated at the time

subtopic_detail: PCOS amenorrhoea - endometrial protection
stem: A 24-year-old woman with PCOS (Rotterdam criteria, hyperandrogenism plus oligomenorrhoea plus polycystic ovaries) attends for review. She has had no menstrual bleeding for 9 months. She is not sexually active, not contemplating pregnancy in the next 2 years, and finds daily medication burdensome. Her BMI is 31 kg/m2. She has tried metformin in the past without benefit.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 122/78 mmHg, weight 84 kg, height 165 cm
data_table.Examination: Mild acne and hirsutism on the chin, no acanthosis nigricans, no galactorrhoea
data_table.Investigations: Pregnancy test negative, TSH 1.8 mU/L, prolactin 320 mU/L, fasting glucose 5.4 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate strategy to protect the endometrium?

options.text: Cyclical medroxyprogesterone 10 mg orally daily for 12 days every 8 weeks
Levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system inserted for 5 years' protection
Continued metformin 1 g twice daily as monotherapy with lifestyle support
Combined oral contraceptive ethinylestradiol 30 mcg with levonorgestrel daily
Hysterectomy with ovarian conservation as a definitive long-term solution

subtopic_detail: Postmenopausal bleeding - endometrial assessment
stem: A 62-year-old woman presents with a single episode of vaginal bleeding lasting 2 days, 9 years after her last menstrual period. She is not on hormone therapy. She has no abdominal pain, weight loss or vaginal discharge. She has a BMI of 33 kg/m2 and a history of type 2 diabetes on metformin. She is otherwise well and has had normal cervical screening for the last 10 years.

data_table.Examination: Speculum shows a healthy cervix with no visible lesion; bimanual examination reveals a non-tender, mobile, normal-sized uterus
data_table.Investigations: Pregnancy test not required; FBC normal; cervical screening up to date and HPV negative

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Repeat cervical screening test from the cervix and the vaginal vault now
Outpatient hysteroscopy with Pipelle biopsy at the next available clinic
Transvaginal ultrasound to measure the endometrial thickness now
Pelvic magnetic resonance imaging with intravenous contrast next week
Reassure that a single short bleed without other symptoms needs no work-up

subtopic_detail: Intrauterine resuscitation
stem: A 32-year-old G3P2 at 39+6 weeks is in established labour at 6 cm dilation. Oxytocin augmentation was commenced 90 minutes ago for slow progress. Over the last 20 minutes the CTG shows repetitive late decelerations to 90 beats per minute with reduced variability between contractions. Contractions are occurring every 90 seconds. The fetal heart rate baseline is 150. The midwife has called you and you are at the bedside.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal BP 102/64 mmHg, HR 96, SpO2 99% in room air
data_table.Examination: Cervix 6 cm dilated, station -1, intact membranes; contractions every 90 seconds lasting 70 seconds
data_table.Investigations: CTG: repetitive late decelerations, reduced variability, baseline 150

lead_in: What is the single best initial intrauterine resuscitation step?

options.text: Increase the oxytocin infusion rate to strengthen contraction quality
Proceed directly to category 1 caesarean section under general anaesthesia
Administer subcutaneous terbutaline 250 mcg and continue oxytocin infusion
Stop the oxytocin infusion and reposition the woman to left lateral
Perform a fetal scalp lactate sample before any other intrauterine action

subtopic_detail: Twin chorionicity determination
stem: A 30-year-old G1P0 attends for her dating ultrasound at 11+5 weeks. Two viable fetuses are seen with appropriate crown-rump lengths. You are reviewing the images with the sonographer. The placental territories are partly contiguous and a thin inter-twin membrane is visible.

data_table.Investigations: Two fetuses with CRL 48 and 50 mm, both with cardiac activity, inter-twin membrane visualised, placental masses contiguous

lead_in: Which single ultrasound finding most reliably establishes chorionicity at this gestation?

options.text: Two separate placental masses identified on a single ultrasound image
Detection of two separate amniotic sacs around the twins on the scan
Discordant fetal sex documented on transabdominal scanning at this gestation
Inter-twin membrane thickness measured greater than 2 mm at the midpoint
Lambda twin-peak sign at the inter-twin membrane placental insertion now

subtopic_detail: Cervical screening HPV16+ HSIL
stem: A 34-year-old woman returns to her general practitioner for her cervical screening result. She is well, sexually active and uses a copper IUD for contraception. The cervical screening test reports oncogenic HPV detected, type 16, with reflex liquid-based cytology showing possible high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion. She has had previous normal results.

data_table.Investigations: HPV: oncogenic type 16 detected; LBC: possible HSIL; previous CSTs normal 2.5 years ago

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat the cervical screening test in 12 months from today's date
Refer to colposcopy for assessment and directed biopsy without delay
Arrange a large loop excision of the transformation zone (LLETZ) procedure
Order pelvic magnetic resonance imaging for cervical staging this week
Remove the copper intrauterine device prior to any further evaluation

subtopic_detail: Antepartum haemorrhage - placenta praevia
stem: A 33-year-old G3P2 at 32+0 weeks presents with sudden painless bright red vaginal bleeding that filled half a pad in 20 minutes and has now slowed. She has had two previous caesarean sections. The fetal movement chart shows normal movement. She has no contractions and no abdominal pain. She is haemodynamically stable on arrival but anxious.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 112/68 mmHg, HR 96, SpO2 99% in room air, Temp 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender abdomen, fundal height appropriate, fetal heart rate 145 with normal variability, no contractions, NO digital vaginal examination performed
data_table.Investigations: Blood group A Rh-positive, Hb 116 g/L, platelets 245, group and hold sent; routine 20-week ultrasound noted placenta covering the internal cervical os

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Sterile speculum examination after transabdominal ultrasound now
Digital vaginal examination to assess cervical dilation today
Intramuscular ergometrine 250 micrograms to control the bleeding
Immediate elective caesarean section under spinal anaesthesia today
Discharge home with general practitioner review in 48 hours plus pad chart

subtopic_detail: Induction of labour - Bishop's score
stem: A 28-year-old G1P0 at 41+3 weeks is admitted for induction of labour for prolonged pregnancy. She is well and has had normal antenatal care. Her membranes are intact. The fetal heart rate is reassuring on CTG. She declines artificial rupture of membranes today and is keen for the least invasive starting option.

data_table.Examination: Cervix posterior, firm, 1 cm long, 1 cm dilated, vertex at station -3, Bishop's score 3
data_table.Investigations: CTG reassuring, deepest pool of liquor 4 cm, estimated fetal weight 3.4 kg on growth scan 2 weeks ago

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate initial method of induction?

options.text: Artificial rupture of membranes immediately followed by an oxytocin infusion
Mechanical cervical ripening using a transcervical balloon catheter overnight
Vaginal misoprostol 25 micrograms every 4 hours up to a maximum of 6 doses
Outpatient weekly membrane sweeping until spontaneous onset of labour
Elective caesarean section under spinal anaesthesia scheduled tomorrow morning

subtopic_detail: Threatened miscarriage options
stem: A 27-year-old G2P1 woman at 8 weeks by LMP presents to ED with 12 hours of light vaginal bleeding and mild cramping. She has no fever, no foul discharge and no shoulder-tip pain. She is Rh D positive. A transvaginal ultrasound shows an intrauterine sac with an embryo of crown-rump length 16 mm and a fetal heart rate of 160 bpm. There is a small subchorionic haematoma. The cervix is closed on examination.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 36.7 degrees Celsius, HR 84, RR 16, BP 118/72 mmHg, SpO2 99% in room air
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft non-tender, cervix closed on speculum with small amount of blood in vault, no adnexal tenderness, uterus consistent with dates
data_table.Investigations: Beta-hCG 64,000 IU/L; haemoglobin 124 g/L; blood group A Rh D positive

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Offer misoprostol 800 microgram vaginally as outpatient medical management of likely miscarriage
Commence vaginal progesterone 400 mg twice daily until 16 weeks to prevent miscarriage
Administer anti-D immunoglobulin 250 IU intramuscularly to prevent maternal alloimmunisation
Admit overnight for bed rest, intravenous fluids and serial beta-hCG measurements before discharge
Reassure her, discharge home with safety-net advice and arrange GP follow-up in 2 weeks

subtopic_detail: MHT initiation intact uterus
stem: A 52-year-old woman with an intact uterus and no menstruation for 14 months presents to her GP for severe daily vasomotor symptoms disrupting sleep and work. She has no history of breast cancer, VTE, ischaemic heart disease or migraine with aura. Her BMI is 26 kg/m^2 and BP is 122/76 mmHg. A recent FBC, lipid profile and breast examination are normal. She declines non-hormonal therapies and asks about menopausal hormone therapy.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 36.8 degrees Celsius, HR 72, RR 14, BP 122/76 mmHg, SpO2 99% in room air
data_table.Examination: Well, no breast lump, no thyromegaly, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: Cervical screening up to date and negative; mammography normal in past 12 months

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate MHT regimen?

options.text: Topical low-dose vaginal oestrogen alone for systemic vasomotor symptoms and sleep disturbance
Oestradiol-only patch without a progestogen because she is past her final menstrual period
Sequential combined regimen with monthly progestogen withdrawal bleeds for the first year of treatment
Tibolone 2.5 mg orally daily as first-line treatment for moderate to severe vasomotor symptoms
Continuous combined oestradiol with micronised progesterone for endometrial protection

subtopic_detail: Postnatal contraception breastfeeding
stem: A 31-year-old woman presents to her GP at 6 weeks postpartum for routine review. She is exclusively breastfeeding her healthy term infant 8 times in 24 hours including overnight. She wants effective long-term contraception because the family is complete. Her BMI is 24 kg/m^2, BP is 116/72 mmHg, and there is no personal or family history of VTE or breast cancer. She had an uncomplicated vaginal birth and would prefer not to have surgery for sterilisation at this time.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 36.7 degrees Celsius, HR 70, RR 14, BP 116/72 mmHg, SpO2 99% in room air
data_table.Examination: Well-healed perineum, uterus involuted, no abnormal discharge, BMI 24 kg/m^2

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate contraceptive option?

options.text: Combined oral contraceptive pill starting today as effective contraception during breastfeeding
Insertion of a levonorgestrel intrauterine device at this visit with safety-net advice
Lactational amenorrhoea method as primary contraception until the infant is 12 months of age
Vaginal contraceptive ring inserted today and changed every 3 weeks for ongoing protection
Condoms with safety-net of emergency contraception until laparoscopic tubal ligation is arranged

subtopic_detail: Lactational mastitis
stem: A 28-year-old woman presents to her GP 3 weeks postpartum with 24 hours of fever, rigors and a painful left breast. She is exclusively breastfeeding her well infant. She has no penicillin allergy. On examination, the lateral upper quadrant of the left breast is red, warm and indurated with no fluctuance or skin breach. She is producing good volumes of milk on both sides. She has no axillary lymphadenopathy. The infant is feeding well.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 38.6 degrees Celsius, HR 100, RR 16, BP 118/74 mmHg, SpO2 99% in room air
data_table.Examination: Left breast lateral upper quadrant erythema with induration, no fluctuance, no skin necrosis, no axillary nodes, nipples intact without cracks

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate management?

options.text: Oral amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily for 7 days and cessation of breastfeeding from the affected breast
Oral flucloxacillin 500 mg four times daily for 5 to 7 days with continued breastfeeding from both breasts
Symptomatic management with paracetamol and ibuprofen and review in 48 hours if not improving
Refer for urgent breast ultrasound to exclude abscess and defer antibiotics until imaging is reviewed
Oral cefalexin 500 mg twice daily for 14 days with cabergoline to suppress lactation temporarily

subtopic_detail: Severe pre-eclampsia delivery timing
stem: A 32-year-old G1P0 woman at 36+0 weeks is admitted to a tertiary obstetric unit with severe headache, epigastric pain and brisk reflexes. Her BP on admission is 168/108 mmHg confirmed on two readings 15 minutes apart. She has received IV labetalol and magnesium sulfate. The fetus is cephalic with a reassuring CTG and estimated fetal weight at the 40th centile. Her cervix is unfavourable (Bishop score 2). Investigations show evidence of severe disease.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 36.8 degrees Celsius, HR 96, RR 18, BP 162/106 mmHg after labetalol, SpO2 99% in room air
data_table.Examination: Brisk reflexes, no clonus, no visual disturbance after analgesia; epigastric tenderness; uterus non-tender; CTG with normal baseline and accelerations
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 86 x10^9/L, ALT 142 U/L, AST 156 U/L, creatinine 96 micromol/L, urine protein-creatinine ratio 380 mg/mmol

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue magnesium and antihypertensive therapy as outpatient pending fetal movement diary monitoring
Administer antenatal corticosteroids and continue conservative management to 37+0 weeks
Arrange elective caesarean section because the cervix is unfavourable for induction at term
Proceed with planned delivery during this admission with intrapartum magnesium continuation
Transfer to a quaternary intensive care unit for plasma exchange before considering operative delivery

subtopic_detail: Suspected placental abruption preterm
stem: A 28-year-old G3P2 woman at 32+0 weeks presents to a tertiary maternity unit by ambulance with sudden onset constant abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding 200 mL. The uterus is tense and tender between contractions. CTG shows a baseline of 160 with reduced variability and recurrent late decelerations. There is no placenta praevia on the routine 20-week ultrasound. Her BP is 102/64 mmHg after a 500 mL crystalloid bolus.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 36.8 degrees Celsius, HR 122, RR 22, BP 102/64 mmHg, SpO2 98% in room air
data_table.Examination: Pale, anxious, tense tender uterus, palpable contractions every 2 minutes, cervix dilated 2 cm with old and fresh blood at os, fetal parts difficult to palpate
data_table.Investigations: Hb 96 g/L, platelets 168 x10^9/L, fibrinogen 1.8 g/L, INR 1.4, group and screen sent; bedside ultrasound confirms cephalic presentation, posterior placenta with no praevia

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Augment labour with oxytocin and aim for vaginal delivery within the next 2 hours under monitoring
Administer antenatal corticosteroids and tocolysis with nifedipine to delay delivery for 48 hours
Activate the obstetric emergency team and proceed to emergency caesarean section with massive transfusion protocol on standby
Transfer to a quaternary fetal medicine unit for cordocentesis before deciding on delivery mode
Continue conservative management with intravenous fluids and serial CTG every 2 hours overnight

subtopic_detail: Recurrent pregnancy loss workup
stem: A 33-year-old woman presents with her partner to a gynaecology clinic after three consecutive first-trimester miscarriages. All losses were before 10 weeks with confirmed intrauterine pregnancies on ultrasound. She has regular cycles, BMI 24 kg/m^2, no smoking and no thrombotic history. The couple's karyotypes and a pelvic ultrasound are normal. There is no family history of recurrent miscarriage or VTE. She has not had previous investigations performed.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 36.8 degrees Celsius, HR 72, RR 14, BP 116/72 mmHg, SpO2 99% in room air
data_table.Examination: Normal external genitalia and bimanual examination, no abdominal tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Pelvic ultrasound with 3D imaging shows normal uterine cavity; thyroid function normal; HbA1c 5.2%; karyotypes of both partners normal

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next test?

options.text: Inherited thrombophilia panel including factor V Leiden and prothrombin gene variant testing
Antiphospholipid antibody screen including lupus anticoagulant and anticardiolipin antibodies on two occasions
Hysteroscopy to assess the uterine cavity for septum or polyps missed by ultrasound imaging
Natural killer cell phenotyping and uterine immunohistochemistry to assess immune cause of loss
Anti-Mullerian hormone level and antral follicle count to assess ovarian reserve before reassurance

subtopic_detail: Postpartum eclampsia magnesium
stem: A 30-year-old G2P2 woman is on the postnatal ward 12 hours after a normal vaginal birth at 39 weeks. Her antenatal course was complicated by gestational hypertension. She has a witnessed 2-minute generalised tonic-clonic seizure. After airway management and oxygen, she is loaded with magnesium sulfate 4 g IV over 15 minutes followed by an infusion of 1 g per hour. Twenty minutes later she has a second seizure. BP is 162/108 mmHg.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 36.9 degrees Celsius, HR 110, RR 18, BP 162/108 mmHg, SpO2 98% on 6 L oxygen via mask
data_table.Examination: Postictal, GCS 13 then improves to 15 over 15 minutes, brisk reflexes, no focal neurology, uterus well contracted with minimal lochia
data_table.Investigations: Magnesium level 1.8 mmol/L, platelets 132 x10^9/L, creatinine 88 micromol/L, ALT 64 U/L, glucose 5.4 mmol/L

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Load with intravenous phenytoin 20 mg/kg as the magnesium has failed to prevent the second seizure
Administer a further 2 g magnesium sulfate intravenously over 5 to 10 minutes and increase the infusion rate
Cease magnesium sulfate, give intravenous calcium gluconate 1 g and commence intravenous diazepam infusion
Arrange urgent non-contrast CT brain before any further antiseizure therapy is administered
Administer intravenous labetalol 20 mg and intramuscular hydralazine 5 mg without further magnesium therapy

subtopic_detail: Symptomatic BV in pregnancy
stem: A 28-year-old G2P1 at 14 weeks of gestation presents to her general practitioner with 1 week of grey malodorous vaginal discharge and mild vulval irritation. She has no fever, abdominal pain or bleeding. Her first pregnancy was uncomplicated with a term vaginal birth. She is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander. She has no allergies and is taking pregnancy multivitamins only.

data_table.Examination: Speculum: thin homogeneous grey-white discharge coating vaginal walls; cervix appears healthy with no friability; uterus appropriate size for gestation
data_table.Investigations: Vaginal pH greater than 4.5; wet mount: clue cells present; whiff test positive; NAAT for chlamydia and gonorrhoea negative

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Oral fluconazole 150 mg as a single dose targeting vulvovaginal candidiasis as cause
Intravaginal clindamycin 2% cream once daily at night for 7 nights as topical therapy
Reassure that bacterial vaginosis does not require treatment in low-risk pregnancy currently
Oral metronidazole 400 mg twice daily for 7 days as systemic antibiotic therapy treatment
Intravaginal metronidazole gel 0.75% once daily at night for 5 nights as topical therapy

subtopic_detail: GDM initial management lifestyle first
stem: A 32-year-old G1 at 26 weeks of gestation attends her midwife appointment with the results of her routine 75 g oral glucose tolerance test. She is asymptomatic and has had an uncomplicated pregnancy to date. She has no family history of diabetes. Her booking BMI was 27. She is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander and has no other risk factors.

data_table.Examination: Symphysis-fundal height appropriate for gestation, fetal heart 145 beats per minute, no oedema; BP 118/72
data_table.Investigations: 75 g OGTT (mmol/L): fasting 5.4, 1 hour 10.6, 2 hour 8.8 (ADIPS thresholds 5.1 / 10.0 / 8.5); HbA1c 5.4%

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Commence metformin 500 mg twice daily titrating to a maximum of 2 g daily over 2 weeks
Refer to obstetrician for insulin initiation given multiple abnormal OGTT values today
Repeat the 75 g OGTT in 4 weeks for confirmation before initiating any management
Defer treatment until 32 weeks to allow physiological glucose changes to stabilise first
Initiate medical nutrition therapy, exercise advice and home glucose monitoring with review in 1-2 weeks

subtopic_detail: Most effective EC at 96 hours UPSI
stem: A 22-year-old nulliparous woman presents to her GP requesting emergency contraception. She had a single act of unprotected vaginal intercourse 96 hours ago. Her last menstrual period began 12 days ago and her cycles are regular at 28 days. She has no contraindications to hormonal or non-hormonal contraception and wishes to also commence ongoing contraception. Her BMI is 26.

data_table.Examination: Vital signs within normal limits; abdomen soft and non-tender; no current vaginal bleeding
data_table.Investigations: Urine beta-hCG negative; NAAT for chlamydia and gonorrhoea sent

lead_in: Which is the single most effective emergency contraception option?

options.text: Insertion of a copper intrauterine device within the next 24 hours
Oral levonorgestrel 1.5 mg as a single dose taken as soon as possible today
Oral ulipristal acetate 30 mg as a single dose taken as soon as possible today
Combined oral contraceptive Yuzpe regimen with high-dose oestrogen and progestogen
Reassurance as conception is unlikely beyond the standard emergency contraception window

subtopic_detail: Neonatal hepatitis B prophylaxis
stem: A 30-year-old G1 attends her first antenatal appointment at 12 weeks. Routine booking bloods return HBsAg positive, HBeAg negative, anti-HBe positive, ALT 38, HBV DNA 5,000 IU/mL. She is otherwise well, has no symptoms of liver disease, and her physical examination is unremarkable. She is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander. She plans a vaginal birth at term in a tertiary maternity unit.

data_table.Examination: No stigmata of chronic liver disease, no hepatosplenomegaly, mucous membranes pink
data_table.Investigations: HBsAg positive, HBeAg negative, anti-HBe positive, anti-HBc IgG positive; ALT 38 (normal less than 35), AST 30; HBV DNA 5,000 IU/mL; HIV and hepatitis C negative

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate plan for the neonate at birth?

options.text: Routine immunisation schedule commencing with hepatitis B vaccine at 6 weeks of age only
Hepatitis B immunoglobulin 100 IU plus birth-dose monovalent vaccine within 12 hours of birth
Defer infant immunisation until maternal HBV DNA is repeated postpartum to confirm need
Plan elective caesarean section to reduce vertical hepatitis B transmission risk for the infant
Test cord blood for HBsAg and only immunise the infant if cord blood comes back positive

subtopic_detail: HELLP at late preterm requires delivery
stem: A 31-year-old G2P1 at 34 weeks 2 days of gestation presents to the birth suite with 3 days of right upper quadrant and epigastric pain, nausea and one episode of vomiting. She has no headache or visual disturbance. CTG is reactive. She is not in labour. Cervix is unfavourable with a Bishop score of 3. There is no vaginal bleeding.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 168/108, HR 96, RR 18, SpO2 99% in room air, temp 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Right upper quadrant tenderness, hyperreflexia without clonus, no peripheral oedema, no abdominal tenderness elsewhere
data_table.Investigations: Hb 102, platelets 78, ALT 220, AST 250, LDH 800, urate 0.46, urine PCR 0.5, creatinine 78; coagulation normal

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate management?

options.text: Antihypertensive control with oral nifedipine and expectant management to 37 weeks
IV magnesium sulfate seizure prophylaxis and observation only with daily bloods on the ward
IV labetalol, IV magnesium sulfate seizure prophylaxis, and proceed to delivery after maternal stabilisation
Urgent plasma exchange for suspected thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura instead of delivery
IM betamethasone 12 mg and delay delivery 48 hours to allow full course for lung maturation

subtopic_detail: PPROM at 28 weeks expectant management bundle
stem: A 25-year-old G1 at 28 weeks 4 days of gestation presents 4 hours after a sudden gush of clear fluid per vagina, with continued small leakage. She has no contractions, abdominal pain or vaginal bleeding. She has no fevers or other systemic symptoms. She is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander. Group B streptococcus status is unknown.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 36.8 degrees Celsius, HR 84, BP 118/72, RR 16, SpO2 99% in room air
data_table.Examination: Sterile speculum: clear amniotic fluid pooling in posterior fornix, no offensive odour, cervix appears closed; uterus soft and non-tender; CTG reactive with fetal heart rate 145
data_table.Investigations: WCC 11.5, CRP 8, urinalysis negative; high vaginal swab and low vaginal swab for GBS sent

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate management?

options.text: Immediate induction with vaginal prostaglandin gel given adequate fetal lung maturity at this gestation
Discharge home with twice weekly outpatient review and a course of antenatal corticosteroids only
Oral nifedipine tocolysis for 48 hours to allow steroid course completion then proceed to delivery
Admit, IM betamethasone, IV erythromycin, magnesium sulfate if delivery imminent, expectant care to 34 weeks
Emergency caesarean section to avoid chorioamnionitis given the risk of prolonged latency on the ward

subtopic_detail: Indicated GBS chemoprophylaxis in labour
stem: A 30-year-old G2P1 at 38 weeks of gestation presents in established labour. Her previous baby had culture-confirmed early-onset group B streptococcal sepsis at 36 hours of life and required NICU admission. She has no penicillin allergy. Her current pregnancy has been uncomplicated. On examination she is in active labour with intact membranes and a cervix dilated 5 cm.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 36.9 degrees Celsius, HR 88, BP 118/72, RR 16
data_table.Examination: Cephalic presentation, fetal heart rate 145 with reassuring CTG, uterine contractions 3 in 10 minutes lasting 60 seconds; cervix 5 cm dilated with intact membranes

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate intrapartum chemoprophylaxis?

options.text: Oral cefalexin 500 mg six-hourly during labour as outpatient style cover
IV vancomycin 1 g eight-hourly during labour due to GBS resistance concerns nationally
Withhold antibiotics until membrane rupture has been present for more than 18 hours
IV cefazolin 2 g loading dose then 1 g eight-hourly during labour as first-line prophylaxis
IV benzylpenicillin 3 g loading dose then 1.8 g four-hourly until delivery completes

subtopic_detail: Amniotic fluid embolism with DIC
stem: A 32-year-old G3P2 at 39 weeks of gestation collapsed in second stage of labour with sudden dyspnoea, cyanosis and hypotension. She received CPR for 4 minutes with return of spontaneous circulation. She is now intubated and ventilated on an adrenaline infusion. Massive vaginal bleeding has started since collapse with no clot formation visible. The team has activated the obstetric emergency code.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 80/40 on adrenaline 0.1 mcg/kg/min, HR 130, RR 18 ventilated, SpO2 88% on FiO2 1.0, temp 36.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Generalised oozing from intravenous sites and gums; ongoing brisk bleeding per vagina with no clot; uterus boggy; fetal heart rate 90 with prolonged deceleration
data_table.Investigations: Hb 78, platelets 60, fibrinogen 0.8, PT 30 seconds, APTT 65 seconds, lactate 8.4, pH 7.18; cross-match in progress

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate immediate priority while continuing resuscitation?

options.text: Massive transfusion protocol with balanced blood products, expedite delivery and intensive care
IV unfractionated heparin 5000 unit bolus then continuous infusion targeting APTT 60-80 seconds
IV tranexamic acid 1 g and IM ergometrine 250 micrograms given postpartum haemorrhage features
Defer delivery until coagulation parameters are corrected then proceed to caesarean section here
IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 3 days targeting the anaphylactoid component of embolism

subtopic_detail: PCOS first-line management in primary care
stem: A 24-year-old nulliparous woman presents to her GP with 9 months of secondary amenorrhoea, gradual weight gain and increased terminal hair growth on her chin and lower abdomen. She is not currently sexually active, has no plans for pregnancy in the next 2 years, and has no personal or family history of thromboembolism. Her cycles before this episode were always irregular at 6 to 10 weeks apart since menarche at age 14.

data_table.Examination: Mild acne on jawline; Ferriman-Gallwey score 11; no acanthosis; thyroid not palpable
data_table.Investigations: TSH, prolactin, 17-hydroxyprogesterone all within reference range; total testosterone 3.8 nmol/L; LH:FSH ratio 2.6; HbA1c 5.8%; TVS shows 14 antral follicles in one ovary, 16 in the other, ovarian volume 12 mL bilaterally

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate initial management plan?

options.text: Lifestyle modification targeting 5 to 10 percent weight loss plus a combined oral contraceptive for cycle regulation and androgen control
Clomifene citrate 50 mg on days 2 to 6 of an induced cycle to restore ovulation and reduce androgen burden
Spironolactone 100 mg daily as monotherapy to suppress androgens, with no other contraceptive cover added
Referral for laparoscopic ovarian drilling as a definitive surgical solution to the underlying ovarian pathology
Empiric metformin 500 mg twice daily alone, without lifestyle counselling or contraceptive review at this visit

subtopic_detail: Severe pre-eclampsia with HELLP features at 34 weeks
stem: A 31-year-old G2P1 presents to birth suite at 34+5 weeks with 8 hours of right upper quadrant pain, nausea and a frontal headache. Her booking BP was 110/68; today three repeat readings 15 minutes apart give consistent values around 168/112 mmHg. She has had one normal vaginal delivery at term previously and is on no regular medications. The fetus is cephalic, CTG is reactive with no decelerations, and the cervix is 1 cm dilated and 1 cm long.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 168/112, HR 96, RR 18, SpO2 98% room air, Temp 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Tender right upper quadrant; brisk patellar reflexes; no clonus; no peripheral oedema beyond mild ankle puffiness
data_table.Investigations: Hb 102 g/L, platelets 78 x10^9/L, ALT 142 U/L, AST 168 U/L, LDH 720 U/L, creatinine 92 micromol/L, urate 0.42 mmol/L, urinary protein creatinine ratio 78 mg/mmol, fibrinogen 3.1 g/L, INR 1.0

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Oral nifedipine 20 mg single dose, no magnesium sulfate, and steroid course before considering delivery in 48 hours
Intravenous magnesium sulfate 4 g loading then 1 g/hour, intravenous labetalol titrated to BP under 160/110, and proceed to delivery today
Intramuscular betamethasone 11.4 mg now, intravenous hydralazine boluses, and expectant management to 37 weeks
Intravenous furosemide 40 mg, oral methyldopa loading, and admission for cardiotocograph surveillance for 24 hours
Platelet transfusion targeting count above 100 x10^9/L, vitamin K 10 mg intravenous, and elective caesarean tomorrow morning

subtopic_detail: Primary atonic PPH refractory to first-line oxytocin
stem: A 28-year-old G2P2 is 15 minutes after a spontaneous vaginal birth at 39+2 weeks following a 3-hour second stage. Active management of the third stage included intramuscular oxytocin 10 IU. She has lost an estimated 900 mL of blood with continuing brisk PV bleed. The uterus palpates soft and boggy at the umbilicus despite fundal massage, an IV oxytocin 5 IU bolus and a 40 IU oxytocin infusion already running. The placenta appears complete and the perineum has no significant tear.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 96/58, HR 118, SpO2 99% on 2 L nasal prongs, Temp 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Soft non-contracting uterus, no obvious cervical or vaginal tear on speculum, bladder catheterised and empty
data_table.Investigations: Hb 92 g/L on point-of-care, platelets 184 x10^9/L, fibrinogen pending; booking BP 118/72; no personal or family history of hypertension

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next pharmacological step?

options.text: Repeat intramuscular oxytocin 10 IU and continue the existing oxytocin infusion at the same rate while awaiting further bleeding
Intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g without adding any further uterotonic agent or escalation of bimanual compression
Intramuscular ergometrine 250 micrograms plus intramuscular carboprost 250 micrograms with intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g concurrently
Insertion of an intrauterine balloon tamponade device immediately, before any further pharmacological uterotonic escalation is attempted
Activation of the massive transfusion protocol with 4 units of packed red cells and 2 units of fresh frozen plasma immediately

subtopic_detail: Cord prolapse at 4 cm dilation
stem: A 33-year-old G3P2 at 38+4 weeks is admitted in early labour at 4 cm dilation with intact membranes. Twenty minutes after artificial rupture of membranes by the midwife to augment progress, the CTG shows a prolonged deceleration to 70 bpm lasting longer than 3 minutes. On vaginal examination there is a soft pulsatile loop of cord palpable in the vagina, below a high cephalic presenting part. Senior obstetric and anaesthetic registrars and the neonatal team have been called.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal BP 124/74, HR 92, SpO2 98% on room air
data_table.Examination: Cervix 4 cm dilated, vertex high above the spines, palpable pulsating cord loop in vagina
data_table.Investigations: Booking BMI 26, no scar; CTG demonstrates a sustained bradycardia at 70 bpm with no recovery on lateral position change

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Move the woman to theatre for forceps-assisted vaginal delivery at the current cervical dilation as the most expeditious route
Reduce the cord gently back into the uterine cavity by hand and continue augmentation with oxytocin to expedite labour
Apply continuous CTG monitoring in the left lateral position and reassess in 10 minutes before deciding on mode of delivery
Manually elevate the presenting part off the cord, place the woman in knee-chest or Trendelenburg position, and proceed to category 1 caesarean section
Administer terbutaline 250 micrograms subcutaneously for tocolysis and continue intrapartum vaginal birth in the current labour ward bed

subtopic_detail: Shoulder dystocia HELPERR algorithm first manoeuvres
stem: A 32-year-old G2P1 at 40+6 weeks is having a spontaneous vaginal birth. After delivery of the fetal head there is no restitution and the chin retracts against the perineum (turtle sign). Routine downward traction on the next contraction does not deliver the anterior shoulder. The estimated fetal weight at 38 weeks was 4.2 kg, and her previous baby was 4.0 kg. The clock is started by the midwife and an obstetric emergency call is made for theatre, neonatal and anaesthetic backup.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal BP 128/76, HR 102; FHR last 5 minutes 130 bpm with variable decelerations
data_table.Examination: Fetal head delivered, no restitution, turtle sign positive; second stage 35 minutes
data_table.Investigations: GDM diagnosed at 28 weeks, well controlled on diet; HbA1c 5.4% at booking; BMI 32 at booking

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate first set of manoeuvres?

options.text: Apply firm fundal pressure as the woman continues to push to drive the anterior shoulder under the symphysis pubis
Proceed immediately to symphysiotomy under local anaesthesia as the first surgical step in this dystocia algorithm
Push the fetal head back into the pelvis (Zavanelli) and prepare for an emergency caesarean section as the first response
Cut a generous mediolateral episiotomy now to enlarge the bony outlet and then apply downward traction to deliver the anterior shoulder
Hyperflex the maternal hips onto the abdomen (McRoberts position) and apply suprapubic pressure on the posterior aspect of the anterior shoulder

subtopic_detail: Lactational mastitis at day 7 postpartum
stem: A 29-year-old primipara presents to her GP on day 7 postpartum with a 24-hour history of a painful, red right breast and fevers to 38.7 degrees Celsius. She is exclusively breastfeeding with deep nipple cracking on the right. The baby is feeding well and gaining weight appropriately. There is no fluctuance and no overlying skin breakdown beyond a 2 mm nipple fissure. She has no penicillin allergy and is otherwise well.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 38.7 degrees Celsius, BP 118/72, HR 102, RR 16, SpO2 99% on room air
data_table.Examination: Right outer upper quadrant of breast erythematous, warm, tender with palpable engorgement; no fluctuant mass; nipple fissure 2 mm
data_table.Investigations: Bedside ultrasound performed: no organised collection or rim-enhancing fluid pocket; FBC and CRP not yet available

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue breastfeeding from both breasts, ensure effective milk drainage, and start oral dicloxacillin 500 mg four times daily for 5 days
Stop breastfeeding from the affected breast immediately, suppress lactation with cabergoline, and commence oral cefalexin 500 mg six hourly
Refer urgently to breast surgical clinic for incision and drainage today before any antibiotic therapy is commenced in the primary care setting
Trial oral paracetamol and warm compresses for 72 hours before considering antibiotic therapy or surgical referral by the GP at review
Start oral amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg twice daily for 10 days and book a follow-up review in 2 weeks at the practice

subtopic_detail: Hyperemesis gravidarum with ketonuria
stem: A 27-year-old G1P0 presents to ED at 9+4 weeks gestation with 5 days of intractable nausea and vomiting 10 to 12 times daily, unable to tolerate oral fluids for 24 hours. She has lost 3.5 kg since her booking 2 weeks ago. She is otherwise well, with no abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding or features of pre-existing eating disorder. Her dating ultrasound at 7 weeks showed a singleton intrauterine pregnancy with cardiac activity. She has tried oral pyridoxine without benefit.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 102/64, HR 112, RR 16, SpO2 99% on room air, Temp 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Dry mucosae, sunken eyes, capillary refill 3 seconds, abdomen soft and non-tender
data_table.Investigations: Urine ketones 3+, urine specific gravity 1.030, Na 132 mmol/L, K 3.2 mmol/L, urea 8.1 mmol/L, creatinine 78 micromol/L, TSH 0.4 mU/L

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Discharge home with oral metoclopramide 10 mg three times daily and ginger capsules with planned GP review in 48 hours
Admit, give intravenous thiamine 100 mg before commencing intravenous fluids with normal saline plus potassium replacement and ondansetron 4 mg IV
Commence intravenous 5 percent dextrose at 125 mL/hour without prior thiamine to address hypoglycaemia and ketosis quickly in the department
Commence oral prednisolone 40 mg daily as an outpatient with weekly clinical review for 2 weeks in the obstetric day assessment unit
Send her home with subcutaneous ondansetron 8 mg pumps and arrange community midwife daily review and outpatient bloods at the local pathology

subtopic_detail: Ectopic pregnancy medical management criteria
stem: A 28-year-old G2P0 presents to the early pregnancy assessment service with 4 days of mild right iliac fossa discomfort and small amounts of dark vaginal spotting. Her last menstrual period was 6 weeks and 2 days ago. She is haemodynamically stable, has no peritonism and no fertility concerns about future pregnancies. She has no liver, renal or haematological disease and is happy to attend twice-weekly follow-up. She is not breastfeeding and is using no medications.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 116/72, HR 78, RR 14, SpO2 99% on room air, Temp 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Mild right iliac fossa tenderness, no guarding, no rebound; cervical os closed
data_table.Investigations: Serum beta-hCG 2400 IU/L; TVS shows an empty uterus, a 28 mm right tubal mass without fetal cardiac activity and no free fluid in the pouch of Douglas; LFTs and FBC normal; creatinine 64 micromol/L

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate management option?

options.text: Expectant management with weekly serum beta-hCG until the level falls below 5 IU/L and no further imaging required during follow-up
Urgent laparoscopic salpingectomy under general anaesthesia as the safest definitive treatment regardless of the patient's clinical stability today
