Single-dose intramuscular methotrexate 50 mg/m2 with day 4 and day 7 serum beta-hCG to assess response and rule out rising titres
Diagnostic uterine evacuation and curettage to confirm absence of intrauterine villi before deciding on any further treatment route
Repeat the serum beta-hCG and ultrasound in 48 hours, with no specific treatment initiated today regardless of the current imaging findings

subtopic_detail: VBAC suitability after one previous lower segment caesarean
stem: A 32-year-old G2P1 attends her 36-week appointment to discuss mode of birth after one previous lower segment caesarean section at term for breech presentation 2 years ago. The current pregnancy is uncomplicated with a cephalic singleton, estimated fetal weight on the 60th centile. She has no diabetes, no hypertension, no prior uterine rupture and a uterine scar interval over 18 months. She is well informed and would prefer to avoid repeat caesarean if her risk profile permits.

data_table.Examination: Symphyseal-fundal height appropriate at 35 cm; fetus cephalic; cervix unfavourable for ripening yet
data_table.Investigations: Booking bloods normal; placenta fundal anterior on 20-week morphology and 32-week growth scan; uterine artery Doppler indices normal

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate counselling and plan?

options.text: Counsel that elective repeat caesarean at 39 weeks is mandatory because trial of labour is contraindicated after any prior caesarean delivery in Australia
Recommend induction of labour with prostaglandin gel at 39 weeks regardless of cervical favourability to optimise the spontaneous labour window
Plan home birth with a private midwife given the otherwise low-risk pregnancy and her strong preference to avoid hospital intervention this time
Offer a planned trial of labour after caesarean in a hospital with continuous CTG and immediate theatre access, with elective repeat caesarean from 39 weeks as an alternative
Offer external cephalic version now to confirm presentation and book elective caesarean if the fetus reverts to a non-cephalic lie at 38 weeks

subtopic_detail: GBS-positive women in labour at term
stem: A 30-year-old G1P0 at 39+4 weeks arrives in spontaneous early labour with regular contractions every 5 minutes for 2 hours. Her low-vaginal and rectal swab at 36 weeks returned positive for Group B Streptococcus. She has no penicillin allergy, no history of GBS bacteriuria in this pregnancy and no preterm rupture of membranes. The fetus is cephalic with a reassuring CTG. The cervix is 3 cm dilated and 1 cm long.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal BP 122/74, HR 88, Temp 36.7 degrees Celsius, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Cervix 3 cm dilated, fully effaced; membranes intact
data_table.Investigations: Booking bloods unremarkable; GBS swab at 36+2 weeks positive on culture; no prior infant with invasive GBS disease

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate intrapartum management?

options.text: Withhold antibiotics entirely until rupture of membranes occurs, then commence intravenous benzylpenicillin 3 g loading and 1.8 g every 4 hours until birth
Commence intravenous benzylpenicillin 3 g loading then 1.8 g every 4 hours throughout labour with monitoring for anaphylaxis and signs of chorioamnionitis
Commence intravenous vancomycin 1 g every 12 hours as a broad-spectrum substitute since the GBS may be penicillin-tolerant on culture
Offer oral amoxicillin 1 g eight hourly throughout labour because oral absorption is rapid enough to achieve protective neonatal blood levels at delivery
Recommend immediate caesarean section to avoid vaginal transit and eliminate the need for any intrapartum antimicrobial prophylaxis whatsoever today

subtopic_detail: Urinary tract infection in first trimester
stem: A 25-year-old G1P0 at 11+2 weeks attends her GP with 2 days of urinary frequency, dysuria and suprapubic discomfort. She has no fever, no flank pain and no vaginal discharge. She has no penicillin allergy and no history of antibiotic-resistant infections. She is otherwise well, takes folic acid and iodine, and is afebrile in clinic. Her last menstrual period was 11 weeks and 2 days ago with a confirmed intrauterine pregnancy at the dating scan.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 36.7 degrees Celsius, BP 110/68, HR 76, RR 14
data_table.Examination: Mild suprapubic tenderness, no costovertebral angle tenderness, no abdominal guarding
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick: leukocytes 3+, nitrites positive, protein trace, blood negative; midstream urine sent for culture; HbA1c 5.0% at booking

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate empirical antibiotic choice?

options.text: Oral trimethoprim 300 mg daily for 3 days as the first-line agent for uncomplicated lower UTI in the first trimester of pregnancy in this woman
Oral nitrofurantoin 100 mg four times daily for 5 days as the first-line agent for first-trimester urinary tract infection in this otherwise well woman
Oral cefalexin 500 mg twice daily for 5 days commenced today, with the midstream urine culture follow-up and rescript adjustment if resistance is identified
Oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily for 5 days as a broad-spectrum option for empirical treatment of uncomplicated lower UTI in a pregnant patient today
Symptomatic management with oral fluids and urinary alkaliniser only, with a planned review and dipstick check in 48 hours at the GP practice

subtopic_detail: Heavy menstrual bleeding refractory to LNG-IUS
stem: A 44-year-old multiparous woman has had a levonorgestrel intrauterine system inserted 9 months ago for heavy menstrual bleeding with intramural fibroids up to 4 cm. She continues to bleed heavily for 7 days each cycle with daily flooding, and her ferritin has dropped to 12 micrograms/L despite oral iron supplementation. She has completed her family and is keen to avoid hysterectomy if a stepwise medical option remains. The Mirena is correctly sited on transvaginal ultrasound.

data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender abdomen, no palpable mass; cervical os closed, IUD strings visible at expected length
data_table.Investigations: Hb 98 g/L (was 124 g/L 1 year ago), ferritin 12 micrograms/L, TSH 1.6 mU/L, coagulation profile normal; TVS shows three intramural fibroids 2 to 4 cm, endometrial thickness 6 mm, LNG-IUS in situ correctly

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next medical option?

options.text: Refer urgently for total abdominal hysterectomy and bilateral salpingectomy as the only definitive option given her age, parity and family completion at this point
Switch to a depot medroxyprogesterone acetate injection every 12 weeks alongside the existing intrauterine device for additive progestogenic suppression of the endometrium
Commence oral combined oral contraceptive cyclically with the LNG-IUS in situ to add oestrogen-mediated endometrial stabilisation across her remaining cycles
Add oral tranexamic acid 1 g three times daily during the heaviest 4 days of menstrual flow each cycle plus oral iron, with surgical review if no improvement in 3 months
Commence a GnRH agonist as long-term monotherapy without add-back hormonal therapy for ongoing suppression of fibroid-associated bleeding in this woman over the next 12 months

subtopic_detail: Cervical screening with HPV 16/18 detected
stem: A 38-year-old asymptomatic woman attends for her routine 5-yearly cervical screening test. Her result returns HPV 16 detected, with reflex liquid-based cytology showing low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (LSIL). She has no abnormal bleeding, no postcoital bleeding and is in a monogamous relationship. She has had two normal-result smears in the past 10 years. She is not pregnant and not on any immunosuppression at present.

data_table.Examination: Speculum examination at the time of screening was unremarkable; cervix appeared normal macroscopically
data_table.Investigations: Cervical screening test: HPV 16 detected; reflex LBC: LSIL; previous CSTs at 28 and 33 years HPV not detected with negative cytology; no immunosuppression

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat the human papillomavirus test in 12 months and refer to colposcopy only if the same oncogenic type persists at the 12-month follow-up assessment
Refer directly to colposcopy for assessment, given oncogenic HPV type 16 detection regardless of the cytology grade reported on the reflex liquid-based cytology
Recommend hysterectomy as a definitive treatment to remove the risk of progression to invasive cervical cancer in this woman with a high-risk HPV type detected today
Offer adult human papillomavirus vaccination as the sole intervention and rebook a screening test in 5 years rather than referral to colposcopy at this time
Repeat the cervical screening test in 5 years as per a routine asymptomatic-woman recall interval since she has no symptoms today in primary care

subtopic_detail: Anti-D prophylaxis in Rhesus D-negative women
stem: A 26-year-old G1P0 at 27+5 weeks attends her midwifery appointment. Her booking blood group is O Rhesus D negative and her antibody screen at booking was negative for atypical red cell antibodies. The pregnancy is uncomplicated, the fetus is singleton, and there have been no sensitising events such as bleeding, abdominal trauma or procedures. She has no relevant medical history, takes only folate and iodine, and has had no antenatal injections so far.

data_table.Examination: Symphyseal-fundal height appropriate at 28 cm; fetal heart rate 142 by Doppler
data_table.Investigations: Booking: blood group O RhD negative, antibody screen negative, repeat antibody screen at 28 weeks pending; partner blood group unknown; no sensitising events documented this pregnancy

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate plan for anti-D prophylaxis?

options.text: Withhold routine anti-D until a sensitising event occurs or fetal RhD status is established as positive, since prophylaxis is not standard practice in Australian antenatal care
Administer a single dose of anti-D immunoglobulin 625 IU intramuscular at 36 weeks gestation only, with no second dose given before the postpartum cord-blood test result
Administer anti-D immunoglobulin 625 IU intramuscular now at around 28 weeks and again at around 34 weeks, with a postpartum dose dependent on the cord blood RhD result
Administer two doses of anti-D immunoglobulin 250 IU intramuscular at 28 and 34 weeks gestation as the recommended Australian antenatal prophylaxis dosing in non-sensitised women
Send a Kleihauer-Betke test today and only administer anti-D immunoglobulin if there is evidence of fetomaternal haemorrhage above the 4 mL fetal red cell threshold today

subtopic_detail: Recurrent miscarriage workup after three first-trimester losses
stem: A 33-year-old G3P0 has had three consecutive first-trimester miscarriages between 7 and 10 weeks, the most recent 8 weeks ago. She is otherwise well with regular cycles and no thrombotic history. Her body mass index is 23 and she does not smoke. Her partner has fathered no children. She and her partner are keen to optimise her chance of a future ongoing pregnancy and ask about evidence-based investigation before they try again.

data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender abdomen; secondary sexual characteristics normal; cervical os closed
data_table.Investigations: TSH 1.6 mU/L, HbA1c 5.1%, FBC normal, midluteal progesterone consistent with ovulation; cycle 28 days; no prior thromboembolism

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Request a hysterosalpingogram to assess tubal patency as the priority investigation after a third first-trimester pregnancy loss in this woman before further blood work
Refer for assisted reproductive technology including in vitro fertilisation with pre-implantation genetic testing as the first-line approach for recurrent miscarriage workup today
Empirically commence low-dose aspirin 100 mg daily preconception and during early pregnancy without any further targeted laboratory investigations before a fourth pregnancy

Test for antiphospholipid antibodies (lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin and anti-beta2-glycoprotein I), with parental karyotype if products of conception cytogenetics suggest a parental rearrangement
Send a thrombophilia panel including factor V Leiden, prothrombin gene mutation and protein C/S as the first-line investigation in this woman with no thrombotic history this presentation

subtopic_detail: Postpartum long-acting reversible contraception at 6 weeks
stem: A 28-year-old woman attends her 6-week postnatal visit. She is breastfeeding her healthy term baby on demand. She has no thromboembolic history and her BP is normotensive. She does not want another pregnancy for at least 3 years and asks about reliable contraception that does not interfere with breastfeeding. She has had no postnatal complications, normal lochia and a normal pelvic examination today. She has had her postnatal mood and EPDS screening completed.

data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender abdomen, well-healed perineum, cervix appears parous and closed
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count and ferritin within normal range; no current medications other than postnatal vitamins; baby thriving and feeding

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate first-line contraceptive recommendation?

options.text: Recommend reliance on the lactational amenorrhoea method for the next 12 months as the most effective postpartum contraceptive strategy for this woman who is currently breastfeeding her infant
Offer immediate insertion of an etonogestrel subdermal implant at this visit or a copper or progestogen-releasing intrauterine device after counselling about LARC efficacy
Commence a combined oral contraceptive containing 30 micrograms ethinylestradiol and 150 micrograms levonorgestrel daily as the first-line agent for this breastfeeding woman at 6 weeks
Recommend tubal ligation by laparoscopy at the next available theatre list as the most effective contraceptive option in this woman who would like 3 years between pregnancies
Suggest condom use alone for the next 6 months and reassess at her routine cervical screening visit in 4 years for a definitive longer-acting method of contraception then

subtopic_detail: Threatened miscarriage with subchorionic haematoma
stem: A 26-year-old G1P0 at 9+1 weeks presents to the early pregnancy clinic with light fresh PV spotting for 24 hours, no clots and no abdominal pain. She is haemodynamically stable, afebrile and feels well. She has no fevers, no foul-smelling discharge and no chemical or recreational drug exposure. Her booking bloods at 8 weeks were unremarkable. A bedside transvaginal ultrasound today demonstrates a live intrauterine pregnancy with appropriate biometry and a small 1.5 cm subchorionic haematoma.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/70, HR 76, Temp 36.7 degrees Celsius, SpO2 99% on room air
data_table.Examination: Speculum: small amount of fresh blood in posterior fornix; cervical os closed; uterus soft non-tender on bimanual examination
data_table.Investigations: TVS: live intrauterine singleton pregnancy with CRL 24 mm consistent with 9 weeks 1 day; FHB 162 bpm; 1.5 cm subchorionic haematoma; serum bHCG and progesterone not yet measured

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Prescribe oral misoprostol 800 micrograms vaginally as a single dose to expedite resolution of the threatened miscarriage and avoid prolonged uncertainty for this woman today
Admit for bed rest for 7 to 10 days and intravenous progesterone supplementation as the routine management for threatened miscarriage at 9 weeks gestation in primary care
Reassure with safety-net advice, provide RhD typing if not yet done, and arrange clinic follow-up with repeat ultrasound in 1 to 2 weeks if symptoms persist or worsen
Arrange immediate surgical evacuation by suction curettage as the best management option for this woman with confirmed threatened miscarriage at 9 weeks gestation today in the operating theatre
Administer methotrexate 50 mg per square metre intramuscularly as the standard first-line approach to threatened miscarriage with a small subchorionic haematoma today

subtopic_detail: Antiepileptic switch from valproate before pregnancy
stem: A 28-year-old woman with generalised tonic-clonic seizures on sodium valproate 1500 mg daily for 6 years attends preconception clinic. Her last seizure was 2 years ago. She is keen to conceive within the next 12 months. She has no history of focal seizures, no other antiepileptic, no liver disease, no migraine and no contraindications to alternative antiepileptics. She does not drink alcohol and is on the AU pregnancy prevention program for valproate users currently.

data_table.Examination: Normal neurological examination; no focal deficits, no skin lesions suggestive of phakomatosis
data_table.Investigations: EEG 12 months ago without epileptiform activity on routine recording; LFT, FBC normal; on long-acting reversible contraception currently

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate preconception management plan?

options.text: Continue sodium valproate at the current dose and add folic acid 5 mg daily without altering the antiepileptic regimen, with monthly serum valproate monitoring during conception attempts
Stop sodium valproate immediately today and conceive in the next 6 months without commencing any alternative antiepileptic, relying on her current 2-year seizure-free interval
Switch directly to topiramate 100 mg twice daily at standard dose with folic acid 0.5 mg daily as the safer alternative for generalised tonic-clonic seizures in this woman before conception

Gradually cross-taper sodium valproate to levetiracetam over months under neurology supervision with folic acid 5 mg daily, continue contraception until seizure-free on monotherapy, then attempt conception
Add lamotrigine to her current valproate at standard maintenance dose and continue dual therapy throughout the pregnancy to minimise risk of breakthrough seizures occurring at any point

subtopic_detail: Endometriosis stepwise management after failed COCP
stem: A 30-year-old nulliparous woman has had chronic cyclical pelvic pain and dyspareunia for 4 years. She has been on continuous combined oral contraceptive for 12 months with persistent symptoms despite adherence and tolerable side effects. NSAIDs provide partial relief only. She has no current fertility plans. She has no current bowel or urinary symptoms, no haematuria or rectal bleeding, no abnormal cervical screening, and her pelvic examination is unremarkable today.

data_table.Examination: Mild tenderness in the posterior fornix; no adnexal mass or nodules palpable on bimanual examination; cervix appears normal
data_table.Investigations: Pelvic ultrasound: no endometrioma, no hydrosalpinx, no obvious deep infiltrating endometriosis; CA-125 not measured

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next management option?

options.text: Switch the combined oral contraceptive to a progestogen-only pill at standard dose and continue NSAIDs alone with planned review at 6 months in the gynaecology clinic
Refer for total abdominal hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy as the definitive treatment of suspected endometriosis in this woman with persistent symptoms at age 30
Commence empirical danazol 200 mg three times daily for 6 months to suppress endometriotic implants and reduce her cyclical pelvic pain symptoms in this woman before any laparoscopic intervention
Offer the levonorgestrel intrauterine system at standard dose as a sole next intervention without considering laparoscopy for diagnostic confirmation and treatment in the same operative setting today
Offer diagnostic laparoscopy with excision or ablation of any visible endometriotic lesions in the same operative setting, with postoperative hormonal suppression to reduce symptom recurrence

subtopic_detail: Abnormal uterine bleeding in a peri-menopausal woman with obesity
stem: A 47-year-old woman presents with 6 months of increasingly heavy and irregular menstrual bleeding. Her BMI is 34 kg/m2 and she has type 2 diabetes. She has had two children and uses no hormonal contraception. She has no postcoital bleeding, no urinary symptoms and is up to date with cervical screening. She has not noticed any weight loss or systemic symptoms. There is no first-degree relative with endometrial or colorectal malignancy.

data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender abdomen, bulky uterus on bimanual; cervix appears macroscopically normal
data_table.Investigations: Hb 102 g/L, MCV 78 fL, ferritin 14 microgram/L, beta-hCG negative, TSH 1.4 mIU/L; cervical screening test 6 months ago: HPV not detected

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Initiate a levonorgestrel intrauterine system empirically without any imaging or histological evaluation of the endometrium and review the patient in 6 months for ongoing review
Transvaginal ultrasound to measure endometrial thickness only, without any plan for endometrial biopsy regardless of findings or risk factors in this patient's presentation today
Transvaginal ultrasound to assess endometrial thickness and structural lesions plus endometrial biopsy by pipelle, given her age, obesity and diabetes, with management determined by histology
Proceed to dilatation and curettage under general anaesthesia in the next 4 weeks without any prior pipelle sampling or transvaginal ultrasound being attempted at this initial outpatient assessment
Commence the combined oral contraceptive pill empirically as the first investigation and management step without imaging or histological evaluation of the endometrium in this peri-menopausal patient

subtopic_detail: Preconception counselling and medication review in type 2 diabetes
stem: A 32-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes for 5 years presents for preconception counselling. Her current medications include metformin, an ACE inhibitor for diabetic nephropathy with mild albuminuria, and a statin. Her HbA1c is 8.4 percent. She is on the combined oral contraceptive for cycle regulation. She wants to start trying for pregnancy in 6 to 12 months. She has had no diabetic retinopathy on her last screen, and has had no microvascular complications outside mild albuminuria.

data_table.Examination: Normal cardiovascular examination, no peripheral neuropathy on monofilament
data_table.Investigations: HbA1c 8.4%, eGFR 86, urine albumin-creatinine ratio 8 mg/mmol, TSH 1.8 mIU/L, B12 220 pmol/L, fundoscopy at 12 months unremarkable

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate preconception plan?

options.text: Continue all current medications including the ACE inhibitor and statin into pregnancy with no specific glycaemic target and no folate prescribing initiated at this visit
Continue all current medications into pregnancy unchanged on the basis that her glycaemic control has been adequate over the last 12 months at the current regimen for this patient
Cease all diabetes medications before any future conception, with no glycaemic targets set, no folate prescribing initiated and no further follow-up arranged before the next clinic visit

Aim for HbA1c under 6.5 percent before conception with insulin (metformin may continue), cease ACE inhibitor and statin before conception, start folic acid 5 mg daily, schedule retinal and renal review
Counsel her to avoid pregnancy until HbA1c is under 5 percent, with no other medication adjustments, no folate prescribing initiated, and no further microvascular complication screening at this visit

subtopic_detail: Heavy menstrual bleeding: first-line management in a 38 year old
stem: A 38-year-old woman presents with a 12 month history of progressively heavier and prolonged menses, with passage of clots and tiredness. She has two children and her family is complete. Pelvic ultrasound shows a normal sized uterus with no fibroids or polyps. Her cervical screening is up to date. Her ferritin is 14 micrograms/L and Hb is 109 g/L. She is otherwise well, with regular cycles every 28 days, and is not pursuing pregnancy.

data_table.Examination: Pelvic examination normal, no adnexal mass; speculum normal cervix
data_table.Investigations: Hb 109 g/L, ferritin 14 micrograms/L, TSH 2.1 mIU/L, beta-hCG negative, TVUS normal uterus and ovaries

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

options.text: Total laparoscopic hysterectomy after iron infusion as a definitive primary management plan
Oral tranexamic acid 1 g three times daily on day 1 to 4 of menses as long-term therapy only
Endometrial ablation now as definitive treatment with no other contraceptive considerations
Insertion of a 52 mg levonorgestrel intrauterine system at the next available appointment
Combined oral contraceptive pill cyclically with iron supplementation and review in 6 months

subtopic_detail: Vulvovaginal candidiasis vs bacterial vaginosis vs trichomoniasis
stem: A 26-year-old non-pregnant woman presents with a 5 day history of vulval itch, soreness, and a thick white discharge. She has had two similar episodes in the last 12 months treated with over-the-counter therapy. She is in a monogamous heterosexual relationship and uses combined oral contraceptive pill. There is no abnormal bleeding or pelvic pain. Speculum examination shows a thick white adherent discharge and erythema; pH of vaginal fluid is 4.2 and there is no fishy odour.

data_table.Examination: Vulval erythema, thick adherent curdy white discharge, no cervical motion tenderness, no adnexal mass, vaginal pH 4.2, negative amine test
data_table.Investigations: Microscopy pseudohyphae visible; high vaginal swab for STIs sent; urine pregnancy test negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Oral metronidazole 400 mg twice daily for 7 days for bacterial vaginosis treatment cover
Single dose oral fluconazole 150 mg with patient education on triggers and self-care
Oral tinidazole 2 g single dose for both partners as empirical trichomoniasis treatment
Topical hydrocortisone 1% twice daily for 2 weeks without antifungal therapy added today
Oral cefalexin 500 mg four times daily for 7 days based on empirical bacterial superinfection

subtopic_detail: Contraceptive choice for a woman on enzyme-inducing antiepileptic
stem: A 24-year-old woman with epilepsy currently controlled on carbamazepine 400 mg twice daily presents to discuss contraception. She is sexually active with her male partner and uses condoms inconsistently. She would prefer not to take a daily pill and has no contraindications to hormonal contraception. Her cycles are regular and her last menstrual period was 1 week ago. She is not breastfeeding.

data_table.Examination: No abnormality detected
data_table.Investigations: Beta hCG negative; no current sexually transmitted infection screen abnormalities

lead_in: What is the most appropriate contraceptive option?

options.text: Standard depot medroxyprogesterone acetate 150 mg intramuscular every 12 weeks consistently
Combined oral contraceptive pill with 50 micrograms ethinylestradiol as enhanced dose therapy
Etonogestrel subdermal implant on the same day with no contraceptive interaction concern
Progestogen-only pill at standard daily dose with backup condoms during enzyme inducer use
Copper intrauterine device inserted at the next available appointment for long-term cover

subtopic_detail: Hyperemesis gravidarum: first-line antiemetic ladder
stem: A 24-year-old woman in her first pregnancy presents at 9 weeks gestation with persistent vomiting since 6 weeks, unable to keep fluids down for 36 hours. She has lost 4 kg from her booking weight and reports dizziness on standing. Urine ketones are 3+. She has tried dietary modification, small frequent meals, and ginger without benefit. Pulse rate is 110 and blood pressure 96/58 standing.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 110 supine 124 standing, BP 96/58, T 36.9, RR 18, SpO2 99%
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes, mild epigastric tenderness, no thyroid mass, no abdominal mass
data_table.Investigations: Urine ketones 3+, sodium 132 mmol/L, potassium 3.2 mmol/L, beta hCG 78000 IU/L; TFTs pending; ultrasound singleton pregnancy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Single dose intramuscular ondansetron 8 mg and discharge home with a 7 day script for ondansetron
Outpatient oral metoclopramide 10 mg three times daily with general practitioner review tomorrow
Admit for intravenous Hartmann solution with thiamine 100 mg IV and oral pyridoxine doxylamine
Oral prochlorperazine 5 mg three times daily and ginger 250 mg four times daily for 3 days
Termination of pregnancy counselling because of failure of conservative management at 9 weeks

subtopic_detail: Asymptomatic bacteriuria detected at antenatal booking
stem: A 28-year-old woman attends her antenatal booking visit at 13 weeks gestation. She is asymptomatic. The midstream urine culture from booking grows greater than 10 to the 8 colony forming units per litre of Escherichia coli sensitive to nitrofurantoin, cefalexin and trimethoprim. She has no allergies and no known renal disease. Pregnancy has otherwise been uncomplicated.

data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender abdomen, no flank tenderness, no suprapubic tenderness
data_table.Investigations: MSU E. coli >10^8 CFU/L; urine dipstick leucocytes 1+ nitrites positive; renal function normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Oral trimethoprim 300 mg daily for 3 days regardless of trimester or folate status
Repeat the MSU in 6 weeks before deciding to treat asymptomatic bacterial growth
Single dose oral fosfomycin 3 g sachet without further test of cure because of pregnancy
Oral nitrofurantoin 100 mg four times daily for 5 days with repeat MSU after treatment
Continuous low dose nitrofurantoin 50 mg nightly until 36 weeks gestation without test of cure

subtopic_detail: Endometrial polyp on TVUS in a postmenopausal woman
stem: A 62-year-old postmenopausal woman presents with a single episode of postmenopausal bleeding 6 weeks ago. She has not bled since. Transvaginal ultrasound shows a thickened endometrium of 9 mm with a discrete focal lesion suggestive of an endometrial polyp. She has no significant medical history, is not on tamoxifen, and has a BMI of 26. She has a normal cervical screening history.

data_table.Examination: Pelvic examination normal, no cervical lesion on speculum, no adnexal mass
data_table.Investigations: TVUS endometrium 9 mm with discrete focal hyperechoic lesion 12 mm consistent with polyp; CA-125 normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer for total laparoscopic hysterectomy without prior histological diagnosis being obtained
Repeat transvaginal ultrasound in 6 months without immediate biopsy or hysteroscopy
Pipelle endometrial biopsy alone as outpatient procedure without removing the polyp
Initiate continuous combined hormone replacement therapy to thin the endometrium
Outpatient hysteroscopy and polyp resection with directed endometrial biopsy

subtopic_detail: Threatened miscarriage in early first trimester
stem: A 31-year-old woman with a desired pregnancy presents at 7 weeks 3 days by last menstrual period with a 2 day history of light per-vaginal spotting and mild cramping. She has no fever, no shoulder tip pain, and her observations are normal. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an intrauterine gestation sac with a yolk sac and a 5 mm crown-rump length embryo with cardiac activity present at 110 beats per minute. The cervix is closed on speculum examination.

data_table.Examination: Soft abdomen, no peritonism, no shoulder tip pain, closed cervix on speculum
data_table.Investigations: Beta hCG 18000 IU/L, blood group O Rh positive; TVUS intrauterine gestation, CRL 5 mm, FHR 110 bpm, no subchorionic haematoma

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassurance, pelvic rest, follow up ultrasound in 1 to 2 weeks if symptoms continue
Immediate dilatation and curettage to clear products and prevent further bleeding
Vaginal progesterone 400 mg twice daily for all women with threatened miscarriage and bleeding
Anti-D 250 IU intramuscular as a single dose given to this Rh-positive woman today
Methotrexate 50 mg per m2 intramuscularly to manage a suspected ectopic pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Postpartum contraception in a breastfeeding mother
stem: A 32-year-old woman is reviewed 4 weeks after an uncomplicated spontaneous vaginal delivery of her first child. She is exclusively breastfeeding and her child is gaining weight well. She and her partner want effective contraception and are willing to consider any method including long-acting reversible contraception. She has no history of venous thromboembolism, hypertension, or migraine with aura. Her smoking status is non-smoker.

data_table.Examination: Postnatal examination unremarkable, fundus involuted, no abnormal bleeding
data_table.Investigations: Not indicated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line contraceptive option?

options.text: Levonorgestrel intrauterine system inserted at 6 weeks postpartum is delayed by current uterine state
Combined oral contraceptive pill 30 micrograms ethinylestradiol started today as effective option
Lactational amenorrhoea method alone as exclusive contraception without other supplementary method
Etonogestrel subdermal implant inserted today with timely follow up arranged for monitoring
Diaphragm fitted in clinic today as primary method without backup contraceptive arrangements

subtopic_detail: Carriage in an earlier pregnancy with a negative swab in this one
stem: A 33-year-old woman in her second pregnancy arrives in established labour at 39 weeks. Her first baby was born vaginally at term and remained well throughout the newborn period.

data_table.Swabs: Positive at 36 weeks in the first pregnancy, negative at 36 weeks in this one
data_table.Labour: Cervix 5 cm, membranes ruptured 40 minutes ago, clear liquor, afebrile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Routine labour care without an intravenous antibiotic for carriage
Intravenous benzylpenicillin now, because carriage carries over in time
Intravenous cefazolin now, as a narrower option than penicillin in labour
Send a further swab now and start an antibiotic while awaiting the result
Withhold the antibiotic but arrange a blood culture on the baby after birth

subtopic_detail: Cervical screening HSIL result and colposcopy pathway
stem: A 32-year-old woman attends to discuss her latest cervical screening result. She had a routine self-collected cervical screening test, which returned positive for HPV-16. Reflex liquid-based cytology shows high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion. She is asymptomatic, sexually active in a monogamous relationship, and has never had an abnormal screen previously. She is not pregnant and has a copper IUD in place.

data_table.Examination: Speculum examination normal at routine follow up appointment
data_table.Investigations: HPV-16 positive; reflex LBC HSIL; pregnancy test negative

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat cervical screening test in 6 months with referral only if HPV remains positive
Repeat the HPV cervical screening test in 12 months without colposcopy referral first
Remove the copper IUD before any further investigation can be safely performed today
Empirical large loop excision of the transformation zone without prior colposcopy
Refer for colposcopy within 2 weeks for directed biopsy and treatment planning

subtopic_detail: Recurrent pregnancy loss workup at three losses
stem: A 34-year-old woman attends gynaecology with her partner after a third consecutive first-trimester miscarriage. All losses were spontaneous and confirmed on ultrasound. There is no history of stillbirth or second trimester loss. She has regular menstrual cycles, BMI 24, and no medical conditions. She does not smoke or drink. The partner is well and 36 years old. The previous loss had products of conception that were not karyotyped.

data_table.Examination: Pelvic examination normal, no abnormal bleeding
data_table.Investigations: Previous TVUS showed normal uterine cavity; FBC, TSH, fasting glucose all normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial workup?

options.text: Antiphospholipid antibody panel plus parental karyotype and pelvic cavity imaging assessment
Empirical heparin and aspirin in next pregnancy with no investigations performed today now
Inherited thrombophilia screen for factor V Leiden and prothrombin gene mutations only
Pre-implantation genetic testing for aneuploidy referral for the next attempt without other tests
Endometrial biopsy in the secretory phase to screen for chronic endometritis alone

subtopic_detail: Operative vaginal delivery: vacuum versus forceps selection
stem: A 30-year-old primigravida is in the second stage of labour at 40 weeks gestation. She has been pushing for 90 minutes with adequate contractions. The fetal head is at +2 station in direct occipito-anterior position with no caput or moulding. The cardiotocograph shows late decelerations with reduced variability. She has an effective epidural in situ. The obstetric registrar is supervised by an experienced consultant in the labour ward.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal BP 116/74, HR 96, T 36.8; fetal CTG late decelerations, baseline 145, reduced variability
data_table.Examination: Fully dilated cervix, head at +2 station, direct OA position, no caput, no moulding, intact perineum
data_table.Investigations: Bedside ultrasound confirms OA position; bedside fetal scalp lactate 4.0 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Category 1 caesarean section in theatre transferring immediately for delivery within 30 minutes
Vacuum-assisted vaginal delivery using a Kiwi cup with appropriate analgesia in situ
Continue active pushing for a further 30 minutes with maternal repositioning techniques first
Apply intrauterine pressure catheter to titrate oxytocin and increase the contraction frequency
Mid-cavity rotational forceps without prior vacuum attempt as primary instrument selection

subtopic_detail: Severe pre-eclampsia at 36 weeks: timing of delivery
stem: A 30-year-old primigravida at 36 weeks gestation is admitted with blood pressure 168/108 mmHg, 3+ proteinuria on dipstick, and headache. Bloods show platelets 92 x10^9/L, ALT 80 U/L, creatinine 88 micromol/L, and urate 0.42 mmol/L. The cardiotocograph is reassuring with baseline 140 and normal variability. She has had a single dose of nifedipine slow release 20 mg with BP reduction to 152/96 and started intravenous magnesium sulfate. She has had a course of corticosteroids 4 days ago.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 152/96 after nifedipine, HR 86, T 36.9, RR 18, SpO2 99%
data_table.Examination: Brisk reflexes, no clonus, no visual disturbance now, headache persisting; CTG reassuring
data_table.Investigations: Plt 92 x10^9/L, ALT 80 U/L, creatinine 88 micromol/L, urate 0.42 mmol/L, urine PCR 320 mg/mmol

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Expectant management with daily monitoring and aim to reach 39 weeks gestation for delivery
Delivery is recommended now given severe pre-eclampsia with end-organ involvement at 36 weeks
Continue magnesium sulfate for 48 hours and reassess for delivery once severity has stabilised
Repeat course of corticosteroids today and plan delivery in 48 hours after second course completes
Outpatient management with daily blood pressure monitoring and twice weekly bloods until 38 weeks

subtopic_detail: Lactational mastitis versus inflammatory breast cancer
stem: A 34-year-old breastfeeding mother presents to the GP 6 weeks postpartum with a 5 day history of right breast pain, redness, and warmth that has progressed despite frequent feeding and warm compresses. The right breast skin shows diffuse erythema involving more than one quadrant, with non-tender peau d orange in the upper outer area but no discrete fluctuant lump. She is afebrile and clinically well. She has tried paracetamol and continued breastfeeding without resolution. There is no nipple discharge.

data_table.Examination: Diffuse erythema upper outer quadrant right breast with peau d orange; non-tender; no discrete mass; no axillary lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Bedside ultrasound shows no abscess; skin and milk swab pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer urgently to a breast clinic for assessment including ultrasound, mammogram, and core biopsy
Start oral flucloxacillin 500 mg four times daily for 10 days and review in 7 days as needed
Encourage cessation of breastfeeding to allow resolution and review the patient in 1 week time
Empirical incision and drainage in the emergency department for suspected occult breast abscess
Hot compresses, milk expression, and follow up in 4 weeks without further investigation now

subtopic_detail: OASIS classification and immediate repair planning
stem: A 28-year-old woman has just delivered a 3.8 kg infant via spontaneous vaginal delivery with vacuum assistance at 40 weeks gestation. On perineal examination by the obstetric registrar, there is a tear through the perineal skin, perineal muscles, external anal sphincter, internal anal sphincter, and rectal mucosa. The vacuum was used because of fetal distress. She has an epidural in situ and is haemodynamically stable. The consultant has been called to attend.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 122/80, HR 86, T 36.9, blood loss 350 mL
data_table.Examination: Tear extending through external and internal anal sphincters and rectal mucosa, epidural functional
data_table.Investigations: Not currently indicated; recheck Hb in 6 hours postpartum

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Repair only the perineal skin and external anal sphincter in delivery suite with local anaesthesia
Repair the tear at the bedside in delivery suite using local anaesthetic infiltration only
Leave the tear unrepaired and review by colorectal surgery in clinic at 2 weeks postpartum
Refer urgently for primary defunctioning colostomy by colorectal surgery this admission
Transfer to theatre for repair under regional anaesthesia with antibiotic prophylaxis cover

subtopic_detail: Maternal sepsis: hour-1 bundle in pregnancy
stem: A 27-year-old woman at 32 weeks gestation presents to the emergency department with rigors, lower abdominal pain, and foul smelling vaginal loss for 12 hours. Her temperature is 39.1 degrees Celsius, heart rate 130, respiratory rate 26, blood pressure 92/56, oxygen saturation 95% on room air. The cardiotocograph shows a baseline of 175 with absent variability and frequent uterine contractions. She is 4 cm dilated on examination, with cloudy fluid noted. Bedside lactate is 4.2 mmol/L.

data_table.Examination: Cervix 4 cm dilated, cloudy malodorous liquor draining, uterine tenderness, fetal tachycardia
data_table.Investigations: Lactate 4.2 mmol/L, WCC 22 x10^9/L, CRP 250 mg/L, blood cultures taken, urine taken, MSU pending

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Intravenous tocolytic therapy with terbutaline to prolong pregnancy and reduce uterine activity
Immediate emergency caesarean section without antibiotic dose first being administered
Intravenous fluid resuscitation 30 mL/kg and intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam within 1 hour
Intravenous antibiotics after blood culture growth and identification of causative organism
Single dose intravenous corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity before any other intervention

subtopic_detail: Anovulatory infertility in PCOS: ovulation induction agent
stem: A 28-year-old woman with a BMI of 31 has been trying to conceive for 14 months with her partner. Her cycles are irregular at 35 to 60 days. She has clinical hyperandrogenism with acne and hirsutism. Pelvic ultrasound shows polycystic ovarian morphology. Her partner has a normal semen analysis. Her thyroid function and prolactin are normal. Her HbA1c is 5.4%, fasting glucose 5.0 mmol/L, and she has had a normal hysterosalpingogram. She declines fertility supplements and tracks ovulation reliably.

data_table.Examination: Mild acne and hirsutism, no acanthosis nigricans, otherwise normal pelvic exam
data_table.Investigations: TSH normal, prolactin normal, day 21 progesterone consistent with anovulation; partner semen analysis normal; HSG patent tubes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line ovulation induction agent?

options.text: Metformin 1500 mg daily monotherapy without additional ovulation induction agent in cycle
Oral clomifene citrate 50 mg daily on cycle days 2 to 6 as standard first-line therapy
Oral letrozole 2.5 mg daily on cycle days 2 to 6 with monitoring of follicular response
Gonadotropin injections starting low dose without trial of oral ovulation induction first
Direct referral for in vitro fertilisation without trial of ovulation induction agents first

subtopic_detail: First episode postmenopausal bleeding
stem: A 62-year-old presents with a single episode of spotting 4 days ago, occurring 9 years after her last menstrual period. She has never been on hormone therapy. Her body mass index is 31 and she has type 2 diabetes managed with metformin. There is no family history of endometrial or colorectal cancer. She has had no abnormal cervical screening tests.

data_table.Examination: Speculum reveals a parous atrophic cervix with no obvious cervical lesion; bimanual examination reveals a non-tender mobile uterus of normal size; no adnexal mass
data_table.Investigations: Cervical screening 18 months ago: negative for HPV oncogenic strains; pregnancy test not applicable

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Repeat the cervical screening test today and review again in 3 months from the general practitioner if no further bleeding occurs in the interim
Schedule an outpatient hysteroscopy and dilatation and curettage under general anaesthesia within 6 weeks as the initial investigation
Arrange transvaginal ultrasound endometrial thickness within 2 weeks with onward referral if thickness exceeds 4 mm or imaging is non-diagnostic
Order serum cancer antigen 125 and a contrast-enhanced computed tomography scan of the abdomen and pelvis for initial workup
Reassure as a single bleed without bleeding for 12 months thereafter is a self-limited atrophic event needing no further follow-up

subtopic_detail: Anovulatory subfertility in polycystic ovary syndrome
stem: A 28-year-old presents for fertility advice after 14 months of unprotected intercourse without conception. She has oligomenorrhoea with cycles every 50 to 70 days and a body mass index of 29. Her partner has had a recent semen analysis showing normal count and motility. Pelvic ultrasound shows polycystic ovarian morphology bilaterally. Anti-Mullerian hormone is elevated. There is no tubal pathology on hysterosalpingogram.

data_table.Investigations: Day-3 FSH 5.5 IU/L, LH 9 IU/L, TSH 1.8 mIU/L, prolactin 320 mIU/L, fasting glucose 5.6, HbA1c 5.4%, total testosterone 2.6 nmol/L, sex hormone binding globulin 28 nmol/L

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate first-line pharmacological intervention for ovulation induction?

options.text: Combined oral contraceptive pill for 3 months followed by clomifene citrate 50 mg daily for days 2 to 6 of the next withdrawal bleed
Subcutaneous recombinant follicle stimulating hormone with daily ultrasound monitoring as first-line ovulation induction
Metformin 500 mg twice daily monotherapy with no other ovulation induction agent for the next 6 months
Laparoscopic ovarian drilling as the initial intervention to restore monthly ovulation without the need for medication
Letrozole 2.5 mg daily for days 2 to 6 of the cycle with mid-luteal progesterone confirmation of ovulation

subtopic_detail: Anti-D immunoglobulin after antepartum sensitising event
stem: A 26-year-old in her first pregnancy at 21 weeks presents 3 hours after a moderate fall down two stairs at home with right-sided abdominal contact with the bannister. She is RhD negative with no preformed anti-D antibodies on her booking screen. Her fetal movements are still felt. Routine 28-week prophylaxis has not yet been administered. The on-call obstetric registrar has reviewed her and found no antepartum haemorrhage.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 92, RR 18, T 36.8, BP 116/72, fetal heart rate 148 by handheld Doppler
data_table.Examination: Soft abdomen, no uterine tenderness, no contractions on tocography, mild bruising over the right flank
data_table.Investigations: Speculum shows no bleeding; Kleihauer-Betke 0.5 mL fetal cells per 5 mL maternal blood; group and antibody screen confirms RhD negative with no anti-D

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step for RhD alloimmunisation prevention?

options.text: Administer intramuscular anti-D 250 IU now and avoid routine 28-week and 34-week prophylaxis because of the recent event dose given today
Administer intramuscular anti-D 625 IU within 72 hours of the event and continue routine 28-week and 34-week prophylaxis as scheduled
Administer intravenous anti-D 1500 IU now and titrate with daily Kleihauer-Betke until below 0.1 mL fetal cells per 5 mL maternal blood
Defer anti-D and arrange repeat Kleihauer-Betke at 48 hours, treating only if the level rises above 1 mL fetal cells per 5 mL maternal blood
Defer anti-D because the maternal-fetal haemorrhage is less than 4 mL, and reassess only if she develops new bleeding or contractions overnight

subtopic_detail: Acute ovarian torsion with intermittent pain
stem: A 22-year-old presents with 5 hours of sudden severe right iliac fossa pain that began during exercise. The pain is colicky with two episodes of severe vomiting. She uses condoms only and her last menstrual period was 12 days ago. There is no fever and no abnormal vaginal discharge. There is no urinary frequency or dysuria.

data_table.Examination: Right iliac fossa tenderness with mild guarding, no rebound, no rigidity; bimanual examination reveals tender right adnexal mass approximately 6 cm
data_table.Investigations: Urinary pregnancy test negative, urinalysis bland, FBC WCC 12 with neutrophilia; CRP 22; transabdominal ultrasound shows a 6 cm complex right adnexal cyst with markedly reduced colour Doppler flow within the ovary

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Admit for observation and analgesia, with repeat ultrasound in 6 hours if pain persists or worsens during overnight nursing review
Commence intravenous ceftriaxone plus metronidazole empirically for tubo-ovarian abscess and reassess after 24 hours of antibiotics
Arrange an outpatient magnetic resonance imaging scan within 1 week and gynaecology clinic appointment within 2 weeks for the adnexal mass
Arrange urgent gynaecology referral for same-day diagnostic laparoscopy with detorsion and ovarian conservation if viable
Trial transvaginal ultrasound-guided cyst aspiration in the emergency department as an alternative to laparoscopy

subtopic_detail: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes at 34 weeks gestation
stem: A 31-year-old G2P1 at 34+0 weeks presents with 4 hours of clear fluid leakage confirmed on sterile speculum. She has no contractions, no fever, and is GBS negative on this pregnancy's screening. The fetus is in cephalic presentation with reassuring cardiotocography. She has had no antenatal corticosteroids in this pregnancy. She would like to know about timing of delivery.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 86, RR 16, T 36.7, BP 118/72, fetal heart rate baseline 140 with normal variability
data_table.Examination: Sterile speculum confirms pooling clear amniotic fluid; cervix appears 2 cm dilated with no chorioamnionitis features; uterus non-tender
data_table.Investigations: Maternal FBC WCC 9.6, CRP 6, midstream urine bland; ultrasound confirms cephalic, normal Doppler, estimated fetal weight 2.3 kg, amniotic fluid index 7

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Admit for expectant management with antenatal corticosteroids, infection surveillance, and planned delivery at 37+0 weeks with prophylactic antibiotics if labour starts first
Immediate caesarean delivery today with administration of betamethasone in theatre after delivery to mitigate neonatal respiratory distress syndrome
Discharge home with 7 days of oral erythromycin and weekly outpatient review of fetal welfare and maternal inflammatory markers in clinic
Induce labour immediately with vaginal misoprostol and continue magnesium sulfate infusion for neuroprotection throughout induction
Commence tocolysis with nifedipine and inpatient bed rest until 37 weeks gestation without antibiotics, steroids, or further inflammatory markers

subtopic_detail: Suspected placenta accreta spectrum at 28 weeks
stem: A 34-year-old G4P3 has had three previous caesarean deliveries. Her morphology ultrasound at 22 weeks reported a low-lying anterior placenta covering the previous uterine scar. A repeat scan at 28 weeks now reports loss of the clear retroplacental space, irregular intraplacental lacunae with turbulent flow, and bridging vessels crossing the uterine bladder interface. She is asymptomatic with no antepartum haemorrhage. She lives 90 minutes from the regional referral hospital.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 84, RR 16, T 36.6, BP 116/74, fetal heart rate 142 with normal variability
data_table.Investigations: Targeted ultrasound concerning for placenta accreta spectrum; bloods: Hb 110, platelets 230, fibrinogen 4.2, group and antibody screen for blood bank notification

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate antenatal management plan?

options.text: Continue local antenatal care and plan elective lower segment caesarean section at 39 weeks at her local hospital with on-call gynaecology
Order magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis today and only refer to a tertiary maternal-fetal medicine unit if posterior involvement is confirmed
Admit her at 32 weeks for daily ultrasound surveillance and plan vaginal delivery on the labour ward if cephalic at 37 weeks
Trial of conservative management with placenta in situ at delivery aiming for delayed expulsion and uterine preservation as the primary plan
Refer to a tertiary multidisciplinary placenta accreta service for steroids, blood bank planning, and elective caesarean hysterectomy at 35 to 36 weeks

subtopic_detail: Chorionicity determination and surveillance schedule in twin pregnancy
stem: A 32-year-old G2P1 first attends maternity booking at 13+2 weeks gestation by her last menstrual period. Her booking ultrasound demonstrates a viable twin pregnancy. The sonographer identifies a thin inter-twin membrane with a T-sign at the placental insertion. There is a single shared placental disc visible. Both fetuses appear concordant for crown-rump length and nuchal translucency. She has no significant past obstetric history.

data_table.Investigations: Crown-rump length twin 1: 71 mm; twin 2: 73 mm; nuchal translucency twin 1: 1.6 mm, twin 2: 1.7 mm; combined first trimester screen low chance; cervical length 38 mm
data_table.Examination: Booking observations within normal range; uterus consistent with twin pregnancy

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate surveillance plan?

options.text: Continue routine singleton antenatal schedule with ultrasound only at the 20 to 22 week morphology assessment and 36 weeks growth scan
Schedule fortnightly ultrasound only after 24 weeks to monitor growth discordance and reserve middle cerebral artery Doppler for symptomatic events
Schedule fortnightly ultrasound from 16 weeks for twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome surveillance and plan elective delivery at 36 to 37 weeks
Recommend selective fetal reduction at 14 weeks given the higher pregnancy complication rate in monochorionic-diamniotic twins
Plan elective caesarean delivery at 32 weeks to avoid twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome and ensure neonatal intensive care availability

subtopic_detail: Antiphospholipid syndrome thromboprophylaxis in pregnancy
stem: A 33-year-old G4P0 attends for preconception counselling. She has had three first trimester miscarriages and one stillbirth at 22 weeks 4 months ago. Investigations after the stillbirth showed persistent lupus anticoagulant positivity on two samples 12 weeks apart and elevated anticardiolipin IgG. She has no personal venous thromboembolism history. Her partner is supportive and she would like to conceive again.

data_table.Examination: BMI 24, BP 118/76, no skin lesions, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: Persistent lupus anticoagulant on two occasions 12 weeks apart; anticardiolipin IgG 60 GPL; beta-2 glycoprotein-I 45 SGU; antinuclear antibody and double-stranded DNA negative; FBC, renal and liver function normal

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate pharmacological plan once pregnancy is confirmed?

options.text: Aspirin 100 mg daily alone from positive pregnancy test, continuing throughout pregnancy and the puerperium without anticoagulation
Aspirin 100 mg daily plus prophylactic enoxaparin 40 mg daily from confirmation of pregnancy through to 6 weeks postpartum
Warfarin titrated to an INR of 2 to 3 from the second trimester onwards with bridging enoxaparin at delivery and post-partum
Hydroxychloroquine 200 mg twice daily alone in lieu of anticoagulation throughout pregnancy and postpartum
Therapeutic enoxaparin 1.5 mg/kg daily plus prednisolone 10 mg daily from the first positive pregnancy test

subtopic_detail: Severe aortic stenosis with limited exercise capacity in pregnancy planning
stem: A 29-year-old G1P0 attends for preconception counselling. She has bicuspid aortic valve disease with a peak gradient of 75 mmHg and mean gradient of 52 mmHg on echocardiography last month. The aortic valve area is 0.9 cm2. She walks 600 m on flat ground before stopping for dyspnoea and has had one syncopal episode while running. Left ventricular ejection fraction is 60%. Her cardiologist's letter notes no aortopathy. She has no other comorbidity.

data_table.Examination: Ejection systolic murmur grade 3 over 6 at the right upper sternal edge radiating to carotids; soft second heart sound; no displaced apex; no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: Echocardiogram: peak gradient 75 mmHg, mean gradient 52 mmHg, valve area 0.9 cm2, no left ventricular hypertrophy, ascending aortic diameter 38 mm; ECG sinus rhythm with normal axis

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate counselling and management plan now?

options.text: Counsel that her cardiac lesion is modified World Health Organization class II and proceed with planned conception now with shared-care obstetric review
Recommend pregnancy can proceed but with combined cardiology-obstetric monthly review and elective caesarean delivery at 39 weeks under regional anaesthesia
Advise the use of oestrogen-containing combined oral contraception to avoid pregnancy while continuing routine annual cardiology follow-up appointments
Counsel that the lesion is modified World Health Organization class IV, advise pregnancy avoidance, and refer for valve intervention with reassessment afterwards
Plan immediate valve replacement using a mechanical prosthesis followed by warfarin throughout future pregnancies for thromboprophylaxis

subtopic_detail: Iron deficiency anaemia in pregnancy
stem: A 30-year-old G2P1 woman attends antenatal clinic at 28+3 weeks for routine review. Her booking ferritin was 18 mcg/L and she was started on oral iron polymaltose 100 mg daily at 16 weeks. She has taken it consistently but feels increasingly fatigued and short of breath climbing one flight of stairs. There is no history of menorrhagia, no current GI bleeding, no antepartum bleeding, and her diet includes red meat twice weekly.

data_table.Examination: Pale conjunctivae, no jaundice, fundal height 28 cm, fetal heart 142, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: Hb 92 g/L, MCV 76 fL, ferritin 11 mcg/L, transferrin saturation 9%, CRP 3 mg/L, platelets 268 x10^9/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Continue oral iron polymaltose and recheck full blood count in six weeks
Switch to oral ferrous sulfate 325 mg three times daily plus ascorbic acid
Arrange ferric carboxymaltose 1000 mg intravenously as a day-case infusion
Cross-match and transfuse two units of packed red blood cells overnight
Commence subcutaneous erythropoietin alfa weekly and recheck reticulocytes

subtopic_detail: Continuing prophylaxis when threatened preterm labour settles
stem: A 28-year-old woman admitted at 31 weeks with contractions was started overnight by the night team on nifedipine and an intravenous antibiotic. She now has no contractions and feels well.

data_table.Cervix: Closed on speculum, unchanged from admission, membranes intact
data_table.Screening: No vagino-rectal swab taken this pregnancy, temperature 36.8 degC

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of the antibiotic?

options.text: Stop the infusion now and give no further doses
Continue it four hourly until she is discharged home
Continue it until a vagino-rectal swab result returns
Change it to a ten day oral course of erythromycin
Give one further dose, then swab her and stop it

subtopic_detail: Term prelabour rupture of membranes
stem: A 32-year-old G2P1 woman presents at 38+5 weeks reporting a gush of clear fluid 4 hours ago with continuing leakage. Her previous pregnancy ended with a spontaneous vaginal birth at 39 weeks; this pregnancy has been uncomplicated and her 36-week GBS swab was negative. She is afebrile, the fetus is moving, and she is not contracting. Speculum confirms clear liquor pooling in the posterior fornix with positive amnisure.

data_table.Examination: Fundal height 38 cm, longitudinal lie, cephalic, FHR 140, no uterine tenderness; speculum clear liquor, cervix appears closed visually
data_table.Investigations: GBS swab 36 weeks negative; CTG reactive; group B and D Rh-positive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan of care?

options.text: Discharge home with daily review and induction if not in labour by 96 hours
Commence prophylactic intravenous benzylpenicillin and expectant management to 48 hours
Perform prostaglandin gel insertion immediately to ripen the cervix further first
Offer induction of labour with oxytocin infusion within 24 hours of rupture
Recommend an immediate elective caesarean section due to ruptured membranes risk

subtopic_detail: Lactational mastitis
stem: A 31-year-old woman 3 weeks postpartum following an uncomplicated vaginal birth presents with 36 hours of right-sided breast pain, redness and a flu-like illness. She has been exclusively breastfeeding her infant but feeding on the affected side has become very painful. She has no penicillin allergy and is otherwise well. She wants to continue breastfeeding if possible.

data_table.Examination: Right upper outer breast: 6 cm wedge-shaped erythema, warm and tender, no fluctuance, no nipple cracks; left breast normal; infant suckling well
data_table.Investigations: Not performed; routine bloods not indicated at this stage

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Cease breastfeeding from the right breast and pump until the redness resolves completely
Arrange urgent ultrasound and incision and drainage of the breast under anaesthetic
Switch to oral cefalexin 500 mg every 6 hours and warm compresses three times daily
Trial 24 hours of cabbage leaves, ibuprofen and effective milk removal with no antibiotics
Commence oral flucloxacillin 500 mg four times daily plus continued breastfeeding

subtopic_detail: Gestational diabetes diagnosis
stem: A 33-year-old G2P1 woman attends for her 26-week OGTT. Her previous pregnancy was uncomplicated with a 3400 g infant born at 39 weeks. Pre-pregnancy BMI is 24.5; she has no family history of diabetes. Her booking HbA1c was 36 mmol/mol. She has been well throughout this pregnancy and the morphology scan was normal. She is anxious about the result and wants to know what happens next.

data_table.Examination: Fundal height 26 cm, longitudinal lie, FHR 144; no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: 75 g OGTT (mmol/L): fasting 5.4, 1 hour 9.8, 2 hour 7.9

lead_in: Which step most appropriately progresses her management?

options.text: Reassure her that all values are within the normal range for pregnancy
Repeat the OGTT in 4 weeks with the same 75 g loading dose for confirmation
Commence metformin 500 mg twice daily and arrange dietitian review within two weeks
Refer urgently to endocrinology for insulin commencement before the next antenatal visit
Diagnose gestational diabetes and refer for diabetes educator and home BSL monitoring

subtopic_detail: Combined oral contraceptive pill initiation
stem: A 22-year-old non-smoking woman attends her GP wanting to start a contraceptive pill. She has regular 28-day cycles and her last period started 5 days ago. She has migraines without aura roughly once a month, well controlled with paracetamol. BP at this visit is 118/72 and BMI 23. She wants the most effective pill option starting today and to know when she can rely on it.

data_table.Examination: Soft abdomen, no peripheral oedema; cardiovascular exam unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: Pregnancy test negative; cervical screening up to date

lead_in: Which approach most appropriately initiates contraception today?

options.text: Defer starting until her next period and recommend condoms for the next three weeks
Use a progesterone-only pill instead of a combined pill due to her migraine history
Prescribe the combined pill but only after she completes 3 months of cycle tracking
Insert a copper IUD today as it is the most effective hormone-free contraceptive method
Start the combined pill today and use back-up contraception for 7 days from today

subtopic_detail: Threatened miscarriage with subchorionic haematoma
stem: A 27-year-old G3P1 woman at 8+4 weeks by certain dates presents with light fresh vaginal bleeding for 6 hours and lower abdominal cramping. She has no syncope and the bleeding has now slowed. Her previous miscarriage was at 7 weeks two years ago; this pregnancy was planned and otherwise well. She is Rh-positive and her booking bloods are unremarkable.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 116/76, HR 78, T 36.6°C, abdomen soft non-tender
data_table.Examination: Speculum: closed cervical os, minimal fresh blood in vault, no products visible
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound: single intrauterine sac with fetal pole CRL 18 mm, FHR 162; small 12 mm subchorionic haematoma adjacent to sac

lead_in: Which management plan is most appropriate?

options.text: Bed rest for 7 days with daily progesterone pessaries and weekly ultrasound review
Admit for 48 hours of intravenous tranexamic acid and crossmatched blood standby
Offer surgical evacuation of the haematoma to reduce ongoing miscarriage risk later
Commence vaginal micronised progesterone 400 mg twice daily until 16 weeks routinely
Reassure, continue normal activities and review with repeat ultrasound in 2 weeks

subtopic_detail: VBAC counselling
stem: A 31-year-old G2P1 woman at 36 weeks attends to discuss her birth options. Her first child was born by emergency lower-segment caesarean section for failure to progress at 6 cm dilation, with no intraoperative complications. This pregnancy has been uncomplicated, the fetus is cephalic and growth is on the 50th centile. She wants to know her chances of a successful vaginal birth and the main maternal risk to consider.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 122/78, HR 80, fundal height 36 cm, fetal heart 144
data_table.Examination: Vertex cephalic, longitudinal lie, free above pelvic brim, normal liquor volume
data_table.Investigations: Previous operative note: low transverse uterine incision, no extension, single layer closure

lead_in: Which counselling point is most accurate?

options.text: Her chance of vaginal birth is about 70 percent with uterine rupture risk around 0.5 percent
Her chance of vaginal birth is around 90 percent with uterine rupture risk under 0.1 percent
Her chance of vaginal birth is around 40 percent with uterine rupture risk around 2 percent
Her chance of vaginal birth is around 70 percent with uterine rupture risk around 4 percent
Her chance of vaginal birth is around 50 percent with uterine rupture risk under 0.05 percent

subtopic_detail: Induction of labour with unfavourable cervix
stem: A 32-year-old G1P0 at 41+3 weeks attends for planned induction of labour. She has no significant medical history and the pregnancy has been uncomplicated. She declines membrane sweep at this visit and is keen for the gentlest induction option. Fetal movements are normal and she is not contracting. The neonatal cot is available and theatre is staffed for emergencies.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 122/80, HR 82, T 36.6°C; CTG reactive, no decelerations
data_table.Examination: Vertex, cephalic, head 2/5 palpable, station -3; cervix posterior, firm, 1 cm long, closed (Bishop score 2)
data_table.Investigations: Estimated fetal weight 3850 g (75th centile); amniotic fluid index 9 cm; group B negative at 36 weeks

lead_in: Which induction approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Intravenous oxytocin infusion commenced at 1 mU/min titrated to contractions
Artificial rupture of membranes followed by titrated oxytocin infusion within an hour
Dinoprostone 10 mg controlled-release pessary intravaginally for ripening over 24 hours
Expectant management with daily CTG and amniotic fluid index for a further week
Insertion of a transcervical balloon (Foley or Cook) catheter for mechanical ripening overnight

subtopic_detail: Recurrent miscarriage investigation
stem: A 33-year-old woman attends 6 weeks after a third consecutive first-trimester miscarriage with her partner. All three losses were at 8 to 10 weeks; the most recent had a sac with no embryo seen and there was no chromosomal sample taken. She is otherwise well, has regular cycles and her BMI is 24. She has had two unprovoked late-term DVTs and is anxious about further losses.

data_table.Examination: Cardiovascular and obstetric examination unremarkable; no skin lesions
data_table.Investigations: TSH 2.1 mIU/L, HbA1c 33 mmol/mol, pelvic ultrasound: normal uterus with no Mullerian anomaly

lead_in: Which investigation should be prioritised at this visit?

options.text: Endometrial biopsy for chronic endometritis with CD138 immunohistochemistry staining
Parental karyotype testing of both partners for balanced translocation screening currently
Hysterosalpingography to evaluate the uterine cavity for an intrauterine adhesion or septum
Antiphospholipid antibody panel (lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, anti-beta2-glycoprotein-I)
Inherited thrombophilia screen (Factor V Leiden, prothrombin G20210A, antithrombin, protein C/S)

subtopic_detail: Atypical pre-eclampsia
stem: A 35-year-old G3P2 woman at 35+2 weeks presents with two days of bilateral hand swelling and intermittent epigastric pain. She has had three blood pressure readings in clinic ranging from 134 to 142 systolic and 84 to 89 diastolic over the past week. Urine dipstick at this visit is trace protein; she has had no headache, no visual disturbance and the fetus is moving normally. There is no past hypertension.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 138/89, HR 88, T 36.6°C, RR 16; reflexes brisk but no clonus
data_table.Examination: Mild bilateral pitting oedema, epigastric tenderness, fundal height 33 cm (small for dates), FHR 142
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 95 x10^9/L (was 220 at booking), creatinine 88 micromol/L (was 56), AST 78 U/L, ALT 64 U/L, LDH 380 U/L, spot urine PCR 38 mg/mmol

lead_in: Which assessment most accurately characterises this presentation?

options.text: Gestational hypertension only as her blood pressure remains under 140/90 mmHg today
Atypical pre-eclampsia with HELLP-spectrum features warranting admission and delivery planning
Acute fatty liver of pregnancy with secondary blood pressure and renal involvement
Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura with pregnancy-related microangiopathic haemolysis
Chronic hypertension with superimposed proteinuria from incidental urinary tract infection

subtopic_detail: Anti-D prophylaxis after threatened miscarriage
stem: A 28-year-old G2P1 woman who is blood group O Rh-negative attends ED with light fresh vaginal bleeding at 13+2 weeks. Her partner is known to be Rh-positive. She has had no previous sensitising events and her booking antibody screen 6 weeks ago was negative. The bleeding has settled but she remains anxious about pregnancy loss and Rh sensitisation.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/72, HR 80, T 36.5°C; abdomen soft non-tender
data_table.Examination: Speculum: small amount of old blood, cervix closed; uterus consistent with dates
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound: viable intrauterine pregnancy, CRL 76 mm, FHR 158; rhesus screen confirmed Rh-negative; antibody screen pending

lead_in: Which step regarding Rh-isoimmunisation prevention is most appropriate?

options.text: No Anti-D required as bleeding was very light and the pregnancy remains viable today
Anti-D 250 IU intramuscularly now without need for Kleihauer testing today
Anti-D 1500 IU intramuscularly with mandatory Kleihauer-Betke testing today
Anti-D 625 IU intramuscularly within 72 hours and routine antenatal doses at 28 and 34 weeks
Withhold Anti-D until paternal genotyping confirms his Rh status and zygosity definitively

subtopic_detail: Vasa praevia antenatal management
stem: A 30-year-old G2P1 woman has her morphology ultrasound at 22 weeks following IVF conception. She is asymptomatic. The fetus is structurally normal. A repeat targeted transvaginal scan at 32 weeks now confirms a velamentous cord insertion with a single vessel crossing the internal cervical os, consistent with type I vasa praevia. She has no antepartum bleeding and the fetus is growing on the 60th centile.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 116/72, HR 78, fundal height 32 cm, FHR 142
data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender abdomen, no cervical change clinically
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound 32 weeks: fetal vessel crosses internal os; cervix 32 mm long; estimated fetal weight 1850 g (60th centile)

lead_in: Which antenatal plan is most appropriate?

options.text: Plan elective caesarean section at 34 to 36 weeks after antenatal corticosteroids for fetal lungs
Plan for vaginal birth with continuous CTG and immediate caesarean if FHR abnormality
Plan elective caesarean at 39 weeks once the pregnancy is at full term gestation
Admit for inpatient monitoring from 28 weeks with daily CTG until delivery is planned
Repeat ultrasound at 36 weeks to assess for vessel migration before deciding on mode of birth

subtopic_detail: Twin chorionicity determination
stem: A 29-year-old G1P0 woman attends her dating scan at 12+1 weeks following spontaneous conception. The sonographer reports two viable fetuses with concordant CRLs of 56 and 58 mm. The lambda (twin peak) sign is clearly visible at the placental junction and the intertwin membrane is thick. The patient is well and has no significant past medical history.

data_table.Examination: Soft abdomen, no peripheral oedema, gravid uterus consistent with twin pregnancy
data_table.Investigations: Ultrasound: two viable fetuses, lambda sign positive, intertwin membrane thickness 2.2 mm, two placental masses described

lead_in: Which conclusion about chorionicity is most accurate?

options.text: Monochorionic monoamniotic twins requiring weekly ultrasound from 16 weeks onwards
Monochorionic diamniotic twins with a planned scan schedule every two weeks from 16 weeks
Conjoined twins requiring tertiary referral for early MRI to delineate organ sharing pattern
Dichorionic diamniotic twins requiring growth scans every 4 weeks from 24 weeks onwards
Chorionicity cannot be assigned reliably until 16 to 18 weeks of gestation by ultrasound

subtopic_detail: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome
stem: A 32-year-old woman with polycystic ovary syndrome presents 6 days after IVF oocyte retrieval with rapidly worsening abdominal distension, nausea and shortness of breath. She required collection of 28 oocytes and had a fresh embryo transfer 2 days ago. She is now unable to keep fluids down and has had no urine for 8 hours.

data_table.Examination: Tense ascites, dull lung bases bilaterally, no peripheral oedema; abdomen distended and tender
data_table.Investigations: Hb 168 g/L (was 122), haematocrit 0.52, WCC 16, Na 130 mmol/L, K 5.2 mmol/L, creatinine 142 micromol/L (was 60), albumin 28 g/L, beta-hCG 220 IU/L

lead_in: Which is the single most important next intervention?

options.text: Admit for intravenous crystalloid resuscitation with thromboprophylactic enoxaparin
Commence high-dose oral cabergoline 0.5 mg daily and discharge with daily review
Arrange urgent paracentesis as first measure to relieve abdominal pressure and dyspnoea
Prescribe oral diuretics (furosemide 40 mg daily) to mobilise the third-space fluid quickly
Continue luteal phase progesterone and review symptomatically in the fertility clinic next week

subtopic_detail: Gestational trophoblastic neoplasia
stem: A 34-year-old woman is being followed up after a complete hydatidiform mole evacuated 10 weeks ago. Her serial weekly beta-hCG has been: 32,400 then 4,100 then 580 then 220 then 195 then 185 then 188 IU/L. She has no vaginal bleeding and her cervix is closed; chest is clear and there is no abdominal mass. She is using effective contraception and her FIGO score is 4.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/74, HR 76, T 36.6°C; physical examination unremarkable
data_table.Examination: Abdominal exam: no masses; speculum: closed os, normal vault
data_table.Investigations: Pelvic ultrasound: small intrauterine echogenic focus only, no invasive disease; CXR clear; routine bloods normal

lead_in: Which management plan is most appropriate?

options.text: Refer to a gestational trophoblastic disease centre for single-agent methotrexate chemotherapy
Continue weekly beta-hCG monitoring for another 8 weeks before considering active treatment
Perform a repeat suction evacuation under anaesthetic this admission to clear residual trophoblast
Commence multi-agent EMA-CO chemotherapy as primary treatment for residual molar disease now
Recommend total abdominal hysterectomy as definitive curative treatment given completed family

subtopic_detail: Amniotic fluid embolism
stem: You are the obstetric registrar called urgently to the birth suite. A 38-year-old multiparous woman at 39+5 weeks has just delivered her third child. Immediately after delivery of the placenta she became acutely breathless, hypotensive, and developed a tonic-clonic seizure. The seizure has terminated after 30 seconds but she is now poorly responsive and has copious oozing from the episiotomy site and intravenous puncture sites. The blood loss is approximately 1500 mL and ongoing. Cardiac arrest team has been called. No fluid bolus has yet been given.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 138 bpm, BP 72/40 mmHg, RR 38, SpO2 84% room air, Temp 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy GCS 10, central cyanosis, oozing from venepuncture sites, soft uterus, ongoing PV bleeding
data_table.Investigations: Point-of-care Hb 88 g/L, INR > 4.0, platelets 78 x10^9/L, fibrinogen 0.8 g/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management priority?
