options.text: Commence intravenous magnesium sulfate 4 g loading dose for eclampsia and continue at 1 g per hour
Administer intramuscular adrenaline 500 micrograms for presumed anaphylactoid reaction to oxytocin
Activate massive transfusion protocol while supporting airway, breathing and circulation with fluids and uterotonics
Administer intravenous tissue plasminogen activator for presumed pulmonary thromboembolism
Defer transfusion until laboratory-confirmed coagulation results return and place urgent type-and-cross-match

subtopic_detail: GDM screening and diagnosis
stem: You are the antenatal clinic registrar reviewing a 32-year-old G2P1 woman at 26 weeks gestation with a BMI of 31. Her first child was 4.3 kg at term with no documented dysglycaemia in pregnancy. She has just completed a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test in the morning after appropriate fasting and brings the printout to the appointment.

data_table.Examination: Fundal height appropriate for dates, fetal movements present
data_table.Investigations: OGTT: fasting 5.4 mmol/L, 1 hour 9.8 mmol/L, 2 hour 7.9 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Order an HbA1c level to differentiate between gestational diabetes and overt pregestational diabetes that may have been missed at initial booking visit
Reassure the patient as none of the OGTT values meet the diagnostic threshold for gestational diabetes and continue routine antenatal care without changes
Commence metformin immediately as first-line pharmacological therapy without a trial of dietary intervention given the elevated body mass index
Repeat the OGTT in two weeks to confirm the diagnosis before any intervention or referral as a single test may produce false positive results
Diagnose gestational diabetes and commence dietary advice with capillary glucose monitoring four times daily and dietitian referral

subtopic_detail: Postpartum haemorrhage first-line management
stem: You are the obstetrics registrar called urgently to the birthing suite for a multiparous woman ten minutes after a spontaneous vaginal birth with active third stage management. The placenta is out and appears complete. The midwife reports estimated blood loss of 900 mL with continuing brisk bleeding. The uterus is palpably soft and rises above the umbilicus on examination.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 102/58, HR 116, RR 22, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Uterus boggy at 24 weeks size, no perineal lacerations, bladder palpable
data_table.Investigations: Group and screen on file, FBC and coags being sent
data_table.Medications: IV oxytocin 10 units given at delivery; nil drug allergies; BP 144/92 on antenatal booking with no other features

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next action?

options.text: Transfer the patient to the operating theatre for examination under anaesthesia and exploration without further attempts at conservative bedside management
Administer carboprost 250 micrograms intramuscularly as the first additional uterotonic without bimanual compression or further bladder management
Empty the bladder, perform bimanual compression, and administer a further uterotonic such as syntometrine while calling for senior assistance
Administer tranexamic acid one gram intravenously as the sole pharmacological response to ongoing postpartum bleeding from a soft uterus
Reassure the team that 900 mL is within acceptable physiological blood loss after vaginal birth and continue observation without intervention

subtopic_detail: Antepartum haemorrhage placenta praevia
stem: You are the obstetrics RMO assessing a 29-year-old G2P1 woman at 32 weeks gestation presenting with sudden onset painless bright red vaginal bleeding while at home. Her morphology scan at 20 weeks documented an anterior placenta covering the internal os. She reports no contractions, normal fetal movements, and a soaked maternity pad on the way in.

data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender uterus, no contractions, CTG reactive, no speculum yet performed
data_table.Investigations: Group and screen on file, FBC and coags being sent

lead_in: Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate step?

options.text: Avoid digital vaginal examination, admit for monitoring, and arrange ultrasound to assess placental location and fetal wellbeing
Perform a gentle digital vaginal examination to assess cervical dilatation and determine the source of bleeding before arranging further imaging
Discharge home with safety netting and outpatient ultrasound in the next forty-eight hours once the patient is haemodynamically stable on observation
Proceed to immediate category one caesarean section regardless of current haemodynamic stability or current cardiotocograph findings on assessment
Commence intravenous tocolysis with nifedipine to prevent preterm labour and continue conservative outpatient management following initial review

subtopic_detail: Severe pre-eclampsia magnesium sulfate
stem: You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 34-year-old primigravid woman at 33 weeks gestation referred with worsening headache and visual scotomata over the last six hours. She has had right upper quadrant pain since this morning. BP at her last antenatal visit four days ago was 132/86. There has been no per-vaginal bleeding and the fetal movements are present.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 168/108 repeated 15 minutes later 162/106, HR 96, RR 18, SpO2 98%
data_table.Examination: Hyperreflexia with two-beat clonus, mild epigastric tenderness, no peripheral oedema, fundi sharp
data_table.Investigations: Urine protein:creatinine 86 mg/mmol, platelets 92 x10^9/L, ALT 138, AST 142, creatinine 78, urate 0.42, LDH 480
data_table.Medications: Aspirin 100 mg from 14 weeks, pregnancy multivitamin

lead_in: Which intervention has the strongest evidence for reducing maternal morbidity in this scenario?

options.text: Phenytoin loading dose intravenously for seizure prophylaxis in severe pre-eclampsia given its established efficacy in non-pregnant populations
Intravenous hydralazine bolus titrated to a target systolic blood pressure under 130 mmHg before further evaluation or specialist input is obtained
Magnesium sulfate intravenous loading dose followed by infusion to reduce the risk of eclamptic seizures while delivery is being planned
Furosemide intravenous bolus to manage presumed fluid overload contributing to the rise in blood pressure during this preterm gestation
Aspirin dose increase to 300 mg daily for the duration of admission to optimise placental perfusion and reduce ongoing maternal morbidity

subtopic_detail: Role of episiotomy when the anterior shoulder is impacted
stem: You are called to a birth where the head has delivered and the shoulders have not followed with the next contraction. Help has arrived and the first line manoeuvres have already failed.

data_table.Perineum: Intact, no episiotomy, epidural in situ and working well
data_table.Timing: Ninety seconds since the head delivered, no bleeding

lead_in: What is the most appropriate approach to the perineum?

options.text: Cut one only if the perineum blocks a hand entering the vagina
Cut a generous mediolateral episiotomy now to release the shoulder
Cut a midline episiotomy now, as it gives more room than mediolateral
Cut one now and then apply firmer downward traction on the head
Never cut one, as the perineum plays no part in this emergency

subtopic_detail: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes management
stem: You are the obstetrics registrar reviewing a 28-year-old G3P2 woman at 33 weeks gestation referred with a sudden gush of clear fluid two hours ago followed by ongoing leakage. There are no contractions, no abdominal pain, and fetal movements are present. Speculum confirms pooling in the posterior fornix. The patient is afebrile and has no rupture or trauma history.

data_table.Examination: Soft uterus, no tenderness, no contractions on tocography, CTG reactive, speculum confirms pooling, cervix appears closed and uneffaced
data_table.Investigations: FBC normal, CRP 6, high vaginal swab and urine MSU sent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Place an emergency cervical cerclage to maintain pregnancy and reduce risk of preterm birth following confirmed rupture of membranes at this gestation
Commence immediate induction of labour with vaginal prostaglandins given the gestation has reached the 33-week threshold for expedited delivery in current practice
Discharge home with daily temperature monitoring and outpatient follow-up in two days for review and ongoing assessment of fetal wellbeing
Administer tocolysis with nifedipine prophylactically to allow steroid completion before planning further antenatal management strategy with senior input
Admit for inpatient monitoring with antenatal corticosteroids, prophylactic antibiotics, and expectant management with planned delivery around 34 weeks

subtopic_detail: Acute fatty liver of pregnancy recognition
stem: You are the obstetric medicine registrar called to ED to assess a 30-year-old primigravid woman at 35 weeks gestation with three days of nausea, vomiting, and right upper quadrant pain followed by progressive lethargy. She has no past medical history and is on routine prenatal care. She is mildly confused this morning. Her sister was admitted with similar symptoms when pregnant 8 years ago.

data_table.Examination: Mildly jaundiced, mild RUQ tenderness, no peripheral oedema, no asterixis but slow to follow commands, abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: ALT 248, AST 312, bilirubin 92 (predominantly conjugated), INR 1.8, ammonia 84, glucose 2.6, urate 0.48, creatinine 124, platelets 138, urine protein 1+, fibrinogen 1.2 g/L

lead_in: Which feature most strongly favours acute fatty liver of pregnancy over HELLP syndrome?

options.text: Onset in the third trimester with right upper quadrant pain and a transaminase elevation similar to a typical HELLP syndrome biochemical profile
The presence of mild hypertension above the booking value in association with bilirubin elevation and right upper quadrant tenderness on examination
Mild proteinuria one plus on dipstick and a modest reduction in the maternal platelet count to below normal limits without other systemic features
Hypoglycaemia with coagulopathy out of proportion to platelet count and the presence of encephalopathy on clinical assessment
A family history of similar symptoms in a sister during pregnancy with full recovery after expedited delivery and supportive management

subtopic_detail: Second trimester cervical insufficiency
stem: You are the maternal-fetal medicine fellow seeing a 31-year-old G3P0 woman at 18 weeks gestation referred for a transvaginal cervical length scan. She has had two prior mid-trimester losses at 21 and 19 weeks with painless cervical dilatation noted on each occasion. There is no current contraction activity and no bleeding or fluid leak. The cervix appears closed externally.

data_table.Examination: Soft uterus, no contractions, speculum shows closed external os and no pooling
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal cervical length 18 mm with funnelling, no debris in amniotic fluid, fetus appropriately grown, anatomy normal
data_table.Medications: Pregnancy multivitamin only; no progesterone yet started

lead_in: What is the most appropriate intervention?

options.text: Arrange a transabdominal cerclage as the first-line intervention given recurrent loss and counsel for elective caesarean section at term
Recommend vaginal progesterone 200 mg nightly without cerclage and arrange surveillance ultrasound every two weeks until twenty-four weeks gestation
Offer an ultrasound-indicated McDonald cerclage with adjunctive vaginal progesterone and counsel about procedural and pregnancy risks
Commence high-dose nifedipine prophylactically and arrange admission for inpatient bed rest until twenty-eight weeks gestation as the primary intervention
Place a pessary in the outpatient clinic today and review in two weeks with transvaginal scan and counsel about preterm birth risk reduction

subtopic_detail: Pre-eclampsia BP threshold and drug choice
stem: You are the obstetrics registrar reviewing a 32-year-old primigravida at 33+2 weeks of gestation with BP 162/106 on two readings 15 minutes apart. She has new-onset proteinuria of 1+ on urinalysis and a headache, with no visual disturbance or epigastric pain. Reflexes are not pathologically brisk. CTG is reassuring. Her booking BP was 110/70 and no prior antihypertensive history.

data_table.Examination: Headache, no visual changes, no epigastric pain, no clonus
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis: protein 1+, PCR pending; FBC normal; LFTs normal; uric acid 0.38; platelets 218

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate antihypertensive choice?

options.text: Oral nifedipine immediate-release 10 mg sublingually with repeat BP at 30 minutes
Oral labetalol 200 mg with repeat BP at 30 minutes and escalate if not below target
Sublingual captopril 25 mg with repeat BP at 30 minutes and consider escalation if uncontrolled
IV magnesium sulfate 4 g loading dose with immediate transfer to a labour ward for delivery
Oral methyldopa 250 mg twice daily as a first-line oral agent in severe pregnancy hypertension

subtopic_detail: OGTT screening at 24 to 28 weeks
stem: You are the GP shared-care doctor for a 31-year-old G2P1 at 26 weeks of gestation. She has no diabetes risk factors apart from a BMI of 31 at booking and a previous baby weighing 4150 g. Her early pregnancy fasting glucose at 11 weeks was 4.6 mmol/L. She would like to know what GDM screening she should have now.

data_table.Examination: Fundal height appropriate
data_table.Investigations: Early pregnancy fasting glucose 4.6; HbA1c not done; recent urinalysis nil

lead_in: What is the most appropriate GDM screening test now?

options.text: HbA1c with a diagnostic threshold of 6.5% as the screening test of choice at 24 to 28 weeks
Repeat fasting glucose alone with same 5.1 mmol/L cut-off as in early pregnancy screening
75 g 2-hour oral glucose tolerance test with fasting and 1 and 2 hour samples taken
50 g 1-hour glucose challenge test followed by 100 g 3-hour OGTT if positive at 7.8 mmol/L
Random capillary glucose with a 7.8 mmol/L cut-off and reflex to a confirmatory test if positive

subtopic_detail: Routine anti-D administration
stem: You are the antenatal clinic registrar reviewing a 26-year-old G1 at 28+0 weeks with blood group O Rh negative and negative antibody screen. The booking ultrasound and 20-week morphology scan were normal. Her partner is Rh positive but the fetal Rh status is not known. There has been no antepartum bleeding or invasive procedure to date. She is well.

data_table.Examination: Symphysis-fundal height 28 cm
data_table.Investigations: Blood group O Rh negative; antibody screen negative; FBC normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Defer anti-D until evidence of sensitising event such as bleeding or amniocentesis arises
Administer 1500 IU anti-D immunoglobulin intramuscularly at 28 weeks only with no further dose
Administer 250 IU anti-D immunoglobulin intramuscularly now and reassess at 34 weeks for further
Administer 625 IU anti-D immunoglobulin intramuscularly at 28 weeks and again at 34 weeks
Test fetal Rh status by maternal cell-free DNA and only treat if fetus confirmed Rh positive

subtopic_detail: PPROM management at 30 weeks
stem: You are the obstetrics registrar admitting a 28-year-old G2P1 at 30+1 weeks with confirmed PPROM by sterile speculum showing pooling and positive amniSure. She has no contractions, no abdominal pain, no fever and no bleeding. The CTG is reassuring. Fetal growth is appropriate for gestation. She has no penicillin allergy.

data_table.Examination: Pooling of clear liquor in posterior fornix; cervix appears closed on speculum
data_table.Investigations: FBC normal; CRP 4; group B Strep culture pending; fetal fibronectin not done

lead_in: Which combination of immediate interventions is most appropriate?

options.text: Tocolysis with nifedipine for 48 hours and discharge home with weekly outpatient review
Betamethasone 11.4 mg IM with broad-spectrum coverage by IV ampicillin and IV gentamicin
Betamethasone 11.4 mg IM with amoxicillin and clavulanic acid orally for 7 days as cover
Magnesium sulfate neuroprotection only with planned delivery within 24 hours of diagnosis
Betamethasone 11.4 mg IM with erythromycin 250 mg orally four times daily for 10 days

subtopic_detail: Second-line uterotonic choice
stem: You are the obstetrics registrar called for ongoing atonic PPH after a vaginal delivery in a 33-year-old G2P2. The patient had pre-eclampsia in this pregnancy with peak BP 160/105 on the day of delivery. She has received 10 IU oxytocin IM at delivery and then 40 IU oxytocin in 1 L Hartmann's by infusion. Her BP is now 154/96. Estimated blood loss is 1200 mL and ongoing. She has asthma well controlled by salbutamol PRN with no recent flares. The bladder is empty and the uterus is boggy on bimanual.

data_table.Examination: Boggy uterus to umbilicus, ongoing PV loss, no perineal trauma, no retained placenta on inspection
data_table.Investigations: Hb 92 (pre-delivery 118); platelets 218; INR 1.1; fibrinogen 3.4
data_table.Medications: Salbutamol PRN; recent labetalol 200 mg in labour for BP control

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next uterotonic to give?

options.text: Misoprostol 800 micrograms sublingually as second-line uterotonic for ongoing atonic PPH
Carboprost 250 micrograms IM as a second-line uterotonic for ongoing atonic PPH now
Ergometrine 250 micrograms IM as a second-line uterotonic for ongoing atonic PPH now
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV slowly with no additional uterotonic until atony reassessed
Repeat oxytocin 10 IU IM and continue oxytocin infusion at 40 IU per litre Hartmann's now

subtopic_detail: Shoulder dystocia HELPERR sequence
stem: You are the obstetrics registrar called for shoulder dystocia in a 28-year-old G2P1. She is fully dilated and the fetal head has delivered but the anterior shoulder will not deliver despite gentle traction. Estimated fetal weight at last scan was 4200 g. She has GDM on insulin. There is no maternal exhaustion or epidural. Last documented fetal heart rate two minutes ago was 140 bpm. Help has been called and the senior registrar will be in 90 seconds.

data_table.Examination: Head delivered, no shoulder rotation, turtle sign present, no cord visible
data_table.Investigations: Recent FBC normal; group and hold valid

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate next manoeuvre?

options.text: Zavanelli manoeuvre with cephalic replacement followed by urgent emergency caesarean now
McRoberts manoeuvre with suprapubic pressure applied diagonally toward the anterior shoulder
Fundal pressure applied steadily for 60 seconds to push the anterior shoulder below symphysis
Internal rotation manoeuvre (Woods corkscrew) using fingers to rotate the posterior shoulder
Symphysiotomy with deliberate division of the maternal pubic symphysis to widen the pelvis

subtopic_detail: Gestational hypertension threshold for admission
stem: You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 28-year-old G1P0 at 33+2 weeks gestation, referred from antenatal clinic with new hypertension. Her booking BP was 110/68. Today repeated BP measurements are 152/98 and 148/94 on the contralateral arm after 15 minutes rest. She is asymptomatic with no headache, no visual disturbance, no epigastric pain, and no ankle swelling beyond mild dependent oedema. Fetal movements are normal and recent growth scan was on the 40th centile. Routine bloods and urinalysis have been sent.

data_table.Examination: No epigastric tenderness, no clonus, no facial oedema, mild ankle oedema bilaterally, gravid uterus consistent with dates, fetal heart 142
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis: protein nil, blood nil; PCR 8 mg/mmol (normal <30); Hb 118, plt 244, ALT 24, AST 22, creatinine 64; uric acid 0.34; CTG: reassuring

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Discharge with twice weekly community midwifery BP monitoring and review at the antenatal clinic in 2 weeks
Admit for IV magnesium sulfate seizure prophylaxis and urgent delivery by induction of labour within 24 hours
Commence oral labetalol 100 mg twice daily and arrange day assessment unit review twice weekly
Start oral methyldopa 250 mg three times daily and arrange routine antenatal follow-up in 4 weeks
Reassure as white-coat hypertension and provide a home BP monitor for daily readings over 7 days

subtopic_detail: Group B Streptococcus prophylaxis
stem: You are the obstetrics registrar reviewing a 32-year-old G2P1 at 37+5 weeks gestation in established labour (4 cm dilated, ROM 6 hours ago). Her booking notes show vaginal-rectal GBS swab at 36 weeks was negative. Her first child was born vaginally 3 years ago at another hospital without complication; that baby had no neonatal infection. Today she is afebrile, has been on no antibiotics, and has had no urinary GBS at any time this pregnancy. Fetal heart rate is reassuring.

data_table.Examination: Cervix 4 cm, fully effaced, vertex at 0 station, intact membranes ruptured 6 hours ago with clear liquor; uterus relaxed between contractions
data_table.Investigations: GBS swab at 36 weeks: negative; urinalysis: clear; FBC and group and hold valid

lead_in: What is the most appropriate intrapartum management?

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin 3 g loading then 1.8 g 4 hourly throughout labour as routine GBS prophylaxis
Repeat vaginal-rectal GBS swab now and start IV benzylpenicillin pending results during labour
Intravenous cefazolin 2 g 8 hourly throughout labour as routine GBS prophylaxis given the duration of ROM
Routine labour care with continuous CTG monitoring and no intrapartum antibiotic for GBS now
Intravenous clindamycin 900 mg 8 hourly throughout labour as routine GBS prophylaxis cover

subtopic_detail: Threatened miscarriage management
stem: You are the gynaecology registrar in the early pregnancy assessment service reviewing a 29-year-old G2P1 at 8+3 weeks by LMP with 12 hours of light fresh PV bleeding and mild lower abdominal cramping. She is haemodynamically stable. Her previous pregnancy was uncomplicated. She is rhesus negative. Speculum examination shows cervical os closed and minimal fresh blood in the vaginal vault. Transvaginal ultrasound shows a viable intrauterine pregnancy with crown-rump length consistent with 8+2 weeks and fetal heart present at 168 bpm.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft, non-tender, no peritonism; speculum: cervical os closed, minimal fresh blood; bimanual: uterus 8 weeks size, no adnexal mass or tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Hb 124, group and hold sent (Rh negative), beta-hCG 78 000; TVUS: viable IUP, CRL consistent with 8+2 weeks, fetal heart 168, no subchorionic haematoma

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Reassure, advise rest and abstain from intercourse, no anti-D required at this gestation and follow-up with GP
Administer 250 IU anti-D immunoglobulin intramuscularly for the bleeding event and arrange repeat scan in 7 days
Commence vaginal progesterone 400 mg twice daily until 16 weeks based on the PRISM trial evidence
Admit for serial beta hCG monitoring with repeat scan in 48 hours to assess for early pregnancy loss progression
Surgical evacuation of retained products of conception by suction curettage in theatre within 24 hours arranged

subtopic_detail: HRT initiation in symptomatic perimenopause
stem: You are the GP registrar reviewing a 51-year-old woman with 12 months of disabling hot flushes, night sweats waking her 4 times per night, and new mood lability affecting work performance. Her last menstrual period was 8 months ago. Her BMI is 26. She has no personal or family history of breast cancer, VTE, or cardiovascular disease. Her BP today is 122/74. She still has her uterus and ovaries. She has read about menopausal hormone therapy and wishes to start treatment.

data_table.Examination: No abnormalities of breasts, abdomen, or pelvis on examination
data_table.Investigations: FSH not required for diagnosis at this age with classic symptoms; mammogram up to date; cervical screening up to date

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial menopausal hormone therapy regimen?

options.text: Oral conjugated equine oestrogen 0.625 mg daily as monotherapy with annual review of risk profile arranged
Transdermal oestradiol patch 50 mcg twice weekly with continuous oral micronised progesterone 100 mg daily
Transdermal oestradiol patch 50 mcg twice weekly with cyclical oral micronised progesterone 200 mg for 12 days
Tibolone 2.5 mg orally daily as combined synthetic steroid for vasomotor and mood symptoms in this patient
Vaginal oestradiol pessary 10 mcg twice weekly with SSRI venlafaxine 75 mg daily for vasomotor symptoms

subtopic_detail: Twin chorionicity and surveillance
stem: You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 31-year-old G1P0 at 11+5 weeks for her booking dating scan. The sonographer identifies a twin pregnancy. Both fetuses are appropriately grown for dates. There is a single placental mass with a thin inter-twin membrane and absence of the lambda sign at the membrane-placenta junction; T-sign is present. Each fetus has its own amniotic cavity. The woman has no significant medical history and conceived spontaneously without fertility treatment.

data_table.Examination: Uterus 14 weeks size
data_table.Investigations: Dating ultrasound: dichorionic vs monochorionic differentiation - single placental mass, T-sign present at membrane insertion, lambda sign absent, thin inter-twin membrane, 2 separate amniotic cavities, both fetuses CRL consistent with 11+5; routine first-trimester bloods sent

lead_in: What chorionicity does this represent and what surveillance is appropriate?

options.text: Dichorionic-diamniotic twins requiring growth scan and umbilical artery Doppler at 28, 32, and 36 weeks gestation
Dichorionic-monoamniotic twins requiring growth scan and umbilical artery Doppler 4-weekly from 24 weeks onwards
Monochorionic-monoamniotic twins requiring inpatient surveillance and elective caesarean at 32 to 34 weeks
Monochorionic-diamniotic twins requiring fortnightly growth and TTTS screening ultrasound from 16 weeks
Conjoined twins requiring tertiary referral and detailed anomaly scan at 12 to 14 weeks gestation

subtopic_detail: Rhesus negative pregnancy and Kleihauer-guided anti-D
stem: You are the obstetrics registrar called to maternity assessment at 30+2 weeks. A 27-year-old G2P1 rhesus-negative woman has been involved in a low-speed motor vehicle accident as restrained driver 2 hours ago, with seat belt across the gravid abdomen. She has mild lower abdominal tenderness. No PV bleeding. CTG over 4 hours is reassuring with no uterine activity. Routine antenatal anti-D 625 IU was given at 28 weeks. Kleihauer test on maternal blood returns showing 35 mL fetal red blood cells in maternal circulation (well above 6 mL threshold).

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal BP 118/76, HR 92, T 36.8, FHR 142 with normal variability
data_table.Examination: Soft seatbelt bruise across the lower abdomen, uterus non-tender, no PV loss, cervix closed on speculum
data_table.Investigations: FBC: Hb 116, plt 244; group: O-negative; antibody screen negative; Kleihauer: 35 mL fetal RBC; CTG: reassuring 4-hour trace
data_table.Medications: Pregnancy multivitamin; routine anti-D 625 IU at 28 weeks 2 weeks ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step regarding anti-D administration?

options.text: No further anti-D needed because routine 28-week prophylaxis was given 2 weeks ago covering this event
Repeat Kleihauer test in 48 hours and administer additional anti-D only if fetal cells still detected
Administer additional anti-D 625 IU intramuscularly as second dose within the 72 hour preventive window
Administer additional anti-D 3500 IU (100 IU per mL fetal RBC) within 72 hours and recheck Kleihauer at 48 hours
Administer IV immunoglobulin 1 g/kg as second line because the Kleihauer is well above the standard threshold

subtopic_detail: Cervical cerclage indication
stem: You are the obstetrics registrar reviewing a 33-year-old G3P0+2 at 18 weeks in the high-risk antenatal clinic. Her obstetric history is significant: 2 previous pregnancy losses at 21 and 23 weeks, both with painless cervical dilation followed by rapid delivery. She had no PV bleeding, no abruption, no infection, and no contractions before either loss. Transvaginal ultrasound today shows a cervical length of 22 mm (below 25 mm threshold) without funnelling. Her cervix is closed on digital examination and she is asymptomatic.

data_table.Examination: Cervix closed on digital examination, no PV bleeding or discharge
data_table.Investigations: TVUS: cervical length 22 mm, no funnelling, fetal anatomy normal; FBC, urine MC&S, MSU sent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Vaginal progesterone 200 mg nightly from 20 weeks until 36 weeks without cerclage consideration this pregnancy
Bed rest at home, abstain from intercourse, and weekly cervical length scans from 18 to 24 weeks gestation
Ultrasound-indicated cervical cerclage (McDonald or Shirodkar) this admission given short cervix on TVUS today
Arabin pessary inserted in clinic with weekly review and removal at 36 weeks or earlier if labour develops
17-hydroxyprogesterone caproate weekly intramuscular injection from 16 to 36 weeks for preterm birth prevention
